items.title: [Bug] Kimi-K3 DCP a2a produces garbled decode output on 2-node GB300; NCCL_GRAPH_REGISTER=0 restores smoke-test output
items.author: Phoenix3334
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

On a two-node GB300 MNNVL deployment (4 GPUs/node, TP8/DCP8) serving Kimi-K3, DCP `a2a` can produce degenerate decode output under CUDA graphs when NCCL graph buffer registration is enabled. In the original 12-prompt greedy smoke probe, the failing configuration produced **12/12 degenerate outputs**; restarting with `NCCL_GRAPH_REGISTER=0` restored coherent output (**0/12**).

Follow-up controlled experiments now narrow the failure to a **buffer-lifetime/address-stability mismatch between NCCL graph registration and graph-pool-temporary DCP `a2a` exchange buffers**. A full 2x2 showed that correctness is restored either by disabling graph registration or by keeping the exchange buffers persistent across graph replay. The exact transient replay-time access that clobbers or reuses released storage has not been directly observed.

There are now two validated fix shapes:

- **#45371 (Plan A, ready for review):** minimal startup safeguard; resolved DCP `a2a` defaults `NCCL_GRAPH_REGISTER=0` while preserving explicit overrides.
- **#45824 (Plan B, ready for review):** keep graph registration enabled and make the DCP `a2a` exchange buffers persistent. The exact current head `9cb1de5` has been re-validated on the reported deployment with the #45371 guard absent: **12/12 correct, 0/12 degenerate**, including `17 * 23 -> 391`. Focused regression tests also passed locally (**23 tests + 5 subtests**).

These are alternative fixes for the same failure and are **not intended to be merged as-is together**.

## Observed correctness results

Two-node GB300, Kimi-K3, TP8/DCP8, real prefill + decode:

| Configuration | Degenerate outputs / 12 prompts |
| --- | ---: |
| DCP `a2a`, original registration environment | 12/12 |
| DCP `a2a`, `NCCL_GRAPH_REGISTER=0` | 0/12 |
| DCP `a2a`, startup guard applied on both nodes | 0/12 |
| DCP `fi_a2a` control | 0/12 |

The passing runs include `17 * 23 -> 391`.

The smoke probe is not a full task-accuracy evaluation, but it is sufficient to distinguish the reported failure: failing outputs often begin with a plausible token and then degenerate into repeated `!` characters.

## Mechanism isolation: registration × buffer lifetime

A persistent-buffer variant was implemented and tested on the same two-node GB300 / TP8-DCP8 Kimi-K3 deployment. The resulting 2x2 is:

| | graph-pool temporaries | persistent held buffers |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `NCCL_GRAPH_REGISTER=1` | **12/12 garbage** | **0/12 correct** |
| `NCCL_GRAPH_REGISTER=0` | 0/12 correct | 0/12 correct |

This is the strongest mechanism evidence so far:

- graph registration alone does not fail;
- temporary-buffer lifetime alone does not fail;
- the reproduced failure requires the combination of **graph registration + graph-pool-temporary buffers**;
- holding the exchange buffers persistent restores correctness while keeping registration enabled.

The remaining low-level detail is which transient replay-time access is responsible for the released-storage clobber/reuse. That exact access has not been directly observed, so this issue does not claim a more specific NCCL/CUDA-graph internal mechanism than the lifetime/address-stability mismatch supported by the 2x2.

## Negative controls / ruled-out necessary ingredients

The failing cell (`NCCL_GRAPH_REGISTER=1` + graph-pool temporaries) remained **12/12 garbage** with each of the following controls:

- `NCCL_CUMEM_ENABLE=0`;
- CUDA allocator `expandable_segments` disabled;
- `NCCL_NVLS_ENABLE=0`;
- `NCCL_P2P_DISABLE=1`.

Therefore, no particular cuMem/VMM allocator backend, expandable-segment behavior, NVLS path, or P2P path is a necessary ingredient in this reproduction.

Allocator instrumentation during decode sampled `torch.cuda.memory_snapshot()` every ~2 seconds while recording more than 11k DCP `a2a` buffer-address observations on the head node. It found no persistent `ACTIVE_ALLOCATED` block overlapping the recorded ranges. This argues against the simple explanation that another long-lived tensor permanently occupies the registered address; it does not exclude transient released-storage reuse that the snapshots miss.

A smaller 8-rank synthetic harness calling the real `dcp_a2a_lse_reduce` did not reproduce the model-level corruption with registration left at its default setting. A single-node 4-GPU toy also did not reproduce. These are only non-reproductions and are not treated as proof that cross-node topology or full-model context is strictly required.

## High-concurrency stability

The guarded `a2a` path was re-tested at **concurrency 128** on the configuration that had previously failed with `CUDA illegal memory access`:

- MF=0.94;
- `max-running-requests=112`;
- decode CUDA graphs up to batch size 112;
- TP8/DCP8;
- 60K input / 1K output.

With the startup guard active and no manual `NCCL_GRAPH_REGISTER` override:

- **640/640 requests completed**;
- no CUDA illegal-memory-access error, scheduler exception, or hang was observed;
- repeated-`!` garbage scan: **0 matches**;
- output throughput: **1932.8 tok/s**;
- mean TPOT: **32.94 ms** (P99 **33.43 ms**).

This is consistent with the earlier C64 corruption and C128 crash belonging to the same registration/lifetime failure family.

## Performance follow-up

Because Plan A changes a process-wide NCCL setting, we checked for visible throughput impact.

A same-settings `fi_a2a` anchor measured:

- original registration environment: **1643.7 tok/s**;
- `NCCL_GRAPH_REGISTER=0`: **1641.3 tok/s**;
- delta: **-0.15%**, within run-to-run noise for this setup.

After restoring `a2a` correctness, the following C64 comparison was also measured:

| TP path | `fi_a2a` | corrected `a2a` | a2a vs fi |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| NCCL all-reduce | 1673.5 tok/s | 1649.7 tok/s | -1.42% |
| CustomAllReduceV2 | 1841.6 tok/s | 1820.9 tok/s | -1.12% |
| CustomAllReduceV2 + K3 all-reduce fusion | 1977.2 tok/s | 1935.0 tok/s | -2.13% |

The earlier much larger apparent `a2a` speedup must not be used as performa

items.title: [Bug] pause_generation(mode="abort") with --tokenizer-worker-num > 1 can let a request reach the scheduler after the KV cache is released
items.author: galletas1712
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Please use English.

### Describe the bug

With `--tokenizer-worker-num > 1`, `/pause_generation` with `mode="abort"` can return while another tokenizer worker still has a request in flight. That request reaches the scheduler after the pause, and the scheduler is not paused in `abort` mode, so it schedules it. If the caller then releases the KV cache (`/release_memory_occupation`, the usual RL weight-update flow), the request runs against a released KV cache.

The pause holds requests back per worker:

- Each tokenizer worker has its own `is_pause` and `model_update_lock`. A request passes the pause gate, then tokenizes under the reader lock and sends to the scheduler ([tokenizer_manager.py#L954-L956](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/c64886f9e383695c954e5f651a146e70c803a05a/python/sglang/srt/managers/tokenizer_manager.py#L954-L956)).
- The router broadcasts `is_pause` to all workers, but does not forward an `abort` pause to the scheduler, so `_engine_paused` stays `False` ([multi_tokenizer_mixin.py#L694-L703](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/c64886f9e383695c954e5f651a146e70c803a05a/python/sglang/srt/managers/multi_tokenizer_mixin.py#L694-L703)).
- The worker that received the pause aborts all requests, then waits only for its own `model_update_lock` ("only the originator checks its own lock state", [multi_tokenizer_mixin.py#L880-L896](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/c64886f9e383695c954e5f651a146e70c803a05a/python/sglang/srt/managers/multi_tokenizer_mixin.py#L880-L896)).

Interleaving:

1. Worker B accepts a request, passes the pause gate, and is still tokenizing it (holding B's reader lock).
2. Worker A receives `/pause_generation` with `mode="abort"`, broadcasts `is_pause`, and sends `abort_all`. The scheduler does not have B's request yet, so nothing is aborted.
3. A's own lock is free, so the pause returns.
4. The caller calls `/release_memory_occupation`. The scheduler is idle, so the idle assertion in [weight_updater.py#L339-L341](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/c64886f9e383695c954e5f651a146e70c803a05a/python/sglang/srt/managers/scheduler_components/weight_updater.py#L339-L341) passes and the KV cache is released.
5. B finishes tokenizing and sends the request. The scheduler is not paused and schedules it without a KV cache.

With one tokenizer worker this cannot happen: the pausing worker's lock covers its own in-flight request. `retract` and `in_place` pauses are not affected, because they pause the scheduler and a late request waits in its queue.

Possible fixes:

- Pause the scheduler for `abort` too (as `in_place` does: set `_engine_paused`), so a late request waits in the waiting queue until `continue_generation`.
- Or have every worker wait for its own `model_update_lock` before the pause completes, not only the originator.

### Reproduction

Found by reading the code; not reproduced on hardware yet. Conditions: `--tokenizer-worker-num 2` or more, `--enable-memory-saver`, steady traffic with slow tokenization (long prompts or multimodal inputs), then `/pause_generation` with `{"mode": "abort"}` followed by `/release_memory_occupation`. Expected failure: a request scheduled after the release, accessing freed KV cache memory.

### Environment

Code-level issue at c64886f9e383695c954e5f651a146e70c803a05a, independent of hardware.

items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

- bug report:

```
Hello vLLM team, I'm running into a suspicious ZMQ socket bug with my 2P 4D configuration for DeepSeek-V3 (see below). I thought it is caused by reusing same nodes for many vLLM launches, but now it happened also at a clean node. Seems like a DP bug of sorts. Please find logs attached. vllm==0.11.0.

```

### 🐛 Describe the bug

From Nick:
```
I think the problem is that each DP worker finds/assigns free ports dynamically/independently.. so there is a race condtion. I'm not sure of an immediate workaround apart from just re-attempt to start things when this happens. We'll have to look at how to catch and re-find a port if possible (though I have a memory this might be nontrivial).
```

From Reporter:
```
Received init message: EngineHandshakeMetadata(addresses=EngineZmqAddresses(inputs=['tcp://slurm-h200-207-083:60613'], outputs=['tcp://slurm-h200-207-083:36865'], coordinator_input='tcp://slurm-h200-207-083:34575', coordinator_output='tcp://slurm-h200-207-083:48025', frontend_stats_publish_address='ipc:///tmp/88ec875f-3de9-46ec-9947-6d1d6573b910'), parallel_config={'data_parallel_master_ip': 'slurm-h200-207-083', 'data_parallel_master_port': 41917, '_data_parallel_master_port_list': [60545, 36835, 47971, 37001], 'data_parallel_size': 32})
```

I'm looking at the code and I see that all code paths for getting ports eventually to go to _get_open_port, and that in _get_open_port there is basically no defence against choosing the same port twice. Can you please confirm my understanding?

_get_open_port in main is here: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/utils/network_utils.py#L177

UPD: I imagine the assumption here is that once a code path gets a port, that code path will use it immediately, and thus the port will be come busy. It doesn't seem to hold though.


Even where all sockets that vLLM chose for itself are unique, I get the stack trace below.
I have the following explanation in mind:

- vLLM chooses zmq ports before launching the engines
- launching the engines takes ~5 mins
- by the time the engines are launched, something can listen on this port, like for example Ray
- **It looks the right solution is to hold on to then chosen ports immediately are they are chosen.**

items.title: [Bug]: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash(-1017) returns U+FFFD for a 12-token prompt, clean one token longer (v0.31.0/v0.32.0, TP8+EP, 8xH20)
items.author: CodeSlogan
items.body_excerpt:
# [Bug]: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash(-1017) returns U+FFFD for a 12-token prompt, clean one token longer (v0.31.0/v0.32.0, TP8+EP, 8xH20)

### Your current environment

I can attach the full `collect_env` output on request. The fields that matter:

|             |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| ----------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| vLLM        | **`0.31.0` and `0.32.0` both reproduce** (0.32.0 confirmed by `system_fingerprint`: `vllm-0.32.0-tp8-ep-2ec77c92`)                                                                                                                      |
| GPU         | 8x NVIDIA H20, single node                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| Parallelism | TP8 + EP (`--tensor-parallel-size 8 --enable-expert-parallel`)                                                                                                                                                                          |
| Checkpoint  | `DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017`, and the non-1017 `DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash`. **Both reproduce**, so it is not a 1017 weight regression. The checkpoint is an internal mirror; `config.json` and tokenizer are identical to the upstream release. |
| Thinking    | off (fast mode) — response reports `reasoning_tokens: 0`                                                                                                                                                                                |
| CUDA graphs | not overridden, i.e. the default `FULL_AND_PIECEWISE`                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| Spec decode | DSpark k=5 + adaptive verification in the base config; **removing `--speculative-config` entirely does not fix it**                                                                                                                     |

### 🐛 Describe the bug

A single-turn chat request whose prompt tokenizes to **12 tokens** comes back with U+FFFD replacement characters embedded in the reply. Extending the same user text by one character (`您好` -> `您好啊`) makes the corruption disappear.

The corruption is not a semantic degradation. The reply is fluent, the model answers the right question, `finish_reason` is `stop`, HTTP is 200, and nothing is logged. Only one or two character positions are destroyed.

This tracks **prompt token count**, not prompt content, which is why I am filing it separately from the general "DSpark corrupts chat output" reports — and DSpark turns out not to be required (see below).

### Serve command

```bash
vllm serve <DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017> \
  --tensor-parallel-size 8 \
  --tokenizer-mode deepseek_v41 \
  --engram-config '{"cpu_offload":true}' \
  --max-num-batched-tokens 4096 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.92 \
  --enable-expert-parallel \
  --reasoning-parser deepseek_v41 \
  --speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","num_speculative_tokens":5,"draft_sample_method":"probabilistic","rejection_sample_method":"block","enable_adaptive_verification":true}' \
  --mm-encoder-tp-mode data \
  --tool-call-parser deepseek_v41 \
  --enable-auto-tool-choice
```

### Reproduction

```bash
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/chat/completions \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{
    "model": "DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017",
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "你好"}],
    "temperature": 0,
    "max_tokens": 64,
    "stream": false
  }'
```

Observed `message.content`, verbatim from the client log with U+FFFD made explicit:

```
你好！有什么我可以帮<U+FFFD>帮<U+FFFD>帮助你的吗？
```

`您好` and `嘿` show the same class of corruption. `您好啊` does not.

### Response metadata

```json
{
  "choices": [{
    "finish_reason": "stop",
    "index": 0,
    "logprobs": null,
    "message": {
      "content": "你好！有什么我可以帮<U+FFFD>帮<U+FFFD>帮助你的吗？",
      "reasoning": null,
      "role": "assistant",
      "tool_calls": null
    }
  }],
  "system_fingerprint": "vllm-0.32.0-tp8-ep-2ec77c92",
  "usage": {
    "prompt_tokens": 12,
    "completion_tokens": 12,
    "total_tokens": 24,
    "completion_tokens_details": { "reasoning_tokens": 0 }
  }
}
```

Five observations that constrain the cause:

1. **`reasoning_tokens: 0`** — non-thinking path, so the `deepseek_v41` reasoning parser is not splitting anything. The U+FFFD is inside `content`.
2. **`prompt_tokens: 12`** — the prompt fits inside the first 128 positions of a fresh sequence and inside a single prefill chunk.
3. **Non-streaming** — `stream: false`, so the string is built from the final token list, not from an incremental detokenizer. That removes the usual "partial UTF-8 across stream boundaries" explanation.
4. **A one-token-longer prompt is clean** — the trigger is token count, not meaning.

### What has been ruled out

| Ruled out                                    | Evidence                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| -------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.title: [Onboarding 2026] Good first issues — start contributing to LMCache in one PR
items.author: maobaolong
items.body_excerpt:
👋 Welcome to join lmcache slack channel. https://join.slack.com/t/lmcacheworkspace/shared_invite/zt-4d1c2uk6t-55YZVvOQnJFNeAJK32U~Gg 

👋 Welcome to LMCache! This umbrella issue is the **single entry point** for first-time
contributors. If you've never sent a PR to LMCache before, start here.

> If you're looking for the older onboarding thread, see #627. This 2026 version
> focuses on smaller, well-scoped tasks with a friendly step-by-step PR workflow.

---

## 0. Before you start

- Read [`CONTRIBUTING.md`](../blob/dev/CONTRIBUTING.md). The most important parts:
  - Base branch is `dev`. Open PRs against `dev`, not `main`.
  - Every Python file starts with `# SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0`.
  - Imports are grouped as `# Standard / # Third Party / # First Party / # Local`.
  - Line length is **88**, formatter is `ruff format`, lint is `ruff check`.
  - Never access `_private` members of other classes (SLF rule).
  - Public functions/methods need **type hints** + **docstring**.
- Set up the environment:
  ```bash
  uv venv --python 3.12 && source .venv/bin/activate
  uv pip install -e . --no-build-isolation
  uv pip install -r requirements/test.txt
  pre-commit install
  ```

## 1. How to claim a task

These tasks are mainly for new contributors to learn the LMCache issue-to-PR workflow. Please claim **only one good-first issue at a time**. If you already have an assigned good-first issue or an open good-first PR, finish that work before taking another one, and leave the remaining tasks for other newcomers.

1. Pick **one** sub-issue below that has no assignee and no `🔒 claimed` comment.
2. Comment exactly: `/claim` (or `I'd like to work on this 🙋`).
   A maintainer will assign it to you within ~2 business days.
3. If you go silent for 7 days we'll un-assign so others can pick it up — totally fine,
   just leave a comment if you need more time.

## 2. Branch & commit

```bash
git checkout dev && git pull
git checkout -b gfi/<issue-number>-short-slug
# ... do the work ...
git commit -s -m "short imperative summary"   # -s is required (DCO)
```

- **Sign-off is required** (`-s`). PRs without DCO sign-off cannot be merged.
- Keep the PR small: one issue = one PR.

## 3. Local checks (must pass before pushing)

```bash
pre-commit run --all-files
pytest -xvs tests/<the_file_you_touched>.py    # if applicable
```

## 4. Open the PR

**PR title format** (please follow):

```
[good-first-issue] <area>: <imperative summary>  (#<sub-issue-number>)
```

Examples:
- `[good-first-issue] docs: fix broken link in quickstart (#1801)`
- `[good-first-issue] tests: add unit test for FooBar.flush (#1802)`
- `[good-first-issue] lint: add SPDX header to scripts/foo.py (#1803)`

**PR description** — please use this template (the repo's PR template already
gives you the skeleton; just fill it in):

```markdown
**What this PR does / why we need it**:
Closes #<sub-issue-number>
Refs #<this umbrella issue number>

<one or two sentences describing the change>

**Special notes for your reviewers**:
- This is my first PR to LMCache 🙇 please be gentle.
- I ran `pre-commit run --all-files` locally — all green.
- I ran `pytest -xvs tests/...` — all green.

**If applicable**:
- [ ] this PR contains user facing changes - docs added
- [ ] this PR contains unit tests
```

> Tip: writing `Closes #1234` in the description auto-closes the sub-issue when the
> PR is merged. Keep `Refs #<umbrella>` so the umbrella stays linked.

## 5. Finding a reviewer

You don't need to find one yourself — `.github/CODEOWNERS` will auto-request
the right people based on the files you changed. If the PR sits idle for **3 working
days**, leave a polite comment like:

> Friendly ping — PTAL when you have a moment 🙏 cc @<one CODEOWNER from the file you changed>

If you really can't tell who to ping, default to:
- Tests / CI / packaging → @hickeyma @sammshen @ApostaC @deng451e
- Docs / examples → @sammshen @deng451e
- Storage backends → @maobaolong @sammshen @chunxiaozheng
- Core engine / memory → @ApostaC @YaoJiayi @sammshen
- Multiprocess → @ApostaC @OasisGit @hlin99

(See [`.github/CODEOWNERS`](../blob/dev/.github/CODEOWNERS) for the full map.)

## 6. Responding to review comments

This is the part most newcomers miss — please follow it, it makes everyone happier:

1. **Address every comment.** For each thread:
   - If you agree → push a fix and reply `Done in <commit-sha>`.
   - If you disagree → explain politely, propose an alternative.
   - If you don't understand → ask! Reviewers expect questions.
2. **Don't force-push** during review (it loses inline-comment context). Just add
   commits; we'll squash on merge.
3. **Re-request review explicitly** once all threads are resolved:
   > Addressed all comments, PTAL again 🙏 @reviewer1 @reviewer2

   `PTAL` = "Please Take Another Look". Tag every reviewer who left comments.
4. If CI is red, fix it before pinging — reviewers will skip red PRs.


---

## 7. How to create and claim a sub-issues

- You can extend the new cli commend line tools, ref to https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/pull/3719 and https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/pull/3678

---

Stuck? Drop a message in the `#contributors` channel of our
[Slack](https://join.slack.com/t/lmcacheworkspace/shared_invite/zt-3g8e6xzz8-KzS_HI8bPERGFK5PTB~MYg)
or comment here. We're happy to help. 🙌


**Maintainers**: please update this checklist as sub-issues are filed.

---

## Next step: Good second issues

Finished your first PR? Head over to **#5751 — [Good second issues — next step after your first PR](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/issues/5751)** for your next small, well-scoped task.

items.title: Support KV cache events in MP mode (for Dynamo KV-aware routing)
items.author: glbyktjys
items.body_excerpt:
### Background

In non-MP mode, LMCache emits a [CacheStoreEvent](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/dev/lmcache/v1/cache_engine.py#L507) on each chunk store. vLLM pulls these event through the connector's [take_events() ](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/base.py)and publishes them as [BlockStored events](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/distributed/kv_events.py) (--kv-events-config) for consumers like Dynamo's KV-aware router. 

See docs/source/production/kv_cache_events.rst.

### Problem

In MP mode, the cache engine runs in the LMCache server process rather than alongside the inference engine. As a result, cache store events are not propagated to the upstream engine.

### Goal

In MP mode, chunks stored by the LMCache server produce KV cache events published directly from the LMCache server to Dynamo's KV-aware router through Dynamo's KvEventPublisher, carrying the same information as non-MP BlockStored events. This bypasses vLLM's event path entirely.

###  Task (not limited to the following)

1. Write a design doc for the event path. Good reference: https://docs.nvidia.com/dynamo/v1.1.1/integrations/kv-events-for-custom-engines
2. Event creation in the MP server when a chunk is stored.
3. Integrate Dynamo's KvEventPublisher with the MP server.

items.title: [Bug] Shutdown and L1 TTL expiry can reclaim a buffer an L2 adapter is still loading into
items.author: JulianZJN
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

`L2AdapterInterface` makes the *caller* responsible for keeping a load buffer
valid "until the load task is completed", but gives the caller no way to find out
that a load it is no longer waiting for has stopped touching that buffer.
`PrefetchController.stop()` therefore frees L1 write reservations that an adapter
still owns, and, independently, the L1 write lock guarding such a reservation
is a TTL lock that expires after 600 s by default, after which the object becomes
readable by other requests and evictable by the eviction controller.

Both are reproducible on `dev` with in-tree components only.

## Affected version

`dev` at `dd35168c801fec49889b34b083a12204d3c02a2a` (reproduced there).

## Background: the contract gap

`lmcache/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/base.py:321-328` (`submit_load_task`):

> The caller is responsible for managing the lifecycle of the memory objects, and
> should make sure that the memory buffer is valid until the load task is
> completed.

`base.py:93-96`: *"The L2 adapter is not supposed to manage the lifecycle of the
memory objects."* But "completed" is defined only as `query_load_result`
returning non-`None` (`base.py:335-353`), and `close()`, `base.py:587-593`, says
nothing at all about in-flight loads. There is no `drain`, `join`, `quiesce`,
`wait_for_idle` or `num_inflight` anywhere in `L2AdapterInterface`.

From reading each adapter's `close()`, they do not agree on this. Some wait for their workers (`dax`, `raw_block`, `valkey`), several cancel their tasks and tear down, and at least two do neither for work that is already running:

* `p2p` (`p2p_l2_adapter.py:353-368`) unregisters its fds and removes the transfer-channel client without cancelling or joining posted reads.
* `fs` cancels a coroutine whose actual read runs on the default executor (`run_in_executor(None, self._read_with_odirect, ...)`, `fs_l2_adapter.py:707-718`), which cancellation cannot stop and `close()` never shuts down.

`serde_wrapper.py:350-355` already documents the hazard and asserts the guarantee
it needs, *"Both close() calls block until their in-flight reads / writes against
the temp MemoryObjs finish"*, which does not hold for the second and third
groups above.

## Repro 1, shutdown frees a buffer a pending load still owns

The test below (drop it in as `tests/v1/distributed/test_shutdown_ownership_repro.py`) drives the real `PrefetchController` and
`L1Manager` with a mock adapter whose gate sits before the copy into the
caller's buffers, so at the moment of shutdown the adapter has written nothing
and still holds the `MemoryObj`s it was handed. It asserts the safety contract
and is therefore RED:

```
E  AssertionError: shutdown reclaimed 4 of 4 L1 buffers that a pending L2 load
   still owns and has not written; PrefetchController.stop() joins only its own
   loop thread and no in-tree L2 adapter exposes a quiescence guarantee for
   in-flight loads (L2AdapterInterface.close() says nothing about them)
```

Mechanism, `storage_manager.py:1113-1127`:

```
    self._prefetch_controller.stop()     # joins its own thread, then frees
    ...
    for adapter in self._l2_adapters.values():
        adapter.close()                  # adapters consulted only afterwards
    self._l1_manager.close()
```

`PrefetchController.stop()` (`prefetch_controller.py:600-611` on dev) calls
`_cleanup_in_flight_requests()` (`prefetch_controller.py:1474-1491` on dev),
which does

```
    if request.phase == PrefetchPhase.PLAN_AND_LOAD:
        if request.write_reserved_keys:
            l1_mgr.finish_write_and_delete(request.write_reserved_keys)
```

`L1Manager.close()` (`l1_manager.py:902-909`) then frees everything else
unconditionally, with no lock check, so any adapter in the "cancel" or "neither"
group that returned from `close()` with work still in flight lands on freed
memory.

Swapping the two `close()` calls is not a fix by itself, since not every adapter's `close()` waits for in-flight loads.

## Repro 2, L1 write-lock TTL expiry, with `write_ttl_seconds=1`

The L1 read/write locks are `TTLLock` (`csrc/lmcache_native/ttl_lock.{h,cpp}`)
and the entire rule is `ttl_lock.cpp:74`:

```cpp
  return (counter_ > 0) && (current_time < expiration);
```

No TTL is ever refreshed for the duration of an operation: `write_lock.lock()` is
called once at `reserve_write` (`l1_manager.py:486`, `:522`), and neither
`unsafe_read` (`l1_manager.py:306-310`) nor `touch_keys`
(`l1_manager.py:782-796`) touches it. So the default 600 s
(`config.py:213-217`) is a hard wall-clock cap on how long an L2 load may hold a
reserved L1 buffer, unrelated to any L2 timeout.

Against the real `L1Manager` with `write_ttl_seconds=1` and `finish_write` never
called, exactly the state of a buffer a stalled load still owns:

```python
m.reserve_write([k], [False], layout)                     # SUCCESS
m.is_key_evictable(k), m.reserve_read([k])[k][0]          # False, KEY_NOT_READABLE
time.sleep(1.6)                                            # TTL expires
m.is_key_evictable(k), m.reserve_read([k])[k][0]          # True,  SUCCESS  <-- hands out the MemoryObj
m.delete([k])                                              # SUCCESS         <-- buffer returned to the allocator
m.finish_write([k])                                        # KEY_IN_WRONG_STATE
# WARNING L1Manager: finish write on non-write-locked key ...,
#         potential inconsistent data might be written
```

Consequences:

1. A second request reads a half-written buffer. `reserve_read` passes
   `available_for_read()` (`l1_manager.py:53-59`, "not write-locked") and returns
   `entry.memory_obj` (`l1_manager.py:288`).
2. Eviction frees it. `is_key_evictable` (`l1_manager.py:867-884`) returns
   True; the eviction controller passes it as the filter and calls plain
   `delete()` (`eviction_controller.py:184-198`); `delete`'s own "check again"
   safety net (`l1_manager.py:728-736`) uses the same expired `is_locked()`, so
   it does not help. The buffer goes back

items.title: [RFC][MP][L2] End-to-end integrity check for the fs L2 adapter (CRC32 trailer, verify on load)
items.author: malikoyv
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

The MP `fs` L2 adapter checks only a file's **length** when it loads a KV chunk. A file of the right size but with wrong bytes is served to the engine as a cache hit. The model then produces fluent garbage, and users debug the model rather than the cache.

This RFC proposes an **opt-in** integrity check:
- On store, write a small trailer (magic + CRC32) after the payload.
- On load, verify it; a mismatch becomes a cache miss and the file is deleted.

A draft implementation with tests is ready. I'd like agreement on the on-disk format and the failure semantics before opening the PR.

## Motivation

Silent-corruption reports keep reaching the tracker, and each was found by a person reading bad output rather than by LMCache:

- **#4991:** `fs_native` failed stores stay visible and cache hits produce gibberish. The analysis there found two concurrent writers of one key sharing a staging file, which leaves a torn file in place.
- **#5263:** a buffer is reclaimed while an L2 load is still writing into it.

A checksum does not fix any of these root causes. It turns an L2 content error into a detected miss, so the engine recomputes instead of silently serving wrong KV. Some related reports are not L2 content errors and a checksum would **not** catch them: #5344 (a tensor-parallel shard never written to L1) and #4247 (layout/view mismatch). This RFC is scoped to the L2 bytes.

Ways the same-size wrong bytes can reach `fs` today:
1. **Torn concurrent writes.** Writers of the same key share one temp path. The Python `fs` adapter uses the same `<name>.tmp` pattern as `fs_native`.
2. **Files from another writer or version** in a shared or reused directory.
3. **Media or firmware errors** (silent data corruption): rare per drive, but non-zero at fleet scale.
4. **Power loss or crash.** There is no `fsync` before rename, so after a crash a renamed file can contain stale or zeroed blocks.

What exists today:

| Mechanism | Covers |
|---|---|
| `fs` load length check | Truncated files only |
| AES-GCM serde | Tampering, but only when encryption with key management is enabled |
| `POST /cache/checksums` | Manual GPU-block debugging, not the load path |

## Proposal

**Config.** A new `fs` adapter field, a string rather than a boolean so it can gain algorithms later:

```json
{"type": "fs", "base_path": "/data/lmcache/l2", "checksum": "crc32"}
```

`"none"` is the default and keeps today's on-disk format byte for byte.

**On-disk format** (with `crc32`):

```
<payload bytes> | trailer: magic "LMC1" (4 B) | zlib.crc32(payload) (4 B, little-endian)
```

- Under `use_odirect`, the trailer is padded to one filesystem block so all writes stay aligned. Readers only look at the first 8 bytes after the payload, so buffered and O_DIRECT files are readable by either mode.
- The magic carries a format version (`LMC1`), so the layout can change later without misreading old files.

**Load semantics.**
- The payload is re-hashed off the adapter's event loop (`run_in_executor`; `zlib.crc32` releases the GIL on large buffers).
- A mismatch, missing trailer or unknown magic becomes a **miss** for that key. The prefetch controller already treats it as a gap, and the engine recomputes.
- The file is **deleted**, and listeners get `on_l2_keys_deleted`. Otherwise the key would miss forever: `_execute_store` skips existing files, and `fs` never evicts.

**Accounting.** Store reports the full file length, so usage stays consistent with `delete()`, which subtracts `st_size`.

**Related fix.** On the O_DIRECT path, check the byte count `os.write` returns. Today a short write is renamed into place as if complete.

## Cost

A typical chunk: Llama-3-8B, bf16, 256 tokens, about 32 MiB.

| | Overhead |
|---|---|
| Space | 8 B per file (one extra 4 KiB block allocated; 4 KiB under O_DIRECT), about 0.01% |
| Extra read bandwidth | 8 B per load (at most one extra 4 KiB page) |
| CPU per store and per load | One CRC32 pass. Measured on one host with zlib-ng 1.3.1: about 48 GB/s per core, about 0.7 ms per 32 MiB. Classic zlib is several times slower. |

Space and bandwidth are negligible; the real cost is **latency**. `_execute_load` handles keys sequentially, so each CRC adds directly to that chunk's load time. That's why this is opt-in. Hashing chunk N while reading chunk N+1 is the obvious follow-up. I'll post a `none` vs `crc32` load-throughput table on NVMe with the PR.

## Compatibility

- **Default `"none"`:** no behaviour or format change.
- **Enabling `"crc32"` on an existing directory:** old files have no trailer, so each is discarded on first access, a one-time miss.
- **A `"none"` reader on files written with `"crc32"`:** reads the payload length and ignores the trailer, so it works.
- **Shared directories:** all writers sharing a directory should use the same setting. It's documented.
- **Shared directories with `fs_native`:** it uses the same filenames, so the same rule applies. This RFC changes only the Python `fs` adapter.

## Alternatives considered

| Option | Why not (for now) |
|---|---|
| A checksum serde type (runs through the existing `SerdeL2AdapterWrapper`) | Covers every backend, but an adapter takes only one serde today, so it can't combine with fp8/turboquant; it also adds a temp-buffer copy. It's a good follow-up once serdes can chain. |
| xattr for the CRC | Not available on every filesystem (some NFS/FUSE setups); lost when files are copied. |
| A separate checksum file per object | Two files per object, and no atomic publish of both. |
| XOR / parity | No faster in practice (numpy XOR fold about 42 GB/s vs zlib-ng CRC32 about 48 GB/s on the same host), and it misses word reordering and paired bit flips. |
| crc32c (`google-crc32c`) / xxh3 | Faster on some CPUs but adds a dependency. The `checksum` string leaves room to add them. |
| Verifying at lookup | Would need a full read per lookup; load time is the natural point. |

## Open questions for maintainers

1. **Delete on mismatch:** is deleting t

items.title: [Bug] HiCache + hybrid (SSM/Mamba): failed cudaHostRegister on a secondary host pool aborts the whole instance, and the error path throws TypeError thereby hiding the real rc
items.author: flymysql
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

On sglang `0.5.19` (torch `2.13.0+cu130`, CUDA 13.0, H20), starting a **hybrid SSM/Mamba** model
with `--enable-hierarchical-cache --hicache-storage-backend dynamic` fails during
`attach_hybrid_pool_to_unified_cache` and **kills the entire instance**.

Two coupled defects:

1. **`cudaHostRegister` failure is treated as fatal.** `alloc_with_host_register` raises, which
   aborts scheduler init for all TP ranks. But the failure only means "this host pool is not
   zero-copy registered" — and sglang's own non-zero-copy path (`_generic_page_get/_set`) is
   fully functional without registration. A missing acceleration is escalated into a full outage.
2. **The error path destroys its own diagnostic.** Inside the `raise`, `cudart.cudaGetErrorString(rc)`
   is called with a **plain `int`**, which raises `TypeError` on this torch build — so the real
   `rc`/`offset`/`size` are swallowed. Operators only see a bare `TypeError`.

Additionally, the failure **leaves a sticky CUDA error**, which then surfaces later at an unrelated
call site (`_create_sync_groups` → `all_gather_object` → `torch.zeros`), which made this
considerably harder to root-cause.

### Environment

- sglang `0.5.19`
- torch `2.13.0+cu130`, CUDA 13.0
- 8 × H20 (96 GiB) / 8 × H20-3e (141 GiB), driver `535.161.08`
- Model: `Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-FP8` (`Qwen3_5MoeForConditionalGeneration`, pool stack **KV + MAMBA**)
- Backend: `--hicache-storage-backend dynamic` with `interface_v1: 1` in the extra config
  (this selects the zero-copy page functions; the crash itself is in host-pool allocation and is
  not specific to any particular dynamic backend)
- Relevant flags: `--mamba-full-memory-ratio 0.37 --mamba-radix-cache-strategy extra_buffer_lazy
  --mamba-ssm-dtype bfloat16 --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3 --hicache-mem-layout page_first_direct
  --hicache-io-backend direct --tp 8`

### Reproduction

```bash
python -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path <hybrid SSM/Mamba model, e.g. Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-FP8> \
  --tp-size 8 --trust-remote-code \
  --mem-fraction-static 0.80 \
  --enable-hierarchical-cache --hicache-ratio 1.0 \
  --hicache-storage-backend dynamic \
  --hicache-mem-layout page_first_direct \
  --hicache-io-backend direct \
  --mamba-full-memory-ratio 0.37 \
  --mamba-radix-cache-strategy extra_buffer_lazy \
  --mamba-ssm-dtype bfloat16 \
  --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3 \
  --hicache-storage-backend-extra-config '{"backend_name":"...","module_path":"...","class_name":"...","interface_v1":1,...}'
```

Failures are **not deterministic per machine** — we observed the same config **succeed on a 96 GiB
box and fail on a 141 GiB box**, consistent with a pool-geometry / allocation-order dependence.

### Observed failure trace (verbatim)

```
[TP5] attach_hybrid_pool_to_unified_cache failed
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File ".../mem_cache/hybrid_cache/hybrid_pool_assembler.py", line 1759, in attach_hybrid_pool_to_unified_cache
    result = strategy.build(
  File ".../hybrid_pool_assembler.py", line 1329, in build
    host_pool_group, cache_controller = build_hybrid_mamba_stack(
  File ".../hybrid_pool_assembler.py", line 735, in build_hybrid_mamba_stack
    kv_host_pool = build_kv_host_pool(
  File ".../hybrid_pool_assembler.py", line 160, in build_kv_host_pool
    return kv_host_pool_cls(
  File ".../mem_cache/pool_host/mha.py", line 89, in __init__
    super().__init__(
  File ".../mem_cache/pool_host/base.py", line 205, in __init__
    self.kv_buffer = self.init_kv_buffer()
  File ".../mem_cache/pool_host/mha.py", line 191, in init_kv_buffer
    buffer = alloc_func(
  File ".../mem_cache/pool_host/common.py", line 235, in alloc_with_host_register
    _cuda_host_register(buffer, registration_granularity_bytes)
  File ".../mem_cache/pool_host/common.py", line 163, in _cuda_host_register
    f"{cudart.cudaGetErrorString(rc)}) at offset={offset} size={size} "
       ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: cudaGetErrorString(): incompatible function arguments. The following argument types are supported:
    1. (arg0: torch._C._cudart.cudaError) -> str
Invoked with: 1                      <-- the real rc is only visible here, by accident
```

A second, later-surfacing variant of the same root cause (sticky CUDA error), reached when the
first pool *does* register successfully:

```
[TP6] Scheduler hit an exception: ...
  File ".../mem_cache/hybrid_cache/hybrid_cache_controller.py", line 161, in attach_storage_backend
    super().attach_storage_backend(
  File ".../managers/cache_controller.py", line 590, in attach_storage_backend
    self.prefetch_hits_sync_groups = self._create_sync_groups()
  File ".../managers/cache_controller.py", line 415, in _create_sync_groups
    create_custom_parallel_group(
  File ".../distributed/parallel_state.py", line 2762, in create_custom_parallel_group
    torch.distributed.all_gather_object(gathered_configs, local_config)
  File ".../torch/distributed/distributed_c10d.py", line 3506, in all_gather_object
    object_sizes_tensor = torch.zeros(
torch.AcceleratorError: CUDA error: invalid argument
```

Note `cache_controller.py:590` calls `_create_sync_groups()` **immediately** after the storage
backend is attached — i.e. right where the sticky error from a failed registration lands.

### Minimal evidence that this is the registration call

Instrumenting `_cuda_host_register` on the failing box (141 GiB) shows the KV pool registers fine
and a **secondary** pool is the one that fails:

```
reg#1 total=49676820480 (46.27GiB) granularity=3840        -> OK
reg#2 total=17765498880 (16.55GiB) granularity=11796480    -> FAILED rc=1 (cudaErrorInvalidValue) at offset=0
reg#3 total=623738880  ( 0.58GiB) granularity=414720       -> (never reached)
```

`offset=0`, the size is page aligned, and `chunk_limit=256 GiB` (i.e. a single call) — so this is
**not** an alignment, chunking, or size problem. The same three pools register fine in an

items.title: [RFC / HiCache] Same-node peer L2 sharing across DP ranks via /dev/shm
items.author: VNG-VMONITOR
items.body_excerpt:
# [RFC / HiCache] Same-node peer L2 sharing across DP ranks via `/dev/shm`

## Motivation

In deployments running multiple DP ranks on a **single node** (e.g. one host with 8 GPUs and `--dp-size 8`), each rank maintains a fully private L2 host KV cache. When two ranks receive requests with the same prefix — a common pattern for system prompts, few-shot examples, or shared document context — Rank B cannot see the KV pages that Rank A already produced, and must recompute the prefix from scratch.

Existing HiCache L3 backends (Mooncake, NIXL, AIBrix, 3FS, LMCache) do solve cross-instance sharing, but they all go through a networked / service-mediated data path. For **same-node** sharing that is common in single-box multi-DP deployments, the network round-trip is pure overhead — the ranks are all local processes with access to the same physical DRAM.

## Proposed design: `shm_peer_l2` HiCache storage backend

Two DP ranks on the same node map the same L2 host pool via named shared memory (`/dev/shm` tmpfs). Metadata (key → owner rank + slot address) is exchanged through a small direct-mapped index (also in `/dev/shm`). When Rank B misses in its own L1/L2, it looks up the index; on a hit, it performs one `memcpy` within the shared SHM to bring the peer's page into its own slot, then DMAs to GPU — no recompute.

Compared to a hypothetical "share via existing L3 file" approach (see `shm_cross_dp` below), the peer variant eliminates the L3 data copy: only a 288-byte pointer per page is written, giving:

- **Storage overhead**: ~55 MB total for a 475 GB L2 (vs. ~L2_size for a full mirror)
- **Read path**: 1 index lookup + 1 SHM memcpy + 1 DMA (vs. L3→CPU_buf→L2 + memcpy + DMA)
- **Write path**: 1 GPU→shared_L2 DMA + 1 index write (vs. + 1 memcpy to L3 file)

### Correctness

A per-page **generation counter** in shared memory prevents stale reads: when Rank A evicts and reallocates a slot, its generation counter increments. Rank B compares the stored generation against the current one; a mismatch is treated as a miss instead of copying whatever bytes now occupy the slot. The check is best-effort (no full memory barrier) — the tiny TOCTOU window between the generation read and the memcpy is accepted as per the "stale reads may be silently accepted" contract already present in HiCache read paths.

### Operational envelope

- `--dp-size >= 2`
- All DP ranks on the **same node** (`/dev/shm` is node-local tmpfs)
- `--hicache-write-policy write_through` required (`write_back` only flushes on eviction, so Rank B would not see data timely)
- Optionally with `--hicache-io-backend kernel` and `page_first`/`page_first_direct` layouts

Auto-computed capacity (`page_num × 4`, 25% load factor) at startup; explicit override via `--hicache-storage-backend-extra-config '{"peer_l2_capacity": N}'`.

Collision rate emitted every 10,000 writes; WARNING once it exceeds 10% (actionable — increase capacity).

## Existing prototype

A working implementation exists in a downstream fork. It shipped as two related backends registered through `backend_factory.py`:

- `shm_cross_dp` — shared L2 pool + full SHM L3 data file (simpler, more memory, extra copy)
- `shm_peer_l2` — shared L2 pool + tiny SHM index only (optimized; strict improvement)

Both reuse a common `ShmHostTensorAllocator` and named-SHM helpers added to `pool_host/common.py` and `storage/mmap/mmap_allocator.py`. Tests included: `test/registered/mem_cache/test_shared_l2_hicache.py` (CPU-only, `register_cpu_ci`), covering allocator wiring, slot partitioning, index CRUD, generation-counter stale-slot behavior, collision detection, auto-capacity, and a cross-process shared-L2 round-trip via subprocess.

The prototype hooks into:
- `HiRadixCache` — for `shm_name` derivation, `dp_rank/dp_size` forwarding to `MHATokenToKVPoolHost`
- `HostKVCache` (`pool_host/base.py`) — `clear()` partitions `free_slots` to `[slot_start, slot_start+local_size)`; `alloc()` fires registered callbacks; `slot_used` spans the full pool for cross-DP double-free detection
- `cache_controller` — `shm_peer_l2` added to the V1 interface allow-list

## The upstreaming question

We noticed [#40787](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/40787) (merged 2026-09-22) removed `HiRadixCache` since [#35081](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/35081) migrated HiCache to `UnifiedRadixCache`. The prototype above was written against `HiRadixCache` and does **not** apply cleanly to current `main`.

Before we invest in porting to `UnifiedRadixCache`, we would like guidance from HiCache maintainers on a few design points:

1. **Integration point in UnifiedRadixCache** — where is the equivalent of `HiRadixCache.write_backup`, `_inc_hit_count`, and `prefetch_from_storage` in the unified architecture? Is there a documented extension surface for backends that need per-page alloc callbacks and slot-partitioned allocators?

2. **Shared L2 pool ownership** — is there interest in a first-class "shared host pool" concept inside `MHATokenToKVPoolHost` (dp_rank / dp_size / shm_name parameters)? The prototype adds them minimally, but a maintainer-blessed shape would be preferable.

3. **Scope split** — would you prefer:
   - (a) A single PR introducing the shared L2 pool infrastructure + one backend using it (either `shm_cross_dp` or `shm_peer_l2`), then a follow-up for the other, or
   - (b) The infrastructure alone first (no backend), then backends as separate PRs?

4. **Naming / positioning** — `shm_peer_l2` vs `shm_cross_dp` overlap significantly; would maintainers prefer we upstream only `shm_peer_l2` (the optimized variant) and drop `shm_cross_dp`, or keep both as complementary options?

5. **Alternative direction** — is there an existing or planned effort (Mooncake local mode, an internal HiCache broadcast, etc.) that already covers the same-node peer sharing use case and would make this redundant? We searched issues/PRs and did not find one but want to double-check.

Happy to open a draft PR against `main

items.title: [Bug] `/hicache/storage-backend/clear` returns "Hierarchical cache storage backend cleared." with a 400 when it did not clear anything
items.author: Yunzez
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

Simply purely a reporting defect. 

Both the current endpoint and its deprecated alias build a **fixed** response body and vary only the status code, so the failure path returns a message that affirmatively claims the operation succeeded, and the reason it actually failed, which the handler is holding in `ret`, is discarded.

```python
# python/sglang/srt/entrypoints/http_server.py:1072
@app.api_route("/hicache/storage-backend/clear", methods=["POST"])
@auth_level(AuthLevel.ADMIN_OPTIONAL)
async def clear_hicache_storage_backend():
    ret = await _global_state.tokenizer_manager.clear_hicache_storage()
    return Response(
        content="Hierarchical cache storage backend cleared.\n",     # <- always this
        status_code=200 if ret.success else HTTPStatus.BAD_REQUEST,
    )
```

The deprecated `/clear_hicache_storage_backend` (line ~1059) has the same shape, with the deprecation notice prepended to the same unconditional "cleared" sentence.

The body is `text/plain`, not JSON, so a client that reads the message, which is the natural thing to do for a plain-text endpoint, is told the cache was cleared when it was not.



### Reproduction

On a server with no hierarchical cache configured:

```bash
python -m sglang.launch_server --model-path Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B --port 30000
curl -i -X POST http://127.0.0.1:30000/hicache/storage-backend/clear
```

```
HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request
...
Hierarchical cache storage backend cleared.
```

## Expected

The body should reflect the outcome and carry the reason the handler already has, e.g.

```
HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request
{"success": false, "message": "<whatever ret carries, e.g. no hierarchical cache storage backend is configured>"}
```

Status says the request failed; body says the work was done; neither says why.

items.title: [Perf] HiCache Throughput Loss Analysis in Long-Context MLA Workloads
items.author: githlangub
items.body_excerpt:
---

## 1. Background

In our long-context MLA benchmarks, enabling HiCache L2 causes up to 44.6%–66.6% effective throughput loss at an 80% hit rate—revealing that hit-length-dependent overhead severely erodes the expected speedup of prefix caching.

Specifically, given a cache hit rate `r`, only `(1 - r)` of the tokens require new prefill computation (`extend` tokens). Ideally, if cache hits incurred zero overhead, the effective throughput of the uncached `extend` tokens would remain constant (equal to the 0%-hit baseline), and total throughput `ITPS` would scale by `1 / (1 - r)`. In practice, however, **the effective throughput of `extend` tokens degrades substantially as hit rate increases**—and this deviation widens sharply when L2 cache offloading is enabled.

This phenomenon indicates that cache hits introduce overhead proportional to the matched prefix length (e.g., attention computation over cached KV history, radix tree management, and L2<->L1 data transfers). To quantify this overhead, we evaluate cache performance internally using the following methodology:

We care deeply about actual compute efficiency under cache hits. Internally, we evaluate cache performance using the following methodology:


### 1.1. Defining Cache Performance via "Throughput Loss"
1. We measure pure Prefill throughput with Prefix Cache disabled (`--disable-radix-cache`) as the upper-bound throughput for computing newly extended (`extend`) tokens, denoted as `ITPS_baseline`.
2. With Prefix Cache enabled, the throughput of the `extend` tokens is `(1 - HitRate) * ITPS`, denoted as `ITPS_uncached` (written as `FTPS` in the result table below).
3. We define **Cache Loss** as:
   `Loss = 1 - (ITPS_uncached / ITPS_baseline)`

### 1.2. Why Define Loss This Way?
1. If cache hits were completely zero-cost, `ITPS_uncached` would equal `ITPS_baseline` under any hit rate (`Loss = 0%`).
2. Because cache hits incur non-trivial overhead in practice, `ITPS_uncached` drops below `ITPS_baseline`. We use the gap between the two as **Loss** to measure cache performance.

### 1.3. How We Measure Loss
1. We only benchmark **Prefill** instances. We use the fake bootstrap feature (`--disaggregation-transfer-backend fake`) to replace PD transfer with a no-op, and enable `--ep-dispatch-algorithm fake` to test the upper-bound Prefill throughput.
2. **0% Hit Rate Scenario:** Send 60K fixed-length requests directly to obtain `ITPS_baseline`.
3. **80% Hit Rate Scenario (taking L2 Cache as an example):**
   * **a.** First, send a batch of completely distinct 48K-token requests to populate the cache.
   * **b.** Clear the L1 Cache so that cached prefixes only reside in L2.
   * **c.** Append 12K new tokens to each of the previous requests (total 60K tokens, 80% hit rate) and run the benchmark to obtain `ITPS_uncached` (`FTPS`).

---

items.title: [Bug] NGRAM speculative decoding corrupts radix-cached KV with the overlap scheduler when requests end on a stop token (0.5.22)
items.author: DiaaAj
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary
With `speculative_algorithm="NGRAM"` and otherwise default settings, greedy (temperature 0) outputs of a
few concurrent requests are wrong. The radix cache, overlap scheduler and CUDA graphs are all on by
default; on 0.5.21, disabling any one of them made the outputs exact, and on 0.5.22 disabling the overlap
scheduler does. The trigger is requests that share prefixes, in a workload where requests end on a stop
token. Greedy speculative decoding should be lossless, so
this is silent corruption.

- **History:** in 0.5.21 it also showed with `ignore_eos` and `max_new_tokens` endings. A bisection of
  main pins its disappearance for those endings to #42720 ("Skip the decode for a request whose last
  token is already in flight"). #42720 skips the discarded trailing decode only for requests that finish
  by length.
- **0.5.22 still fails:** with stop-token endings, 3/192 requests are wrong, the same ones as on 0.5.21.
- **Same defect:** switching off only #42720's skip (one line) brings 0.5.22 back to 0.5.21's exact
  8/192 failure.
- **Probable mechanism:** the trailing NGRAM verify step that runs for a request whose last token is
  already in flight writes KV that ends up in, or over, radix-cached prefixes.
- **EOS endings:** they use the same finish check as stop tokens (`_check_token_based_finish`), so
  ordinary EOS-terminated traffic is most likely affected too. We did not measure EOS directly.

## How it was found
With probec: exact known-answer probe checkpoints, with synthetic weights whose correct outputs are known
exactly and are insensitive to floating-point reduction order, so any deviation is an engine error, not
numerics. The probe is a Qwen3ForCausalLM twin of Qwen3-0.6B (same shapes, synthetic weights).

## Environment
- **0.5.22:** pip, with torch 2.14.1, sglang-kernel 0.4.9 and flashinfer-python 0.7.1. RTX 3090 (SM86), driver 595.84.
- **0.5.21:** torch 2.13.0, sglang-kernel 0.4.7, flashinfer 0.6.18. It also reproduces on an H100 SXM.
- **Engine:** `sgl.Engine(model_path=probe, skip_tokenizer_init=True, dtype="bfloat16", random_seed=0,
  context_length=16512, mem_fraction_static=0.8, attention_backend="flashinfer",
  speculative_algorithm="NGRAM", speculative_num_draft_tokens=4)`.
- **Workload:** 192 requests submitted together. Prompts are 130–16,000 tokens, and about 30% share a long
  prefix with an earlier request. Up to 256 new tokens each, at temperature 0.
  - Stop-token endings: each request gets `stop_token_ids=[t]`, where t is its correct answer's token at a
    random position 8–240 that does not occur earlier; `ignore_eos=False`.
  - Length endings: `ignore_eos=True`.

## Results (deterministic; the run without speculation is exact in every row)
| Version | Endings | Variant | Wrong requests / 192 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.5.22 | stop token | defaults | **3** (58, 109, 185) |
| 0.5.22 | stop token | `disable_overlap_schedule=True` | 0 |
| 0.5.22 | length | defaults | 0 |
| 0.5.22 | length | #42720's `self.enable_skip_finishing_decode = True` (in `event_loop_overlap`) changed to `False` | **8**, the same as 0.5.21 |
| 0.5.22 | length | `SGLANG_TEST_RETRACT=1` | 0 |
| 0.5.21 | stop token | defaults | 3, the same requests and verify counts as 0.5.22 |
| 0.5.21 | length | defaults | 8 (1,793 wrong tokens) |
| 0.5.21 | length | `attention_backend="triton"` | 8 |
| 0.5.21 | length | `speculative_num_draft_tokens=2` | 1 |
| 0.5.21 | length | `disable_radix_cache=True`, `disable_overlap_schedule=True`, `disable_cuda_graph=True`, `max_running_requests=1`, or no shared prefixes | 0 |
| 0.5.21 on an H100 | length | defaults | 6 (first failure identical to the RTX 3090's) |

### Which requests break
Each time, one request that owns a cached prefix goes wrong mid-generation, and the requests reusing its
cached prefix are wrong from their first reads:
- **Length endings:** request 15 (1,471-token prompt, no cache hit) diverges at generated token 151.
  Requests 48 and 100 reuse its cached prefix, 54 and 63 reuse 48's, and 67 reuses 63's; all are wrong
  from their first token. Request 116 (5,267 tokens) diverges at token 104, and 125 reuses its prefix.
- **Stop-token endings:** request 58 (3,408 tokens) diverges at token 137. Request 109 reuses 3,407 of its
  tokens and request 185 reuses 2,034 cached tokens of request 139's prompt; both are wrong from token 4.
  All three then miss their stop tokens.

### Bisection
- **Range:** main from bd78095 (v0.5.21 is a release-branch tag two cherry-picks past it) to d0a098b.
- **Method:** each commit was built from source with the Rust extensions.
- **Result:** the first clean commit for length endings is e14ef4b (#42720). Its parent 1fc6b89, a docs-only
  commit, fails the same 8 requests, and both were tested twice.
- **Dependencies ruled out:** the torch, sglang-kernel and FlashInfer upgrades all land at commits that
  still fail.

### Real model
On Qwen3-0.6B with real weights (greedy, 96 repetitive prompts), NGRAM and no-spec outputs diverge in
17/96 requests. But two no-spec runs, default and `--enable-deterministic-inference`, already diverge in
21/96. So real-model comparisons can't separate this bug from benign numerics; the probe's exact oracle
can.

## Related
- #23392 (shared-prefix load corrupts unrelated requests under NGRAM; involved cancellations; closed)
- #22819 (radix block-boundary corruption with deterministic inference; closed)
- #42720 (the change that hides it for length endings)

## Repro
```
git clone https://github.com/DiaaAj/probec && cd probec
pip install -e . "sglang[all]==0.5.22"
probec compile --like Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B --no-scale-check -o twin
python tools/repro_sglang_ngram.py twin --finish stop
```
On 0.5.22 it prints "NGRAM vs no-spec: 3/192 requests differ; NGRAM vs exact oracle: 3 wrong". Without
`--finish stop` it prints 0/192 on 0.5.22 and 8/192 on 0.5.21.

comments.author: he-yufeng
comments.body:
I can't reproduce this on stock v0.21.0, and after tracing the whole streaming path I don't think stock code can produce this exact signature. Writing up what I found.

**What the glyphs are**

`Ċ`, `åĹ¯`, `ï¼Į` are exactly what `tokenizer.convert_ids_to_tokens()` returns for those token ids (verified with a DeepSeek-R1 family tokenizer: 198 -> `Ċ`, 106287 -> `åĹ¯`, 3837 -> `ï¼Į`). So the reasoning stream is raw token strings that never went through the byte-level decode step.

**Why stock v0.21.0 shouldn't be able to emit that**

The streaming chain with `--reasoning-parser deepseek_r1` is:

1. The engine detokenizer produces `output.text` (already byte-decoded, incremental).
2. serving_chat sets `delta_text = output.text` and feeds it to the unified parser that `ParserManager.get_parser(reasoning_parser_name="deepseek_r1")` builds, which delegates to `DeepSeekR1ReasoningParser`.
3. That parser only slices `delta_text` around the `</think>` boundary. I audited every branch of `basic_parsers.py` and `deepseek_r1_reasoning_parser.py`: each return value is a substring of `delta_text`. There is no `convert_ids_to_tokens` anywhere in `vllm/entrypoints`, `vllm/parser`, or `vllm/reasoning` (the only hit is the unrelated `/tokenize` endpoint).

Your control experiments are the tell. Without the parser, the same `output.text` arrives as clean content, and non-streaming is clean too. So your detokenizer output is clean. The parser can only cut up what it receives; slicing clean text cannot turn one field back into raw token strings while the other stays clean. Something in your deployment is replacing the reasoning path with a token-string implementation between the detokenizer and the wire.

**Verification I ran**

In-process simulation of the exact serving chain (real tokenizer, CJK reasoning stream, token-at-a-time detokenization, then the same `_WrappedParser.parse_delta` the server uses):

- v0.21.0 tag + transformers 5.8.1 (your versions), fast detokenizer path: clean
- v0.21.0 tag + transformers 5.8.1, forced slow `detokenize_incrementally` path: clean
- current main + transformers 5.14.1, both paths: clean

Reasoning and content reconstruct byte-exact in every combination, zero glyphs. Script below, you can run it inside your container (no GPU needed, point it at your local model dir):

<details><summary>repro script</summary>

```python
"""Simulates the v0.21.0 streaming chain for --reasoning-parser deepseek_r1.
Runs in-process, no GPU needed. Usage: python repro.py [model_path]
"""
import sys
from types import SimpleNamespace

import transformers
from vllm.entrypoints.openai.chat_completion.protocol import ChatCompletionRequest
from vllm.parser.parser_manager import ParserManager
from vllm.tokenizers.registry import get_tokenizer
from vllm.v1.engine.detokenizer import IncrementalDetokenizer, SlowIncrementalDetokenizer

MODEL = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B"
tok = get_tokenizer(MODEL)
print("transformers:", transformers.__version__, "| tokenizer:", type(tok).__name__)

prompt_ids = tok.encode("<｜User｜>请用三句话介绍一下你自己。<｜Assistant｜><think>\n")
gen_ids = tok.encode("\n嗯，让我想想。</think>好的！很高兴认识你。", add_special_tokens=False)

def run(force_slow):
    sampling = SimpleNamespace(stop=None, min_tokens=0, include_stop_str_in_output=False,

items.title: [Question]: Qwen4Exp PLE n-gram table is materialised dense in bf16 — can it stay compressed in pinned host memory?
items.author: tellmewhattodo
items.body_excerpt:
### Environment

| | |
|---|---|
| vLLM | `0.32.0` |
| Python | `3.12.15` |
| torch | `2.13.0+cu130` |
| transformers | `5.19.0` |
| triton | `3.7.1` |
| glq | `0.8.28` |
| CUDA / driver | `13.0` / `595.91.07` |
| GPU | 2x consumer Blackwell (`sm_120`), 31.85 GiB total |

> **Note on older versions**: with `glq 0.8.16 / vLLM 0.30.0 / Python 3.10`, loading the same checkpoint
> fails earlier, at engine-core init, with a *different* error:
> `NotImplementedError: Qwen4Exp PLE embedding does not support quantization config GLQvLLMConfig`.
> That whitelist issue is fixed in `glq 0.8.28` (see "Confirmed working" below) and is *not* the subject
> of this report. It is mentioned only so that readers on older versions know which error they are looking at.

### What happens

With the combination above the PLE embedding **loads successfully**, but the engine cannot come up on a
host with **94.27 GiB** of RAM: the PLE n-gram table is materialised **dense in bf16** during init, the
allocation exceeds host memory, and the process is **OOM-killed**.

### Steps to reproduce

```sh
vllm serve <checkpoint-dir> \
    --tensor-parallel-size 2 \
    --cpu-offload-gb 40
```

**Expected**: engine starts.
**Observed**: process is killed by the kernel OOM killer during engine init.

`--cpu-offload-gb` does not govern this allocation: lowering it from `60 -> 40` moved `shmem-rss` by only
~2 GB (`93.5 -> 91.3 GB`), i.e. a large block is allocated outside it.

### Why it is not a size-on-disk problem

| tensor | dtype | shape | bytes |
|---|---|---|---:|
| `...ple_embedding.ngram_embedding.trellis_packed` | I16 | [320001536, 40] | **25.600 GB** |
| `...ple_embedding.ngram_embedding.Wscale` | F16 | [320001536] | 0.640 GB |
| PLE total on disk | | | **26.253 GB** |

Row width at 4 bpw = `40 x 16 / 4` = **160** weights; this cross-checks with
`ple_embed_dim 2560 / ngram_heads 16 = 160`.

=> **Dense bf16 = 320001536 x 160 x 2 B = 102.4 GB ~= 95.4 GiB**, versus **94.27 GiB** of host RAM.

### Confirmed working (so the whitelist part is settled)

```
Initialized PLE embedding ...ngram_embedding:
  quantization_method=GLQEmbeddingMethod, weight_device=cpu, pinned=True
```

### The concrete ask

**Can the PLE n-gram table stay in its trellis-compressed form in pinned host memory, instead of being
materialised dense in bf16?**

### Questions (not a demand)

1. Is the PLE n-gram table intended to be materialised dense (bf16/fp16) regardless of the checkpoint's
   quantization, or is there a path that keeps it compressed and decodes on lookup?
2. If dense materialisation is required by design, what is the intended host-memory sizing rule, so a
   deployment can be checked **before** a ~26 GB download?
3. Could the loader emit the projected dense size at startup (one log line), so an under-provisioned host
   fails with a clear "needs N GiB" message instead of an OOM kill?

items.title: CPU-only lmcache server + CUDA vLLM worker: REGISTER_KV_CACHE fails with 'Device UUID not found' (examples/multi_process + docstring mismatch)
items.author: zhaotyer
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

When the `lmcache server` runs in a CPU-only container (no GPU visible → `StubCPUDevice`) and the vLLM worker has CUDA GPUs, the worker's `REGISTER_KV_CACHE` request fails at server side with:

```
RuntimeError: Device UUID f231cc14-0922-0ca9-5c57-efd8982e6c5e not found in the discovered devices. Please make sure the process can see all the accelerator devices
```

The `examples/multi_process/` k8s YAMLs describe exactly this topology (CPU-only DaemonSet + CUDA vLLM Deployment) but never set `lmcache.mp.mp_transfer_mode=engine_driven` on the client, so they appear to hit the same failure. Two related doc bugs make it hard to diagnose: the connector docstring describes `engine_driven` / `lmcache_driven` exactly opposite to what the factory code does.

## Reproduction

### Server (CPU-only container)

```bash
lmcache server \
    --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 \
    --l1-size-gb 20 --eviction-policy LRU --chunk-size 16
```

Startup log shows the server fell back to the CPU stub:

```
LMCache INFO:  torch_dev=StubCPUDevice(device_type=cpu), torch_device_type=cpu
...
LMCache INFO: Supported transfer mode: auto
LMCache INFO: LMCache ZMQ cache server is running on tcp://0.0.0.0:8000
```

### Client (vLLM with GPU, default `mp_transfer_mode=auto`)

```
vllm serve <model> --kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"LMCacheMPConnector", "kv_role":"kv_both", "kv_connector_extra_config": {"lmcache.mp.host": "tcp://<server>", "lmcache.mp.port": 8000}}'
```

### Error (server-side)

```
LMCache ERROR: Error handling request RequestType.REGISTER_KV_CACHE
...
  File ".../lmcache/v1/platform/cache_context.py", line 149, in _detect_device_type
    device_types = {w.to_tensor().device.type for w in kv_caches}
  File ".../lmcache/v1/multiprocess/custom_types.py", line 145, in to_tensor
    device_index = self._get_device_index_from_uuid(self.device_uuid)
  File ".../lmcache/v1/multiprocess/custom_types.py", line 79, in _get_device_index_from_uuid
    raise RuntimeError(
RuntimeError: Device UUID f231cc14-0922-0ca9-5c57-efd8982e6c5e not found in the discovered devices. Please make sure the process can see all the accelerator devices
```

## Root cause

1. Client-side default `mp_transfer_mode=auto` routes CUDA workers to `LMCacheDrivenTransferContext` (CUDA IPC path):
   ```python
   # lmcache/v1/multiprocess/transfer_context/worker_transfer.py:547-550
   # AUTO: dispatch by device type (CUDA -> handle path, else -> data path).
   if device_type == "cuda":
       return LMCacheDrivenTransferContext()
   return EngineDrivenTransferContext()
   ```
2. Worker wraps its KV tensors with `CudaIPCWrapper`, embedding the worker GPU's `device_uuid` (`lmcache/v1/multiprocess/custom_types.py:135-136`).
3. On `REGISTER_KV_CACHE`, the server calls `create_cache_context()` → `_detect_device_type()` → `w.to_tensor()` → `_get_device_index_from_uuid()` (`cache_context.py:149`, `custom_types.py:145`).
4. `_discover_devices()` returns immediately when `torch_dev.is_available()` is `False` (`custom_types.py:56-57`), and `StubCPUDevice.is_available()` is always `False` (`lmcache/v1/platform/cpu/stub_cpu_device.py:214-220`). So `_discovered_device_mapping` stays empty and any UUID lookup raises.

Server-side `--supported-transfer-mode auto` loads both transfer modules (`lmcache/v1/multiprocess/server.py:198-200`), so it cannot rescue this — the failure happens earlier, in `REGISTER_KV_CACHE` routing on the client side.

## Expected behavior

One of:
- The `examples/multi_process/` YAMLs set `lmcache.mp.mp_transfer_mode=engine_driven` on the vLLM side (the documented escape hatch for this topology — see `docs/source/getting_started/quickstart.rst:452-455`).
- OR the server detects "CUDA worker IPC arrived but I have no GPU" and returns a clear error message at `REGISTER_KV_CACHE` time pointing the user at `engine_driven`, rather than a generic "Device UUID not found".
- OR `auto` on a CUDA worker falls back to `engine_driven` when the server is CPU-only (harder — needs a capability handshake).

## Environment

- LMCache: v0.5.0 (g389b9cfc)
- Server container: CPU-only (`torch_dev=StubCPUDevice`)
- vLLM worker: has CUDA GPUs
- Topology: same as `examples/multi_process/` (CPU-only lmcache DaemonSet + CUDA vLLM Deployment, co-located via `/dev/shm` hostPath)

## Workaround

Set `lmcache.mp.mp_transfer_mode=engine_driven` in `kv_connector_extra_config` on the vLLM side, or `export LMCACHE_MP_TRANSFER_MODE=engine_driven` in the vLLM container. This routes the worker through `EngineDrivenTransferContext` (worker-side gather/scatter copy), which does not require the server to open CUDA IPC handles.

## Doc bugs found while debugging

### 1. `examples/multi_process/` does not set `engine_driven`

`examples/multi_process/vllm-deployment.yaml` (line 39) only sets `lmcache.mp.host` / `lmcache.mp.port`, relying on the default `auto`. With a CPU-only server (`lmcache-daemonset.yaml` has no `nvidia.com/gpu` resource request) and a CUDA worker, this should hit the error above. Either the example needs `engine_driven` in `kv_connector_extra_config`, or the deployment doc (`docs/source/mp/deployment.rst`) should call out the topology assumption.

### 2. Connector docstring swaps `engine_driven` / `lmcache_driven` descriptions

`lmcache/integration/vllm/lmcache_mp_connector_0201.py:476-480`:

```python
- lmcache.mp.mp_transfer_mode: routing mode for the worker -> server
  transfer context. One of ``auto`` (default; CUDA -> engine_driven,
  others -> lmcache_driven), ``engine_driven`` (force IPC / SHM
  zero-copy), ``lmcache_driven`` (force worker-side gather/scatter
  copy). Overrides the ``LMCACHE_MP_TRANSFER_MODE`` env var when set.
```

This says `engine_driven` = "force IPC / SHM zero-copy" and `lmcache_driven` = "force worker-side gather/scatter copy". The factory code says the opposite:

```python
# lmcache/v1/multiprocess/transfer_context/worker_transfer.py:543-550
if resolved_mode is MPTransferMode.LMCACHE_DRIVEN:
    return _build_lmca

items.title: [Bug][MP] "full" prefetch drops columns that are partly in L1 when an L1 reservation fails
items.author: theminjunchoi
items.body_excerpt:
**Describe the bug**

With `fetching_policy="full"`, if any L1 staging reservation fails, the prefetch controller trims the request to whole columns (Step 3.5 in `_transition_to_load_phase`, added in #5434). The trim only looks at `l1_reserved_keys`, so rows of a column that are already in L1 (`l1_locked_keys`) don't count. A column that is partly in L1 and partly loaded from L2 is never seen as whole, gets released, and turns into a miss.

`_finish_request` does count L1 rows when it picks the whole columns, so the same column is a hit when every reservation succeeds and a miss when some other column's reservation fails.

This affects the "full" callers: the blend sparse leg, warm prefetch and P2P. It shows up under L1 pressure, which is also when some rows of a chunk tend to get evicted.

**To Reproduce**

Three rows, two columns. Column 0 is in L1 for rows 0 and 2 and only in L2 for row 1. Column 1 is only in L2. L1 has room for three staging buffers, so the last row's reservation fails.

```python
rows = [make_group([make_object_key(i, gid=g) for i in range(2)], gid=g) for g in range(3)]
write_keys_to_l1(l1_manager, [rows[0].keys[0], rows[2].keys[0]], layout)
store_keys_in_l2(adapter, [rows[1].keys[0]] + [r.keys[1] for r in rows], layout)
# L1Manager sized for 5 objects
```

(helpers from `tests/v1/distributed/test_prefetch_controller.py`)

| case | hits |
| --- | --- |
| `full`, L1 big enough | `[[0, 1], [0, 1], [0, 1]]` |
| `full`, one reservation fails | `[[], [], []]` |
| `prefix`, one reservation fails | `[[0], [0], [0]]` |

**Expected behavior**

Column 0 is complete (two rows in L1, one loaded from L2), so the second case should return `[[0], [0], [0]]`.

**Additional context**

Seen on `dev` at 6448b447. Adding `l1_locked_keys` to the cells the trim checks fixes it.

items.title: Compressed LLMs by 85% that scores higher for llama.cpp's own 2-bit at the same size. Free one-click build.
items.author: harshit-genrius
items.body_excerpt: We made a new 2-bit format for local models. It makes **Qwen3-4B 85% smaller (8 GB -> 1.24 GB)** and **Llama 3.1 8B 85% smaller (16 GB -> 2.4 GB)**, and at the same file size it scores clearly better than llama.cpp's IQ2_XXS and ik_llama.cpp's IQ2_KT. **Try it in 2 minutes (Windows, NVIDIA RTX 30/40/50):** download the zip from the [release page](https://github.com/Genrius-AI/pingala8-llm/releases/tag/v2.4-oneclick), unzip, double-click `run_qwen3_4b.bat`. It downloads the model once and opens a chat page in your browser. Linux: `./run.sh qwen`. **How good is it? (Qwen3-4B, all files the same 1.24 GB size)** |Test (plain words)|Original model|llama.cpp IQ2_XXS|IQ2_KT (best rival)|**This**| |:-|:-|:-|:-|:-| |Quiz score: average of 5 standard tests (HellaSwag, WinoGrande, ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, MMLU)|56.3|41.9|46.5|**50.8**| |Share of the original's quiz score kept|100%|74%|83%|**90%**| |Quality lost vs the original model (lower is better)|0%|130%|46%|**34%**| |Picks the same next word as the original model|-|-|63.7%|**71.3%**| On Llama 3.1 8B (2.4 GB, 85% smaller) the same pattern holds: IQ2_XXS's error score is 35% higher than this one's, IQ2_KT's 10% higher. (For the technical crowd: "quality lost" is WikiText-2 perplexity relative to the original, 16.64 vs 12.46; IQ2_XXS 28.61, IQ2_KT 18.15; Llama 9.14 vs 10.04 vs 12.35. Context 4096, same imatrix for every file. "Same next word" is top-1 agreement with Q8_0 over 72 chunks. "Original" quiz column is the 8-bit Q8_0 file. Held-out C4 text keeps the same order.) **Speed** (one RTX 5070 Ti Laptop, compared with llama.cpp's IQ2_XXS at the same size): * Chatting (how fast it writes the reply): about the same, 1.10x * Reading a long prompt or document before replying: 26% slower (0.74x) * Serving several chats at once: 3-5x slower (0.18-0.34x) * Running on CPU only: about 40% slower (0.56-0.62x) **Where it loses (please read):** * Qwen3-14B: it loses slightly to IQ2_KT (about 2% worse; perplexity 9.57 vs 9.40, tie on C4 text). The prediction was written down before the run, so it's a real loss. * The Qwen3-4B number is from my last of many builds, so treat it as tuned. C4, Llama and 14B were held out or pre-registered. * Needs a patched llama.cpp (CUDA). Stock llama.cpp, Ollama and LM Studio can't load it yet. No Metal/Vulkan. How: an 8-state trellis code (Ungerboeck) over groups of 4 weights, after a Hadamard rotation and QuIP-style LDLQ rounding. Builds on QTIP / QuIP# and ikawrakow's IQ2_KT. Links: * One-click build: https://github.com/Genrius-AI/pingala8-llm/releases/tag/v2.4-oneclick * Code, patch, all logs: https://github.com/Genrius-AI/pingala8-llm * Models: https://huggingface.co/Genrius-AI/Qwen3-4B-Pingala8-2bit and https://huggingface.co/Genrius-AI/Llama-3.1-8B-Pingala8-2bit * Paper: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23481757
