items.title: [Doc]: Out-of-tree quantization plugin guide uses the removed FusedMoE class and an outdated MoE method API
items.author: SohamDutta02
items.body_excerpt:
### 📚 The doc issue


The MoE example in the "Out-of-Tree Quantization Plugins" section of the quantization docs ([`[docs/features/quantization/README.md](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/2d8efee9a73366d6b4e753780af32443d2fef91a/docs/features/quantization/README.md)`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/2d8efee9a73366d6b4e753780af32443d2fef91a/docs/features/quantization/README.md), rendered at https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/features/quantization/) no longer works on `main`. A plugin copied from it fails at import time. Even with the imports fixed, its `apply` method has a signature the MoE layer can't call.

I checked this against `main` at `2d8efee9a73366d6b4e753780af32443d2fef91a`:

**1. `FusedMoE` no longer exists.**
The example imports it ([[L111](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/2d8efee9a73366d6b4e753780af32443d2fef91a/docs/features/quantization/README.md#L111)](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/2d8efee9a73366d6b4e753780af32443d2fef91a/docs/features/quantization/README.md#L111)) and dispatches on `isinstance(layer, FusedMoE)` ([[L145](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/2d8efee9a73366d6b4e753780af32443d2fef91a/docs/features/quantization/README.md#L145)](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/2d8efee9a73366d6b4e753780af32443d2fef91a/docs/features/quantization/README.md#L145)). #40735 introduced `RoutedExperts`, and #44941 renamed `FusedMoE` to `FusedMoEFactory`, which is a factory function rather than a layer class. `vllm.model_executor.layers.fused_moe` no longer exports `FusedMoE`, so the import raises `ImportError`. The in-tree configs now dispatch on `RoutedExperts` instead (e.g. [`fp8.py` L191](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/2d8efee9a73366d6b4e753780af32443d2fef91a/vllm/model_executor/layers/quantization/fp8.py#L191)).

**2. `UnquantizedFusedMoEMethod` is no longer in `fused_moe.layer`.**
The example imports it from `vllm.model_executor.layers.fused_moe.layer` ([[L194](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/2d8efee9a73366d6b4e753780af32443d2fef91a/docs/features/quantization/README.md#L194)](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/2d8efee9a73366d6b4e753780af32443d2fef91a/docs/features/quantization/README.md#L194)). Since #41184, `layer.py` no longer imports it. The class lives in `fused_moe/unquantized_fused_moe_method.py` and is re-exported from `vllm.model_executor.layers.fused_moe` ([`__init__.py` L75](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/2d8efee9a73366d6b4e753780af32443d2fef91a/vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/__init__.py#L75)). The documented import path is therefore also an `ImportError`.

**3. `MyQuantMoEMethod.apply` has a signature the layer can't call.**
The example defines `apply(self, layer, router: "FusedMoERouter", x, router_logits)` ([[L215-L221](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/2d8efee9a73366d6b4e753780af32443d2fef91a/docs/features/quantization/README.md#L215-L221)](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/2d8efee9a73366d6b4e753780af32443d2fef91a/docs/features/quantization/README.md#L215-L221)). `FusedMoEMethodBase` now has two entry points ([`fused_moe_method_base.py` L143-L173](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/2d8efee9a73366d6b4e753780af32443d2fef91a/vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/fused_moe_method_base.py#L143-L173)):

- `apply(layer, x, topk_weights, topk_ids, shared_experts, shared_experts_input)` for modular kernels.
- `apply_monolithic(layer, x, router_logits, input_ids=None)` for kernels that do their own routing.

`RoutedExperts` calls `apply` with keyword arguments ([`routed_experts.py` L1397-L1404](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/2d8efee9a73366d6b4e753780af32443d2fef91a/vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/routed_experts.py#L1397-L1404)), so a method written from the docs fails with:

```
TypeError: MyQuantMoEMethod.apply() got an unexpected keyword argument 'topk_weights'
```

The linear-layer half of the example and the `QuantizationConfig` table still match the current APIs; only the MoE parts are stale. None of the refactor PRs above touched `docs/`, which is probably how the guide drifted.


### Suggest a potential alternative/fix


Update the MoE parts of the example to the current API.

In `MyQuantConfig`:

```python
from vllm.model_executor.layers.fused_moe import RoutedExperts

...
        elif isinstance(layer, RoutedExperts):
            return MyQuantMoEMethod(layer.moe_config)
```

The MoE method:

```python
import torch

from vllm.model_executor.layers.fused_moe import (
    FusedMoEMethodBase,
    FusedMoEQuantConfig,
    RoutedExperts,
    SharedExperts,
    UnquantizedFusedMoEMethod,  # return this to leave MoE layers unquantized
)


class MyQuantMoEMethod(FusedMoEMethodBase):
    """Custom quantization method for MoE layers."""

    def create_weights(
        self,
        layer: RoutedExperts,
        num_experts: int,
        hidden_size: int,
        intermediate_size_per_partition: int,
        params_dtype: torch.dtype,
        **extra_weight_attrs,
    ):
        # Create quantized weights for the MoE layer
        ...

    def get_fused_moe_quant_config(
        self, layer: RoutedExperts
    ) -> FusedMoEQuantConfig | None:
        # Return the MoE quantization configuration
        ...

    def apply(
        self,
        layer: RoutedExperts,
        x: torch.Tensor,
        topk_weights: torch.Tensor,
        topk_ids: torch.Tensor,
        shared_experts: SharedExperts | None,
        shared_experts_input: torch.Tensor | None,
    ) -> torch.Tensor:
        # Routing has already run; apply the experts with quantized weights
        ...
```

It would also help to add a short note that a method which does its own routing should make `is_monolithic` return `True` and implement `apply_monolithic(layer, x, router_logits, input_ids=None)` instead of `apply`.

A small test that imports and registers the example config might keep this section from drifting during future MoE refactors.

I'm happy to open a PR with the fix.

items.title: [MP][ARC] Clarify ghost readmission semantics across L1 and L2
items.author: Mengmj
items.body_excerpt:
**Label**

`discussion`, `mp_mode`.

**Summary**

ARC currently classifies a key returning from B1/B2 differently depending on the listener path: L1 reservation followed by admission leaves it in T1, while L2 storage completion puts it in T2. I would like to clarify whether this difference is intentional and add coverage for the agreed behavior. I am interested in taking ownership of the follow-up PR.

**Details**

Inspected revision: `dev` at `d66c61d9d08a78e6fd56d0d43eafb3e6fc52279f`.

For a key that is already in B1 or B2:

| Path | Policy callbacks | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| L1 write | `on_keys_reserved` followed by `on_keys_created` | T1 |
| L2 store | `on_keys_created` directly | T2 |

In the [L1 reservation handler](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/d66c61d9d08a78e6fd56d0d43eafb3e6fc52279f/lmcache/v1/distributed/eviction_policy/arc.py#L121-L154), ARC applies ghost feedback, removes the ghost entry, inserts the key into T1, and marks admission as pending. The subsequent creation notification consumes that pending marker without changing its classification.

The [L2 listener](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/d66c61d9d08a78e6fd56d0d43eafb3e6fc52279f/lmcache/v1/distributed/eviction.py#L233-L234) calls `on_keys_created` directly. Its [B1/B2 branches](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/d66c61d9d08a78e6fd56d0d43eafb3e6fc52279f/lmcache/v1/distributed/eviction_policy/arc.py#L98-L113) apply ghost feedback and insert the key into T2.

The reservation docstring describes keeping reservations in T1, but does not separately explain ghost readmission or the difference between L1 and L2.

**Steps / Reproduction**

At the policy/listener level, start each case from equivalent ghost state:

1. Create a key, optionally touch it to move it into T2, then select and confirm its eviction to produce a B1 or B2 entry.
2. For L1, call `on_l1_keys_reserved_write([key])`, then `on_l1_keys_write_finished([key])`.
3. In a separate equivalent case, call `on_l2_keys_stored([key], [size])`.
4. Compare `get_debug_state()`: the L1 case puts the key in T1; the L2 case puts it in T2.

This report is based on source and existing-test inspection. I have not run a full MP server or measured a performance regression for this issue.

**Expected Outcome / Goal**

Could maintainers clarify whether ghost readmission should intentionally differ between L1 and L2? If the paths should agree, which classification should they use?

I would like to take this on and prepare a focused PR once the intended behavior is confirmed. I can:

- Align the callbacks if the difference is unintended, or document the rationale if it is intentional.
- Add public-interface tests covering B1/B2 readmission through both listener paths, including repeated L1 reservations.
- Preserve coverage that cold writes stay in T1 and explicit accesses promote them to T2.

**Actual Outcome / Test Coverage**

The [L1 lifecycle test](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/d66c61d9d08a78e6fd56d0d43eafb3e6fc52279f/tests/v1/distributed/test_arc_eviction_policy.py#L203-L220) verifies cold admission and eviction into B1, but stops before readmission. The [existing ghost tests](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/d66c61d9d08a78e6fd56d0d43eafb3e6fc52279f/tests/v1/distributed/test_arc_eviction_policy.py#L108-L143) exercise `on_keys_created` directly and expect T2 behavior. I could not find a test covering ghost readmission through L1's reserve-then-admit sequence.

**Additional Context**

Related: #5347 and #5348 addressed duplicate notifications promoting cold L1 writes to T2; this question concerns keys returning from ghost history after eviction.

vLLM's CPU-offload ARC [explicitly documents insertion into T1 even for ghost entries](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/494663940b9b44f667c4f61c8c2407ba8e725ceb/vllm/v1/kv_offload/cpu/policies/arc.py#L30-L44). I am therefore asking about LMCache's intended contract before proposing a change based on classical ARC semantics.

items.title: [Roadmap] LMCache Roadmap 2026 Q4
items.author: ApostaC
items.body_excerpt:
# LMCache 2026 Q4 Roadmap

The main topic for Q4 is to make LMCache faster, safer, more stable, and more pluggable.


## 1. In-process mode deprecation and deletion

We don't list concrete tasks for the in-process mode deprecation because it will need a lot of ad hoc changes.
At a high level, we will separate in-process mode code to `lmcache/in_process` folder first, and then drop them together. (See #5831 and #5839 )



## 2. Security enhancements

As LMCache is continuously evolving, we noticed that some vulnerabilities have been introduced. Therefore, we will push more security enhancements into LMCache in Q4. 

- [ ] Deprecating the use of pickle
- [ ] Authentication to all user-facing HTTP APIs

## 3. Core improvements

In Q4, we are still going to keep making LMCache faster and better, with the following optimizations:

- [ ] Unfull-chunk persistence
- [ ] LMCache-native PD disaggregation
- [ ] Multi-tier L1 memory support (e.g., CXL, Remote RDMA memory server, and NIXL)
- [ ] GDS L2 storage adapters support
- [ ] General performance optimization (data copies, L2 adapter performance, and metadata management overheads).
- [ ] Centralized config source and support dynamic configuration



## 4. LMCache plugins and pluggable interfaces

We really appreciate the innovations in the community. To make sure that all the cool ideas can easily land in LMCache, we are going to introduce the LMCache plugin system. Once this is landed, everyone can add plugins and modify LMCache based on customized use cases and algorithms. 

- [ ] Standardize plugin interface and SDK
- [ ] Move out of tree of some L2 Adapters
- [ ] Move out of tree of some device backends
- [ ] Support out-of-tree GDS backend
- [ ] Extension module for layerwise transfers
- [ ] (Experimental) Token dropping outside inference engine
- [ ] (Experimental) Token dropping in inference engine

## 5. SGLang integration

For a long while, LMCache has had the most native integration with vLLM. In Q4, we want to improve and stabilize the SGLang integration with their latest interfaces. 

- [ ] Support SGLang external linker interface
- [ ] Improve SGLang integration tests
- [ ] Performance optimization with SGLang
- [ ] Stability enhancement


## 5. CI/CD and release pipeline

- [ ] Release `lmcache-client` package for a more lightweight integration with different inference engines (no extra dependencies is introduced)
- [ ] Performance dashboard and auto regression testing
- [ ] Better PyPI release with different hardware vendors and platforms

------

### For contributors

Since most of the items on the roadmap are pretty big topics, if you would like to participate in some of them, please directly reach out to the core team in the LMCache Slack workspace with the design docs so that we can discuss them. 
We generally don't accept big PRs without a discussed and converged design.

items.title: [RFC] Native PD disaggregation
items.author: hlin99
items.body_excerpt:
# 1. Motivation

**Heterogeneous hardware is becoming an increasingly important direction for PD disaggregation.** As more alternatives to NVIDIA GPUs emerge, different accelerators may offer advantages in performance, cost, or energy efficiency for prefill and decode respectively. Deployments therefore have a growing reason to choose different hardware for the two stages.

**The best inference engine may differ as well.** An engine optimized for the prefill hardware may not be the best choice—or even available—on the decode hardware. Requiring the same engine on both sides constrains these hardware choices, creating a need for cross-engine PD.

Cross-engine interoperability is not a primary focus of individual inference engines. **LMCache is naturally positioned to bridge this gap:** it already integrates with multiple engines and provides cache offloading and transfer infrastructure. Extending these foundations with compatible KV and recurrent-state representations offers a path to cross-engine PD.

With the rise of agentic workloads, deployments that prioritize end-to-end task efficiency over minimum TTFT may find the additional cross-engine PD handoff overhead an acceptable trade-off for better hardware–engine combinations.

# 2. Known Gaps

We identified seven known gaps for cross-engine PD interoperability.

- The [prototype](https://github.com/hlin99/LMCache/tree/pd_pd) includes fixes and workarounds for the first four.
- Checkpoint/prefix compatibility remains a limitation.
- Saving partial chunks needs to be addressed but has not been attempted.
- Asymmetric TP has not been attempted.

| Gap | Description | Prototype solution / status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **FULL KV layout** | The tested engines use different K/V layouts. | **[w/a]** Adapt SGLang to match vLLM's layout with extra packing/unpacking copies. Commit: [77b1dd67](https://github.com/hlin99/LMCache/commit/77b1dd67). |
| **Object-group identity and order** | Component registration order differs, making positional group IDs incompatible. | **[fix]** Map component groups explicitly, preserving device indices and identifying FULL token-slot ownership. Commit: [6701bfd1](https://github.com/hlin99/LMCache/commit/6701bfd1). |
| **GDN state byte format** | Convolution and recurrent states differ in layout, dtype, offsets, and padding. | **[w/a]** Adapt SGLang to match vLLM's packed state representation with extra packing/unpacking copies. Commit: [a86d3a63](https://github.com/hlin99/LMCache/commit/a86d3a63). |
| **GDN logical-layer order** | Physical grouping produces different recurrent-layer orders. | **[w/a]** Reorder SGLang's state tensor references to match the tested vLLM round-robin grouping, without an extra layer-copy pass. Only unpadded grouping is supported. Commit: [8b515db7](https://github.com/hlin99/LMCache/commit/8b515db7). |
| **Checkpoint/prefix boundaries** | FULL KV and GDN state must represent exactly the same token prefix, despite different checkpoint grids and snapshot availability. | **[limitation]** Reuse is restricted to shared aligned boundaries with the required GDN snapshot available. Arbitrary-boundary checkpoints are not supported. Configuration and limitations: [057706cf](https://github.com/hlin99/LMCache/commit/057706cf). |
| **Saving partial chunks** | A prefix may end with an incomplete LMCache chunk that also needs to be saved for PD handoff. | **[not attempted]** Saving partial/tail chunks needs to be implemented. Padding model input with dummy tokens is not a valid workaround because it changes recurrent state. |
| **Asymmetric TP** | Different TP degrees require repartitioning KV and recurrent state across workers. | **[not attempted]** Matching TP is required by the prototype. |

# 3. Validation Results

All runs below used BF16, matching TP, and two independent CPU caches connected through NIXL:

**P engine GPU → P CPU cache → NIXL → D CPU cache → D engine GPU**

The copy-mode column identifies who performs GPU/CPU transfers on **both** sides: the cache daemons for `lmcache_driven`, or the engine workers for `engine_driven`. This is separate from the CPU-to-CPU NIXL transfer.

| Model | Prefill engine | Decode engine | TP (P → D) | GPU/CPU copy mode | Restored prefix | Cold-reference result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Qwen3.5-0.8B** | vLLM | SGLang | 1 → 1 | `lmcache_driven` | 2176 tokens | All 31 continuation token IDs matched fresh SGLang with LMCache disabled. |
| **Qwen3.5-0.8B** | vLLM | SGLang | 2 → 2 | `lmcache_driven` | 2176 tokens | All 31 continuation token IDs matched fresh SGLang with LMCache disabled. |
| **Qwen3.5-0.8B** | SGLang | vLLM | 2 → 2 | `lmcache_driven` | 2176 tokens | All 31 continuation token IDs matched fresh vLLM without the LMCache connector. |
| **Llama-3.1-8B** | vLLM | SGLang | 2 → 2 | `engine_driven` (inline IPC) | 512 tokens | All 31 continuation token IDs matched fresh SGLang with LMCache disabled. |

- These are correctness checks, not performance benchmarks.

# 4. Design Trade-offs and Boundaries

- **Interoperability over minimum transfer latency.** This design prioritizes cross-engine compatibility rather than the lowest-latency GPU-direct RDMA (GDR) path. Normalizing engine-specific KV layouts into a canonical transfer representation and staging through CPU memory can introduce additional conversion, copy, and synchronization latency. The benefit is enabling PD handoff between different inference engines. This path is not intended to replace engine-native PD; same-engine deployments prioritizing minimum handoff latency may prefer a native direct-transfer path. The current prototype uses the tested vLLM representation as an interim format, not a finalized canonical representation.

- **Native engine chunking remains unchanged.** We do not modify either engine's native block/checkpoint granularity. For cross-engine PD, the LMCache chunk size must therefore be a common multiple of both engines' granularities, with the least comm

items.title: Eval bug: [SYCL][mtmd] llama-mtmd-cli aborts with 0xC0000409 after threadpool init on Intel Arc Pro B70 (Windows) — before image encode
items.author: matthew-rutledge-dev
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

Official Windows SYCL binary **b11064** (`llama-b11064-bin-win-sycl-x64` / local tree `E:\llama-cpp-sycl\b11064`).
Binary used: `llama-mtmd-cli.exe`.

### Operating systems

Windows 11

### GGML backends

SYCL (Level Zero)

### Hardware

Intel Arc Pro B70, 32 GB VRAM (Xe2 / Battlemage). Dual-GPU host also has an NVIDIA RTX 5080; Arc runs were launched with:

```
ONEAPI_DEVICE_SELECTOR=level_zero:0
ZES_ENABLE_SYSMAN=1
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=-1
```

### Models

- `gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf` (Unsloth)
- `mmproj-BF16.gguf` (same model set)

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

`llama-mtmd-cli` on Windows SYCL **aborts with `STATUS_STACK_BUFFER_OVERRUN` (`0xC0000409` / exit `-1073740791`)** roughly **12s after** logging `llama threadpool init, n_threads = 24`, **before any image encode**, with **empty stdout**.

**Text `llama-cli` on the same GGUF (no mmproj) passes** on this B70 SYCL build.

Reproduced on a dedicated re-run (2026-09-21) with the same fixture + prompt; wall ~18.15s; abort reproduced yes.

Minimal shape used:

```text
llama-mtmd-cli.exe ^
  -m gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf ^
  --mmproj mmproj-BF16.gguf ^
  --image phase-b-shapes-42.png ^
  -p "Describe this image in one short sentence. Name colors and any numbers you see." ^
  -ngl 99 -n 128 --perf
```

Also failed previously with `--no-mmproj-offload` (same abort signature).

### Closest known issue

Closest match by **exit code + post-threadpool timing**:

- https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/issues/27128 — Win SYCL, dies right after threadpool init, exit `-1073740791`. That report shows Level Zero `UR_RESULT_ERROR_INVALID_VALUE` on VMM `phys->map`. **Our stderr is quieter**: no UR/SYCL error line — only load warnings, then threadpool init, then silent abort.

**Question for maintainers:** do the workarounds suggested on #27128 apply to the **mtmd** path as well?

- `GGML_SYCL_ENABLE_VMM=0`
- `--no-mmap` / `--load-mode none`

We have **not** re-tested those env/flags yet on this mtmd lane (filing first). Happy to try and report back.

Related B70 SYCL context (different symptom — garbage output, not this abort):
- https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/issues/21893 (`GGML_SYCL_DISABLE_OPT=1`)

### First Bad Commit

Unknown — observed on official **b11064** win-sycl. Not bisected.

### Relevant log output

items.title: [RFC]: Hot Standby Mode for Master Service Metadata High Availability
items.author: Libotry
items.body_excerpt: ## Introduction To address the issue where all metadata is lost after a master service failure and recovery, this solution proposes a **hot-standby synchronization mechanism** and a **hybrid approach** combining hot standby with snapshots, ensuring rapid data recovery following a master service failure. ## Motivation The current HA (High Availability) mode only supports rapid restart of the master service after a failure but cannot guarantee fast data recovery. The pain points of the current HA mode are as follows: | Issue | Impact | Severity | | -------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------- | | **Complete loss of metadata after Leader failure** | All KV cache location information is lost and must be rebuilt | 🔴 Critical | | **Follower lacks data pre-warming** | After successful election, the new Leader must start serving from scratch | 🟠 Medium | | **Long recovery time** | Relies on clients to re-register; may take several minutes to tens of minutes | 🟠 Medium | | **Service unavailability window** | Requests cannot be processed during Leader failover | 🟡 Low | ## Goals: 1. **Near-zero RPO**: Minimize the data loss window 2. **Fast failover**: Achieve second-level RTO (Recovery Time Objective) 3. **Data consistency guarantee**: Ensure correct synchronization between primary and standby 4. **Verifiability**: Include mechanisms to validate data integrity 5. **Low performance overhead**: Avoid impacting normal business operations ## Proposal ### 1. Core Design Approach **Use etcd as an intermediate reliability component to implement OpLog primary-standby synchronization**: - **OpLog Mechanism**: Primary Master records all state change operations to OpLog - **etcd Storage**: OpLog is written to etcd, leveraging etcd's strong consistency and persistence capabilities - **Watch Mechanism**: Standby Master receives OpLog in real-time through etcd Watch mechanism - **Ordering Guarantee**: Guarantee operation order through global sequence_id and key-level key_sequence_id ### 2. Architecture Design #### (1) Overall Architecture The overall architecture diagram shows the interaction relationships between Primary Master, etcd Cluster, and Standby Master: **Architecture Description**: - **Primary Master**: Handles client requests, records OpLog and writes to etcd - **etcd Cluster**: Acts as intermediate storage, providing strong consistency and Watch mechanism - **Standby Master**: Receives OpLog in real-time by watching etcd and applies to local metadata store #### (2) Data Flow Diagram The data flow diagram shows the complete flow from Client request to Standby synchronization: **Flow Description**: a. Client sends `PutEnd` request to Primary Master b. Primary Master records operation through `OpLogManager`, generating sequence_id c. `EtcdOpLogStore` writes OpLog to etcd d. etcd notifies Standby Master through Watch mechanism e. `OpLogWatcher` receives events and passes to `OpLogApplier` f. `OpLogApplier` checks order and applies to Standby's metadata store #### (3) Failover Sequence The failover sequence diagram shows the complete process from Primary failure to Standby promotion to Primary: **Flow Description**: a. **Normal Operation**: Primary maintains Lease, Standby continuously synchronizes OpLog through Watch b. **Primary Failure**: Primary's Lease expires, etcd notifies Standby c. **Standby Promotion**: Stop Standby service, initialize Lease, clean expired metadata, start leader election ### 3. Core Component Design #### (1) OpLogManager (Primary Side) **Responsibilities**: - Record all state change operations (PUT_END, PUT_REVOKE, REMOVE) - Generate global sequence_id and key-level key_sequence_id - Maintain memory buffer (for fast queries) **Key Methods**: ```cpp class OpLogManager { uint64_t Append(OpType type, const std::string& key, const std::string& payload = ""); std::vector GetEntriesSince(uint64_t since_seq_id, size_t limit = 1000) const; uint64_t GetLastSequenceId() const; }; ``` #### (2) EtcdOpLogStore (Primary Side) **Responsibilities**: - Write OpLog to etcd - Update latest sequence_id - Record snapshot corresponding sequence_id - Clean up old OpLog **etcd Key Design**: - OpLog Entry: `mooncake-store/oplog/{cluster_id}/{sequence_id}` - Latest Sequence ID: `mooncake-store/oplog/{cluster_id}/latest` - Snapshot Sequence ID: `mooncake-store/oplog/{cluster_id}/snapshot/{snapshot_id}/sequence_id` #### (3) OpLogWatcher (Standby Side) **Responsibilities**: - Watch etcd OpLog changes - Read historical OpLog (for initial synchronization) - Process Watch events and pass to OpLogApplier **Key Methods**: ```cpp class OpLogWatcher { void Start(); void Stop(); bool ReadOpLogSince(uint64_t start_seq_id, std::vector& entries); }; ``` #### (4) OpLogApplier (Standby Side) **Responsibilities**: - Apply OpLog Entry to local metadata store - Check global and key-level order - Handle sequence number discontinuities and out-of-order cases - Periodically clean up key_sequence_map_ (memory optimization) **Key Methods**: ```cpp class OpLogApplier { bool ApplyOpLogEntry(const OpLogEntry& entry); bool CheckSequenceOrder(const OpLogEntry& entry); void CleanupStaleKey

comments.body: ### 1. Problem & Assumptions #### 1.1 Problem After a `Delete` (or eviction) on the primary master: - The primary frees a replica’s memory (returns buffer to allocator’s free list). - The `Delete` event is **not** replicated to the standby master. - The primary then crashes; the standby is promoted to new master. - The new master still believes that this replica exists, and returns its address to clients. - That buffer may already have been **reused by another object**, or may still contain **logically deleted data**. We must **never** return data that belongs to some other key/object/tenant due to buffer reuse, even if we allow some metadata loss. #### 1.2 Accepted Semantic Constraints We explicitly accept the following semantics: - **Metadata / delete operations may be lost across failover**: - A delete acknowledged by the old master may be “rolled back” after failover. - That is acceptable because the KV cache can be recomputed. - **Hard safety requirement**: - It is strictly forbidden to read data that **belongs to another key/object/tenant** as if it were the requested key. - In other words: buffer reuse must not cause **cross-key contamination**. Under these constraints, it is acceptable that: - A key that was “deleted” on the old master may reappear after failover (logical delete rolled back). - But it is **not** acceptable to read someone else’s data due to buffer reuse. --- ### 2. Idea We upgrade each replica from a “raw pointer” into a **versioned capability**: - In-memory layout of a replica buffer becomes: - The master generates a **64-bit version** for each successful `Put` of a key. - This `version` is stored: - In `ObjectMetadata` on the master. - In the `ReplicaDescriptor` returned to clients. - In the first 8 bytes of the actual buffer in the KV store. - On **Get**, the client always verifies: - Read the first 8 bytes of the buffer. - Compare with the expected version from `ReplicaDescriptor`. - If versions match → buffer still belongs to this key/epoch → safe to read payload. - If versions differ → buffer was reused by someone else → mark this replica invalid, do not use it. Thus, even if the physical address is reused for a different object, the client will detect it and reject the replica. --- ### 3. Data Model Changes #### 3.1 Version Type ```cpp using Version = uint64_t; ``` Version can be constructed as: - High bits: timestamp (e.g., microseconds since epoch). - Low bits: per-node monotonic sequence ID. Requirements: - For a single master process, each successful `Put` for a given key gets a **unique, monotonically increasing** version. - Version collisions are practically impossible within a process lifetime. #### 3.2 Replica Descriptor Extension Extend `Replica::Descriptor` (or equivalent) to carry version information: On `PutStart`, the master generates `version`, stores it in metadata, and includes it in each replica descriptor. --- ### 4. Write Path (Put) Design #### 4.1 Master: PutStart 1. Client invokes `Put(key, slices, config)`. 2. `MasterService::PutStart(key, slice_lengths, config)`: - Validates input. - Allocates replicas as it does today (segments, buffers, etc.). - Generates a new `Version version = MakeVersion()` for this key. - Stores `version` in `ObjectMetadata` for this key. - Fills `ReplicaDescriptor.version = version` for each allocated replica. - Returns the list of descriptors to the client. All replicas of the same key for this `Put` share the same version. #### 4.2 Client: Writing to Store We enhance `TransferWrite` to enforce the following **write order** per replica: 1. Write **8-byte version header** at `buffer_address`. 2. Write **payload** at `buffer_address + 8` for length `size`. There are two implementation options: - **Option A: Two-step write** (simpler): - First,

comments.author: ykwd
comments.body:
Thanks for sharing the proposal. Unfortunately, this approach is not safe and does not actually guarantee the hard safety requirement you described, for two reasons:

First, RDMA reads and writes do not provide ordering and atomicity guarantees, which breaks the version-only validation scheme. In your design, correctness relies on the assumption that the first 8 bytes (the version) and the payload are written and observed atomically and in order. That assumption does not hold.

Second, the allocator does not guarantee alignment between successive allocations, which makes the embedded-version assumption invalid. Your scheme assumes that when a buffer is freed and later reused, the next allocation will reuse the same start address and layout, so that the version stored in the first 8 bytes corresponds exactly to the logical object boundary.

items.title: [Roadmap] SGLang dLLM Serving
items.author: rwang5203
items.body_excerpt:
# Goal

This roadmap continues #14199, initiated by @ClawSeven, and builds on the community's work toward robust, efficient block-diffusion serving and Jev-style decisions on diffusion LLMs.

Carry forward unfinished serving goals alongside newer work. Fixes for crashes and wrong results on main come before new features. Full-sequence models get baseline compatibility. Checked items record merged work. Unchecked items track remaining work or evaluation. Phases can overlap. Jev-style decisions on causal models are tracked separately, starting with #40826.

# Roadmap

### Phase 1: Shared runtime and request lifecycle

- [ ] Complete shared scheduling support.

  - [x] Dynamic batching. #14883
  - [x] Prefill/decode separation. #17484
  - [x] Algorithm-independent FDFO and early block departure. #27551
  - [ ] Refine scheduling interfaces and isolate model behavior.
  - [ ] FDFO + LowConfidence overlap scheduling. @Betelgeu #40756
  - [ ] Extend overlap to other algorithms after state-lifetime qualification.
  - [ ] Derive the default running-request count and graph capture sizes from available memory instead of serving one request at a time.

- [ ] Fail early on unsupported configurations.

  - [ ] Refuse speculative decoding, two-batch overlap, unsupported deterministic backends, and logprob requests. #43452
  - [ ] Refuse or support attention data parallelism, which crashes today.
  - [ ] Refuse or fix the FA3 attention backend, which crashes on the first request.
  - [ ] Reject sampling and grammar fields that the selected algorithm does not apply.
  - [ ] Reject unknown algorithm configuration keys instead of falling back to defaults.

- [ ] Harden request lifecycle and caching.

  - [x] Block-level radix caching. #18724
  - [x] Retain block KV and request slots. #27877
  - [x] Keep one request row across FDFO blocks. #42846
  - [ ] Qualify aborted FDFO cleanup and retained KV recovery.
  - [ ] Apply the waiting timeout to requests queued for dLLM scheduling. @lsnchow #42453
  - [ ] Bound staging admission by block size and available capacity. #32992
  - [ ] Fix the radix double count that stops an idle scheduler. #35781
  - [ ] Settle how literal mask text and caller input IDs holding the mask id are handled. #35998
  - [ ] Qualify committed streaming, EOS/stops, cancellation, and final assembly. @zxr-creator
  - [ ] Define opt-in provisional output separately from committed streaming.

### Phase 2: Prefill and CUDA graphs

- [ ] Expand attention and prefill support.

  - [ ] Round preparation and staging liveness, split from #31586.
  - [ ] Multi-block pure prefill in eager mode.
  - [ ] CUDA graphs for multi-block prefill through generic padded buckets.
  - [ ] Native block-extend attention. FlashInfer #2722
  - [ ] Block-extend attention adapter. #39739
  - [ ] Custom and block-causal masks across backends. @0z5a #39703
  - [ ] Preserve prefix-cache, prompt-tail, and literal-mask semantics. @0z5a #39592
  - [ ] Mixed prefill/decode rounds. #33196

- [ ] Extend CUDA graph coverage.

  - [x] Fixed-block CUDA graphs. #14203
  - [ ] Fit decode graph capture to memory without `--max-running-requests`. #40941
  - [ ] Piecewise prefill graphs on compatible backends.
  - [ ] Qualify variable-length prefill and graph buckets.

### Phase 3: Models, decoding, and backends

- [ ] Expand model support.

  - [x] LLaDA2.0 model family. #12588
  - [x] SDAR dense and MoE models. #19044
  - [x] DiffusionGemma text and image-input serving. #34061
  - [x] DiffusionGemma FA4 and CUDA graphs on Blackwell. #42239
  - [ ] Route `sglang serve` dLLM launches to the LLM runtime. #40942
  - [ ] Quantized DiffusionGemma checkpoints, FP8 first.
  - [ ] Radix cache and chunked prefill for DiffusionGemma.
  - [x] LLaDA2.2 block routing. #31768
  - [x] LLaDA2.2 insertion/deletion decoding. #31773
  - [ ] LLaDA2.2 routing and editing on Ascend. #32280
  - [ ] Qualify LLaDA2.2 mini and 128K context with a documented launch command.
  - [ ] Nemotron Labs Diffusion with its autoregressive, block-diffusion, and LinearSpec modes. #25803
  - [ ] Dream full-sequence baseline. #36881
  - [ ] Read block size, mask id, and default algorithm from checkpoint metadata.
  - [ ] Qualify the Fast-dLLM v2 continuation and batching support. @SensenGao #22156
  - [ ] GFusion model support. #29776
  - [ ] LLaDA-Image as a related image-generation extension. #37907

- [ ] Extend decoding support.

  - [x] Threshold-based LowConfidence decoding. #14412
  - [x] JointThreshold token editing. #18171
  - [ ] Per-request temperature, top-p, and top-k sampling with greedy defaults unless the checkpoint sets others. @Dayuxiaoshui #41242
  - [ ] Entropy-bounded sampling as a shared algorithm.
  - [ ] Decoding step maps and deterministic seeds for RL rollout. #27943

- [ ] Evaluate broader hardware and distributed serving.

  - [x] AMD Triton backend. #15560
  - [x] Ascend graph execution. #18485
  - [ ] Qualify AMD AITER coverage.
  - [ ] Qualify Ascend Triton coverage.
  - [ ] Fix the Intel XPU warmup crash in `DLLM_EXTEND`. #42627
  - [ ] Evaluate DPA support.
  - [ ] Evaluate context parallelism.
  - [ ] Evaluate pipeline parallelism.
  - [ ] Evaluate attention/FFN disaggregation.

### Phase 4: Kernels, profiling, and evaluation

- [ ] Optimize kernels and runtime overhead.

  - [x] FP8 SwapAB for eligible H20 MoE shapes. #15712
  - [ ] Profile remaining MoE shapes and backends.
  - [x] Vectorized JointThreshold with the NPU default. #21094
  - [ ] Enable the vectorized JointThreshold CUDA default. #34122
  - [ ] Adapt fused LowConfidence processing to the step interface. #18810
  - [ ] Reuse block-attention and token-selection kernels.
  - [ ] Fold the KV commit of a resolved block into the next block's first forward.

items.title: [Bug] A silent DP rank leaves /flush_cache waiting without a deadline and blocks subsequent flush calls
items.author: Adeshen
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] Searched related issues and PRs; related work and limitations are noted below.
- [ ] Reproduced on the latest version. The service observations are from the pinned v0.5.17 image; current main was inspected as source only.
- [x] Included reproduction steps and the available environment information.
- [x] Report written in English.

### Describe the bug

In the pinned v0.5.17 deployment with DP=2, suspending one scheduler rank leaves `/flush_cache` without an HTTP response until the client times out. `FanOutCommunicator.queueing_call` waits for all expected replies while holding its queueing lock, without an internal wait deadline. Subsequent calls on the **same communicator** cannot dispatch until the active call finishes.

This is a worker-failure/deadline limitation of an existing all-rank collection contract. Related PRs already discuss the trade-off; this report adds a real-service reproduction and the observed health behavior, rather than claiming the mechanism was previously unknown.

### Reproduction

Use a dedicated test service in the image below with two NPUs:

```bash
python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path /models/qwen3-0.6b --served-model-name qwen3 \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --port 30130 \
  --device npu --attention-backend ascend --trust-remote-code \
  --context-length 4096 --mem-fraction-static 0.4 \
  --dp-size 2 --tp-size 1
```

1. After readiness, confirm `POST /flush_cache`, `GET /health` and a short generation request succeed.
2. In that test container's PID namespace, identify one scheduler rank with `ps -eo pid,stat,args`. Suspend that specific scheduler PID with `kill -STOP <scheduler-pid>`; keep the other rank and HTTP/tokenizer process running.
3. Run:

```bash
curl -sS --max-time 45 -X POST \
  -w '\nHTTP_CODE=%{http_code} TIME=%{time_total}\n' \
  http://127.0.0.1:30130/flush_cache
```

4. Resume the same PID with `kill -CONT <scheduler-pid>`, and check that a new flush succeeds. For the recovery observation, another flush was started while the rank was still stopped and allowed to remain pending across SIGCONT.

### Recorded results

These are measured real-service observations, not a model of the scheduler:

| Observation | Result |
|---|---|
| Baseline flush | HTTP 200, 0.006699 s |
| One rank stopped, flush | curl exit 28, HTTP code 000, 45.000981 s |
| Health probes during the quiet stopped-rank period | 503 / 200 / 503 |
| Four health probes with paced generation traffic during the same stopped-rank window | all 200 |
| Eight paced generation requests in that window | six HTTP 200 in under 0.1 s; two client timeouts |
| Flush started while stopped and spanning recovery | HTTP 200, total request time 41.384738 s |
| New flush after recovery | HTTP 200, 0.004737 s |

The 41.38 s figure includes waiting before SIGCONT; it is **not** a post-resume recovery latency. A second real-service variant stopped both ranks and also observed a 45 s flush timeout, with health checks returning 503.

A separate CPU integration test of the real communicator and control path supplied only one reply for fan-out 2: the first call stayed pending and a second caller did not dispatch (`dispatch_count=1`). Its transport/rank replies were declared fixtures. This is the direct measurement of same-communicator head-of-line blocking; no claim is made that every other control endpoint shares that lock.

### Code path and expected behavior

The relevant structure is:

```python
async with self._queueing_lock:
    # dispatch and initialize the per-call collector
    ...
    await self._result_event.wait()
    ...
```

The event is set when the expected reply count is reached. With a missing rank, the wait itself has no deadline. **Changing the count comparison from == to >= would not fix missing replies**; fewer than the expected count satisfies neither comparison.

On 2026-10-21, main at [`573b5716f5b4`](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/573b5716f5b47c77a5fb5f2c24ae9b0e596dc3d1/python/sglang/srt/managers/communicator.py#L41-L57) still has the bare event wait inside the lock. This is source inspection, not a fresh full-service reproduction.

Expected behavior to discuss: an explicit control-call deadline and a defined worker-failure/recovery outcome, rather than relying solely on the HTTP client's timeout. Any solution needs to preserve response ownership: simply releasing the lock after timeout can allow late replies to be consumed by a later call. Partial results must not be reported as successful all-rank completion.

### Related work and limits

- #30022 explicitly acknowledged that a scheduler which never replies can keep a control slot held.
- #30606 addresses FIFO serialization.
- #42694 addresses cancellation and late-reply ownership; its description explicitly states that it does not add worker-failure recovery or a drain timeout.
- #39562 concerns aggregating flush results; #40119 and #36152 concern exposing/forwarding the scheduler-side flush timeout. These are distinct from bounding the tokenizer-side reply wait when a rank cannot respond.

SIGSTOP is deliberate fault injection. No production frequency, irreversible deadlock, or permanent whole-service failure is claimed: resuming the rank allowed progress. Other control operations, real client-disconnect cancellation, and gateway behavior were not validated by this real-service run. Healthy responses occurred in the observed traffic window, not under all possible loads.

### Environment

Historical real-service runs were performed on 2026-10-11 with:
- SGLang v0.5.17, recorded commit `29481685462732237d80d86076d6563e1f658102`.
- Image: `quay.io/ascend/sglang:v0.5.17-cann9.0.0-910b`.
- Resolved image digest: `sha256:35852210819ac0d388bce69c24960189c0412a300dc3add13234b549ba00abda`.
- Ascend 910B3; Python 3.11.15; model: Qwen3-0.6B, mounted at `/models/qwen3-0.6b`.
- Full `python3 -m sglang.check_env` output was not captured in the historical archive; the information above is from the recorded i

items.title: [Roadmap] Rust Frontend Feature Parity
items.author: BugenZhao
items.body_excerpt:
## Motivation

The Rust frontend has landed in the vLLM repository as a drop-in alternative to the Python API server process. It is enabled through `VLLM_USE_RUST_FRONTEND=1` and uses the existing vLLM engine/core boundary.

The Rust frontend is still experimental and not yet feature-complete relative to the Python frontend. This issue tracks the roadmap for the remaining gaps in feature parity and provides community contributors with a place to find scoped work.

This roadmap prioritizes user value and the Rust frontend's architectural goals over blanket 1:1 parity with the Python frontend. In particular, we may skip:

- Features / endpoints / options that are not commonly used in production
- Options that mainly reflect Python frontend implementation details or Python-side workarounds
- Features whose Python implementation has accumulated enough complexity that redesigning or removing them may be better than porting them directly

**For items marked with 🧭:** Please start with a design discussion before implementation, covering the intended API/architecture, co-design with the engine if needed, and the testing plan.

Related context:

- Original RFC: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/40846
- Integration PRs
  * https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/40848
  * https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/43283

## Current status

- [x] Rust code lives in the main vLLM repository under `rust/`
- [x] `vllm-rs` integrates with `vllm serve` as a Python-supervised frontend subprocess
- [x] Core `/v1/chat/completions` support (streaming & non-streaming)
- [x] Core `/v1/completions` support (streaming & non-streaming)
- [x] Tool calling and reasoning output support for several key model families
- [x] Commonly used OpenAI-compatible sampling options
- [x] Image, audio, and video multimodal chat inputs for registered processor/model specs
- [x] Multi-engine internal load balancing with scheduler-stat-aware routing
- [x] Admin and operational routes: health, load, version, metrics, reset-cache, sleep/wake
- [x] Mock-engine and HTTP integration-test infrastructure for Rust frontend development

## Roadmap

### Distributed serving and large-scale control plane

items.title: [RFC]: DeepSeek-V4 Performance Optimization on ROCm (Phase Two)
items.author: shen-shanshan
items.body_excerpt:
## Motivation

> Continue working on phase one: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/41820.

DeepSeek-V4 introduces CSA (Compressed Sparse Attention, `compress_ratio=4`), HCA layers, and a large MoE backbone. A side-by-side trace comparison of the vLLM decode path against vLLM-ATOM on ROCm shows that vLLM still leaves measurable performance on the table. The gaps cluster into three areas:

1. **Unfused mHC kernels.** vLLM runs `mhc_post` and `mhc_pre` as separate kernels, and `mhc_pre_big_fuse` + `add_rmsnorm_quant` as two kernels, while ATOM fuses each pair into a single kernel (`mhc_fused_post_pre` and `mhc_pre_big_fuse_rmsnorm`). Every extra kernel launch on the decode critical path costs launch latency and cache/register thrash.
2. **Serial execution where overlap is possible.** ATOM forks auxiliary HIP streams to run compressor GEMMs (CSA pre-attention), SWA KV insertion (HCA), and the MoE router/shared experts concurrently with the main stream. vLLM executes all of these serially.
3. **Slower attention support kernels.** ATOM replaces the vLLM CSA top-k selection kernels and the post-attention batched GEMMs (`torch.mm` + `manual_unroll`) with dedicated optimized kernels (e.g., `batched_gemm_bf16_kernel`).

An earlier attempt at closing gap #2 — PR #51794, which enables three-stream overlap for CSA pre-attention — is currently a draft: the overlapped region itself is faster when there is no bubble, but some ranks see a much slower tail all-reduce due to inter-rank latency jitter. The un-optimized kernels running in the parallel streams contend for hardware resources and desynchronize ranks. This suggests the correct order of work is: **replace the kernels with ATOM's optimized versions first, then enable stream overlap on top of them.**

## Proposed Change

Port the ATOM-optimized decode path into vLLM's ROCm DeepSeek-V4 implementation, using the ATOM trace as the reference for each change. The work is organized per module:

### CSA:

- [x] **Fuse mHC kernels:** merge `mhc_post` + `mhc_pre` into `mhc_fused_post_pre`, and `mhc_pre_big_fuse` + `add_rmsnorm_quant` into `mhc_pre_big_fuse_rmsnorm`. #52737 @shen-shanshan 
- [x] **Fuse SWA q/kv RMSNorm and q FP8 group quant:** #53540 @shen-shanshan 
- [x] **Fuse main-compressor and indexer-compressor projection:** https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/53838 @Fangzhou-Ai 
- [x] **Pre-attention three-stream overlap:** Before the input GEMMs, fork three HIP streams: (1) **default stream**: fused wqa+wkv GEMM → q/kv RMSNorm → wq_b → qnorm/RoPE → SWA KV insert; (2) **aux stream 0**: main-compressor wkv_gate GEMM → compress kernels (compressed KV cache write); (3) **aux stream 1**: indexer-compressor wkv_gate GEMM → K-cache write. After the join, the indexer weights GEMM, the indexer q-side (wq_b + fused q RoPE+quant), the sparse indexer op (top-k selection), and the MLA attention run serially on the main stream. Each aux stream is a self-contained chain starting from `hidden_states`, so no fine-grained cross-stream dependencies are required. **This item stays disabled (draft) until the kernels in the parallel streams are replaced with ATOM's**.
  - [ ] https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50866 @shen-shanshan 
  - [x] https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/51794 @shen-shanshan 
  - [ ] https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/54571 @shen-shanshan 
  - [x] https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/61378 @shen-shanshan 
- [x] **Support FP4 indexer:**
  - [ ] https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/56834 @LiuYinfeng01
  - [x] https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/60834 @shen-shanshan 
- [x] **Remove MQA temporary fix:** https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/55808 @shen-shanshan 
- [x] **Replace top-k kernels:** between `gluon_deepgemm_fp8_paged_mqa_logits_preshuffle` and the core `sparse_attention`, replace the vLLM top-k implementation with ATOM's fused sparse-indexer kernels. #52882 @Fangzhou-Ai 
- [x] **Support FP8 attention output projection:** https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/54894 @LiuYinfeng01 

### HCA:

- [x] **Pre-attention two-stream overlap:** for `c128a` layers (which have no indexer), run the main KV compression concurrently with SWA token insertion on an auxiliary stream. https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/56853 @shen-shanshan 

### MoE:

- [x] **Router and shared-experts dual-stream overlap:** run the router computation concurrently with the shared experts on a second stream, then join before the routed experts. https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/56098 @mawong-amd 
- [x] Enable AITER heterogeneous fused MoE:
  - [x] TP: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/53161 @Fangzhou-Ai 
  - [ ] DP: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/54134 (not needed now, prefer to use dual-stream MoE for DP) @LiuYinfeng01
- [x] Enable mega MoE: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/59685 @micah-wil 

### Others:

- [x] Prefill optimization:
  - [x] https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/54855 @jiacao-amd 
  - [x] https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57773 @shen-shanshan 
  - [x] https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/58405 @ZhengGong-amd 

## Feedback Period

_No response_

## CC List

@Fangzhou-Ai @qli88 @tjtanaa @ChuanLi1101

items.title: [RFC]: Reduce descriptor and WR overhead to improve Mooncake KV transfer bandwidth
items.author: zhou-yuhan
items.body_excerpt:
### Motivation.

## Overview

**Problem**: Mooncake approaches NIXL performance on hybrid attention model (Qwen3.5) but has substantially lower KV-transfer bandwidth (-35% to \-67%) and higher TTFT on full-attention (Qwen3).   
**Profiled bottleneck**: Measurements point to: 1\) numerous small transfer requests and RDMA work requests (WRs) incurred by a large number of transfer descriptors; 2\) serialized WRs construction and posting in Mooncake Transfer Engine (TE) implementation.  
**Solution**: We propose three optimization phases across vLLM and Mooncake TE

## Benchmark results

### Setup and metric definitions

Two nodes, each with 8 NVIDIA H20 GPUs (96 GiB each) and four RDMA HCAs; one prefill instance and one decode instance. Each run has fixed-length synthetic prompts, one output token, three warmup requests, a 300-second arrival window, and 10-second metric intervals. Connectors share the trace at each length.

Network: 200 GBps RoCE per GPU, Mooncake `transfer_engine_bench` test gives \~48 GBps per GPU

- **Qwen3-235B-A22B:** full GQA attention; 0.5 requests/s and 150 requests at every length.  
- **Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-FP8:** three GDN layers per full-attention layer; 0.5 requests/s at 1K–16K, 0.25/s at 32K, and 0.1/s at 64K–128K: 150/75/30 requests.

<details>
<summary>vLLM and router launch commands</summary>

```bash
export P_IP="<prefill-ip>" D_IP="<decode-ip>"
export MODEL="/path/to/Qwen3-235B-A22B" MAX_MODEL_LEN=40960
export CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7 WITH_NVIDIA_PEERMEM=1
export VLLM_LOG_STATS_INTERVAL=10 VLLM_LOGGING_LEVEL=INFO VLLM_LOGGING_COLOR=0
export HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 VLLM_NO_USAGE_STATS=1

# tune Mooncake:
export MC_RDMA_SIGNAL_INTERVAL=32
export MC_MAX_WR=4096

# For Qwen3.5:
# export MODEL="/path/to/Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-FP8" MAX_MODEL_LEN=139264
# export VLLM_SSM_CONV_STATE_LAYOUT=DS

# Mooncake prefill (P)
VLLM_HOST_IP="$P_IP" VLLM_MOONCAKE_BOOTSTRAP_PORT=8998 VLLM_MOONCAKE_ABORT_REQUEST_TIMEOUT=360 \
vllm serve "$MODEL" \
  --served-model-name pd-connector-bench --dtype bfloat16 \
  --tensor-parallel-size 8 --pipeline-parallel-size 1 --data-parallel-size 1 \
  --max-model-len "$MAX_MODEL_LEN" --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 \
  --block-size 16 --kv-cache-dtype auto --no-enable-prefix-caching \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8100 \
  --kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"MooncakeConnector","kv_role":"kv_producer","kv_load_failure_policy":"fail","kv_connector_extra_config":{"mooncake_protocol":"rdma","num_workers":10}}'

# Mooncake Decode (D)
VLLM_HOST_IP="$D_IP" VLLM_MOONCAKE_BOOTSTRAP_PORT=8998 VLLM_MOONCAKE_ABORT_REQUEST_TIMEOUT=360 \
vllm serve "$MODEL" \
  --served-model-name pd-connector-bench --dtype bfloat16 \
  --tensor-parallel-size 8 --pipeline-parallel-size 1 --data-parallel-size 1 \
  --max-model-len "$MAX_MODEL_LEN" --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 \
  --block-size 16 --kv-cache-dtype auto --no-enable-prefix-caching \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8200 \
  --kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"MooncakeConnector","kv_role":"kv_consumer","kv_load_failure_policy":"fail","kv_connector_extra_config":{"mooncake_protocol":"rdma","num_workers":10}}'

# Mooncake router
vllm-router --vllm-pd-disaggregation --kv-connector mooncake \
  --prefill "http://$P_IP:8100" 8998 --decode "http://$D_IP:8200" \
  --intra-node-data-parallel-size 1 --policy round_robin --disable-retries \
  --request-timeout-secs 300 --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 \
  --prometheus-host 127.0.0.1 --prometheus-port 29000

# NIXL prefill (P)
VLLM_HOST_IP="$P_IP" VLLM_NIXL_SIDE_CHANNEL_HOST="$P_IP" VLLM_NIXL_SIDE_CHANNEL_PORT=5600 \
vllm serve "$MODEL" \
  --served-model-name pd-connector-bench --dtype bfloat16 \
  --tensor-parallel-size 8 --pipeline-parallel-size 1 --data-parallel-size 1 \
  --max-model-len "$MAX_MODEL_LEN" --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 \
  --block-size 16 --kv-cache-dtype auto --no-enable-prefix-caching \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8100 \
  --kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"NixlConnector","kv_role":"kv_producer","kv_load_failure_policy":"fail","kv_connector_extra_config":{"backends":["UCX"]}}'

# NIXL decode (D)
VLLM_HOST_IP="$D_IP" VLLM_NIXL_SIDE_CHANNEL_HOST="$D_IP" VLLM_NIXL_SIDE_CHANNEL_PORT=5600 \
vllm serve "$MODEL" \
  --served-model-name pd-connector-bench --dtype bfloat16 \
  --tensor-parallel-size 8 --pipeline-parallel-size 1 --data-parallel-size 1 \
  --max-model-len "$MAX_MODEL_LEN" --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 \
  --block-size 16 --kv-cache-dtype auto --no-enable-prefix-caching \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8200 \
  --kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"NixlConnector","kv_role":"kv_consumer","kv_load_failure_policy":"fail","kv_connector_extra_config":{"backends":["UCX"]}}'

# NIXL router
vllm-router --vllm-pd-disaggregation --kv-connector nixl \
  --prefill "http://$P_IP:8100" --decode "http://$D_IP:8200" \
  --intra-node-data-parallel-size 1 --policy round_robin --disable-retries \
  --request-timeout-secs 300 --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 \
  --prometheus-host 127.0.0.1 --prometheus-port 29000
```

</details>

Tables show **means** from the full prompt-length sweeps. KV BW, Xfer time are collected from `KVConnectorStats` that both Mooncake and NIXL implements. Mooncake times `batch_transfer_sync_write()`, including TE preparation through cleanup, but excluding vLLM's `_build_transfer_params()`. NIXL bandwidth includes **prepare \+ xfer**; its xfer column excludes prepare.

### Qwen3.5: no comparable Mooncake deficit

Mooncake here is v0.3.13.post1

items.title: [Bug]: CUDA builds without FA extensions (Jetson Thor sm_110) cannot start: vllm_flash_attn raises at import time and FA is still auto-selected
items.author: potoior
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment Collected from a Jetson Thor (aarch64, sm_110) dev box; vLLM is a source checkout of `main` @ `b3b0bc3059` running against the box's Jetson-built extension set (torch 2.11.0+cu130, CUDA 13.0, driver 595.78). The failing import chain below is pure Python and does not depend on the local extension set.
The output of python collect_env.py ```text System Info OS : Ubuntu 24.04 (aarch64, Jetson Thor) Python : 3.12.3 PyTorch version : 2.11.0+cu130 CUDA used to build PyTorch : 13.0 GPU 0: NVIDIA Thor (compute capability 11.0 / sm_110) vLLM: main @ b3b0bc3059 (source checkout) ```
### 🐛 Describe the bug Any CUDA build that does not ship the compiled flash-attention extensions (`_vllm_fa2_C` / `_vllm_fa3_C`) cannot start an engine on current `main`, because `vllm.vllm_flash_attn` raises at module import time and the import is unconditional on the CUDA platform. Jetson Thor (sm_110) is such a platform: neither the local Jetson build of vLLM nor NVIDIA's own `ghcr.io/nvidia-ai-iot/vllm:r38.2` container image contains an FA extension (the image ships only `_C`, `_C_stable_libtorch`, `cumem_allocator`, `_moe_C`), and sm_110 has no FA2/FA3 kernels. **1. Import-time hard failure.** `LLM(...)` / `AsyncLLM.from_engine_args` dies during `ModelConfig` construction (and any direct import of the model modules) via: ```text vllm/model_executor/models/.py → vllm/model_executor/layers/attention/__init__.py → vllm/model_executor/layers/attention/mm_encoder_attention.py:33 → vllm/v1/attention/backends/fa_utils.py:24 # unconditional on is_cuda() → vllm/vllm_flash_attn/__init__.py:34 ImportError: vllm.vllm_flash_attn requires the CUDA flash attention extensions (_vllm_fa2_C or _vllm_fa3_C). On ROCm, use upstream flash_attn. ``` The raise was introduced with the FA4 integration (#32974), so this looks deliberate for wheels that always bundle FA — but it turns "no FA on this GPU" into "vLLM cannot even be imported/started", even when a non-FA attention backend would work fine. **2. Auto-selection still picks FA when the raise is removed.** With the `raise ImportError(...)` locally replaced by a no-op (nothing else changed), engine startup then fails inside the selected FA backend instead: ```text (EngineCore) AssertionError: FlashAttention version not detected. # flash_attn.py:1216 ``` i.e. on a CUDA platform without FA extensions the backend still resolves to FlashAttention despite `FA2_AVAILABLE`/`FA3_AVAILABLE` being `False`, rather than falling through to the next backend. **3. Everything else works.** With the raise removed and `--attention-backend TRITON_ATTN` passed (no other local changes), the same checkout runs correctly on the Jetson Thor GPU: ```text LLM(model="facebook/opt-125m", enforce_eager=True, attention_backend="TRITON_ATTN") generate(["Hello, my name is"], temperature=0) → " J.C. and I am a" LLM(model="Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B", enforce_eager=True, attention_backend="TRITON_ATTN") → works pytest tests/v1/e2e/general/test_streaming_input.py → 16 passed # GPU e2e suite ``` So the gap is confined to (a) the unconditional import and (b) backend selection not consulting FA availability on this platform. ### Expected behavior One of, maintainer's choice — this issue is to ask which direction is wanted before proposing a change: 1. Graceful degradation: `vllm_flash_attn` imports without the extensions (unavailable, like any other optional op), and CUDA backend selection skips FA backends whose version is unsupported/unavailable, falling through to FlashInfer/Triton. Jetson-style CUDA platforms then work out of the box with a non-FA backend. 2. Fail-fast kept, but earlier and clearer: an actionable platform-level error ("this build has no FA extension and GPU sm_110 cannot run FlashAttention; pass --attention-backend TRITON_ATTN") instead of an import-time `ImportError` from deep inside the model registry. 3. Out of scope: Jetson is served by NVIDIA's stack and upstream wheels always bundle FA — then this issue at least documents the behavior for anyone building `main` on such platforms. If (1) or (2) is wanted I'm happy to open a PR; I can validate end-to-end on the sm_110 box (the only one I have), and unit-test the selection logic for FA-less CUDA configurations. ### Additional context - Verified against `main` @ `b3b0bc3059`; the import chain and the raise are unchanged there. - NVIDIA's Jetson r38.2 vLLM image (vLLM 0.19-based) works on this hardware and ships no FA extension, so current `main` is effectively a regression for this platform class relative to the Jetson-supported stack. - The same two symptoms would apply to any other CUDA environment where the FA extension is absent (e.g. custom/trimmed builds), not only Jetson. AI assistance (opencode) was used while investigating and drafting this report; the reproductions above were run by me on the Jetson Thor box.

items.title: KV-Cache Persistence Issue with SSD Offloading
items.author: LiuQW519
items.body_excerpt:
**Description:**  
follow the SSD offload guide in :

> https://docs.lmcache.ai/kv_cache/local_storage.html

experimentation with vLLM  and LMCache, we observed that the KV-Cache offloading to SSD works partially but lacks persistence across server restarts.  

**Steps to Reproduce:**  
1. Configure vLLM server with SSD offloading for KV-Cache  
2. Run inference scripts with a specific prompt 
3. Observe 2.4GB `.pt` file generated in the SSD cache directory  
4. Restart the vLLM server process  
5. Query the same prompt again  
6. the kv-cache regenerated in SSD

**Expected Behavior:**  
The existing KV-Cache files should be reused, avoiding redundant computation and disk I/O.  

**Actual Behavior:**  
New identical KV-Cache files are regenerated instead of reusing the existing ones

This optimization would significantly improve latency for recurring queries in production scenarios. I would appreciate guidance on recommended methods to achieve proper KV-Cache persistence across server restarts in this workflow.

comments.author: YaoJiayi
comments.body: Hey, feel free to create a PR on this! It shouldn't be hard. We can store the metadata on disk upon program exit and load it back during the next startup

comments.author: fourierr
comments.body: I'd like to work on this issue.

comments.author: ziruiliu
comments.body:
Which version of vllm and lmcache are you using? Can you show us sample of file names that regenerated time of time?

Latest lmcache has changed data type of hash from str to int and use seed from vllm's NONE_HASH. Such change results in the change of filename in local disk.
If PYTHONHASHSEED is not set, vllm's NONE_HASH changes every time.
see vllm's code
```
def init_none_hash(hash_fn: Callable):
    global NONE_HASH

    hash_seed = os.getenv("PYTHONHASHSEED")
    if hash_seed is None and hash_fn is sha256_cbor_64bit:
        logger.warning(
            "PYTHONHASHSEED is not set. This will lead to non-reproducible "
            "block-hashes when using sha256_cbor_64bit as the hash function."
            "Consider setting PYTHONHASHSEED to a fixed value for "
            "reproducibility.")

    NONE_HASH = (int.from_bytes(os.urandom(32), byteorder="big")
                 if hash_seed is None else hash_fn(hash_seed))
```

You can try to set PYTHONHASHSEED to a fixed value to see if file names are different once you restart vllm and re-query

comments.author: ziruiliu

items.title: [Bug] fs L2 adapter: every store fails at os.open() in _write_with_odirect when use_odirect=true
items.author: h1manshu23
items.body_excerpt:
**Describe the bug**
With the `fs` L2 adapter and `use_odirect: true`, **every** chunk store fails. `FSL2Adapter._write_with_odirect` raises at the `os.open()` call, and each store is logged as failed:

```
[2026-07-31 12:39:27,361] LMCache ERROR: FSL2Adapter failed to store
/mnt/nvme0/-SEP-data-medium-SEP-text-generation-models-SEP-gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-FP8-dynamic-SEP-@0x01000100@1@246ba704d24a7690450504e0a607656c195b4e247501896d103d7d293f9b63dc.data
(fs_l2_adapter.py:629:lmcache.v1.distributed.l2_adapters.fs_l2_adapter)
```

Nothing is ever persisted to L2, so the disk tier is effectively dead while the server continues running and reporting no fatal error.

**This is not an unsupported-storage case.** `base_path=/mnt/nvme0` is a real block-backed filesystem on a 4-device NVMe RAID0 array:

```
md0 : active raid0 nvme3n2[3] nvme2n2[2] nvme1n2[1] nvme4n2[0]
```

Two distinct problems here:

1. **The failure itself.** O_DIRECT should be usable on this mount. Whatever LMCache passes to `os.open()` — flag combination, mode, or path — is being rejected on a filesystem/device stack that otherwise accepts direct I/O.
2. **The failure is undiagnosable and unrecoverable.** The log line prints the target path but not the underlying `OSError`/errno, so there's no way to tell EINVAL from EACCES from ENOENT without reading LMCache's source. And there is no fallback: rather than degrading to buffered I/O or refusing at startup, the adapter fails silently-but-endlessly, once per chunk, for the lifetime of the server.

Note the failure is at **`os.open()`**, not at the write — so this is not an O_DIRECT buffer/offset/length alignment issue, which would surface later in `_write_with_odirect`.

**To Reproduce**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. `base_path` sits on a 4× NVMe md RAID0 (512k chunk) mounted at `/mnt/nvme0`.

2. Start the LMCache server with the `fs` L2 adapter and O_DIRECT enabled:

```bash
lmcache server --host localhost --port 9000 \
  --l1-size-gb 128 --eviction-policy LRU --chunk-size 256 \
  --l2-adapter '{"type": "fs", "base_path": "/mnt/nvme0", "use_odirect": true, "num_workers": 32}' \
  --http-port 8081
```

3. Start vLLM against it on a single GPU:

```bash
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 vllm serve /path/to/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-FP8-dynamic/ \
  --port 9001 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.95 \
  --enable-prefix-caching --enable-chunked-prefill \
  --max-model-len 16384 \
  --kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"LMCacheMPConnector","kv_role":"kv_both","kv_connector_extra_config":{"lmcache.mp.host":"tcp://localhost","lmcache.mp.port":9000}}' \
  --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 --max-num-seqs 12
```

4. Send any request. Every L2 store fails with the traceback below; `/mnt/nvme0` stays empty.

**Expected behavior**

On a direct-I/O-capable filesystem like this one, stores should succeed with `use_odirect: true` — that's the whole point of running the cache on NVMe RAID0.

Failing that, LMCache should:
- include the underlying errno / `OSError` message in the `failed to store` log line, and
- probe `O_DIRECT` support on `base_path` **once at startup**, then either fail fast with an actionable message or fall back to buffered I/O — instead of raising per-chunk for the lifetime of the process.

**Screenshots**
If applicable, add screenshots to help explain your problem.
```
[2026-08-02 14:09:16,887] LMCache ERROR: FSL2Adapter failed to store /mnt/nvme0/-SEP-data-medium-SEP-text-generation-models-SEP-gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-FP8-dynamic-SEP-@0x01000100@1@2fd0d18a24695cedc65b54957836c1ddcde16bfbe2208c8c8425e4fec9c93441.data (fs_l2_adapter.py:629:lmcache.v1.distributed.l2_adapters.fs_l2_adapter)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/miphi/vllm_lib/lib/python3.10/site-packages/lmcache/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/fs_l2_adapter.py", line 611, in _execute_store
    await self._loop.run_in_executor(
  File "/usr/lib/python3.10/concurrent/futures/thread.py", line 58, in run
    result = self.fn(*self.args, **self.kwargs)
  File "/home/miphi/vllm_lib/lib/python3.10/site-packages/lmcache/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/fs_l2_adapter.py", line 563, in _write_with_odirect
    os.write(fd, buf)
OSError: [Errno 22] Invalid argument
[2026-08-02 14:09:16,888] LMCache ERROR: Failed to O_DIRECT write /mnt/nvme0/-SEP-data-medium-SEP-text-generation-models-SEP-gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-FP8-dynamic-SEP-@0x01000100@1@677b099d2ff7f7e2dfbc81af4814264cbe36de448429655a96659cca176790a0.tmp (fs_l2_adapter.py:565:lmcache.v1.distributed.l2_adapters.fs_l2_adapter)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/miphi/vllm_lib/lib/python3.10/site-packages/lmcache/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/fs_l2_adapter.py", line 563, in _write_with_odirect
    os.write(fd, buf)
OSError: [Errno 22] Invalid argument
```

**Environment**
 - OS: Ubuntu 22.04 (Linux x86_64), Python 3.10
 - LMCache version: 0.5.2
 - vLLM version: 0.24.0
 - GPU: 1× SM 8.6 (compute capability 8.6), no tensor parallelism
 - Model: Gemma 4 26B-A4B-it, FP8-dynamic
 - L2 backend: `fs` adapter, `base_path=/mnt/nvme0`, `use_odirect=true`, `num_workers=32`
 - Storage: 4× NVMe in md RAID0 (`md0`, 512k chunks, 4000288768 blocks), mounted at `/mnt/nvme0`
 - Filesystem:
 ```
 Filesystem     Type  1K-blocks  Used  Available Use% Mounted on
/dev/md0       ext4 3936358896    28 3736328048   1% /mnt/nvme0
```

items.title: Restart-proof KV cache for llama-server: 40K-token TTFT 155s to 6s after reboot
items.author: qqkzlm
items.body_excerpt:
Every restart wipes your prefill. Server crash, box reboot, model reload — a 40K-token agentic prompt pays the full ~155s prefill again before the first token.

I patched llama-server to persist KV-cache prefix checkpoints to disk and auto-restore the longest matching prefix on boot. Same prompt after a restart: **first token in ~6s instead of ~155s** (2.1s disk read once + decode). No client changes, no re-architecture — the server just remembers.

Measured on GTX 1080 8GB, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, `-c 92160`:

- Cold: 151s prefill → first token at ~155s
- Warm (post-restart): 2.1s disk read (first request only) → first token at ~6s
- Checkpoints keyed by model + ctx + KV quant (wrong config = ignored, never corrupted); disk-budget eviction included

Single-commit patch (86KB): https://github.com/qqkzlm/llama-cpp-prompt-disk-cache — `git am` onto the PrismML `prism` branch, four flags (`--slot-save-path`, `--checkpoint-min-step`, `--ctx-checkpoints`, `--prompt-cache-disk-budget`).

One MoE lesson from the same box: keep experts on GPU, let KV follow the layers — pushing 20 MoE layers to CPU collapsed prefill 265→30 tok/s, which no cache can fix.

Happy to upstream behind a flag if maintainers are interested.

comments.author: qqkzlm
comments.body:
Update to the README since this went up — three things worth calling out for anyone trying it:

**1. Prebuilt CUDA binaries exist for both platforms.** The `v0.2.3` release ships `llama-server-win-cuda-v0.2.3.zip` and `llama-server-linux-cuda-v0.2.3.tar.gz`. The Linux package is built for `sm_61`/Pascal, so it also runs on GTX 10-series. No build needed:

```bash
./llama-server -m model.gguf -c 32768 --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 \
  --slot-save-path /var/tmp/kvstore/model \
  --prompt-cache-disk-budget 20 --checkpoint-min-step 2048 --ctx-checkpoints 64
```

**2. Only one flag is actually required.** `--slot-save-path` is the only one you must pass — `--prompt-cache-disk-budget` and `--prompt-cache-disk-path` are silently ignored without it, and entries land in `<slot-save-path>/pdcache`. `--prompt-cache-disk` is **enabled by default**, so passing it is optional; use `--no-prompt-cache-disk` to turn the cache off.

**3. Cache hits require a byte-identical prompt prefix.** Only the common prefix from token 0 onward is reused. If you prepend a timestamp or a random ID, everything after it misses and the cache is effectively unused. Put stable content first (system prompt, tool definitions, long docs) and per-turn content last — opencode / Claude Code already do this, so it works out of the box.

The README now has a "when does the cache hit / when does it miss" section covering this, a flag-duty table, and a Chinese-first three-step guide (the repo README is now Chinese-primary). A Windows `start-llama-server.bat` is included in the zip if you want a prompt-driven launcher instead of a command line.

Still happy to upstream this behind a flag if maintainers are interested — the whole feature is one commit touching `tools/server/server-prompt-disk.cpp` (~900 lines) plus slot/task integration.

items.author: farouk09
items.body_excerpt:
Hi everyone! 👋

I'm trying to run the model Qwen/Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct-1M on an NVIDIA RTX A6000 (49.1 GB VRAM) using vllm serve with the --dtype auto option. However, I'm getting the following error:

_`ValueError: The model's max seq len (1010000) is larger than the maximum number of tokens that can be stored in KV cache (73792). Try increasing `gpu_memory_utilization` or decreasing `max_model_len` when initializing the engine.`_

From my understanding:

- The model has ~14B parameters, so in FP16 it should use ~28GB of VRAM (please correct me if that’s inaccurate).
- Running in auto mode (which defaults to FP16), the weights should take ~14GB.
- That leaves ~36GB, which I thought would be enough for the KV cache for a 1M context length. But apparently not?

So I have two questions:

1. Is my assumption about the memory breakdown (weights vs KV cache) correct?
2. How can we estimate the required VRAM for a given number of context tokens? Is there a formula or rule of thumb to calculate the KV cache size needed based on context length and model size?

More broadly, I'd really appreciate if someone could explain how to estimate the total VRAM usage in `vllm serve`, including weights, KV cache, context window, etc.

Thanks in advance!

items.author: hzh0425

## 1. Agentic Cache Scheduling

- Supernode-wide KV Cache Sharing @hzh0425  @Shunkangz @zhengd-nv 
	- Enable sharing of GPU-resident (L1) and host-resident (L2) KV caches across engines within the same super-node domain.
	- Add cache location awareness to the Router to coordinate request placement and KV transfers based on cache availability and engine load.
	- Extend HiCache linker integration to support GPU-to-GPU KV transfers over (NVLink @Shunkangz、AMD UALoE @TianDi101、SAIL's card-to-card interconnect @Vinsmoke86) and remote Grace DRAM access through EGM.
