items.title: [Performance discussion] When do larger CUDA graph capture sizes help?
items.author: tomasruizt
items.body_excerpt:
The Qwen-3.8-Flash-Next [recipe (B300)](https://recipes.vllm.ai/Qwen/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next?hardware=b300) leaves CUDA graph capture sizes at their defaults (1,024-tokens). This results in prefill/mixed steps running eagerly, which is super slow due to the GDN host overhead. Adding a couple CUDA graph capture sizes improves throughput/latency significantly.
Workload and configuration details - We used 4×B300, `Qwen/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP8` and vLLM `58b3298457` (2026-10-02). We followed the recipe, with MTP3 and prefix caching enabled. - We benchmarked with AIPerf 0.13 and SPEED-Bench throughput_1K. We allowed natural EOS, capped output at 1,024 tokens, disabled thinking and used temperature 0 and shuffle seed 42. - We started each variant three times. We ran each concurrency three times after the first startup and once after each additional startup, giving five measurements per point. Each run submitted requests for 30 s (60 s at c256), then allowed up to 120 s for outstanding requests to finish. We reset the prefix cache before each run. - All 90 runs passed, with 32,457 completed requests and no errors or preemptions. - Only the capture grid changes. Up to 2K adds `1280,1536,1792,2048` to the default list. Up to 4K additionally adds `2560,3072,3584,4096`.

Each dot shows one run. The lines connect the averages. The orange line collapses to the "Default" performance at c256 because the mixed batches runs mostly in eager mode (see c256 below). Across all five measurements per point, Up to 4K improves average throughput by 96.8% at c128 and 52.3% at c256 compared with Default.

Bar chart details * A pure decode batch can contain up to `4 × concurrency` query tokens with MTP3. Batches above that size must contain prefill work. The chart shows what percentage of these prefill/mixed batches use CUDA graphs. * Each bar shows the average coverage across five runs. The error bars show the minimum and maximum coverage across those runs. We include when the batch is filling up or draining. Piecewise graphs still run some operations eagerly. * Default never uses CUDA graph at c256. A single 1,080-token prefill alongside 255 decode requests already gives us `1080 + 255 × 4 = 2100` query tokens. That is why the 2K limit is too small here.
### Trade-off Up to 4K uses an extra 1.19 GiB/GPU for CUDA graphs. | Variant | CUDA graph mem | KV cache mem | Token capacity | Graph capture time | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:| | Default | 2.85 GiB/GPU | 198.14 GiB/GPU | 26.64M tokens | 35–38 s | | Up to 2K | 2.68 GiB/GPU (−6.0%) | 198.45 GiB/GPU (+0.2%) | 26.68M tokens (+0.2%) | 36–37 s | | Up to 4K | 4.04 GiB/GPU (+41.8%) | 197.32 GiB/GPU (−0.4%) | 26.53M tokens (−0.4%) | 38–39 s | The memory figures were identical at the reported precision across all three startups per variant, even after switching GPU groups. Up to 2K consistently used less CUDA graph mem and had more KV capacity than Default. This is reproducible in this setup, but we still need to investigate why. Graph capture times are shown as ranges across the three startups. This looks like a very positive trade-off. We get a lot higher performance, while losing only little KV-capacity, and spending a few extra seconds on graph capture with Up to 4K. ## GLM 5.3 Flash | Metric | Concurrency | Default | Up to 4K | Change | |---|---|---:|---:|---:| | Throughput | 64 | 3,326 tok/s | 5,147 tok/s | +54.8% | | Throughput | 128 | 4,963 tok/s | 7,046 tok/s | +42.0% | | TPOT | 64 | 13.89 ms | 10.72 ms | −22.8% | | TPOT | 128 | 16.25 ms | 13.95 ms | −14.2% | The improvements are great, but there are some drawbacks measured below (4×B300 TP4). Nevertheless the overall trade-off is very positive.
Trade-offs | Metric | Default | Up to 4K | Change | Change (%) | |---|---:|---:|---|---:| | CUDA graph mem | 6.23 GiB/GPU | 12.88 GiB/GPU | +6.65 GiB/GPU | +106.7% | | KV cache mem | 152.10 GiB/GPU | 141.41 GiB/GPU | -10.69 GiB/GPU | -7.0% | | Token capacity | 23.63M tokens | 21.97M tokens | -1.66M tokens | -7.0% | | Graph capture time | 38 s | 43 s | +5 s | +13.2% | | Total startup time | 403 s | 393 s | -10 s (probably noise) | -2.5% |
## Root Cause The cause is a discontinuity in runtime when running batches in/out of CUDA graphs. This was documented in August in the [vLLM Blog on adaptive verification](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-08-14-dspark-adaptive-verification) (see below), where the authors used `max_cudagraph_capture_size=4096`. The default caputure-limit of 1024 is surpassed already for 128 requests with 8 speculative tokens plus 1 bonus token (9*128=1152). And mixed prefill/decode batches fall out of the range quickly and run eagerly, even for `FULL_AND_PIECEWISE` execution. These mixed batches have very high host overhead in GDN MoE models, so they tank performance when running eagerly.

items.title: [Installation]: [ROCm] Gemma4 multimodal model fails to start on vLLM 0.32.0 due to excessive video encoder memory reservation (negative KV cache)
items.author: ntkylin
items.body_excerpt:
### My current environment

```text
Hi bro,

**Title:**  
`

[vllm-gemma4.txt](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/33754857/vllm-gemma4.txt)

`

**Description:**

After upgrading from vLLM 0.28.x to **0.32.0+rocm723** on Ubuntu 24.04 with ROCm 7.2.x and 4× AMD Instinct MI210 (64 GB each), the Gemma4-31B multimodal model (`Gemma4ForConditionalGeneration`) fails to initialize.

### Environment
- **vLLM**: 0.32.0+rocm723
- **PyTorch**: 2.13.0+git733fca1 (HIP 7.2.53211)
- **Transformers**: 5.19.0
- **GPUs**: 4× MI210 (TP=4), Fabric Link
- **Model**: `/data2/models/gemma-4-31b-it` (Gemma4-31B-IT, multimodal)
- **ROCm**: 7.2.3

### Symptoms
1. **Early failure (higher `max-model-len`)**: OOM during multi-modal warmup in `_process_video_input` → `vt.encoder`, even though PyTorch only reports ~16.6 GiB allocated and GPU shows 0 free.
2. **Later failure (lower settings)**: After reducing `max-model-len` to 8192 and `gpu-memory-utilization` to 0.5–0.7, the engine gets further but reports **negative available KV cache memory** (e.g. `-15.55 GiB` or `-7.43 GiB`) and raises:
   ```
   ValueError: No available memory for the cache blocks. Try increasing `gpu_memory_utilization`
   ```
3. Model weights themselves only consume ~15.8 GiB per GPU under TP=4.

### Root Cause Observation
The issue appears related to the **video encoder cache reservation** during profiling. Logs show:
```
Encoder cache will be initialized with a budget of 2496 tokens, and profiled with 1 video items of the maximum feature size.
```
This reservation is large enough to push available KV cache into negative territory under normal utilization settings.

### Workaround
Adding the following flag allows the engine to start successfully:
```bash
--limit-mm-per-prompt '{"video":0}'
```
With this flag, available KV cache becomes positive (~1.36 GiB under the test config) and the server starts.

### Steps to Reproduce
```bash
export CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1,2,3,4
vllm serve /path/to/gemma-4-31b-it \
  --tensor-parallel-size 4 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.7 \
  --max-model-len 8192 \
  --dtype bfloat16
```
(Fails with negative KV cache or OOM during video encoder warmup.)

Adding `--limit-mm-per-prompt '{"video":0}'` succeeds.

### Expected Behavior
The model should start with reasonable `gpu-memory-utilization` (e.g. 0.7) and a moderate `max-model-len` without requiring video input to be completely disabled, as it did on previous vLLM versions.

### Additional Notes
- No other processes were using the GPUs during testing.
- `PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True` was set.
- The same configuration worked on the previous vLLM version (0.28.x).
- Speculative decoding (MTP) was not required to trigger the issue.

---

You can paste this directly into a GitHub issue. Adjust the model path or add any extra logs if needed.

The output of `python collect_env.py`
```


### How you are installing vllm

```sh
uv pip install vllm --extra-index-url https://wheels.vllm.ai/rocm/0.32.0/rocm723 --upgrade
```


### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: [L2][fs_native] Failed stores stay visible to lookups — later retrieves serve corrupted KV (gibberish output)
items.author: stefanskiasan
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

With the `fs_native` L2 adapter enabled, `Store task N to adapter 0 failed for
keys: [...]` warnings appear at a low but steady rate — and **every subsequent
retrieve that hits one of those keys returns corrupted KV**. The model answer
degenerates into gibberish, at temperature 0, reproducibly.

The failed store leaves the key visible to lookups. It is only a `WARNING`; no
exception is raised, and the key is not invalidated.

## Environment

- 8× MI355X (gfx950), ROCm 7.2.3, one server per 4-GPU replica
- vLLM with `glm_moe_dsa` (GLM-5.3, full model), TP4, MTP k=4,
  `--kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3`, `--block-size 16`, prefix caching on
- `LMCacheMPConnector`, `lmcache_driven` transfer mode, chunk-size 256
- Server: `--l1-size-gb 150 --separate-object-groups --eviction-policy LRU`
  `--l2-prefetch-policy retain`
  `--l2-adapter '{"type":"fs_native","base_path":"/l2","num_workers":8,"use_odirect":false}'`

## Reproduction

Two replicas, identical except for the L2 adapter:

| | replica A | replica B |
|---|---|---|
| `--l2-adapter fs_native` | yes | **no** |
| failed stores | 44 → 66 during eight requests | **0** in 25 049 stores |
| answers on a cache hit | **gibberish** | correct |

The cleanest probe is `cache_salt`, which changes only the cache key:

```
prompt without salt   (cache hit)   3.4 s   GARBAGE  '0.  district120 is0, the ...'
same prompt, new salt (cache miss)  5.0 s   CORRECT  '73605 The user has provided ...'
same prompt, new salt (cache miss)  5.0 s   CORRECT
prompt without salt   (cache hit)   3.4 s   GARBAGE  '1 district contains1.3,. ...'
```

Note the timing: the corrupted runs are **faster** than the correct ones —
they are served from the cache instead of being computed.

The corruption survives a full vLLM restart (the cache server outlives it) and
survives restarting the cache server itself, because new failures keep
occurring: 22 fresh failures during the eight requests above.

## Not the cause

- Disk: write test 4.9 GB/s into the L2 directory, inodes at 1 %, 459 GB free,
  ext4, no errors in the log and no traceback anywhere.
- vLLM side: with LMCache disabled entirely (prefix caching still on), all
  eight requests are correct.
- Recreating the same server **without** `--l2-adapter` makes the problem
  disappear completely: 0 failed stores, 8/8 correct, needle test 5/5 twice
  (the second run with a warm cache).

## Expected

A store that fails must not leave a lookup-visible key. Either the key is
rolled back on failure, or the retrieve path must validate that all object
groups for a key are actually present before serving it. Silently serving a
partially stored entry turns an I/O warning into a correctness bug that looks
like model failure — it cost us two and a half hours of debugging the model
before we suspected the cache.

Related: #4987 (IPC event churn on ROCm in the same connector).

items.title: [Bug] P2P load timeout can report terminal failure while the transfer is still active
items.author: 0andy
items.body_excerpt:
**Describe the bug**

`P2PL2Adapter.query_load_result()` returns a terminal all-zero `Bitmap` as soon as `load_timeout_s` expires, without querying or cancelling the underlying `TransferChannelClient` read ([p2p_l2_adapter.py#L333-L336](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/p2p_l2_adapter.py#L333-L336)). The read may still be in flight at that point, so the adapter reports "finished (failed)" for a load whose transfer has not reached a terminal state.

The existing test `test_load_deadline_expired_yields_failure` asserts exactly this behaviour, so I am raising it as a contract question rather than a regression: is a terminal load result allowed to precede the end of the transfer?

**To Reproduce**

On `dev` @ 8d7d2c47, add this test to `tests/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/test_p2p_l2_adapter.py`:

```python
def test_load_deadline_does_not_report_terminal_while_read_is_in_flight():
    keys = [_key(0)]
    now = [100.0]
    in_flight = TransferChannelReadResult(finished=False)
    with (
        _adapter(load_timeout_s=0.01) as (adapter, _mq, _tc_ctx, tc_client, _n),
        patch.object(p2p_mod.time, "monotonic", side_effect=lambda: now[0]),
    ):
        adapter._remote_addresses[keys[0]] = TransferChannelAddress(offset=100, size=10)
        tc_client.submit_read.return_value = 123
        tc_client.query_read_status.return_value = in_flight
        task_id = adapter.submit_load_task(
            keys, [MagicMock(shm_offset=0, shm_byte_length=10)]
        )
        now[0] = 100.02  # past the 0.01 s load deadline
        assert not in_flight.is_finished()
        assert adapter.query_load_result(task_id) is None
```

```
pytest -v tests/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/test_p2p_l2_adapter.py -k "deadline or not_finished"
```

Result (CPU-only build, transfer channel mocked):

```
>           assert adapter.query_load_result(task_id) is None
E           assert 0 is None
E            +  where 0 = query_load_result(0)

LMCache WARNING: P2P load task 0 timed out; treating as a failure (p2p_l2_adapter.py:335)

test_lookup_deadline_expired_yields_miss PASSED
test_load_not_finished_returns_none PASSED
test_load_deadline_expired_yields_failure PASSED
test_load_deadline_does_not_report_terminal_while_read_is_in_flight FAILED
1 failed, 3 passed
```

(`0` is the repr of a one-key, all-zero `Bitmap`, i.e. a terminal failure.)

This test only demonstrates the current behaviour; its assertion would need adjusting depending on which direction below is preferred.

**Expected behavior**

Either the adapter does not report a terminal load result while its transfer-channel read may still access the destination buffers, or the contract states explicitly that a terminal result does not imply the transfer has quiesced and callers handle that.

**Additional context**

To be clear about what is and is not shown:

*Reproduced (unit test above):* the read is modelled as unfinished, and after the deadline `query_load_result()` returns a terminal failure.

*Derived from reading the code, not reproduced:*
- On that result, `PrefetchController._poll_load_results()` calls `finish_write_and_delete()` for the failed keys and then `submit_unlock()` ([prefetch_controller.py#L1389-L1395](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/storage_controllers/prefetch_controller.py#L1389-L1395)); for P2P, `submit_unlock()` sends `p2p_unlock_objects` to the peer ([#L277-L280](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/p2p_l2_adapter.py#L277-L280)). So both the destination staging buffer and the source-side lock are released.
- The NIXL transfer channel registers the whole L1 buffer once ([nixl_impl.py#L344](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/transfer_channel/impl/nixl_impl.py#L344)). This creates a window in which a late read may write into memory that has since been reassigned to another key.
- After the timeout the adapter no longer queries the read, so the `NixlTransferChannelClient._tasks` entry and its xfer handle are only released on `close()` ([#L178-L181](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/transfer_channel/impl/nixl_impl.py#L178-L181), [#L202-L206](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/transfer_channel/impl/nixl_impl.py#L202-L206)).

*Not reproduced:* actual stale or corrupted KV data end to end. I have not run a two-instance NIXL test for this.

**Possible directions** (not proposing a specific fix yet)

- **A. Stay pending until the transfer is terminal.** After the deadline, keep polling `query_read_status()` and only report once it finishes. Simple ownership model; a hung transfer would hold its buffers and locks indefinitely.
- **B. Add per-task cancellation to `TransferChannelClient`** ([abstract.py#L52-L88](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/transfer_channel/abstract.py#L52-L88) has only `submit_read`, `query_read_status`, `close`), and report terminal only once the cancel is confirmed. For NIXL this would map to `releaseXferReq`, which the BackendGuide says "can return error, meaning it was not successful in aborting the request", so it still needs A as a fallback. The Mooncake wrapper has no cancel today; I have not checked the engine itself.
- **C. Drop the adapter-level load deadline** and rely on the controller-level deadline from #5255, which already keeps late loads' buffers and locks until the load result arrives.

The P2P adapter is the runtime caller of `submit_read()`; the transfer-channel benchmark also calls it directly, so an API change in B would touch both.

**Related**

- #5263 — same ownership family, on the shutdown / TTL paths rat
items.author_work_intent: If maintainers agree this is a contract gap, I'm happy to work on the fix. I'd especially appreciate guidance on whether the preferred direction is to keep timed-out reads pending until terminal, add a TransferChannel cancell

comments.author: holtwood
comments.body:
I checked another timeout case at [`1ca53a8`](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/1ca53a8aadca1d054f171fd67350be35797cfddc/lmcache/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/p2p_l2_adapter.py#L326-L347) using the original query methods with mocked dependencies. I haven't run a real NIXL transfer.

Even when the transfer is already marked `DONE`, polling after the deadline returns a zero bitmap without calling `query_read_status`. The adapter removes its task, so later adapter polls return `None`. The client's `close()` still has a separate cleanup path.

This seems worth covering in the timeout tests, including cleanup of an already-completed transfer. I can help add that case if it's useful.

items.title: [MP] Qualify bounded profiling and a cost-aware local L2 admission example
items.author: realAaronWu
items.body_excerpt:
Parent: #5780
Dependency: external selector loading child (to be linked).

## Scope

Port only the useful bounded statistics from prior profiling work to current MP events, then provide an external StorePolicy example for DRAM L1 plus local filesystem L2. Keep L1 copies and existing eviction. Reuse canonical ObjectKey; distinguish heuristic reuse score, inter-access distance and true distinct-key reuse distance.

## Experiment

Pin Mooncake FAST25 conversation/toolagent traces and content hashes. Replay historical-only candidate policies against default/LRU/no-offload and a clearly labelled offline upper bound. Freeze capacity, timing/availability and prefix-dependency assumptions. Anonymous hashes are not real tokens: any generated token serving workload must be labelled synthetic.

## Acceptance

- Stats, queues and snapshots remain within declared bounds; no graph or unbounded per-request state is required.
- Actual StoreController submission and fs round-trip demonstrate admission behavior, while L1 copies remain usable.
- Single-GPU data correctness and optional full serving/goodput results are distinguished.

- Default behavior stays unchanged. Model/revision/dtype/layout are fixed and isolated by deployment for this first experiment.

items.title: [Bug] MP connector prometheus metrics crash vLLM startup under Ray Serve: histogram built without buckets
items.author: n-grieger
items.body_excerpt:
The Prometheus metrics of the MP connector added in 0.5.6 crash vLLM engine startup whenever the engine runs under Ray Serve LLM (`ray.serve.llm`). `LMCacheMPPromMetrics.__init__` builds `vllm:lmcache_mp_lookup_duration_seconds` without a `buckets` argument (`lmcache/integration/vllm/lmcache_mp_metrics.py:75`, added in PR #5024):

```python
histogram = self._histogram_cls(
    name="vllm:lmcache_mp_lookup_duration_seconds",
    documentation="LMCache MP lookup latency observed by vLLM.",
    labelnames=labelnames,
)   # no buckets
```

Under plain `vllm serve`, `_histogram_cls` is `prometheus_client.Histogram`, and a missing `buckets` means default buckets, so it works. Under Ray Serve, vLLM swaps in `vllm/v1/metrics/ray_wrappers.py`, whose `RayHistogramWrapper` runs `boundaries = buckets if buckets else []` and hands that to `ray.util.metrics.Histogram`. Ray rejects empty `boundaries` with `ValueError`, by design and since 2020. The engine replica dies inside the `AsyncLLM` constructor, after the engine core is already up:

```text
AsyncLLM.__init__ (StatLoggerManager)
  -> vllm loggers.py (kv_connector_prom)
  -> lmcache_mp_connector.py:1665 (build_prom_metrics)
  -> lmcache_mp_metrics.py:75 (LMCacheMPPromMetrics)
  -> vllm/v1/metrics/ray_wrappers.py:158 (RayHistogramWrapper)
  -> ray.util.metrics.Histogram -> ValueError: boundaries argument should be provided when using the Histogram class.
```

**To Reproduce**
Mirrors `tests/v1/test_mp_connector_metrics.py`, with vLLM's real Ray wrapper types instead of the `_Histogram` stub. Verified on `lmcache 0.5.6` + `vllm 0.31.0` + `ray 2.60.0`:

```python
from types import SimpleNamespace

from prometheus_client import Counter, Gauge, Histogram
from vllm.v1.metrics.ray_wrappers import (
    RayCounterWrapper,
    RayGaugeWrapper,
    RayHistogramWrapper,
)

from lmcache.integration.vllm.lmcache_mp_metrics import LMCacheMPPromMetrics

LMCacheMPPromMetrics(
    SimpleNamespace(kv_transfer_config=object()),
    {Counter: RayCounterWrapper, Gauge: RayGaugeWrapper, Histogram: RayHistogramWrapper},
    ["model_name", "engine"],
    {0: ["model", "0"]},
)
# ValueError: boundaries argument should be provided when using the Histogram class.
```

**Expected behavior**
`LMCacheMPPromMetrics` constructs successfully on every metrics backend. Passing explicit `buckets` fixes it independent of the backend and improves the metric itself: lookup latency ranges from sub-millisecond L1 host hits to seconds on remote backends, which the HTTP-oriented `prometheus_client` default buckets (top end 10s) fit poorly. Something like `buckets=(0.001, 0.005, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.5, 1.0, 5.0)` should match the real distribution.

Please tell me if this is something that should rather be fixed on VLLM's site. It seemed more robust to me to place it here but you will know better 😉

items.title: [Perf] MP server converts token ids to ints and back for every key
items.author: theminjunchoi
items.body_excerpt:
Hi! While profiling the MP server under a replayed vLLM trace, I noticed that a good share of the per-request CPU time goes into handling token ids.

Each key arrives with the token ids on the wire, and the server turns them into a tuple of Python ints, copies that into a list, and then packs every 256-token chunk back into big-endian uint32 bytes with `struct.pack` so blake3 can hash it (`token_hasher.py`). So we end up rebuilding the same bytes that could have been sent as-is.

For a single 2,048-token key, that path takes about 91 µs on my machine, while hashing slices of the packed bytes takes about 12 µs and gives the same chunk hashes.

Would it make sense to send the token ids in `IPCCacheServerKey` as packed bytes and hash them directly? The hashes would stay the same, so existing caches would keep hitting. The catch is that the key's wire format changes, so the client and server would need to be on the same LMCache version.

I have a change ready and will open a PR for it. Any feedback is very welcome.

items.title: Performance comparison for dense shared prefix + block-diagonal local mask: custom mask in BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper vs MultiLevelCascadeAttentionWrapper
items.author: catnanami
items.body_excerpt: I am trying to evaluate the best way to implement an attention pattern with a dense shared/global prefix plus a local block-diagonal suffix. The mask pattern is shown below: I am considering two implementations: BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper with a custom mask MultiLevelCascadeAttentionWrapper Questions: 1. For this pattern, is cascade attention expected to be faster than paged prefill with a custom mask? 2. Or is this pattern better handled by a custom kernel/backend? My use case is speculative decoding, where all verification tokens share the same prefix KV, but each local block should only attend to its own block.

comments.author: VectorPeak
comments.body:
For the mask in the image - a dense shared prefix on the left plus independent block-diagonal local regions on the right - `MultiLevelCascadeAttentionWrapper` is usually the better fit than `BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper` with one large custom mask.

The reason is that the custom-mask prefill path does not really exploit this structure as well: it still treats the problem like one masked attention problem over the full layout, so the block-diagonal sparsity mostly becomes masking overhead. Cascade attention lets you model this as:

- shared/global prefix KV: attended by all verification tokens
- local suffix KV: split into independent blocks/requests
- final result: merge prefix-attention state with each local block’s attention state

For speculative decoding, this is exactly the kind of case where cascade can help, especially when the shared prefix is large and the local verification blocks are relatively small. Each local block can be represented as a separate batch item sharing the same prefix. If the local part also needs causal masking inside each block, use the normal causal/local mask for that per-block suffix attention.

items.title: Feature Request: Disk-based context checkpoint offloading (`--cache-disk`)
items.author: wypiki
items.body_excerpt:
### Prerequisites

- [x] I am running the latest code. Mention the version if possible as well.
- [x] I carefully followed the [README.md](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/README.md).
- [x] I searched using keywords relevant to my issue to make sure that I am creating a new issue that is not already open (or closed).
- [x] I reviewed the [Discussions](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions), and have a new and useful enhancement to share.

### Feature Description

## Problem

Context checkpoints (`--ctx-checkpoints`, `--cache-ram`) are currently stored exclusively in system RAM. On UMA (Unified Memory Architecture) systems such as AMD Strix Halo, system RAM and VRAM are physically the same memory pool. This means checkpoint caching actively competes with model weights and KV cache for the same limited resource, rather than providing relief.

On these systems, `--cache-ram` doesn't offload anything – it just reserves more of the same unified memory that the model already needs, reducing the effective memory available for context or GPU layers.

## Proposed Solution

Add a `--cache-disk <path>` option (or `--cache-ssd`) that allows context checkpoints to be serialized to a fast local storage device (NVMe SSD) instead of being held in RAM.

Modern NVMe SSDs deliver 5-7 GB/s sequential read throughput, which would allow restoring a typical checkpoint (50-100 MiB) in ~10-20ms – negligible compared to the seconds or minutes saved by avoiding full prompt re-processing on hybrid/recurrent models like Qwen 3.5.

### Suggested interface

```
--cache-disk <path>       directory for disk-based checkpoint storage (default: disabled)
--cache-disk-max <MiB>    maximum disk space for checkpoints (default: unlimited)
```

When `--cache-disk` is set, checkpoints would be written to disk instead of (or in addition to) RAM. On restore, the checkpoint is read back from disk into the appropriate memory (GPU/unified).

## Use Case

This is particularly relevant for:

1. **UMA/APU systems** (AMD Strix Halo, Strix Point, future Apple Silicon with large models) where RAM = VRAM and every megabyte of RAM used for checkpoints is a megabyte less for model/context
2. **Multi-user systems**: this kind of almost unlimited caching would make serving multiple users with different system prompts or several agents simultaniously fast on systems with slow prompt processing speeds
3. **Large context windows** (100k+ tokens) where checkpoints can grow large and numerous

## Why not just use `--cache-ram`?

On discrete GPU systems with separate VRAM, `--cache-ram` makes sense – it uses a different memory pool. But on UMA systems:

- RAM **is** VRAM – there's no offloading benefit
- Checkpoint RAM usage directly reduces available memory for model layers, KV cache, and context size
- Users are forced to choose between more checkpoints (faster turn transitions) and more context/layers

Disk-based checkpoints would completely eliminate this trade-off on UMA systems, and also benefit discrete GPU setups where system RAM is also limited.

## Environment

- Hardware: AMD Strix Halo (Ryzen AI Max+ 395, Radeon 8060S, 128 GB unified memory)
- Model: Qwen3.5-122B-A10B (Q5_K_XL, ~85 GB)
- Context: 220k tokens
- Backend: Vulkan
- llama.cpp version: b8398


### Motivation

Making UMA systems like Strix Halo or Apple Silicon a real option for multiple users, also making the experience for single users much better with assistants like OpenClaw, Claude Code etc.

### Possible Implementation

Instead of copying the checkpoints to RAM, they would be copied to the SSD and read from there when matched.

items.title: Misc. bug: Metal aborts on MUL_MAT with BF16 src1 at K >= 64, batch > 8 (no BF16 mul_mm kernel)
items.author: vieduy
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

master @ 7170cad (after b11813), built with AppleClang 21.0.0 for Darwin arm64


### Operating systems

Mac

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

Other (Please specify in the next section)

### Command line

```shell
test-backend-ops test -b MTL0 -o MUL_MAT -p "type_a=bf16,type_b=bf16,m=64,n=17,k=64,"
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

On Metal, a MUL_MAT whose src1 is BF16 aborts once K >= 64 and the batch (n) is above 8:

    kernel not found in any metal library: base = 'kernel_mul_mm_bf16_bf16'
    ggml_metal_encoder_set_pipeline: nil Metal pipeline (missing kernel; see compile_pipeline log above)

**Cause:**

- `ggml_metal_op_mul_mat_use_mm` (`ggml/src/ggml-metal/ggml-metal-common.cpp`) chooses `mul_mm` from the shape alone.
- `mul_mm` is only instantiated for F32 and F16 src1 (`kernel_mul_mm_<src0>_f32` / `_f16`), so a BF16 src1 gets a nil pipeline.
- `mul_mv` does have BF16 src1 kernels (`kernel_mul_mv_bf16_bf16`, `kernel_mul_mv_f32_bf16`), so smaller shapes work.

**Affected pairs:**

| src0 x src1 | K >= 64, n > 8 |
|---|---|
| BF16 x BF16 | abort (`kernel_mul_mm_bf16_bf16` not found) |
| F32 x BF16 | abort (`kernel_mul_mm_f32_bf16` not found) |
| F16 x BF16, Q4_0 x BF16 | not affected: Metal reports them unsupported, so they fall back to CPU |

**Why CI doesn't catch it:** every existing BF16 src1 case in `test-backend-ops` uses K < 64 or n <= 8, so none reaches `mul_mm`.

**Reach:** no model graph in `src/` produces a BF16 src1 for MUL_MAT. Even with a BF16 KV cache and flash attention off, the cache is src0 and the activations stay F32. It is reachable through the ggml API.

**Steps to reproduce:** stock master has no test that hits this. Add these two lines to `make_test_cases_eval()` in `tests/test-backend-ops.cpp`:

```cpp
test_cases.emplace_back(new test_mul_mat(GGML_TYPE_BF16, GGML_TYPE_BF16, 64, 17, 64, {1, 1}, {1, 1}));
test_cases.emplace_back(new test_mul_mat(GGML_TYPE_F32,  GGML_TYPE_BF16, 64, 17, 64, {1, 1}, {1, 1}));
```

Then build and run the command above. It exits with code 134 (abort). The same happens at K = 256.

**Hardware:** Apple M4 (10-core GPU), macOS 27.0.1.

**Proposed fix:** keep BF16 src1 off the `mul_mm` path, so it uses the existing `mul_mv` kernels. This is a one-line condition in `ggml_metal_op_mul_mat_use_mm`
### First Bad Commit

Unknown

items.title: [Bug]: Ascend Direct 跨节点 put host 全局段 "Can't find remoteBuffer"（remote_accessible 未导出）
items.author: gygdh-001
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug
In a PD-disaggregated Ascend deployment, cross-node KV transfer via Ascend Direct fails on the host global segment. The ADXL one-sided `put` reports `Can't find remoteBuffer by key[<host-segment-addr>][8192]` — the buffer is not resolvable from the transferred key.

Environment: Atlas 800I A3, CANN 9.2.0, vLLM 0.30.0, SuperPod topology (inter-node HCCS, no RoCE switch).

Error chain:

    [hccl_one_sided_conn.cc:407] GetTransInfo: Can't find remoteBuffer by key[0x12e480060000][8192]
    [hccl_one_sided_service.cc:1242] InitAicpuTilingDataBuf: hcclRet -> 1
    [exception_handler.cc:24] HcclBatchPut: AICPU launch failed, code: 1
    [comm_channel.cc:469] operator(): ErrorNo: 103900 Failed to invoke DlHcclBatchPut, hccl_result = 1
    [adxl_engine_impl.cc:286] TransferSync: ErrorNo: 103900 Failed to TransferSync, operation:write, op_descs size:12, timeout:33064 ms

### Key observation / evidence
The failing keys are exactly the host-side 24GB global segment registered as `mem type:host`; none of the `mem type:device` KV buffers appears:

    register mem addr:0x12f0c0000000, length:25769803776, mem type:host    # prefill
    register mem addr:0x12e440000000, length:25769803776, mem type:host    # decode
    register mem addr:0x12e480000000, length:25769803776, mem type:host    # decode
    register mem addr:0x12dde3400000, length:1905917952,   mem type:device  # KV buffer

    key[0x12f0c0000000][8192/131072]
    key[0x12e440000000][8192/131072]
    key[0x12e480000000][8192/131072]

Even the prefill node's own host segment (`0x12f0c...`) fails the lookup. Since `remoteBuffer` here means the remote-accessible buffer table (not "buffer on the remote node"), a locally-owned segment also missing from that table is consistent with `remote_accessible` being dropped in `registerLocalMemory()` (the `(void)remote_accessible;` bug fixed by #4363), so the host segment is registered local-only and never exported.

### Suspected root cause
PR #4363 (commit 02bb6b1) — `AscendDirectTransport::registerLocalMemory()` did not propagate `remote_accessible` to the ADXL `MemDesc`, so buffers were registered local-only. Our build appears to run a Mooncake without that fix.

### Question
1. Which Mooncake release contains commit 02bb6b1 (#4363)? Is the host 24GB segment supposed to be registered `remote_accessible=true` for cross-node put?
2. `ASCEND_AUTO_CONNECT=1` did not change the error — does that rule out a connection-timing issue and confirm the buffer-registration flag?

items.title: [Feature] [NPU] Add topology-aware CPU and NUMA affinity for Ascend worker ranks
items.author: Guozhong23
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [ ] If this is not a feature request but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [ ] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Motivation

## Motivation
SGLang supports `SGLANG_SET_CPU_AFFINITY=1`, but the current affinity path does not fully model the topology between an Ascend NPU, its closest NUMA node, the process-visible device index, and the CPUs allowed by the container/cgroup.
On multi-socket Ascend servers, assigning ranks by a flat CPU split can place a scheduler or worker on CPUs from a remote NUMA node. This increases host-side scheduling jitter and remote memory access, especially for workloads with frequent small decode steps and host-driven communication.
The problem is more subtle when `ASCEND_RT_VISIBLE_DEVICES` reorders or filters devices: logical NPU 0 is not necessarily physical NPU 0, so rank-based CPU partitioning alone cannot infer the correct NUMA node.
This feature request proposes a topology-aware NPU affinity provider that:
1. obtains the physical NPU topology, for example from `npu-smi info -t topo`;
2. maps logical visible-device indices to physical NPU IDs;
3. resolves the closest NUMA node for each rank;
4. intersects candidate CPUs with the process/cgroup allowed CPU set;
5. prefers physical cores and handles SMT siblings explicitly;
6. assigns non-overlapping CPU subsets to local ranks when possible;
7. reads the effective affinity back and logs the applied result;
8. degrades safely when topology discovery or NUMA memory binding is unavailable.
This should be implemented as a hardware topology provider under the existing affinity/NUMA abstraction, rather than as model-specific code.
## Expected behavior
- Existing behavior remains unchanged when the feature is disabled.
- With NPU affinity enabled, each worker is bound to CPUs local to its physical NPU whenever the topology and cgroup constraints allow it.
- A reordered `ASCEND_RT_VISIBLE_DEVICES` is handled correctly.
- Binding failures are reported, but do not kill the scheduler unless strict mode is explicitly requested.
- The log reports logical device, physical device, NUMA node, requested CPUs, allowed CPUs, and effective CPUs.
## Proposed implementation direction
Introduce an accelerator topology interface similar to:
```python
class AcceleratorTopologyProvider:    
def logical_to_physical_device(self, logical_id: int) -> int: ...    
def device_numa_node(self, physical_id: int) -> int | None: ...    
def candidate_cpus(self, numa_node: int) -> set[int]: ...
￼
The common affinity layer should remain responsible for cgroup filtering, physical-core allocation, conflict handling, application, and verification. The Ascend provider would only implement NPU-specific topology discovery.

### Related resources

- SGLang Ascend tuning documentation currently recommends `SGLANG_SET_CPU_AFFINITY=1`:  
https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/main/docs/docs/hardware-platforms/ascend-npus/optimization/parameter_tuning.mdx
- Related NUMA failure report: https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/27368
- This proposal is complementary to cgroup/memory-binding fallback fixes: it focuses on mapping each Ascend device to the correct NUMA-local CPU set.

items.title: RFC: Plugin Extension Points Needed for MetaX GPU Support
items.author: yangxin-mx
items.body_excerpt:
# Proposal: Generalize SGLang Hardware Plugin Interfaces for MetaX GPU Support

> Discussion draft based on a SGLang 0.5.19-derived codebase. The names below are proposed API shapes, not claims that they already exist on the latest `main` branch. If an equivalent upstream seam already exists, we would prefer to use or extend it. This is an umbrella discussion that can be split into smaller PRs.

SGLang already has useful foundations: hardware-platform entry points, `SRTPlatform.init_backend()`, an explicit OOT forward registry for fused ops, and MoE runner/fused-function registration. See the [plugin documentation](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/main/docs/docs/hardware-platforms/plugin.mdx) and [expert-parallelism documentation](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/main/docs/docs/advanced_features/expert_parallelism.mdx). When adapting another CUDA-compatible GPU, however, we still encounter framework call sites that select a built-in class, import a vendor implementation, or call a kernel through a module-level symbol before a platform plugin can participate.

Our goal is to make required hardware behavior expressible through platform methods and explicit, typed registries. We do **not** propose replacing module globals or monkey-patching framework functions. A missing optional platform implementation should preserve the current built-in behavior; a selected but unsupported implementation should fail with a clear capability error rather than silently run an incompatible kernel. The plugin owns its vendor kernels and package dependencies. The framework owns common algorithms, selection rules, lifecycle, and validation.

The Python snippets below illustrate **proposed interfaces and call sites, not complete, runnable code already present in the repository**. `ExampleGpuPlatform` and `vendor_ops` stand for any vendor plugin. Exact parameters should be settled against existing types and call paths in the corresponding PRs. Each section shows both where the framework would connect the extension point and how a plugin would use it.

## 1. JIT toolchain and cache identity

### Adaptation problem

In the 0.5.19-derived tree, JIT compilation derives the device compiler, architecture and flags through CUDA/ROCm-oriented paths in `kernels/jit/utils/compile/toolchain.py`. The build path (`ninja.py`) and cache path (`cache.py`) must agree on these values. A plugin cannot safely supply a different device compiler by changing only one path: the cache may reuse a binary built for another SDK or architecture.

### Plugin-oriented proposal

- Add an optional `SRTPlatform.get_jit_toolchain() -> JitToolchainSpec | None`. The immutable spec should include the host/device compilers, toolkit root, target architecture, include/link paths and flags, plus an explicit SDK/ABI cache identity.
- Resolve the spec lazily when compilation starts, and pass the **same resolved spec** to command generation and cache-key generation. `None` keeps the existing built-in toolchain logic.
- Let the vendor plugin package its AOT extensions itself. The common AOT setup need not import or name each vendor SDK.

On the framework side, add the optional method in `srt/platforms/interface.py` and have `kernels/jit/utils/compile/{toolchain,ninja,cache}.py` consume the same spec:

```python
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class JitToolchainSpec:
    host_compiler: str
    device_compiler: str
    toolkit_root: str
    target_arch: str
    device_flags: tuple[str, ...] = ()
    include_dirs: tuple[str, ...] = ()
    link_flags: tuple[str, ...] = ()
    cache_identity: str = ""  # SDK/ABI version

class SRTPlatform(DeviceMixin):
    def get_jit_toolchain(self) -> JitToolchainSpec | None:
        return None

def compile_extension(source, **kwargs):
    spec = resolve_jit_toolchain(get_platform().get_jit_toolchain())
    cache_key = make_cache_key(source, spec=spec, **kwargs)
    return build_with_ninja(source, spec=spec, cache_key=cache_key, **kwargs)
```

The plugin only describes its own SDK; it does not modify global `CUDA_HOME` or framework compiler symbols:

```python
class ExampleGpuPlatform(SRTPlatform):
    def get_jit_toolchain(self) -> JitToolchainSpec:
        return JitToolchainSpec(
            host_compiler="/opt/example/bin/c++",
            device_compiler="/opt/example/bin/device-cc",
            toolkit_root="/opt/example",
            target_arch="example-arch",
            cache_identity="example-sdk-1:abi-1",
        )
```

## 2. Device properties and per-operator Triton tuning

### Adaptation problem

Several launch paths infer hardware behavior from CUDA properties or NVIDIA/AMD architecture names, while `num_stages`, warps, tile sizes and shared-memory limits are selected locally. A plugin may expose a CUDA-compatible device but still need different launch parameters; pretending to be a particular SM is not a sound capability contract.

### Plugin-oriented proposal

- Expose a read-only `DeviceKernelProfile` through the active platform, with architecture identifier, warp size, maximum shared-memory bytes and relevant device capabilities.
- Add an optional `tune_triton_launch(op, shape, dtype, default) -> TritonLaunchConfig`. Each caller first computes its present default, then asks the active platform for a per-operator override and validates it before launch. There should be no global change to Triton's defaults.
- Start with launch sites where hardware differences actually affect correctness or feasibility (MoE, quantization and attention), keeping other paths unchanged.

items.title: KernelLens: Deploying Triton Kernels to C++ Inference Engines (TensorRT & ONNX)
items.author: Just1truc
items.body_excerpt:
# Deploying OpenAI Triton Kernels to C++ Inference Runtimes (ONNX Runtime & TensorRT) with KernelLens

Hey Triton Community!

If you write custom `@triton.jit` kernels in Python for LLM operators (FlashAttention, Fused RMSNorm, SwiGLU, Selective Scans), you’ve probably hit the deployment bottleneck: How do you run your Python Triton kernels inside production C++ inference engines like NVIDIA TensorRT or Microsoft ONNX Runtime?

Traditionally, developers had two frustrating choices:
1. **Stay in Python PyTorch Eager/Dynamo**: Forfeiting TensorRT/ORT global graph optimizations across standard model layers.
2. **Manual C++/CUDA Rewrites**: Throw away Python Triton code and manually rewrite kernels in CUDA C++ (`__global__`) while authoring hundreds of lines of `OrtCustomOp` / `nvinfer1::IPluginV2DynamicExt` boilerplate.

To solve this, we created [**KernelLens**](https://github.com/Just1truc/kernel_lens), an open-source compiler framework from [Galiad Research](https://galiad-research.com) that automatically compiles PyTorch models containing Python `@triton.jit` kernels into native C++ plugins for ONNX Runtime and TensorRT in **1 line of Python**.

---

## Step-by-Step Guide to Run the Working Example

Follow these 3 simple steps to test KernelLens on any CUDA-enabled GPU machine:

### Step 1: Install Dependencies
```bash
pip install torch triton kernel-lens
```

### Step 2: Save the Python Script (`example.py`)
Save the following code into a file named `example.py`:

```python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import triton
import triton.language as tl
import kernel_lens as kl

# 1. Define a standard OpenAI Triton Kernel
@triton.jit
def add_kernel(x_ptr, y_ptr, out_ptr, n_elements, BLOCK_SIZE: tl.constexpr):
    pid = tl.program_id(axis=0)
    block_start = pid * BLOCK_SIZE
    offsets = block_start + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE)
    mask = offsets < n_elements
    x = tl.load(x_ptr + offsets, mask=mask)
    y = tl.load(y_ptr + offsets, mask=mask)
    output = x + y
    tl.store(out_ptr + offsets, output, mask=mask)

# 2. Wrap the Triton Kernel inside a PyTorch Module
class VectorAddModule(nn.Module):
    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor, y: torch.Tensor):
        out = torch.empty_like(x)
        n_elements = x.numel()
        grid = lambda meta: (triton.cdiv(n_elements, meta['BLOCK_SIZE']),)
        add_kernel[grid](<x, y, out, n_elements, BLOCK_SIZE=1024>)
        return out

if __name__ == '__main__':
    device = 'cuda' if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'cpu'
    x = torch.randn(4096, device=device, dtype=torch.float32)
    y = torch.randn(4096, device=device, dtype=torch.float32)
    model = VectorAddModule().to(device)

    print("Compiling PyTorch + Triton Model with KernelLens...")
    
    # 3. Compile Model to C++ Plugins in 1 Line
    compiled_model = kl.compile(
        model, 
        (x, y), 
        name="simple_vector_add", 
        backends=["onnx", "tensorrt"]
    )
    
    print("Executing Zero-Copy Inference in ONNX Runtime...")
    ort_output = compiled_model.run((x, y), backend="onnx")
    
    print("Executing Zero-Copy Inference in TensorRT...")
    trt_output = compiled_model.run((x, y), backend="tensorrt")

    # 4. Verify Numerical Parity against PyTorch Result
    torch_expected = x + y
    max_diff_ort = (ort_output - torch_expected).abs().max().item()
    max_diff_trt = (trt_output - torch_expected).abs().max().item()

    print("Verification Complete!")
    print(f"ORT Max Floating-Point Difference: {max_diff_ort:.6e}")
    print(f"TRT Max Floating-Point Difference: {max_diff_trt:.6e}")
    print(f"Exact Numerical Match (ORT): {torch.allclose(ort_output, torch_expected)}")
    print(f"Exact Numerical Match (TRT): {torch.allclose(trt_output, torch_expected)}")
```

### Step 3: Execute the Test
```bash
python3 example.py
```

### Expected Terminal Output
```text
Compiling PyTorch + Triton Model with KernelLens...
Executing Zero-Copy Inference in ONNX Runtime...
Executing Zero-Copy Inference in TensorRT...
Verification Complete!
ORT Max Floating-Point Difference: 0.000000e+00
TRT Max Floating-Point Difference: 0.000000e+00
Exact Numerical Match (ORT): True
Exact Numerical Match (TRT): True
```

---

## How it Works Under the Hood 🛠️

1. **PTX & Metadata Extraction**: KernelLens intercepts `@triton.jit` launches, extracting compiled PTX assembly strings, dynamic shared memory bytes, and parameter bitwidths directly from Triton’s compiler cache.
2. **SymPy Grid Transpilation**: Triton grid functions (e.g., `grid = lambda META: (triton.cdiv(M, BLOCK_SIZE),)`) are parsed via AST inspection into pure C++ integer arithmetic, evaluated dynamically at inference time with $< 0.5 \ \mu\text{s}$ CPU overhead.
3. **C++/CUDA Plugin Synthesis**: Synthesizes production-ready C++ source files implementing `Ort::CustomOp` and `nvinfer1::IPluginV2DynamicExt`, executing the PTX assembly via CUDA Driver API (`cuModuleLoadData` & `cuLaunchKernel`).
4. **Zero-Copy VRAM Binding**: Directly maps PyTorch VRAM pointers (`data_ptr()`) to ONNX Runtime `IOBinding` and TensorRT `setTensorAddress()`.
5. **Hardware Hardening**: Automatically injects dynamic 16-byte address checks to prevent misaligned vector load crashes (`ld.global.v4.b32`), and applies PTX ISA version clamping (`.version 9.0`) for NVIDIA Blackwell (`sm_120a`) GPU driver compatibility.

---

## Benchmarks & Numerical Parity

Across LLaMA 3, Mistral, Qwen 2.5, and Liger-Kernel operators, KernelLens achieves **$3.4\times$ to $7.0\times$ speedups** over eager PyTorch execution while maintaining exact floating-point numerical parity ($\text{MaxDiff} = 0.00\text{e}+00$).

---

## Links & Resources

* 💻 **GitHub**: [Just1truc/kernel_lens](https://github.com/Just1truc/kernel_lens)
* 📦 **PyPI**: `pip install kernel-lens`
* 📄 **Technical Report (DOI)**: [10.5281/zenodo.23194523](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo

items.title: [RFC]: Support ViT Full CUDA Graph (Tracker)
items.author: shen-shanshan
items.body_excerpt:
### Motivation.

Multimodal large language models (e.g., Qwen3-VL, Qwen3.5, GLM-V, Kimi K2.5) rely on a Vision Transformer (ViT) encoder to process visual inputs before feeding them into the language model backbone. In production serving scenarios, the ViT forward pass involves launching a large number of small CUDA kernels — including patch embedding, layer normalization, multi-head self-attention, and MLP projections — each of which incurs non-trivial kernel launch overhead on the host side.

Currently, vLLM supports CUDA graph capture for the decoder (LLM) portion of the model, which has proven effective at reducing kernel launch costs and improving throughput. However, the ViT encoder is still executed eagerly, meaning every forward pass re-launches all kernels from scratch. Extending full CUDA graph support to the ViT encoder would allow the entire encoder forward pass to be captured and replayed as a single graph, eliminating per-kernel launch overhead and enabling more consistent, low-latency inference for multimodal models.

items.title: [RFC]: Design a shared warmup infrastructure for JITs
items.author: LopezCastroRoberto
items.body_excerpt:
### Motivation.

https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/47451 contains an initial implementation of the proposal described in this RFC.

## Summary

This RFC proposes a standard, extensible warmup infrastructure for JIT kernels in vLLM.

The goal is to let kernels from different JIT backends, including Triton, CuTeDSL, TileLang, and potential future DSLs, expose the set of specializations that should be compiled during engine startup.

This is not intended to be a one-off warmup path for a specific kernel. Instead, it defines a kernel-owned contract where each warmable kernel describes its own compile keys, dispatch logic, warmup search space, and compile-only entry point.

## Motivation

vLLM increasingly relies on JIT-generated kernels from multiple DSLs. Today, warming these kernels is difficult to standardize because each backend exposes different runtime and compilation APIs. This RFC proposes a common infrastructure with several goals:

- Create shared JIT warmup infrastructure for JIT backends in vLLM.
- Keep warmup definitions close to the kernels that own the specialization logic, making the system easier to review and maintain.
- Warm up actual compile keys instead of running representative non-key inputs, such as token sizes, and hoping they map to all required specializations. That mapping is not always obvious or guaranteed, so warmup should target the compile-key space directly.
- Use Python AST dispatch tracing to derive compile-key search spaces from normal Python `dispatch(...)` methods, avoiding duplicated hand-written warmup logic.
- Support compile-only warmup APIs, avoiding dummy runtime launches and dummy tensor allocation. Dummy runs can be expensive and may have side effects; each DSL should expose fake tensor/spec descriptors suitable for compilation only.
- Define a standard interface for new contributors and potentially third-party libraries to expose warmup metadata: compile keys, representative warmup keys, and a compile-only API.

## Proposed Change: Warmup Contract

Each warmable kernel should expose a small wrapper object near the kernel's normal runtime entry point.

The wrapper owns:

- A frozen `CompileKey` dataclass with the fields that identify one compiled specialization.
- A `dispatch(...)` method that maps normal dispatch arguments to `CompileKey`.
- A `get_warmup_keys(...)` method that returns representative keys to compile.
- A `compile(compile_key)` method that compiles one key.

Proposed shape:

```python
class MyKernel(VllmJitKernel["MyKernel.CompileKey"]):

    @dataclass(frozen=True)
    class CompileKey:
        BLOCK_SIZE: int

    @staticmethod
    def kernel(...):
        ...

    def dispatch(self, *, num_tokens: int) -> CompileKey:
        return self.CompileKey(BLOCK_SIZE= ...)

    def get_warmup_keys(self, vllm_config: VllmConfig) -> list[CompileKey]:
        ...

    def compile(self, compile_key: CompileKey) -> None:
        ...
  
    def __call__(self, ...):
        compile_key = self.dispatch(...)
        ...

MY_KERNEL = MyKernel()
```

CompileKey must be hashable. `get_warmup_keys(...)` should deduplicate keys before returning them if multiple representative inputs map to the same compiled specialization.

## Scope

This RFC covers the warmup contract and the minimal shared infrastructure needed to make JIT warmup kernel-owned and backend-extensible.

The initial scope is limited to:

- A generic wrapper interface for warmable kernels.
- AST-assisted expansion of representative dispatch inputs into compile keys.
- Backend-specific compile-only adapters where needed.
- Initial Triton and CuTeDSL examples that exercise the contract.

It does not attempt to migrate every existing warmup path or define a complete backend-neutral fake tensor API for all DSLs in this first step.

## Current And Prior Work

To my knowledge, PR https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/47451 is the first implementation of this proposal. It adds the shared wrapper contract and demonstrates it with one Triton path and one CuTeDSL path.

Before this proposal, warmup logic was mostly backend-specific and ad hoc. In some cases it used representative runtime-like inputs rather than directly expressing the compile-key space.

#### Unified Runtime monitor
* https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/46167
* https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/46621
* https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/46718

## Risks

- Some specialization fields (compile-keys) may be hidden in backend internals and hard to model.
- Over-warming can increase startup time.
- Third-party libraries may need small API additions to expose compile-only entry points, and potentially methods to get warmup compile keys.

### Feedback Period.

_No response_

### CC List.

_No response_

### Any Other Things.

_No response_

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: [Bug]: Paused streaming sessions deadlock the scheduler when the KV cache is full
items.author: damienlaine
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

Scheduler-level repro on CPU, no model or GPU needed. Main at `89a00995c9`. Also hit on GPU with Voxtral realtime, V1 and V2 model runners.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

A paused streaming session (`resumable`, `WAITING_FOR_STREAMING_REQ`) keeps its KV blocks. When its next chunk arrives it goes through `kv_holding_waiting`. If the pool is full, `allocate_slots` fails and the waiting loop breaks. Preemption only takes from `running`, which is empty because every session is between chunks. Nothing gets freed, and every session stays waiting forever.

So once the sessions' KV goes over the pool, all of them freeze, not only the one that doesn't fit.

Repro (4 sessions, 7 usable blocks of 16 tokens, each chunk adds one block):

```python
from unittest.mock import MagicMock

import torch

from vllm.config import DeviceConfig, VllmConfig
from vllm.sampling_params import SamplingParams
from vllm.v1.core.sched.scheduler import Scheduler
from vllm.v1.kv_cache_interface import FullAttentionSpec, KVCacheConfig, KVCacheGroupSpec
from vllm.v1.outputs import ModelRunnerOutput
from vllm.v1.request import Request
from vllm.v1.structured_output import StructuredOutputManager

STOP = 128001
BLOCK = 16
NUM_BLOCKS = 8
NUM_SESSIONS = 4


def make_scheduler():
    cfg = VllmConfig(device_config=DeviceConfig("cpu"))
    cfg.model_config = MagicMock()
    cfg.model_config.skip_tokenizer_init = True
    cfg.model_config.is_multimodal_model = False
    cfg.model_config.supports_multimodal_inputs = False
    cfg.model_config.is_encoder_decoder = False
    cfg.model_config.is_diffusion = False
    cfg.model_config.max_model_len = 1024
    cfg.model_config.enable_return_routed_experts = False
    cfg.cache_config = MagicMock()
    cfg.cache_config.num_gpu_blocks = NUM_BLOCKS
    cfg.cache_config.enable_prefix_caching = False
    kv = KVCacheConfig(
        num_blocks=NUM_BLOCKS,
        kv_cache_tensors=[],
        kv_cache_groups=[KVCacheGroupSpec(["layer"], FullAttentionSpec(
            block_size=BLOCK, num_kv_heads=1, head_size=1, dtype=torch.float32))],
    )
    return Scheduler(vllm_config=cfg, kv_cache_config=kv, log_stats=False,
                     structured_output_manager=StructuredOutputManager(cfg),
                     block_size=BLOCK, hash_block_size=BLOCK)


def chunk(rid, n):
    # One streaming update: n new prompt tokens, generation stops after 1 token.
    return Request(request_id=rid, prompt_token_ids=list(range(1, n + 1)),
                   sampling_params=SamplingParams(stop_token_ids=[STOP], max_tokens=16),
                   pooling_params=None, resumable=True)


s = make_scheduler()
ids = [f"s{i}" for i in range(NUM_SESSIONS)]
for rid in ids:
    s.add_request(chunk(rid, BLOCK - 1))

for step in range(12):
    out = s.schedule()
    sched = list(out.num_scheduled_tokens)
    free = s.kv_cache_manager.block_pool.get_num_free_blocks()
    print(f"step {step}: scheduled={sched} free_blocks={free} "
          f"waiting={len(s.waiting) + len(getattr(s, 'kv_holding_waiting', []))}")
    if not sched:
        continue
    # Every scheduled session ends its chunk (STOP) and pauses, keeping its KV.
    s.update_from_output(out, ModelRunnerOutput(
        req_ids=sched, req_id_to_index={r: i for i, r in enumerate(sched)},
        sampled_token_ids=[[STOP] for _ in sched], logprobs=None,
        prompt_logprobs_dict={}, pooler_output=[]))
    # The client sends the next chunk for each of them.
    for rid in sched:
        s.add_request(chunk(rid, BLOCK))
```

```
step 0: scheduled=['s0', 's1', 's2', 's3'] free_blocks=3 waiting=0
step 1: scheduled=['s0', 's1', 's2'] free_blocks=0 waiting=1
step 2: scheduled=[] free_blocks=0 waiting=4
...
step 11: scheduled=[] free_blocks=0 waiting=4
```

On GPU, Voxtral-Mini-4B-Realtime with a 256 sliding window (~128 MiB KV per session) and `--kv-cache-memory 1GiB`: 7 sessions run fine, with 9 every session stops after a few seconds, 0 tok/s, no preemption, all 9 transcriptions cut. `--max-num-seqs 7` avoids it, the extra sessions just wait.

Expected: preempt a paused session (free its KV, recompute on resume) instead of blocking the queue.

Related: #58776 (a preempted resumable session is dropped). The encoder cache has the same pattern: a paused session keeps its last multimodal item cached until it resumes, and when the cache can't hold them all the waiting loop breaks the same way (seen with a small encoder cache in #45022).

comments.author: he-yufeng
comments.body:
Reproduced on current main (`31e2443c90`, CPU scheduler-level, exact script from the report): deadlock from step 2 on, `scheduled=[]` for the remaining 10 steps with `free_blocks=0` and all 4 sessions waiting.

This is the deadlock #59339 already fixes: it reclaims KV blocks from paused/`kv_holding` sessions at the waiting loop's allocation-failure point, which is the gap described here (preemption only scans `running`, and `running` is empty). I ran the same repro on #59339's head (`a0f422aa`): continuous progress from step 2 through 8 as paused sessions get reclaimed and resumed. The repro then stalls again at steps 9-11, but that is genuine capacity exhaustion, not deadlock: each session's prompt grows one block per round, so by then a single chunk needs ~9 blocks against an 8-block pool and nothing can legitimately fit.

One note for whoever picks up review: #59339's only red check is the pre-run gate (author has 2 merged PRs, needs a `verified`/`ready` label), not a code failure.

comments.author: divyuuu
comments.body:
Checked this on current main (`1e5d0ea`).

Static trace matches the report: the running-loop only preempts from `self.running` (`vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py:776-782`), and the waiting-loop `allocate_slots` failure path just `break`s (`1241-1248`) with no reclaim from `kv_holding_waiting`. So once all sessions are paused holding KV and `running` is empty, every `schedule()` stalls with nothing scheduled and nothing freed.

I also checked #59339 (reclaim at the waiting-loop failure point, updated Oct 6) to avoid duplicating it. Validating next whether it covers this exact 4-session repro on a Linux runner (my Windows host can't build vLLM -- no AMD64 precompiled wheel, only manylinux). Repro script ready from the issue body.

If a regression-test gap remains after #59339, may I take it? Happy to contribute the repro as a scheduler regression test. AI assistance used for the trace; will run the repro and tests before any PR per the contribution guide.

comments.author: damienlaine
comments.body:
Ran #59339 (`a0f422aa`) against its base (`21d93d0d8c`) on GPU with Voxtral realtime: RTX 4090, 256/256 sliding windows, `--max-num-batched-tokens 256`, `--kv-cache-memory-bytes 1GiB` (11,915 tokens), 120 s streams sent in real time.

| | completed | generation | words/stream |
|---|---|---|---|
| base, 9 sessions | 0/9, stalled after ~20 s | 0 tok/s | ~15 |
| #59339, 9 sessions | 0/9 | 65 → ~7 tok/s (~110 needed) | ~60 |
| #59339, 8 sessions | 0/8 | ~6 tok/s | ~80 |
| #59339, 7 sessions (fit in pool) | 7/7 | same output as reference | ~275 |
| default pool (49,152 tokens), 9 sessions | 9/9 | 112 tok/s | ~280 |

The stall is gone and reclaimed sessions produce correct output (97-100% word match with the reference on the same audio). Under overcommit, throughput collapses for all sessions, not only the extra one: a reclaimed session restarts from `num_computed_tokens = 0` and recomputes its full history, encoder included, so the cost per reclaim grows with session age.

Also tried restricting victims to sessions with lower `(priority, arrival_time)` than the requester, as the running-loop preemption does: 0/8 and 0/9, ~10 tok/s, and it breaks 3 of #59339's tests. Victim selection is not the issue.

Regression tests for this case are already in #59339 (14 tests, pass locally).

items.title: Feature Request: MoE expert cache with GPU-resident LRU - cache decisions and copies run on the GPU inside the compute graph
items.author: lich-77
items.body_excerpt:
### Prerequisites

- [x] I am running the latest code. Mention the version if possible as well.
- [x] I carefully followed the [README.md](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/README.md).
- [x] I searched using keywords relevant to my issue to make sure that I am creating a new issue that is not already open (or closed).
- [x] I reviewed the [Discussions](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions), and have a new and useful enhancement to share.

### Feature Description

1. Cache MoE experts on the GPU with an LRU, so that MoE models can run on GPUs with limited VRAM.
2. Everything runs on the GPU - there is no host/GPU switching: no per-step readback of expert ids, no 3. synchronization.
3. Works with MTP speculative decoding, on both HIP and CUDA, including dual-GPU setups.

A working implementation is complete: measured 9.7 -> 37-50 t/s decode on a 24GB 7900 XTX (3.5-4x), depending on workload. Code: [commit c81901a57](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/commit/c81901a57)

### Motivation

GPU-side caching of host-offloaded MoE experts is well proven by now, but none has progressed toward merge
-  #20757 was closed as completed, it confirmed strong temporal locality
-  the RFC in #28248 has received no maintainer response
-  #27861 has seen no author updates for weeks 
- the earlier PRs (#21609, #21614, #21620, #24524) were closed
-  #29887, opened yesterday, implements this differently. In same-machine, same-prompt tests, my implementation measured about 1.5x faster (details in the results section).

### Possible Implementation

A working implementation is complete: [commit c81901a57](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/commit/c81901a57) (branch `lru-upstream-v3`, rebased on current master). Measured 9.7 -> 37-50 t/s decode on a 24GB 7900 XTX (3.5-4x), depending on workload.

Each layer whose expert weights are on the host gets a fixed-size pool of N slots (`--moe-lru-slots N`). Two new graph ops do all the work inside the compute graph:

- `LRU_DECIDE` - a single-thread deterministic kernel (CUDA-graph replay safe) that reads the router's expert ids, updates the LRU state, and returns one flat output: remapped slot ids plus a fill list
- `LRU_FILL` - copies the experts named in the fill list from host memory into their pool slots, and returns a view of the pool that the existing `mul_mat_id` reads directly

The expert weights live in pinned host memory, so the fill kernel reads them directly over PCIe.

No scheduler, fusion, or CPU changes.

Correctness was verified before performance:

- Perplexity is unchanged from the no-pool baseline across slot counts: 1.4290 (no pool) vs 1.4292 (s64 through s192) on the test model
- Greedy decoding is deterministic: 12/12 runs of the same command produce identical output - single text hash, single cache counter set, single hit rate
- Generated text was inspected for every benchmark configuration (English, Chinese, and code-generation prompts)

### Local results (7900 XTX, 24GB, single GPU)

*UD-IQ3_XXS, all 48 layers pooled (`-ncmoe 48`), greedy, natural end-of-sequence, English prompt:*

| config | t/s | hit |
|---|---|---|
| no pool, plain | 9.7 | - |
| no pool + MTP-Q8 | 11.3 | - |
| 160 slots, plain | 37.2 | 89.4% |
| 160 slots + MTP-Q8 | 44.8 | 90.1% |

*UD-IQ4_XS, reverse placement (8 layers with native GPU experts + 40 pooled): pinning all 48
layers would need ~57 GB of locked host memory, above the Windows pinned-memory limit on this
64 GB machine (RAM - 16 GB); 40 layers (~47 GB) fits.*

| config | t/s | hit |
|---|---|---|
| 72 slots, plain (6.4 GiB pool) | 31.2 | 77.9% |
| 40 slots, plain (3.6 GiB pool) | 28.8 | 66.9% |
| 40 slots + MTP-Q4 | 30.5 | 73.3% |

### Remote results (2x RTX 3090, 48GB total)

*UD-IQ4_XS, 48 layers pooled, 320 slots (34.7 GiB pool), MTP-Q8 draft:*

| config | t/s | hit |
|---|---|---|
| EN, plain | 47.6 | 93.6% |
| EN + MTP-Q8 | 59.6 | 96.0% |

Note: MTP gains depend on the workload - about +20% on English prose, but +37-40% on
code-generation prompts (the IQ3 row above reaches 50.0 t/s and the 40-slot IQ4 row 38.5 t/s).

For reference, I also measured #29887 (applied on the same base commit) on the same machine,
same prompt, and equal cache budget (~6.5 GiB, reverse placement):

| implementation | t/s | hit |
|---|---|---|
| #29887 | 20.1 | 75.0% |
| this implementation | 31.2 | 77.9% |

Would this direction be welcome? I can open a PR right away if there is interest.

<details>
<summary>Reproduction (7900 XTX, single GPU)</summary>

Model: [unsloth/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF](https://huggingface.co/unsloth/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF) (UD-IQ3_XXS),
draft: [ggml-org/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF](https://huggingface.co/ggml-org/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF) (mtp-Q8_0).

```bash

items.title: RTX 5060 Ti 16GB: Qwen3.8-27B IQ4_XS + MTP-2 achieves 50.2 tok/s, 37/37 ReAct
items.author: SoundByGAIA
items.body_excerpt:
Sharing results from an internal ORDIS evaluation of Qwen3.8-27B on an NVIDIA RTX 5060 Ti 16GB, using stock llama.cpp, Unsloth UD-IQ4_XS quantization, and an external MTP head.

The goal was to exceed 25 tokens/s while maintaining task performance. MTP-2 reached 50.2 tok/s on the short-prompt decode test, with unchanged aggregate evaluation scores.

## Correction: VRAM units

My original post incorrectly divided the raw MiB readings by 1000 and labelled the results “GB”. The corrected table below uses GiB (1 GiB = 1024 MiB).

VRAM figures are the highest whole-GPU `nvidia-smi memory.used` readings sampled once per second, not isolated server-process allocations. The card reports 16,311 MiB (15.9 GiB) total.

## Performance results

All configurations used UD-IQ4_XS, an 8192-token context, and full GPU offload.

| Configuration | Decode: 30-token prompt | Decode: ~6.6K-token prompt | MTP acceptance | Sampled peak VRAM | Evaluation suite wall time |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| MTP disabled | 27.6 tok/s | 26.5 tok/s | — | 13.2 GiB | 259 s |
| MTP-1 | 45.8 tok/s | 42.1 tok/s | 88.5% | 14.6 GiB | 178 s |
| MTP-2 | 50.2 tok/s | 48.1 tok/s | 77.2% | 14.8 GiB (15,141 MiB) | 156 s |

Decode speeds are the mean of two timed requests per prompt: three requests were sent, and the first was discarded. Each configuration completed one full evaluation pass. There are no repeated full runs or variance estimates.

Suite wall time covers the ReAct, general, and multi-step evaluations at temperature 0, seed 42. Decode throughput is measured separately and is not end-to-end task throughput.

Compared with MTP disabled, MTP-2 increased short-prompt decode throughput by approximately 81.9% and reduced suite wall time by approximately 39.8%.

## Evaluation results

| Configuration | ReAct tool-format suite | General suite | Multi-step suite |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| MTP disabled | 37/37 | 42/44 | 7/8 |
| MTP-1 | 37/37 | 42/44 | 7/8 |
| MTP-2 | 37/37 | 42/44 | 7/8 |

These are internal ORDIS test sets, not standardized public benchmarks. Unchanged aggregate scores do not establish identical generated outputs or equivalent quality on other workloads.

The two general-suite failures occurred in all three configurations:

- A Python word-counting solution used `[a-z]+`, losing Turkish characters and splitting words such as `dünya`.
- A science question returned “Karbon” instead of the expected “karbondioksit”.

The multi-step tasks use a simulated tool world. The harness executes tools in a sandbox and supplies observations to the model. A pass requires the expected value in the final answer within a six-step budget. Across all three configurations, there were zero model-written observations and zero multiple-action steps.

The failed multi-step task asked for “the port value in `config.json`” without specifying a path. The sandbox file existed only at `/app/config.json`, and no search tool resolved a bare filename. The model attempted reads and a shell call, exhausted the six-step budget, and produced no final answer; it did not fabricate a value.

A clarified version with an explicit path was not evaluated. This case is confounded by task ambiguity and the six-step budget; without a clarified rerun, we cannot isolate the cause of failure. It remains scored as a failure in the reported 7/8 result.

## Reproducibility: source and artifacts

| Item | Recorded value |
|---|---|
| Engine source commit | `23b0202a189c44a54625aadcb37a946dd1d6278d` |
| Source tarball SHA-256 | `1fb4e5f71f50526ec7cae25bb1e9279d75d899e089386a82b71e42b951ea5d00` |
| Binary version output | `version: 0.6.0-dev (build 0, commit unknown)` |
| `llama-server` SHA-256 | `b2c18fb08ee2d44e00ef21c1e2eac8e84044914cad377ccd52722099a2b59cc1` |
| Model repository | `unsloth/Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF` |
| Model repository revision | `4ca720788d1e01f1bff70c033e0d0028fd02e502` |
| Model file | `Qwen3.8-27B-UD-IQ4_XS.gguf` |
| Model size | 14,252,845,984 bytes |
| Model SHA-256 | `40fac4050e940397dbf13087afd50f4734a11805bf9d65ef8ddd7483470e6199` |
| External MTP head | `MTP/mtp-Qwen3.8-27B-Q4_0.gguf`, from the same repository revision |
| MTP head size | 1,369,590,656 bytes |
| MTP head SHA-256 | `50d9ce5a6da381bbcfb31061cf73df94a90e6faf8efeddee379a9cb8f1501c6e` |

The source commit was verified through the source tarball: `git get-tar-commit-id` returns the recorded SHA, the build directory’s `CMAKE_HOME_DIRECTORY` points to the extracted source tree, and `diff -r` against a fresh extraction shows the source tree unchanged.

The binary was built from a tarball without `.git`, so it reports `commit unknown`. The commit attribution comes from the source and build records, not from the binary’s version output. Shared `libggml*.so` files were not hashed.

Both GGUF files matched their Hugging Face LFS hashes after download and again after copying to the benchmark host.

### Build environment

- NVIDIA driver 595.99.02
