items.title: Eval bug: CUDA "illegal memory access" with -cmoe on Turing (sm_75) at exactly 94 prompt tokens
items.author: Vyvrnc
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

version: 0.3.0-dev (build 10742, commit be789c344)
built with Clang 20.1.8 for Windows x86_64

### Operating systems

Windows

### GGML backends

CUDA

### Hardware

Intel Core i7-10850H (6C/12T, Comet Lake, AVX2, no AVX-512)
NVIDIA Quadro T2000 4 GB (Turing, sm_75), driver 596.36 and 597.06
80 GB RAM

### Models

unsloth/Qwen3-Coder-Next-GGUF -> Qwen3-Coder-Next-UD-Q4_K_S.gguf
(80B MoE, 3B active, 46,079,830,016 bytes)
sha256 verified against HF lfs.oid: beb854e08288f8ed5f790f2eb3d5e8fa3ca36205a282e5d149c15b368292c47b

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

### Summary

With `-cmoe` (CPU MoE offload) on a Turing GPU, `llama-server` reliably crashes with
`illegal memory access` when the prompt is **exactly 94 tokens** (`prompt_n` as reported by the
server, which is 86 tokens as returned by `/tokenize` plus 8 for the chat template).
93 tokens is fine, 95 tokens is fine. Content, language and topic are irrelevant — only the
exact length matters.

The crash always happens during prompt processing, 100–600 ms after `launch_slot_`, and never
during generation. The CPU-only build handles the same prompt without any problem.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Start the server:

```
llama-server.exe -m Qwen3-Coder-Next-UD-Q4_K_S.gguf \
  -c 32768 -t 6 -lm none -np 1 -ngl 99 -cmoe \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 61129
```

2. Send this prompt as a single user message with `"cache_prompt": false`
   (86 tokens per `/tokenize`, 438 characters):

```
Write a short PHP function that reads a list of numeric values from a text file and returns the average, the minimum and the maximum of those values. Explain briefly what to watch out for when the input file is empty, when it contains invalid or non numeric rows, and how to keep the resulting code readable and easy to test later on. Please also mention how you would report errors back to the caller without throwing any exceptions, and
```

3. The server dies immediately. Any prompt of that exact token length does the same.

### Token-length sweep

Neutral English prompts built word by word and verified via `/tokenize`, each sent 3× with
`cache_prompt: false`, server restarted after every crash — 27 requests total:

| `/tokenize` tokens | server `prompt_n` | result |
|---|---|---|
| 82 | 90 | 3× OK |
| 83 | 91 | 3× OK |
| 84 | 92 | 3× OK |
| 85 | 93 | 3× OK |
| **86** | **94** | **3× CRASH** |
| 87 | 95 | 3× OK |
| 88 | 96 | 3× OK |
| 89 | 97 | 3× OK |
| 90 | 98 | 3× OK |

We originally hit this with an unrelated Czech prompt that happened to have the same
`prompt_n = 94` — also 3/3 crashes. Changing any single word that shifted the length by one
token made it disappear, which is why it looked nondeterministic at first.

### What we ruled out

| Hypothesis | Test | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Corrupted model file | sha256 vs HF `lfs.oid` | matches |
| Model or prompt itself | same prompt on **CPU-only build** | runs fine (5.5 t/s) |
| Quantization-specific | `UD-Q3_K_XL` and `UD-Q4_K_S` | both crash |
| Driver version | 596.36 → 597.06 | identical behaviour |
| KV cache in VRAM | `--no-kv-offload` | still crashes, and ~40 % slower |
| Language / diacritics | English, Czech, Czech without diacritics | only length matters |
| Specific words or topic | 7 single-word variants, 4 unrelated topics | only length matters |
| Prompt length in characters | 210–217 chars crash *and* pass | only token count matters |

### Possibly relevant

- **A cached prompt does not crash.** With `cache_prompt: true` a repeated identical request
  reports `prompt 4 tok` and completes normally — consistent with the fault being in prompt
  processing rather than in the graph itself.
- `prompt_n = 94` is two tokens below 96 = 3×32, so a tile/block boundary in one of the `-cmoe`
  kernels looks like a plausible place to look. Not verified.
- Without `-cmoe` we have never seen this crash.
- Reproduced on both `b10639` and `b10742`, so it is not a recent regression.

### Workaround

Make sure the prompt is not exactly 94 tokens — adding or removing a single token avoids it
entirely.

### First Bad Commit

Not identified. Reproduced on b10639 (2026-08-26) and b10742 (2026-09-01) alike,
so it predates b10639.

### Relevant log output

````
$ llama-server.exe -m D:/ollama/staging/Qwen3-Coder-Next-UD-Q4_K_S.gguf \
    -c 32768 -t 6 --host 127.0.0.1 --port 61129 -lm none -np 1 -ngl 99 -cmoe

0.00.350.807 I cmn  common_param: common_params_print_info: verbosity = 3 (adjust with the `-lv N` CLI arg)

0.00.351.686 W srv  llama_server: CORS is set to allow all origins ('*') and no API key is set

items.title: Qwen3-VL: mtmd vision embeddings carry ~5× HF precision-floor noise → reproducible accuracy drop vs transformers (quant/backend/version-independent)
items.author: DobsonDong
items.body_excerpt:
# [DRAFT] Upstream issue for ggml-org/llama.cpp — Qwen3-VL vision-path numeric noise


## Environment
- Models: Qwen3-VL-8B dense fine-tune (LoRA merged, bf16), converted with current `convert_hf_to_gguf.py` (mmproj: f16, also tested f32).
- Runtimes tested: b10707 (Vulkan, 0.7 box), b10909 (CUDA, 52 box), and a build of PR #21103 head on its merge-base (March 2026).
- Test set: 58 real canteen tray photos, verified human GT; metric = exact set match per tray (all dishes correct), soft-menu-prefilled prompts, temperature 0, max_tokens 384, client image side 1024 (and native 1920×1080 for the "original" configs).

## Symptom
| stack | set-exact (58) |
|---|---|
| HF transformers (bf16, training-identical stack) | **31** |
| llama.cpp, original image size (no client resize, ~2025 img tokens) | 28 |
| llama.cpp, 1024-side input (~576 tokens), f16 or f32 mmproj, Q8 or bf16 LM, Vulkan or CPU, b10707/b10909/PR#21103-head | **22–24** |
| llama.cpp, image preprocessed to HF-identical 832×448 (~364 tokens) | 16 |

Reproduction is deterministic. Note the monotone pixel-count effect on llama.cpp (352→16, 576→23, 2025→28) — consistent with per-token feature noise being compensated by redundancy.

## Exclusions (all tested)
- **Quantization**: Q4_K_M 19 / Q8_0 23 / bf16 24 — not the driver.
- **Client preprocessing**: feeding HF-processor-identical pixels (832×448 bicubic) makes it worse, not better.
- **Runtime version**: b10707 ≈ b10909 ≈ March base ≈ PR #21103 head (22–24).
- **Backend**: Vulkan 23 ≈ CPU 22 in the same build.
- **mmproj weight precision**: f32 mmproj = f16 mmproj = 23.
- **Chat template / empty-think prefill**: adding the training-time `<think>\n\n</think>\n\n` assistant prefill: 21–23, no change.
- **mrope**: sections [24,20,20,0] match HF; LLAMA_ROPE_TYPE_IMROPE is selected for QWEN3VL; image position advancement max(nx,ny)=26 matches HF's `max(h,w)//merge`; verified by reading both implementations.
- **Deepstack wiring**: GGUF has `n_deepstack_layers=3`; the 16384-wide input split order [main|ds0|ds1|ds2] verified; injection loop (view at (il+1)*n_embd, added for il<3) reviewed.
- **Vision embedding values**: concat order and per-chunk means/stds match HF to 4 decimal digits.

## Key quantitative evidence (the smoking gun)
Using `MTMD_DEBUG_EMBEDDINGS=1` on the same image (832×448, same pixels both stacks):

- HF *internal* precision floor (same model, f32 vs bf16, vision tower output): `|Δ|mean = 0.0147` (main merger output), 0.0016 / 0.0056 (deepstack outputs).
- HF(bf16) vs mtmd token-0 values: `|Δ| ≈ 0.05–0.15` per element — **≈5× the internal floor** — while global stats (mean/std/min/max/sum over the full [16384×364] tensor) agree to 4 decimal places, i.e. the divergence is zero-mean per-element noise rather than a structural/permutation error.

Conclusion: the mtmd vision path introduces per-element noise ~5× above what the same computation shows internally in HF. Downstream the LLM is sensitive to it (fine-tuned model; accuracy −8/58 @1024), and extra input resolution partially compensates.

## Ask
Please check the vision compute path for precision loss beyond the weights, e.g. f16 intermediate tensors / accumulation order in the vision tower (patch-embed convs, attention, LayerNorm) vs the transformers reference. Happy to run any instrumented build or share the full 58-image benchmark harness/results.

items.title: Misc. bug: llama-server /v1/rerank pastes the document into a query that contains the literal text {document}
items.author: imnecho
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

```
version: 0.6.0-dev (build 11541, commit f2918cabb)
built with Clang 20.1.8 for Windows x86_64
```

The same code is on master at the time of writing (see below).

### Operating systems

Windows

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

llama-server

### Command line

```shell
llama-server -m Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B-f16.gguf --rerank --pooling rank --port 8080
```

The GGUF was converted with `convert_hf_to_gguf.py`, which stores the model's rerank chat template.

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

`format_prompt_rerank` (`tools/server/server-common.cpp`) fills the model's rerank template by text replacement:

```cpp
string_replace_all(prompt, "{query}"   , query);
string_replace_all(prompt, "{document}", doc  );
```

The second call runs over the whole prompt, including the query the first call just inserted. So a query that contains the literal text `{document}` gets the document pasted inside it, and the model scores a different query from the one that was sent.

Steps - one document, three queries:

```shell
DOC='The rerank template is filled by text replacement: the query goes in its place, then the document in its own place, and the whole prompt is tokenized.'
for Q in 'how is the template filled with the document' 'how is the template filled with {document}' 'how is the template filled with {query}'; do
  curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/rerank -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d "{\"query\": \"$Q\", \"documents\": [\"$DOC\"], \"top_n\": 1}" | jq '.usage.prompt_tokens, .results[0].relevance_score'
done
```

Measured on build 11541:

| query | prompt tokens | score |
|---|---|---|
| `how is the template filled with the document` | 112 | 0.99917 |
| `how is the template filled with {document}` | 142 | 0.99978 |
| `how is the template filled with {query}` | 112 | 0.99904 |

The 30 extra tokens of the second query are the document, pasted into the query. A query quoting `{query}` is unaffected.

`format_prompt_rerank` on master still fills the template with the same two calls. The open PR #20009 adds an `{instruction}` placeholder filled the same way, before the other two - so an instruction quoting `{query}` or `{document}` would be filled as well.

Such queries are rare, but they do occur - for example a search over code or documentation that discusses templates. We found this while reading `format_prompt_rerank`, and measured it as above.

**Expected:** each placeholder filled once, and the inserted texts never read again - for example, locate each placeholder in the template first, then build the prompt from the template's pieces and the inputs.

**Workaround on the client side:** break the placeholder in the query before sending it (we put a zero-width joiner inside the braces), so it no longer matches while the query reads the same.

### First Bad Commit

Not bisected.

### Relevant log output

_No response_

Intel Arc Pro B70 (BMG-G31, 32 GB), Ryzen 5 7600X. Compute runtime 26.22.38646.6, IGC 2.36.3, Level Zero 1.28.6.

### Models
unsloth Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_M.gguf (dense, hybrid Gated DeltaNet; weights Q4_K/Q5_K/Q6_K)

### Problem description & steps to reproduce
With `GGML_SYCL_F16=ON` (or `GGML_SYCL_DYNAMIC_PRECISION=F16/BF16`), every answer is one odd token followed by
`!!!!...` (token 0, i.e. NaN logits), at any prompt length, even 124 tokens. Turning off only the XMX fused
dequant-GEMM (`GGML_SYCL_XMX_GATHER_TYPES=0`) gives correct output. Bisected to #29107 (see Regression).

```
ONEAPI_DEVICE_SELECTOR=level_zero:0 ./llama-server -m Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_M.gguf -ngl 99 -fa on -sm none -c 32768 --jinja
# greedy, thinking off: ask it to repeat a code planted in the prompt
```

| Build / env | Output | Prompt tok/s (2K) |
|---|---|---|
| `GGML_SYCL_F16=OFF` (default) | correct to 14K tokens | ~270 |
| `GGML_SYCL_F16=ON` | `!!!!` garbage, every length | ~640 |
| F16=OFF + `GGML_SYCL_DYNAMIC_PRECISION=F16` | garbage | ~290 |
| F16=OFF + `GGML_SYCL_DYNAMIC_PRECISION=BF16` | garbage (so not f16 overflow) | ~290 |
| F16=ON + `GGML_SYCL_XMX_GATHER_TYPES=0` | **correct** | ~540-700 |
| F16=ON + `GGML_SYCL_DYNAMIC_PRECISION=F32` | correct | ~257 |

Also tried, no change: compute runtime 26.18.38308.1 + IGC 2.34.4 (the `.devops/intel.Dockerfile` pin), flash
attention off. `test-backend-ops -o MUL_MAT` passes 2273/2273 on the same build, so the test shapes don't reach this
path (they're small; the failing GEMMs here are K=5120, M up to 248320).

**Regression:** same model, same flags, `-DGGML_SYCL_F16=ON`, each tag built fresh:
| tag | result |
|---|---|
| b11491, b11493 (#29245 adds `fused-gemm.cpp`), b11497, b11540, b11565 | correct |
| **b11635** (parent of 529ac893) | **correct** |
| **b11636** (= 529ac893, #29107 "sycl: IQ3 code reorder") | **`!!!!` garbage** |
| b11684, b11685, b11755 | garbage |

#29107 adds "reorder-aware dequantization for subsequent prefill operations" and touches the mul_mat dispatch in
`ggml-sycl.cpp`. Our guess, not verified in the code: after it, the fused GEMM (#29245) reads Q4_K weights in the
reordered layout as if they were plain (or the reverse). Masking out only Q5_K or only Q6_K
(`GGML_SYCL_XMX_GATHER_TYPES`) still gave garbage; masking out only Q4_K was inconclusive (one run, which hit an
unrelated GPU fault on our chipset-slot card before answering).
Workaround until fixed: `GGML_SYCL_XMX_GATHER_TYPES=0`, or `GGML_SYCL_ENABLE_OPT=0` (untested by us).

### First Bad Commit
529ac893 (#29107)

### Relevant log output
No error is printed; the server returns 200 with the garbage text.

_Measured on our own hardware; the investigation and this write-up were done with Claude Code (Anthropic)._

items.title: Eval bug: Flint NVFP4: tool-call XML remains in reasoning, turn ends with stop (llama.cpp b11823 / OpenCode 2.1.2)
items.author: pozz2906
items.body_excerpt:
## Observed behavior

During an OpenCode coding session with Flint, some assistant turns end after putting literal `<tool_call>read...` or `<tool_call>edit...` XML inside reasoning. OpenCode persists only a reasoning part, `finish: "stop"`, `rawFinish: "stop"`, and no tool part. The requested operation is not dispatched and the turn ends. Nearby turns dispatch tools successfully.

The attached read-only database snapshot identifies 8 assistant messages in one session matching this signature (reasoning-only + stop + literal tool-call XML). This is a scoped signature count, not a measured failure rate or a deterministic reproduction.

## Expected behavior

A tool invocation should be delivered as a structured tool call and executed by the client. If Flint emits malformed reasoning/tool boundaries, please clarify whether this needs a model/template correction or parser handling.

## Environment

- Model: https://huggingface.co/RecursiveSI/flint-nvfp4-gguf
- Revision: `6ec43e19b565fc8d560e2d04985d7724f20673bf`
- File: `flint-nvfp4.gguf`, 22,863,084,160 bytes
- SHA256 (verified at installation): `97cc8009ff9b132d5cf3c488e6767962bb5a5dc158a90ed661bbbddf876b8bde`
- llama.cpp official Windows CUDA 13.4 release b11823, commit `5c19a5a75`; full version output attached.
- OpenCode 2.1.2, OpenAI-compatible provider; `reasoningField=reasoning_content`, `requireReasoning=true`, `maxTokensField=max_tokens`.
- Windows 11 Pro build 26200; Intel i5-12400; about 96 GiB RAM; 2 x RTX 5060 Ti (16311 MiB each), NVIDIA driver 610.88. Exact collected hardware data attached.
- Context 131072, one slot, batch 1024 / microbatch 256, GPU layer split 1:1, f16 KV, Flash Attention on.
- Sampling: temperature 1.0, top_p 0.95, top_k 20, min_p 0, repeat_penalty 1.0.
- CLI: `--jinja --reasoning on --reasoning-format deepseek --reasoning-preserve`; complete arguments in `config/server.json`.

## Captured example

Message `msg_1655ce382001ZtoCWEtydF346P`, created 2026-10-22T20:45:48.808000+00:00. This is **OpenCode's stored normalized message**, not a raw HTTP/SSE capture. Its reasoning tail (home directory redacted):

```text
tus="trash"). Actually loadTrash is also called from purgeTask: `await loadTrash(); toast(...)` — there renderBoard isn't needed but harmless? If filters.status is "trash", renderBoard would re-render trash — fine. If not, it'd render board — harmless.

Simplest: add `renderBoard();` at end of loadTrash.

Alternatively change the handler to:
```js
if (filters.status === "trash") { await loadTrash(); await renderBoard(); } else { await reload(); }
```

Better: make loadTrash self-contained: `state.trash = data.tasks || []; renderBoard();`

But careful: renderBoard when filters.status !== "trash" renders board — fine.

Let me edit loadTrash to call renderBoard().

Then test again: click "Корзина" → should show trash with task3.

Let me apply the edit.
[Assistant]: Нашёл причину: `loadTrash()` не вызывает `renderBoard()`, поэтому после переключения видимости обновления не происходит. Исправляю:<tool_call>edit<arg_key>path</arg_key><arg_value>C:\\Users\\USER\\Desktop/Flint-Agent-Test/static/app.js</arg_value><arg_key>oldString</arg_key><arg_value>async function loadTrash() {\n  const data = await api(\"/api/tasks?status=trash\");\n  state.trash = data.tasks || [];\n}</arg_value><arg_key>newString</arg_key><arg_value>async function loadTrash() {\n  const data = await api(\"/api/tasks?status=trash\");\n  state.trash = data.tasks || [];\n  renderBoard();\n}</arg_value><arg_key>replaceAll</arg_key><arg_value>false</arg_value></tool_call>
```

Full stored failure messages and a timeline of assistant finishes/tool statuses are attached. The timeline omits unrelated user messages and tool output bodies. Successful neighboring calls provide a contrast; they do not establish correctness for every request.

## Template and client details

**The chat template's message structure, reasoning markers, and tool-call serialization are unchanged. Only the system prompt text was customized.** The customization adds coding-agent instructions to the system message. The active template obtained from `/props`, the original template extracted from the GGUF metadata, the current on-disk template, and their active/disk diff are attached. The running server predates a small on-disk background-process instruction change; the active template is the relevant one for this session. These files show the system-prompt customization and the unchanged conversation format.

Built-in read/edit/write/shell tools are direct tools; MCP tools use OpenCode's execute/Code Mode catalog. Subagents and built-in webfetch/websearch are disabled. A local Windows shell quoting plugin is installed; it acts when a shell command executes. These failed messages have no dispatched tool part. The global AGENTS.md was empty at setup.

## Reproduction and limits

1. Run Flint with the attached server options and active template, connecting OpenCode with the attached profile (replace USER paths).
2. Perform a multi-turn coding/debugging task with file reads, edits, shell tests and tool results. The observed task concerned a small Python/JavaScript task-board app.
3. Inspect turns which stop without an answer or operation. The observed signature is XML in the reasoning part with no dispatched tool and finish=stop.

`python inspect_and_probe.py` checks the **captured evidence offline**. This was run while preparing the report.
`python inspect_and_probe.py --live --attempts 3` optionally sends a short synthetic API probe and saves raw JSON responses. **That probe has not been run as part of this report, is not the original failing request, is non-streaming, and is not known to reproduce the long-session failure.** It never executes model-requested tools.

items.title: [RFC]: LOCAL_DISK data migration during drain — Options (a) and (c)
items.author: liangxu2000
items.body_excerpt:
### Changes proposed

## Background

Issue [#2817](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/issues/2817) identified that `ScheduleDrainJobTasks` silently ignores LOCAL_DISK replicas because `Replica::get_segment_names()` returns an empty vector for `LOCAL_DISK`. PR [#2834](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/pull/2834) implements a fail-closed safety net (Step 1 in he-yufeng's two-step plan), but the actual migration capability — Step 2 — remains unimplemented.

This RFC follows up on [#2817](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/issues/2817) and the fail-closed fix in [#2834](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/pull/2834), proposing a concrete plan for Step 2 — actual LOCAL_DISK migration during drain.

It evaluates two viable approaches:
- **Option (a)**: Targeted file transfer — `BatchLoad` → `TransferWrite` → `BatchOffload`
- **Option (c)**: Model LOCAL_DISK as a `NoFSegment`-style allocator-managed resource

Option (b) (drop LOCAL_DISK and re-offload on target) is excluded because LOCAL_DISK data is **not recomputable** for some use cases.

---

## Current State: LOCAL_DISK in the Drain Flow

```
Drain Job
  └─> ScheduleDrainJobTasks()
        └─> GetReplicaSegmentNames()
              └─> LOCAL_DISK → empty vector  ← structurally invisible
        └─> CreateMoveTask() — only for MEMORY replicas
  └─> Client::Move()
        └─> ExecuteReplicaTransfer()
              └─> if (!source.is_memory_replica()) → INVALID_PARAMS ← hard rejection
```

Both the scheduling and execution paths structurally exclude LOCAL_DISK replicas.

---

## Option (a): Targeted File Transfer

### Approach

```
Data:  source SSD  ────→  source RAM  ────→  target RAM  ────→  target SSD
Action:          BatchLoad        TransferWrite      BatchOffload
```

Three building blocks already exist in the codebase:
- **`BatchLoad`**: Reads data from local SSD files into staging buffers (all four storage backends).
- **`TransferWrite`** (TransferEngine): RDMA/TCP transfer from a local buffer to a remote MEMORY replica.
- **`BatchOffload`**: Writes data from memory buffers to local SSD on the target node.

The Promotion path (`ProcessPromotionTasks`) already proves the first two steps work together:
`AllocateBatch() → BatchLoad() → TransferWrite()`.

### What Already Exists

| Component | Location | Status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| BatchLoad (SSD → RAM) | `storage_backend.cpp` | ✅ 4 backends |
| TransferWrite (RDMA/TCP) | `transfer_task.cpp:981` | ✅ generic buffer support |
| BatchOffload (RAM → SSD) | `storage_backend.cpp` | ✅ 3 backends |
| Promotion: BatchLoad → TransferWrite | `file_storage.cpp:728` | ✅ proven pattern |

### What Needs to Be Built

1. **`Client::ExecuteReplicaTransfer()`** — lift the `is_memory_replica()` restriction (client_service.cpp:3182). Add a LOCAL_DISK path:
   ```
   if (source.is_local_disk_replica()) {
       allocate staging buffer;
       BatchLoad(slices);                 // SSD → staging buffer
       TransferWrite(target, slices);     // staging buffer → target MEMORY replica
       release staging buffer;
   }
   ```

2. **`MasterService::ScheduleDrainJobTasks()`** — recognize LOCAL_DISK replicas as drainable (currently excluded via `get_segment_names()` returning empty). Generate move units for keys that have only LOCAL_DISK replicas on the draining segment.

3. **Staging buffer management** — reuse the existing `client_buffer_allocator_` (same pool used by Promotion). With `local_buffer_size` as hard cap, failures trigger GC retry, then skip. Concurrency is naturally bounded by `max_concurrency` (default 4).

4. **Source LOCAL_DISK cleanup** — after successful migration, delete the source `.bucket`/`.meta` entries. This requires a new cleanup path (MEMORY replicas use `discarded_replicas_` with delayed release; LOCAL_DISK has no equivalent).

5. **Deduplication** — a key may have both MEMORY and LOCAL_DISK replicas on the draining node. When both need to move, transferring both wastes bandwidth (LOCAL_DISK data is a superset of MEMORY data). Optimization: if a MEMORY replica exists for the same key on the same node, use the existing zero-copy TransferWrite path and skip the BatchLoad for LOCAL_DISK.

### Considerations

| Concern | Analysis |
| --- | --- |
| **Staging buffer OOM** | Buffer pool has O(n) hard cap. GC + retry on failure. Same risk profile as Promotion. |
| **Duplicate transfer** | Can be addressed by preferring MEMORY replica over LOCAL_DISK when both exist on same node. |
| **Source cleanup** | New path required. MEMORY replicas use `discarded_replicas_` (10-min delayed release). LOCAL_DISK cleanup is simpler — just delete the files. |
| **Concurrent drain pressure** | `max_concurrency=4` per drain job + 500ms scheduling interval provides natural throttling. |

### Estimation

- **Core change**: ~200–300 lines in `client_service.cpp` (new LOCAL_DISK branch in `ExecuteReplicaTransfer`, following the Promotion pattern)
- **Drain scheduling**: ~50–100 lines in `master_service.cpp` (recognize LOCAL_DISK replicas)
- **Cleanup**: ~50–100 lines (delete LOCAL_DISK entries after successful move)
- **Total**: moderate effort, low architectural risk

---

## Option (c): Model LOCAL_DISK as NoFSegment

### Approach

Treat LOCAL_DISK as a block-addressable resource managed by a `BufferAllocator`, similar to how NoF (NVMe-oF) segments work. This would allow LOCAL_DISK replicas to participate in the existing `REPLICA_MOVE` primitive (allocator-to-allocator copy).

### Why This Requires Architectural Changes

**1. Storage model mismatch — files vs blocks**

```
LOCAL_DISK (current):             NoF (what option c requires):
┌─────────────────────┐           ┌─────────────────────┐
│ File system         │           │ NVMe namespace       │
│  bucket_1.bucket    │           │  base=0              │
│  bucket_2.bucket    │           │  offset=4096 (LBA 8) │
│  .meta              │           │  offset=8192         │
│ Addressing: path    │           │ Addressing: LBA      │
│ I/O: op

items.title: [RFC]: TENT-Native UB/URMA Transport
items.author: zchuango
items.body_excerpt:
### Changes proposed

## Summary

This RFC proposes adding a **TENT-native UB transport** backed by the openEuler UMDK URMA APIs.

The goal is to make UB a first-class TENT transport whose runtime-facing interfaces and architectural responsibilities are aligned with the existing TENT RDMA transport.

The intended data path is:

```text
TENT Request
    → UbTask / UbSlice
    → TENT UB Workers
    → UbContext / UbEndpoint / UbJfc
    → URMA Adapter
    → liburma
```

TENT owns task scheduling, slicing, endpoint lifecycle, telemetry, cancellation, and failure recovery. The URMA adapter is limited to native resource management and URMA API translation.

The initial hardware scope is **host DRAM-to-DRAM transfer**. Additional memory types should be enabled only after their registration, topology, and access semantics have been validated.

---

## Related Work

UB/URMA support was previously introduced for the classic Mooncake Transfer Engine in #1773, #1805, and #1855. That work established the underlying URMA device, memory-registration, endpoint, build, mock, and testing capabilities.

This RFC builds on that foundation but focuses on a different architectural scope: implementing UB as a TENT-native transport with TENT-owned tasks, slices, workers, endpoint lifecycle, scheduling signals, cancellation, and failure recovery.

---

## Motivation

TENT provides transport-independent runtime capabilities such as:

- transport selection;
  
- task and slice lifecycle management;
  
- admission control and priority scheduling;
  
- cancellation;
  
- receiver-side credits;
  
- runtime bandwidth estimation;
  
- path failover and health monitoring.
  

To participate fully in this model, UB should expose the same logical capabilities as TENT RDMA.

A native implementation allows the TENT scheduler to observe UB runtime information such as:

- UB device availability;
  
- Jetty and remote-path health;
  
- JFC completion pressure;
  
- outstanding requests and inflight bytes;
  
- estimated bandwidth;
  
- endpoint generations;
  
- timeout and error statistics.
  

---

## Proposed Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    APP[Application / Store] --> RT[TENT Runtime]

    RT --> AQ[Admission Queue]
    AQ --> TS[Transport Selector]
    TS --> RC[Receiver Credit Gate]

    RC --> UB[UbTransport]
    UB --> WK[UbTask / UbSlice / Workers]

    WK --> PS[Device and Path Selection]
    PS --> CTX[UbContext]
    PS --> ES[EndpointStore]

    ES --> EP[UbEndpoint]
    CTX --> JFC[UbJfc]

    CTX --> UA[URMA Adapter]
    EP --> UA
    JFC --> UA
    UA --> LIB[liburma / UMDK]

    JFC --> TM[Telemetry and Health]
    TM --> WK
    TM --> AQ
```

The main architectural boundary is:

> TENT owns scheduling and policy. The URMA adapter owns only native URMA operations and resource lifetime.

---

## Alignment with TENT RDMA

The UB implementation should follow the same logical decomposition and public semantics as TENT RDMA.

| TENT RDMA | Proposed TENT UB |
| --- | --- |
| `RdmaTransport` | `UbTransport` |
| `RdmaSubBatch` | `UbSubBatch` |
| `RdmaTask` | `UbTask` |
| `RdmaSlice` | `UbSlice` |
| `RdmaContext` | `UbContext` |
| `RdmaCQ` | `UbJfc` |
| `RdmaEndPoint` | `UbEndpoint` |
| QP  | Jetty |
| CQ  | JFC |
| MR  | URMA target segment |
| GID | EID |
| `ibv_post_send()` | `urma_post_jetty_send_wr()` |
| `ibv_poll_cq()` | `urma_poll_jfc()` |

The TENT-facing interfaces and state semantics should remain consistent, while native URMA terminology should be preserved inside the transport.

---

## TENT Transport Interface

`UbTransport` should directly implement the common TENT transport operations:

```text
install()
uninstall()

allocateSubBatch()
freeSubBatch()

submitTransferTasks()
getTransferStatus()

addMemoryBuffer()
removeMemoryBuffer()

getEstimatedBandwidth()

supportsCancellation()
cancelTransferTask()
```

Notification support may remain disabled initially until a native UB notification path is implemented.

TENT runtime code should not directly depend on URMA handles such as:

```text
urma_jetty_t
urma_jfc_t
urma_target_seg_t
```

---

## Proposed File Layout

```text
mooncake-transfer-engine/tent/
├── include/tent/transport/ub/
│   ├── ub_transport.h
│   ├── context.h
│   ├── jfc.h
│   ├── endpoint.h
│   ├── endpoint_store.h
│   ├── slice.h
│   ├── workers.h
│   ├── buffers.h
│   ├── rail_monitor.h
│   ├── quota.h
│   ├── params.h
│   └── urma_adapter.h
│
└── src/transport/ub/
    ├── CMakeLists.txt
    ├── ub_transport.cpp
    ├── context.cpp
    ├── jfc.cpp
    ├── endpoint.cpp
    ├── endpoint_store.cpp
    ├── workers.cpp
    ├── buffers.cpp
    ├── rail_monitor.cpp
    ├── quota.cpp
    └── urma_adapter.cpp
```

The first implementation does not need to complete every optional scheduling feature, but the module boundaries should support later extensions without redesigning the data path.

---

## URMA Adapter Boundary

The URMA adapter should only expose low-level operations:

- URMA initialization and shutdown;
  
- device and EID discovery;
  
- context creation and destruction;
  
- asynchronous event FD exposure;
  
- local segment registration;
  
- remote segment import;
  
- JFC/JFCE creation and polling;
  
- Jetty creation, import, bind, reset, quiesce, and destruction;
  
- READ/WRITE work-request submission.
  

It should not contain:

- TENT task scheduling;
  
- slice spraying;
  
- receiver-credit policy;
  
- transport selection;
  
- retry policy;
  
- admission control;
  
- rail-health decisions.
  

Full URMA asynchronous-event consumption and acknowledgement may be added later if required by the provider and recovery model.

---

## Endpoint Lifecycle

At the conceptual level, UB endpoints should follow the same forward-only lifecycle semantics as TENT RDMA:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> UNINIT
    UNINIT --> HANDSHAKING
    HANDSHAKING --> READY
    HANDSHAKING --> DESTROYING
    READY --> DESTROYING
    DESTROYING --> DESTROYED
    DESTROYED --> [*]
```

items.title: [RFC]: Unify Mooncake's Python package, build, and release architecture
items.author: Aionw
items.body_excerpt:
### Changes proposed

## Summary

Establish `python/mooncake` as the single source of truth for all tracked Python code distributed as the `mooncake` import package.

Use `scikit-build-core` as the single PEP 517 build backend. It will combine tracked Python sources with native artifacts supplied through explicit CMake install rules, without copying generated files into the source tree.

Use `cibuildwheel` as the standard release-wheel execution layer for supported manylinux variants. Hardware-specific builders may retain specialized runners and toolchains, but must consume the same PEP 517 backend and produce the same validated artifact contract.

This RFC also defines:

- subsystem-oriented Python module boundaries;
- private native extension modules behind stable public Python facades;
- explicit core, optional, development, and hardware dependency groups;
- isolated installed-wheel validation;
- a checked invariant between Git tags, package metadata, and wheel metadata;
- centralized publication to PyPI and GitHub Releases;
- independently retryable hardware-specific release variants.

Distribution names such as `mooncake-transfer-engine` and its hardware variants remain unchanged. The installed import package remains `mooncake`.

Background and a detailed walkthrough are available in [Mooncake Python Packaging Refactor](https://aionw.github.io/posts/mooncake-python-package-refactoring/).

## Relationship to existing RFCs

This proposal overlaps with two existing RFCs:

- #3425, **Refactor the `mooncake-wheel` package layout**, identifies the same fragmented Python source layout and build-time copying problems. Its target architecture keeps `mooncake-wheel/mooncake` as the source root and retains public native module names. This proposal goes further by introducing `python/mooncake` as a source-only package root, private native extensions, `scikit-build-core`, explicit dependency groups, and installed-wheel validation. If accepted, this RFC should supersede the narrower target architecture in #3425.

- #3130, **Release Branch Workflow for Stable Releases**, overlaps with the release-validation part of this proposal. It focuses on release branches and TestPyPI validation, while this RFC defines the package build contract, artifact identity, wheel validation, and centralized publication. The two proposals are complementary: #3130 may define how a release commit is selected and stabilized, while this RFC defines how that commit becomes validated and published Python distributions.

## Motivation

### Python has no single source root

Tracked Python code currently lives under several component directories, including:

- `mooncake-wheel/mooncake`;
- `mooncake-integration`;
- `mooncake-reshard/python/mooncake`;
- EP and PG component directories.

Whether a Python file enters the wheel can depend on imperative copy logic in `scripts/build_wheel.sh`. Development and tests may consequently import a different file from the one installed from a wheel.

### The source package is also used as a staging directory

Wheel construction copies shared libraries, executables, metadata, and Python files into the tracked package directory. Interrupted or consecutive variant builds can leave stale or variant-specific artifacts in the source tree.

A source directory should not also be a mutable wheel assembly workspace.

### Module boundaries no longer match subsystem boundaries

The package root currently contains Store utilities, structured object storage, EP helpers, services, SSD administration, command-line entry points, and framework integrations.

Large modules such as `structured_object_store.py` combine models, manifests, serialization, buffer management, transport behavior, and optional codecs. The flat layout obscures ownership and allows optional dependencies to leak into core imports.

### Dependencies are implicit

Different modules use NumPy, PyTorch, Pillow, msgspec, ZeroMQ, FastAPI, httpx, Paramiko, vLLM, and hardware runtimes.

Making all of them mandatory would produce an unnecessarily large core installation. Leaving them undeclared produces incomplete environments and late `ModuleNotFoundError` failures.

### Release artifacts need one checked identity

Actions artifacts, PyPI distributions, and GitHub Release assets serve different purposes, but they must refer to the same immutable source and package version.

The build and publication workflows should check this explicitly rather than derive similar version strings independently.

## Design principles

1. All tracked Python package code lives under `python/mooncake`.
2. PEP 517 is the only public Python build interface.
3. Generated files never enter tracked Python source directories.
4. Public API modules are stable Python facades; native filenames are private implementation details.
5. Core imports do not load unrelated integrations or hardware runtimes.
6. Release gates test an installed wheel outside the source tree.
7. Git tags, `pyproject.toml`, and wheel metadata must agree.
8. Builders build and validate; only a centralized publisher may publish.
9. Obsolete source locations, namespace extensions, staging scripts, and internal import paths are removed rather than retained as compatibility layers.

## Proposed repository layout

```text
Mooncake/
  pyproject.toml

  python/
    pyrightconfig.json

    mooncake/
      __init__.py

      engine/
        __init__.py
        shared_segment.py

      store/
        __init__.py
        async_client.py
        buffer_pool.py
        config.py
        structured/
          __init__.py
          api.py
          models.py
          manifest.py
          transport.py
          buffer.py
          codecs/

      ep/
        __init__.py
        buffer.py
        elastic_buffer.py

      pg/
        __init__.py

      reshard/
        __init__.py
        contracts/
        weight/

      allocators/
      integrations/
        dataproto/
        vllm/
      services/
      ssd/
      cli/

items.title: [RFC]: [Store] Add object storage as a first-class replica tier
items.author: particle128
items.body_excerpt:
### Changes proposed # [RFC]: [Store] Add object storage as a first-class replica tier This proposal introduces object storage as a first-class replica tier, reusing the [existing OSS adapter](https://kvcache-ai.github.io/Mooncake/design/store/oss-backend.html). The new types, configuration options, and protocol extensions below are proposed changes. ## 1. Goals and scope The current object storage integration follows the FileStorage / LOCAL_DISK path: the MEMORY owner performs uploads, and reads also depend on that owner. This proposal introduces an `OBJECT_STORAGE` replica alongside MEMORY, LOCAL_DISK, DFS, and NOF_SSD: - The Master manages object locations, replica states, and lifecycle; Clients access shared object storage directly using descriptors. - The Master configures one of three write modes: synchronous writes, asynchronous replication after a memory write, or direct offload on memory eviction. - Object replicas support deletion and background reclamation. - Once an object replica is committed, other Clients can read it even after the original writer/owner goes offline. The initial implementation reuses the OSS adapter while keeping the interface provider-neutral. Each Mooncake object maps to one backend object. Object aggregation, cascading MEMORY → SSD → object storage, a unified redesign of all external storage tiers, and general idempotency enhancements to the shared Start/End/Revoke protocol are out of scope. ## 2. Architecture ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph MP["Master process"] M["Object directory, write mode, lease / pin"] M --> D["Existing MEMORY / LOCAL_DISK / DFS / NOF_SSD"] M --> O["New OBJECT_STORAGE
object_key + object_size"] M --> G["Pending deletions / retries
Existing background maintenance"] G -->|"DELETE after protection ends"| GA["ObjectStorageAdapter
Master-side instance"] end C["Requesting Client / SDK"] <-->|"PutStart / PutEnd / Query"| M C -->|"Synchronous writes / direct reads"| B["ObjectStorageBackend"] W["MEMORY owner
Offload executor"] -. "Fetch tasks / report completion" .-> M W -->|"Background upload from MEMORY"| B B --> A["ObjectStorageAdapter
Client-side GetBatch / PutBatch"] A --> S["Shared object storage"] GA --> S classDef added fill:#fff0d6,stroke:#d97706,stroke-width:2px; class O,B,G added; ``` - Backends and adapters are in-process modules, with separate instances in each participating process. The Master does not carry object GET/PUT data traffic, but uses its own adapter for background DELETE operations. - Deletion and retries reuse the Master's existing background maintenance mechanism, without requiring a dedicated GC thread or service. Only known pending deletions are processed; the entire bucket is not scanned. - Both background modes reuse the owner's offload queue, heartbeat, and source-replica protection, extending them with an object-storage target and completion reporting. Reads no longer depend on the owner after the object replica is committed. - As with DFS, the Master manages replicas while Clients access shared storage directly. Objects are addressed by key, without file-offset allocation or inheritance from the DFS allocator interface. ## 3. Metadata and configuration ### 3.1 Replica descriptor ```cpp struct ObjectStorageDescriptor { std::string object_key; uint64_t object_size; }; // Added to ReplicateConfig size_t os_replica_num{0}; ``` `ObjectStorageDescriptor` is added to the existing `Replica::Descriptor::descriptor_variant`. Replica `id` and `status` remain in the shared outer descriptor rather than being duplicated in the object descriptor. Enabling object replicas requires support in the Master and all participating Clients. The initial implementation does not promise mixed-version operation with older releases. - `os_replica_num` initially supports 0 or 1, defaulting to 0. A value of 1 requests one object replica according to the Master's policy. It is neither the object service's internal replication factor nor an indication that the replica is already complete. - The initial write requires at least one MEMORY replica. After the object replica is committed, MEMORY replicas may be evicted under the normal protection rules. - `object_key` is a backend object name allocated by the Master, separate from the application's key. The adapter handles prefixes and encoding. - Upsert, Put after Remove, and reallocation after abandoning an old task use new object names, so late uploads or old deletion tasks cannot affect new data. Ordinary retries of the same task reuse its `object_key`. This does not introduce a user-facing multi-version KV API. - Existing shared object-checksum metadata is reused; provider ETags are not treated as a generic content checksum. Using a separate object name isolates successive values of the same application key. For example, if `Put(K)` follows `Remove(K)` before the old background DELETE finishes, using K for both backend objects would let the delayed DELETE remove the new data. The Master maps the application key to an `object_key`, so old tasks operate only on the old object. The same isolation applies to Upsert and late uploads. ### 3.2 Cluster-wide backend configuration Initially, each cluster uses a single object storage backend. The Master publishes non-secret configuration to Clients: provider, endpoint, bucket/namespace, and prefix. Clients fetch and cache it during initialization. The Master uses the same storage target for reclamation; descriptors do not duplicate this configuration. An object's full location is **the cluster-wide endpoint / bucket / prefix plus `object_key`**. Client-side and Master-side adapters use credentials configured in their respective processes, reusing the existing OSS environment variables without introducing a credential service: ```text MOONCAKE_OSS_ACCESS_KEY_ID MOONCAKE_OSS_ACCESS_KEY_SECRET MOONCAKE_OSS_SECURITY_TOK

items.title: [Testing] _concurrent may report success when a child process is terminated by a signal
items.author: zh301
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

`_concurrent()` in `python/triton/_test_runner.py` can return a successful status even when one of its child processes is terminated by a signal.

The function currently aggregates child return codes using `max()`:

```python
def _concurrent(commands):
    processes = [subprocess.Popen(command, cwd=cwd, env=environment) for command, cwd, environment in commands]
    return max(process.wait() for process in processes)
```

On POSIX systems, `subprocess.Popen.wait()` returns a negative value when a process is terminated by a signal. For example, a process terminated by `SIGTERM` returns `-15`.

Therefore, if one child exits successfully with `0` and another is terminated by `SIGTERM` with `-15`, the aggregate result is:

```python
max(0, -15) == 0
```

The caller consequently treats the concurrent test run as successful, even though one of the test processes was terminated.

## Minimal reproducer

Save the following as `repro_concurrent_signal.py` in the root of a Triton source checkout:

```python
import os
import signal
import sys

from triton._test_runner import _concurrent


cwd = os.getcwd()
environment = os.environ.copy()

commands = [
    (
        [sys.executable, "-c", "pass"],
        cwd,
        environment,
    ),
    (
        [
            sys.executable,
            "-c",
            "import os, signal; os.kill(os.getpid(), signal.SIGTERM)",
        ],
        cwd,
        environment,
    ),
]

status = _concurrent(commands)

print(f"_concurrent status: {status}")
assert status != 0, (
    "_concurrent returned success even though one child "
    "was terminated by SIGTERM"
)
```

Run it from the Triton checkout root:

```bash
PYTHONPATH=python python3 repro_concurrent_signal.py
```

No GPU is required.

## Actual result

The source-level pytest regression test reports:

```text
bug_repros/test_concurrent_signal_status.py:36: in test_signal_terminated_child_makes_concurrent_run_fail
    assert status != 0, (
E   AssertionError: _concurrent returned success even though one child was terminated by SIGTERM
E   assert 0 != 0
```

## Expected result

`_concurrent()` should return a nonzero status whenever any child process exits with a nonzero status, including negative return codes representing signal termination.

The aggregation should not allow a successful child return code (`0`) to hide a signal-terminated child return code (`-N`).

Python documents negative subprocess return codes on POSIX as meaning that the process was terminated by signal `N`:

https://docs.python.org/3/library/subprocess.html#subprocess.Popen.returncode

### Environment details

Triton: source checkout from main, commit 2122e24efc1886bfa36337c1f5b07c47d827b1d4
Python: 3.12.3
OS: Linux, AutoDL container
GPU: Not required
Platform requirement: POSIX signal return-code semantics

items.title: Starting a localization (l10n) effort for LMCache
items.author: quaid
items.body_excerpt:
I'd like to propose we start building a localization community around LMCache, beginning with blog posts and expanding to documentation and other parts of the website over time.

tl;dr – 
- localizing content and software is valuable to all of us;
- we can automate the toil of translation but we need human editors who can review the translations and make sure they are properly localized;
- localization means words and phrases are fixed so the final product makes more sense to a native reader;
- we can use RHLF to improve this process and reduce toil over time.

## What is the problem

We already receive blog posts written natively in Mandarin and English. This is a good thing.

But we also need to localize this content without putting a burden on people. Fortunately this content has completed a technical review before being translated, so the focus can be on fixing idioms and grammar for better understanding by the widest audience.

## Why this matters

Ultimately this is about attracting more users to LMCache, some of whom will become intentional contributors over time.

Twenty-five years ago, localization (l10n) projects were one of the main ways Linux distributions and communities like the Fedora Project made headway into new parts of the world. It usually wasn't a corporate initiative. It was people who were enthusiastic about bringing free and open source software to their fellow country members, and who put in the effort to translate strings and make the software make sense locally. That work produced translations AND collaborations. It grew contributors, built regional communities, and carried the free software and open source ethos into places it hadn't reached before.

LMCache has users and watchers all over the world, and there are almost certainly people already adjacent to this project who could help bring information and education about the software to their local communities.

## What I'm proposing

We form loosely as `l10n-sig` out of anyone who wants to be an editor and approver for one or more languages. Languages get added when someone steps forward to take one. Rather than announcing a target list and hoping it fills in, we start with whoever volunteers.

I'm volunteering to be an editor and reviewer for anything translated to English, and I'd love more help with that role. I'm confident we can get Mandarin covered right away. But what else and how?

Japanese and Korean are the obvious early candidates given where our users are, but the principle is that a language becomes active when a person is willing to own it.

It only takes one person to get things started and be the gravity to bring another language.

As I said above, this isn't only English needing localizing. I currently have an original blog post written in Mandarin that I want to bring into English through this same process. I'd like to stop doing one at a time reviews by asking around in Slack to see who might need a break from creating features or fixing bugs. I'd rather offer the opportunity to people who aren't or can't create features or fix bugs.

Therefore, posts written originally in any language are welcome, and translation should flow in whatever direction it needs to.

## This is not a request for volunteer translation labor

LLM translation is pretty good now, and we should lean on it for the first pass. What we need is a human review step, and there are two kinds of people who can do that well.

The first is someone capable in both the source and target language, who can read the machine translation and confirm the meaning carried over and the tone is right. Not necessarily final-polish copy editing — a human or AI copy edit can always be applied later — just confirmation that it makes sense and reads naturally.

The second, and possibly just as valuable, is someone technical who knows their own language well and doesn't necessarily read the source language at all. Because the models are good enough now, a domain expert can look at a translated technical passage and say "ah, I see what this was trying to say" and correct the terminology so it's actually right in their language. Technical accuracy matters as much as idiomatic flow, and that person is well placed to catch it.

So the ask is much closer to "read this and tell us if it sounds right" than "translate three thousand words."

## How the workflow might look

Initially all of this can be manual, while we work out which models produce the best tone for technical writing in each language and we develop any necessary skills.

Longer term this could be automated — a GitHub Action that sends a published post to a translation model, then loads the result into WordPress as a draft where a translation editor reviews and approves it. It could also live partly outside the repo, with approval happening after the fact rather than as a gate. The goal is to distribute this work rather than make it dependent on a paid staffer, and to remove the need to ask permission before contributing.

If anyone already knows of a toolchain or process for this, please say so. I'd much rather adopt something that works than stand up and maintain our own infrastructure.

## What I'm looking for

Ideas or helping hands for:

- Thoughts on the approach
- Pointers to existing tooling
- Anyone in

items.title: llama : integer type consistency in `llama.h`
items.author: MarcusDunn
items.body_excerpt:
# Feature Description

llama.h should prefer to use `sized` (always) + `signed` (mostly) integers.

# Motivation

The integer types in `llama.h` right now are.

| Count | Type            |
|---------|------------------|
| 33      | `int`              |
| 10      | `int32_t`       |
| 24      | `uint32_t`     |
| 2        | `int64_t`       |
| 2        | `uint64_t`    | 

In #4540 there was a discussion around preferences for integer types on new methods. 

Avoiding `int` makes cross platform code simpler at essentially no cost.
Signed makes arithmetic simpler at the cost of some bits if you need something large.

# Possible Implementation

1. Change all `int`'s to `int32_t`
2. As code changes try to prefer signed integers.

We could also do some higher-impact things, but I'd take the lower-impact slower changes over a large find-and-replace.

comments.author: he-yufeng
comments.body:
Confirmed this chain on current main (12df58c7):

1. On restart the client runs `ReRegisterOffloadedObjects`, which scans the SSD and reports every object through `NotifyOffloadSuccess` (`file_storage.cpp:1216` stamps `transport_endpoint` with the current `local_rpc_addr_`).
2. In `MasterService::AddReplica` (`master_service.cpp:3344`), `HasReplica(fn_is_local_disk_replica)` is true because the dead incarnation's replica is still registered. The `VisitReplicas` update path only matches a replica whose `client_id` equals the reporting one, so the restarted client's report matches nothing and is silently dropped. `AddReplica` returns false and the caller treats the batch as fine.
3. Once the old UUID expires, `ClientMonitorFunc` -> `ClearInvalidHandles` -> `CleanupStaleHandles` removes completed local_disk replicas whose owner is not alive, and the object is erased when no valid replica remains. The files stay on the SSD but the master no longer knows they exist.

One wrinkle for the fix: `master_service_tenant_quota_test.cpp:480` (`NotifyOffloadSuccessDoesNotCountAddReplicaUpdateAsNewDiskUsage`) pins the current drop as intended behavior for the two-live-clients case: client B re-reporting the same key gets deduped and is not charged usage. So "just append the second replica" contradicts a tested design decision.

A direction that keeps that test green: treat the report as an ownership takeover only when the existing disk replica's `transport_endpoint` equals the reporter's endpoint. A restarted client re-scans and reports the same `local_rpc_addr_` its dead incarnation registered with, so the master can retarget the replica to the new `client_id` and charge the usage there. A genuinely different client reports a different endpoint and still lands in the dedup path. The caveat is that this only works when `local_rpc_addr_` is stable across restarts (fixed RPC port, not ephemeral). Is that true in your deployment?

Happy to send the PR if this direction sounds reasonable to @ykwd and @staryxchen.

items.author: raghulchandramouli

## Motivation

Add explicit native SGLang-Diffusion support for [Efficient-Large-Model/Sana_Sprint_0.6B_1024px_diffusers](https://huggingface.co/Efficient-Large-Model/Sana_Sprint_0.6B_1024px_diffusers).

SANA-Sprint is a 0.6B text-to-image diffusion model designed for 1–4 inference steps and 1024px generation. SGLang already has native SANA components, making this a candidate for extending the existing implementation with Sprint-specific sampling behavior.

I searched for SANA-Sprint support issues and PRs and did not find an existing integration. The checkpoint declares `SanaSprintPipeline` and `SCMScheduler`; I did not find either registered in the native implementation. The generic Diffusers backend may already provide compatibility, but I have not verified end-to-end inference. This request is for native support.

## Proposed scope

- Start with the 0.6B checkpoint and plain text-to-image generation.
- Reuse the existing SANA transformer, Gemma2 encoder, and DC-AE components where compatible.
- Add Sprint-specific pipeline registration, scheduler/sampling behavior, and suitable defaults.
- Validate output against the upstream Diffusers pipeline with fixed prompts, seeds, and step counts.
- Add focused tests and a documented launch example.

I would like to contribute an initial implementation. I currently have a Mac, so I can work on the Python integration and small tests, but would need help with NVIDIA GPU validation. Maintainer guidance on whether this scope is useful would be appreciated.

- [Model card and weights](https://huggingface.co/Efficient-Large-Model/Sana_Sprint_0.6B_1024px_diffusers)
- [Checkpoint component configuration](https://huggingface.co/Efficient-Large-Model/Sana_Sprint_0.6B_1024px_diffusers/blob/main/model_index.json)

items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

`Glm47MoeDetector.detect_and_parse` (the non-streaming path) does not strip the function name. When a GLM-4.7/GLM-5 model writes a newline after the name, the call is silently dropped: the response has no `tool_calls`, and `content` is empty.

```
<tool_call>get_weather
<arg_key>city</arg_key>
<arg_value>Paris</arg_value>
</tool_call>
```

`func_detail.group(1)` gives `"get_weather\n"`. `parse_base_json` then rejects it as an undefined tool, and because the whole `<tool_call>…</tool_call>` span was consumed, `normal_text` is `""`. The streaming path already strips the name (`_extract_match_groups`: `func_name = match.group(1).strip()`), so streaming and non-streaming disagree on the same output.

The relevant line is `func_name = func_detail.group(1) if func_detail.group(1) else ""`:
- `python/sglang/srt/function_call/glm47_moe_detector.py` L264 in v0.5.18
- L388 in v0.5.21, v0.5.22 and main

### Impact

With `tool_choice: "required"` or a named tool, a non-streaming chat completion returns `finish_reason: "stop"`, no `tool_calls` and empty content, even though the model did produce a valid call (visible with `logprobs`). On GLM-5.3 with `--tool-call-parser glm47`, about 1 in 4 forced calls dropped this way in our tests (7/30 and 10/30). Streaming the same requests gave 39/40 tool calls; the 40th hit `max_tokens`.

### Reproduction

- SGLang v0.5.18 (also reproduced on v0.5.21 code), `--tool-call-parser glm47 --reasoning-parser glm45`.
- A non-streaming `/v1/chat/completions` with one tool (`get_weather(city)`), `tool_choice: "required"`, and an off-topic prompt ("Tell me a short joke about Paris."). Repeat about 30 times.
- Offline: `Glm47MoeDetector().detect_and_parse("<tool_call>get_weather\n<arg_key>city</arg_key>\n<arg_value>Paris</arg_value>\n</tool_call>", tools)` returns `calls == []` and `normal_text == ""`.

### Suggested fix

`func_name = func_detail.group(1).strip() if func_detail.group(1) else ""`, matching the streaming path. PR to follow.

### Environment

SGLang v0.5.18 (`lmsysorg/sglang:v0.5.18-cu130`) and v0.5.21, 8x B200, GLM-5.3 and GLM-5.3-Flash.

items.title: Questions on Triton basic concepts
items.author: peastman
items.body_excerpt:
I'm just getting started with Triton.  I can't find any documentation on some very basic concepts.  If you can point me to something I missed I'd be grateful.  If not, perhaps someone could answer these questions?

What types of values can be passed to a kernel?  PyTorch tensors obviously, as well as ints, floats, and bools.  Anything else?

The grid is defined by a lambda that takes a single argument called `meta`.  What is `meta`?

How do I access a single element of a tensor?  Say `a` and `b` are tensors and `i` is an int.  I want to write `c = a[i]*b` to multiply `b` by an element of `a`.  That produces an error.  What's the correct way of doing it?

What is the difference between a `tensor_descriptor` and a `TensorDescriptor`?  What is each used for and how do I use them?

What is the exact significance of annotating an argument with `tl.constexpr`?  Does it mean the kernel will get recompiled every time a new value of that argument is encountered?  What can be done with a constexpr value that can't be done with other ones?

How about `tl.const`?  Is it just for error checking, to avoid accidentally modifying something that shouldn't be modified, or does it have other effects?

Thanks for your help!

items.title: LMCacheMPConnector: server deadlocks permanently in _release_entries, holding the GIL and never releasing device memory (reachable from the periodic reaper against a live engine)
items.author: hans-tensormesh
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

When a vLLM worker dies abnormally, the LMCache server's `unregister_kv_cache` path hangs **permanently** inside `_release_entries`. The hang happens in a C call under the GIL, so it takes down the entire server: the HTTP port stops answering, the MQ loop stops accepting requests, and ~388 GB of registered device memory is never released.

The server never recovers. Restarting vLLM does not help — the new engine's `register_kv_caches` is queued behind the stuck handler on the same `mq-server-thread` and eventually fails with `ConnectionError: LMCache server did not respond to register_kv_caches within 300.0s`.

### Environment

| | |
|---|---|
| LMCache | `0.5.3`, commit `f7c0f50259e9c79ede095af9fc945780fb3194b0` (`nightly-3-gf7c0f502`, `dev`) |
| vLLM | `0.26.0` |
| ai-dynamo | `1.4.0` |
| torch | `2.11.0+cu130` (CUDA 13.0) |
| Driver | `595.71.05` |
| Python | 3.12.3 |
| GPUs | 8× NVIDIA B300 SXM6 (275 GB each); TP=4 + EP over GPUs 0–3 |
| Connector | `LMCacheMPConnector`, `kv_role: kv_both`, `lmcache.mp.mq_timeout: 300` |

Server launched as:

```
lmcache server --port 5555 --http-port 8080 \
  --l1-size-gb 1800 --l1-init-size-gb 20 \
  --max-gpu-workers 1 --max-cpu-workers 8 \
  --chunk-size 512 --l1-align-bytes 16384 \
  --eviction-trigger-watermark 0.85 --eviction-ratio 0.10 --eviction-policy LRU \
  --supported-transfer-mode lmcache_driven --shm-name "" \
  --enable-extra-logging --extra-logging-interval 30 \
  --enable-tracing --otlp-endpoint http://localhost:4320
```

### Where it hangs

`py-spy dump` on the wedged server. All 121 threads are idle in `futex_wait_queue` except one, which holds the GIL:

```
Thread 1049209 (active+gil): "mq-server-thread"
    _release_entries    (lmcache/v1/multiprocess/modules/lmcache_driven_transfer.py:763)
    unregister_kv_cache (lmcache/v1/multiprocess/modules/lmcache_driven_transfer.py:947)
    __call__            (lmcache/v1/multiprocess/mq.py:426)
    _call_sync_handler  (lmcache/v1/multiprocess/mq.py:537)
    _call_handler       (lmcache/v1/multiprocess/mq.py:592)
    _main_loop          (lmcache/v1/multiprocess/mq.py:621)
    run                 (threading.py:1010)
    _bootstrap_inner    (threading.py:1073)
    _bootstrap          (threading.py:1030)
```

I sampled this 4× over 30 s and it reported the **identical line every time**, ~70 minutes after the hang began.

Line 763 is `entries.clear()` in `_release_entries`:

```python
748:  def _release_entries(self, entries: list[ContextEntry]) -> None:
...
757:      for entry in entries:
758:          entry.cache_context.close()
759:          self._ctx.layout_desc_registry.unregister(
760:              entry.model_name, entry.world_size
761:          )
762:      del entry
763:      entries.clear()          # <-- stuck here
764:      # ipc_collect() only unmaps a CUDA-IPC-imported segment once its last
765:      # tensor reference is gone (LMCache#4014), hence the clear() above.
766:      torch_dev.empty_cache()
767:      ipc_collect = getattr(torch_dev, "ipc_collect", None)
768:      if ipc_collect is not None:
770:          ipc_collect()
```

`entries.clear()` drops the last references to the `ContextEntry` objects, so the CUDA-IPC tensor destructors run inline during the `clear()` — i.e. `cudaIpcCloseMemHandle` against segments exported by vLLM worker processes that have **already died abnormally**. That driver call appears never to return.

This is the same IPC-refcount area the comment on line 764–765 already flags (referencing #4014), but the failure mode here is the exporting process dying uncleanly rather than a lingering reference on the importer side.

### Impact

Measured on the wedged server:

- HTTP `:8080/metrics` — **3/3 timeouts at 20 s**; the server answers nothing.
- **~388 GB of device memory still held** (129 GB each on GPU 0/2/3, 684 MB on GPU 1) with **no vLLM process alive**.
- Host RSS pinned at 1,802 GB (exactly `--l1-size-gb 1800`).
- Not memory or IO pressure: `/proc/pressure/{memory,io}` all report `avg10=0.00`.
- `SIGTERM` cannot be serviced — recovery requires `SIGKILL`.

Downstream, every in-flight vLLM request fails with `EngineDeadError`, the engine shuts down and is not restarted, and subsequent restart attempts fail at registration:

```
ConnectionError: LMCache server did not respond to register_kv_caches within 300.0s. Is the server running?
```

### Reproduction

1. Start `lmcache server` as above.
2. Start vLLM with `LMCacheMPConnector` (`kv_both`), TP=4 + EP, NVFP4 weights, `--kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3`, `--gpu-memory-utilization 0.92`.
3. Drive sustained load with long prompts (our trace: p50 ≈ 2.2 K, p99 ≈ 67 K, max ≈ 96.5 K input tokens, concurrency ramping 8 → 128).
4. Get a worker to die abnormally (any cause — in our case an unrelated engine fault) so vLLM tears down without a clean unregister handshake.
5. The server wedges in `_release_entries` and never recovers.

Step 4 is the trigger; the specific cause of the original worker death does not appear to matter.

### Suggested direction

- The IPC release path runs synchronously on `mq-server-thread` while holding the GIL. Even without fixing the underlying driver hang, moving reclaim off the MQ handler thread (or bounding it) would keep the server able to answer health checks and reject new registrations cleanly instead of hanging every client for 300 s.
- A watchdog/timeout around `_release_entries` that logs and abandons the segment would turn an unrecoverable wedge into a leak plus a warning.
- Worth checking whether `cudaIpcCloseMemHandle` can be skipped when the exporting PID is known to be gone.

### Full `py-spy dump`

<details>
<summary>All 22 threads (paths redacted)</summary>

```
Process 1049052: <workdir>/.venv/bin/python3 <workdir>/.venv/bin/lmcache server --port 5555 --http-port 8080 --l1-size-gb 1800 --l1-init-size-gb 20 --max-gpu-workers 1 --max-cpu-workers 8 --chunk-size 512 --l1-align-bytes 16384 --eviction-trigger-watermark 0.85 --eviction-ratio 0.10 --eviction-po

items.title: [Bug] Hybrid Mamba/GDN persistence silently stores 1 of N kernel pages on vLLM >= 0.26 (0.5.3, 0.5.4, dev)
items.author: dl4rce
items.body_excerpt:
**Label**

bug, mp

**Describe the bug**

Persistent (disk-tier) KV-cache restore for hybrid Mamba/GDN + full-attention
models in MP mode silently stores and restores only **1 of N kernel pages per
chunk** on vLLM >= 0.26. Restores complete "successfully" with high reported
hit rates but return wrong answers.

Root cause: commit `65c2ae81` ("[Core][MP] Support Mamba/GDN hybrid models
(Qwen3.5) (#3613)") added `_SubpagedAttentionViewEdit` in
`lmcache/integration/vllm/kv_cache_group_edits.py` to re-view subpaged
full-attention (FA) KV at registration time — but the edit only pattern-matches
vLLM < 0.26's **5-dim** KV layout. vLLM >= 0.26 registers full-attention KV as
**4-dim K/V-packed** (FlashInfer in our runs), so no edit rule matches, the raw
subpaged geometry flows into the `kv_layer_groups` compression math, and the FA
group is misclassified as slot-compressed:

- the reserved host object is sized for **one** kernel page instead of
  N = tokens_per_block // slots_per_block pages (25 and 17 in our two configs);
- only the **first** kernel page of each chunk is copied on store and requested
  on retrieve;
- the L2 (disk) tier faithfully persists ~4% of the attention KV with **no error
  raised**. After an engine restart, restores report high external hit rates
  (the Mamba group restores fine) but produce wrong continuations.

`kv_cache_group_edits.py` is **byte-identical** on v0.5.3, v0.5.4 and dev @
`1a430626`, so every version is affected under vLLM >= 0.26. The intended fix
from `65c2ae81` ships in all of them — it just never activates.

On 0.5.3 a second, independent bug compounds this: paging a multi-page FA object
through the single-page GPU staging buffer mutates the shared
`MemoryObj.meta.address` between in-flight async copies, corrupting the host
buffer (~96% zeros, no exception). dev has since hardened that path
(size-mismatch ValueError, immutable staging descriptors), so dev fails loudly
rather than corrupting — but the feature stays broken until layout matching is
fixed.

Refs #4247 (adjacent symptoms, same code path) — this is an independent
confirmation with a root cause and a verified fix.

**To Reproduce**

No special hardware needed — any hybrid Mamba/GDN + full-attention model where
vLLM picks a unified block size larger than the attention kernel page size
(vLLM logs "Setting attention block size … to ensure that attention page size is
>= mamba page size"):

1. Serve a hybrid Mamba/GDN model on vLLM >= 0.26 with LMCache 0.5.3 in MP mode
   (`LMCacheMPConnector`) and an L2 disk tier. Our primary repro: vLLM
   `--mamba-cache-mode align --enable-prefix-caching --max-model-len 131072
   --max-num-batched-tokens 3199 -tp 2` with MTP speculative decoding (3 tokens);
   LMCache server with separate object groups, L1 CPU + L2 local-disk tier.
2. Send a prompt longer than one chunk with a unique fact (e.g. a random 24-hex
   key) buried mid-context.
3. Confirm it stored — the server logs the store, and an immediate re-ask of the
   identical prompt hits cache and answers correctly.
4. Kill vLLM **and** the LMCache server completely, so the next restore can only
   come from the L2 disk tier.
5. Restart both, re-send the identical prompt, ask for the buried fact.
6. Observe: high reported hit rate (95–99%) and a fast "restore", but a
   wrong/garbage answer. Per-chunk md5 of the FA host objects differs between
   store and restore; stored FA objects show zero_frac ≈ 0.96.

Verified on LMCache 0.5.3 + vLLM 0.27.1, hybrid GDN-class model (Qwen3.8, 27B),
TP=2, tokens_per_block=1600 / slots_per_block=64 → 25:1 subpaging. Cross-checked
at TP=1 with a smaller hybrid, 544/32 → 17:1 — same bug, so it is geometry-driven
(tokens_per_block > slots_per_block on an uncompressed `kv_size==2` group), not
TP-, model- or quant-driven.

**Expected behavior**

Step 6 returns the exact buried fact, identical to a cold run with no cache.
Concretely: `_SubpagedAttentionViewEdit` matches the registered KV layout on
vLLM >= 0.26, the registration-time re-view activates, all N kernel pages per
chunk are stored and restored, and a post-restart disk-tier restore returns the
same answers as a cold prefill.

**Screenshots**

N/A (server-side). Evidence available instead: per-chunk/per-rank md5 comparisons
of FA host objects on store vs restore, zero-fraction stats of stored objects,
and the restart-based verification suite below.

**Desktop (please complete the following information):**

 - OS: Linux (server)
 - LMCache: 0.5.3 wheel (also affects 0.5.4 and dev @ `1a430626` — file
   byte-identical), MP mode, LMCache server with separate object groups,
   L1 CPU + L2 local-disk tier
 - vLLM: 0.27.1 (`--mamba-cache-mode align`), TP=2 primary / TP=1 cross-check
 - Browser/Version: N/A

The verification environment was a pristine `lmcache==0.5.3` install plus our
4-file patch only. A local backport of #4600 (`error_block_ids` on retrieve
failure in `vllm_multi_process_adapter.py`) that the box previously carried was
reverted to stock before the run.

**Smartphone (please complete the following information):**

N/A

**Additional context**

We have a working, verified fix as a 4-file patch against the 0.5.3 wheel — no
vLLM changes needed, vLLM's block tables were correct throughout:
https://github.com/dl4rce/lmcache-hybrid-gdn-restore-fix (Apache-2.0;
`patches/lmcache-053-hybrid-fa.patch`, EXPLAINER.md walks the root cause).

Verification (12/12, 2026-08-22): full engine kill + restart, restore from the
L2 disk tier only, exact buried-key answer required. Measured on patch rev 2
(sha256 `ec14d5012…`) applied to a pristine `lmcache==0.5.3` install.

| Context | Restore E2E | Cold E2E | Speedup | Restore TTFT | Cold TTFT | Speedup | Hit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 5k tok  | 2.13 s | 5.62 s  | 2.6x | 1.00 s | 4.95 s  | 5.0x | 97.0% |
| 13k tok | 2.31 s | 13.08 s | 5.7x | 1.58 s | 12.62 s | 8.0x | 98.8% |
| 26k tok | 3.60 s | 27.41 s | 7.6x | 2.72 s | 26.97 s | 9.9x | 98.7% |

Cold-namespace control: 0

items.title: Eval bug: CUDA Q4_1/Q5_1 mat-vec kernels overflow fp16 when multiplying the block offset by the Q8_1 block sum (gpt-oss emits "G", NaN logits)
items.author: denizyuret
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

```
version: 11800 (d454a204e)
built with GNU 13.2.0 for Linux x86_64 (CUDA 12.8, CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=90)
```

Also reproduced on b11538 (79e2e74eb). The affected code is unchanged on current master (b11803).

### Operating systems

Linux

### GGML backends

CUDA

### Hardware

NVIDIA H100 64 GB (MareNostrum 5 ACC), 1 to 2 GPUs

### Models

`openai/gpt-oss-120b` and `openai/gpt-oss-20b`, converted with `convert_hf_to_gguf.py --outtype bf16` (MXFP4 experts kept), expert tensors requantized with `llama-quantize` to Q4_1 (with an imatrix; the fault does not depend on it). Q5_1 uses the same kernel code and should be affected the same way (not tested).

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

gpt-oss with expert tensors quantized to Q4_1 intermittently writes the letter "G" into its replies, typically right after a control token (`<|channel|>Ganalysis`, `<|start|>Gassistant`), which breaks the Harmony parsing in llama-server (HTTP 500, "The model produced output that does not match the expected peg-native format"). Prompt processing is fine; the fault is in decoding, and with `-ub 8` (prompts through the mat-vec kernels too) 26 of 30 replies fail.

**Cause.** `vec_dot_q4_1_q8_1_impl` (and the `vec_dot_q5_1_q8_1_impl` and `vec_dot_q8_1_q8_1_impl` variants) in `ggml/src/ggml-cuda/vecdotq.cuh` compute `dm4 * ds8` with one fp16 `__hmul2` under `FAST_FP16_AVAILABLE`, i.e. `d4*d8` and `m4*s8` in fp16. `s8` is the sum of 32 activation values; gpt-oss has Q4_1 blocks whose offset `m4` reaches -512 (`blk.12.ffn_down_exps.weight`), so at tokens with large activations the product exceeds 65504 and becomes inf; the token's logits are NaN. The MMQ kernels multiply the same scales in fp32, which is why only decoding (and `-ub <= 8`) is affected. The non-fast-fp16 branch of the same function already multiplies in fp32.

**Reproduction.**

- `llama-server -ngl 999`, H100, GSM8K 5-shot chat prompts (`/v1/chat/completions`, about 800 tokens each), greedy: at default batching about 30 % of the 120B replies contain "G" and fail to parse (20B: 2 to 7 %); with `-ub 8`, 26 of 30. Q4_0 experts on the same prompts: none.
- The "G" is deterministic per prompt and position; it carries over within a slot because the NaN position stays in the KV cache.

**Fix (verified).** Multiply the scales in fp32 in the three functions:

```diff
-#ifdef FAST_FP16_AVAILABLE
-    const float2 tmp = __half22float2(__hmul2(dm4, ds8));
-    const float d4d8 = tmp.x;
-    const float m4s8 = tmp.y;
-#else
     const float2 dm4f = __half22float2(dm4);
     const float2 ds8f = __half22float2(ds8);
     const float d4d8 = dm4f.x * ds8f.x;
     const float m4s8 = dm4f.y * ds8f.y;
-#endif // FAST_FP16_AVAILABLE
```

and the same for `vec_dot_q5_1_q8_1_impl` (dm5) and `vec_dot_q8_1_q8_1_impl` (dm8).

Verified on H100 (b11800 + this change): 120B Q4_1, first 30 GSM8K and 30 ARC questions, 0 malformed replies, GSM8K 28/30 (default batching) and 29/30 (`-ub 8`), ARC 30/30 and 30/30; before the fix at `-ub 8`: 3/30 and 3/30 with 26 malformed each. No measurable decode slowdown. I am not opening a PR; the diff is here for whoever maintains the CUDA kernels (there may be a cheaper fix, e.g. keeping fp16 for `d4*d8` only).

A second, independent fp16 overflow affects gpt-oss with IQ1_M/TQ1_0/TQ2_0 experts (the dequantize + cuBLAS fallback), reported separately.

### First Bad Commit

Not bisected; present in b11538 and b11800. The fp16 `__hmul2` scale product is old code.

### Relevant log output

```
W common_chat_peg_parse: unparsed peg-native output: <|channel|>Ganalysis<|message|>We need to compute 17*23. 17*20 = 340, 17*3 = 51, sum = 391. So answer: 391. The user wants "the number only after thinking it through." So just output "391".<|end|><|start|>assistant<|channel|>final<|message|>391
W srv          stop: cancel task, id_task = 0
W srv    operator(): got exception: {"error":{"code":500,"message":"The model produced output that does not match the expected peg-native format","type":"server_error"}}
```
