items.title: S3 storage stores only the tail of a large upload when a multipart part times out, and reports success
items.author: wguo7
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

`S3Storage.put_object()` sends data of 5 MiB or more (`multipart_threshold`) through `multipart_upload()`. That call sits inside a `try` whose `except (OSError, IOError, ValueError): pass` is meant only for the case where the size cannot be determined, as its comment says ([s3.py#L102-L122](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/blob/f3300be0e65f81760ec3b0287aebbf1b638a4d1a/python/aibrix/aibrix/storage/s3.py#L102-L122)).

Several botocore errors subclass `OSError`, through the `requests` exception classes vendored in botocore. In botocore 1.43.115 these include `ReadTimeoutError`, `ConnectTimeoutError`, `SSLError` and `ProxyConnectionError`. When one of them is raised while a part uploads, `multipart_upload()` aborts the upload and re-raises ([base.py#L488-L495](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/blob/f3300be0e65f81760ec3b0287aebbf1b638a4d1a/python/aibrix/aibrix/storage/base.py#L488-L495)), and `put_object()` swallows the error and falls through to a single PUT of `reader.read_all()` ([s3.py#L136](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/blob/f3300be0e65f81760ec3b0287aebbf1b638a4d1a/python/aibrix/aibrix/storage/s3.py#L136)).

The reader has already been read up to and including the failed part, so the single PUT stores only the bytes after the failed part, and `put_object()` returns `True`. The Files API upload ([files.py#L205-L208](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/blob/f3300be0e65f81760ec3b0287aebbf1b638a4d1a/python/aibrix/aibrix/metadata/api/v1/files.py#L205-L208)) then reports a successful upload of a file that holds only the data after the failed part. A batch input uploaded this way is missing every request up to the end of the failed part, and nothing reports an error.

S3 errors that are not `OSError` propagate as expected, for example `ClientError` (an HTTP 500 or AccessDenied on a part) and `EndpointConnectionError`. Open PR #3184 moves the multipart upload out of the same kind of `try` in `TOSStorage.put_object()`. It does not change `s3.py`.

### Steps to Reproduce

The script uses an in-process S3 (moto), makes `upload_part` raise `ReadTimeoutError` for part 2, and calls `put_object()` with 10,486,760 bytes: 5 MiB of `A`, 5 MiB of `B` and 1000 bytes of `C`. Output on main (f3300be):

```
put_object returned True (no exception)
stored 1000 bytes, starting with b'C'; the data had 10486760 bytes, starting with b'A'
expected: put_object raises the timeout and no object is stored
```

<details><summary>repro.py</summary>

```python
"""Run: PYTHONPATH=<aibrix>/python/aibrix python repro.py

S3Storage.put_object(): a read timeout on one part of a multipart upload is
swallowed, and the object is stored with only the bytes left after the
failed part.

botocore's ReadTimeoutError subclasses OSError, and put_object() wraps the
multipart path in `except (OSError, IOError, ValueError): pass`, which is
meant for "cannot determine size". It then falls through to a single PUT of
what the reader has left. S3 is simulated in-process with moto.
"""

import asyncio
import logging
import os

os.environ.setdefault("AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID", "testing")
os.environ.setdefault("AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY", "testing")
os.environ.setdefault("AWS_DEFAULT_REGION", "us-east-1")

import boto3  # noqa: E402
from botocore.exceptions import ReadTimeoutError  # noqa: E402
from moto import mock_aws  # noqa: E402

from aibrix.storage.base import StorageConfig  # noqa: E402
from aibrix.storage.s3 import S3Storage  # noqa: E402

logging.disable(logging.CRITICAL)  # keep the storage logs out of the output


async def main():
    with mock_aws():
        boto3.client("s3", region_name="us-east-1").create_bucket(Bucket="bkt-test")
        storage = S3Storage("bkt-test", region_name="us-east-1", config=StorageConfig())
        real_upload_part = storage.client.upload_part

        def flaky_upload_part(**kwargs):
            if kwargs["PartNumber"] == 2:
                raise ReadTimeoutError(endpoint_url="https://s3.example.com")
            return real_upload_part(**kwargs)

        storage.client.upload_part = flaky_upload_part
        part = storage.config.multipart_threshold  # 5 MiB
        data = b"A" * part + b"B" * part + b"C" * 1000  # 3 parts
        try:
            ok = await storage.put_object("out.jsonl", data)
            print("put_object returned", ok, "(no exception)")
        except Exception as e:
            print("put_object raised", type(e).__name__)
        try:
            stored = await storage.get_object("out.jsonl")
            print(
                f"stored {len(stored)} bytes, starting with {stored[:1]!r}; "
                f"the data had {len(data)} bytes, starting with {data[:1]!r}"
            )
        except FileNotFoundError:
            print("object not stored")
    print("expected: put_object raises the timeout and no object is stored")


asyncio.run(main())
```

</details>

### Expected behavior

`put_object()` raises the error from the failed part, and nothing new is stored under the key. Only an error from finding the size should fall back to the single PUT.

### Environment

- AIBrix version: main at f3300be
- Deployment environment: none. The repro uses `S3Storage` in-process against moto (macOS arm64, Python 3.12.15, botocore 1.43.115)
- LLM(s) being used: none

### Area

Batch

I have a fix with a test ready and will open a PR.

items.title: [Bug]: Two-model draft-target speculative decoding with sampling does not preserve the target distribution (1.2.1, PyTorch backend)
items.author: SeverinVisionary
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

- GPU: NVIDIA L4 (SM89, 23 GB), driver 580.82.07, CUDA 13.0 (Google Colab)
- OS: Linux 6.6 x86_64, glibc 2.39; Python 3.12.3
- tensorrt-llm 1.2.1 (pip, NVIDIA index), torch 2.9.1+cu130, transformers 4.57.3
- PyTorch backend: `DraftTargetDecodingConfig(max_draft_len=3)`, `attn_backend="VANILLA"`, `disable_overlap_scheduler=True`, `disable_flashinfer_sampling=True`, `cuda_graph_config=None`

### Who can help?

_No response_

### Information

- [ ] The official example scripts
- [x] My own modified scripts

### Tasks

- [ ] An officially supported task in the `examples` folder (such as GLUE/SQuAD, ...)
- [x] My own task or dataset (give details below)

### Reproduction

I compared the output distribution of two-model draft-target speculative decoding with the same engine without speculation, on tiny Llama models (V = 8, 2 layers) where the whole output distribution can be counted. The script below needs only tensorrt-llm 1.2.1. It writes its own two random models (bf16), samples 20,000 sequences per arm (40,000 without speculation) from the prompt `[1, 2, 3, 1, 2]` with 4 new tokens, and compares the arms with a chi-square test. It also wraps `TorchSampler._process_draft_tokens_rejection_sampling` to count, per verification, the number of draft tokens K, the number of `py_draft_logits` rows R, and how many accepted draft tokens have probability 0 in their own `py_target_probs` row. The only patch to TensorRT-LLM is a workaround for a separate crash (described at the end).

```
python repro_draft_target.py --out ./repro_out      # about 10 min on an L4 after the install
```

<details><summary>repro_draft_target.py</summary>

```python
"""Standalone reproduction: TensorRT-LLM 1.2.1 two-model draft-target speculative decoding with sampling does not
preserve the target's output distribution.

    python repro_draft_target.py --out ./repro_out            # one GPU; about 10 min after the install

Needs only tensorrt-llm==1.2.1 (with the torch it pins), numpy, scipy and safetensors. The script:
1. writes two tiny random Llama checkpoints (V = 8, 2 layers, head_dim 32) with fixed seeds: a target and a draft;
2. samples N sequences from the prompt [1, 2, 3, 1, 2] (4 new tokens, EOS = 7) at temperature 1 and at top-k 3,
   in three arms, each in its own process (2N draws for `base`):
   - `base`: no speculation;
   - `spec`: `DraftTargetDecodingConfig(max_draft_len=3)`;
   - `spec_keeplast`: as `spec`, with `ModelDrafter._create_draft_request` passing
     `exclude_last_generation_logits=False`;
3. in the speculative arms, wraps `TorchSampler._process_draft_tokens_rejection_sampling` to record, per
   verification, the number of draft tokens K, the number of `py_draft_logits` rows R, the number accepted, and how
   many accepted draft tokens have probability 0 in their own `py_target_probs` row;
4. compares each speculative arm's sequence distribution with `base` (total variation and a chi-square test),
   next to `base` split in two halves as the noise floor.

The only change to TensorRT-LLM besides the `spec_keeplast` patch is a workaround for a separate crash: in 1.2.1,
`ModelDrafter.process_decoded_tokens` calls `generation_logits.squeeze_(0)` on an inference tensor outside inference
mode, which kills the executor thread when sampling with VANILLA attention. The script runs that method under
`torch.inference_mode()`. Nothing else is patched; the run is bf16 with stock kernels.
"""
import argparse
import collections
import json
import os
import pathlib
import signal
import subprocess
import sys
import time

V, EOS, MAX_NEW = 8, 7, 4
PROMPT = [1, 2, 3, 1, 2]
SETTINGS = {"T1": dict(temperature=1.0), "topk3": dict(temperature=1.0, top_k=3)}
N = 20_000
BATCH = 2_000
ARM_SEED = {"base": 1000, "spec": 2000, "spec_keeplast": 3000}  # TorchSampler seed, per arm and setting
FATAL = "[TRT-LLM] [E] Error in event loop"


def make_model(path, seed):
    """A tiny Llama with random weights; lm_head scaled up so the next-token distributions are not near uniform.
    Stored in bf16 with torch_dtype bfloat16: an fp32 checkpoint keeps fp32 activations even with LLM(dtype="bfloat16"),
    and FlashInfer's RMSNorm dispatches fp16/bf16 only."""
    import numpy as np
    import torch
    from safetensors.torch import save_file
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    hidden, heads, head_dim, inter, layers = 64, 2, 32, 128, 2

    def w(*shape, std=0.3):
        return (rng.standard_normal(shape) * std).astype(np.float32)

    sd = {"model.embed_tokens.weight": w(V, hidden, std=1.0), "model.norm.weight": np.ones(hidden, np.float32),
          "lm_head.weight": w(V, hidden, std=1.5)}
    for i in range(layers):
        p = f"model.layers.{i}."
        sd |= {p + "input_layernorm.weight": np.ones(hidden, np.float32),
               p + "post_attention_layernorm.weight": np.ones(hidden, np.float32),
               p + "self_attn.q_proj.weight": w(heads * head_dim, hidden),

items.title: Non-persistent `triton_kernels.matmul` with a fused SwiGLU masks the MX output scales with the pre-activation `N` instead of `N // 2`, silently writing past each row's scales
items.author: Hughshine
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug


**TL;DR.** #8865 fixed the MX scale store mask of the persistent `triton_kernels.matmul` kernel to count scale blocks from the output width `yN = N // 2` of a fused SwiGLU instead of the pre-activation `N` ("there is a bug in mask_n_scale which should use yN (N // ACTIVATION_REDUCTION_N) instead N"), but did not change the same mask in the non-persistent kernel (`_matmul.py`), which still uses `N_MX_BLOCK = cdiv(N, 32)`. There, with an MXFP8 or MXFP4 output, the last output tile of a row also stores the scale blocks past the row's `cdiv(yN, 32)` (up to 3 bytes per row at the default `BLOCK_N = 256`, for example N = 576): onto the first scales of the next row, and past the end of the scale tensor for the last row. Possible fix: count from `yN` in the non-persistent kernel too, as #8865 does in the persistent one.

`test_matmul.py` checks this combination under "swiglu together with mxfp8 downcast", but only for the persistent kernel on Blackwell. The script below runs the non-persistent kernel with N = 576 (yN = 288, so 9 scale bytes per row; the output tile is 128 columns, 4 scale bytes) and leaves 3 spare bytes behind every row of the scale tensor, which nothing should write to. N = 512 is the control (yN is a multiple of the output tile):

```python
import sys

import torch
from triton_kernels.matmul import matmul, PrecisionConfig, FusedActivation, FnSpecs, FnName, Epilogue
from triton_kernels.matmul_details import opt_flags
from triton_kernels.numerics_details.mxfp import quantize_mxfp8_fn
from triton_kernels.swiglu import swiglu_fn

swiglu = FusedActivation(FnSpecs("swiglu", swiglu_fn, ("alpha", "limit"), reduction_n=2), (1.0, 1.0))
quantize = Epilogue(FnSpecs(FnName.QUANTIZE_MXFP8.name, quantize_mxfp8_fn, (), ()), (), ())
M, K = 64, 512
bug = False
for N in (512, 576):  # SwiGLU halves N; one scale byte per 32 outputs: 256 outputs = 8 scales per row, 288 outputs = 9
    n_scale = N // 2 // 32
    a = torch.randn(M, K, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
    b = torch.randn(K, N, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
    scales = torch.full((M, n_scale + 3), 0xA5, dtype=torch.uint8, device="cuda")  # 3 spare bytes after each row
    config = PrecisionConfig(out_dtype=torch.float8_e4m3fn, c_mx_scale=scales[:, :n_scale])
    with opt_flags.scoped_opt_flags_constraints({"is_persistent": False}):
        matmul(a, b, None, precision_config=config, epilogue=quantize, fused_activation=swiglu)
    written = int((scales[:, n_scale:] != 0xA5).sum())
    print(f"N={N}: {written} of {M * 3} spare bytes written (expected 0)")
    bug |= written > 0
sys.exit(1 if bug else 0)
```

Observed on main @6fe3348e6 (exit code 1):
```
N=512: 0 of 192 spare bytes written (expected 0)
N=576: 192 of 192 spare bytes written (expected 0)
```
Expected: 0 for both. Every row of N = 576 gets 3 stores at scale columns 9 to 11, which the row does not have. The stored bytes hold 119, the scale byte the epilogue computes for a block that is entirely padding: masked lanes enter the max as -1 ([_downcast_to_mxfp.py#L45](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/6fe3348e6e907584e07e593ab19a35caee95c37a/python/triton_kernels/triton_kernels/numerics_details/mxfp_details/_downcast_to_mxfp.py#L45)), and `-1 / 448` gives byte 119 in the rounding formula at [L55-L56](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/6fe3348e6e907584e07e593ab19a35caee95c37a/python/triton_kernels/triton_kernels/numerics_details/mxfp_details/_downcast_to_mxfp.py#L55-L56) (`-1 / 6` gives 125, the byte seen with an MXFP4 output). A caller passes a contiguous `[M, 9]` scale tensor, where column 9 + j of row r is column j of row r + 1: the stores overwrite the first three scales of the next row (wrong outputs, see below) and, behind the last row, fall outside the tensor. With the change below the script prints 0 for both sizes (exit code 0). On the 3.8.0 wheel with `triton_kernels` from the v3.8.0 tag the output is identical to main.

<details>
<summary>The same with a contiguous scale tensor and a torch reference (3298 of 18432 outputs wrong)</summary>

```python
import sys

import torch
import triton
from triton_kernels.matmul import matmul, PrecisionConfig, FusedActivation, FnSpecs, FnName, Epilogue
from triton_kernels.matmul_details import opt_flags
from triton_kernels.numerics_details.mxfp import quantize_mxfp8_fn, upcast_from_mxfp
from triton_kernels.swiglu import swiglu_fn

M, K, ALPHA, LIMIT = 64, 512, 1.702, 7.0
SENTINEL = 0xA5


def run(N):
    y_n, n_scale = N // 2, triton.cdiv(N // 2, 32)
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    a = torch.randn(M, K, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
    b = torch.randn(K, N, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
    swiglu = FusedActivation(FnSpecs("swiglu", swiglu_fn, ("alpha", "limit"), reduction_n=2), (ALPHA, LIMIT))
    quantize = Epilogue(FnSpecs(FnName.QUANTIZE_MXFP8.name, quantize_mxfp8_fn, (), ()), (), (), effective_itemsize=6.0)
    # the [M, n_scale] scales, followed by 64 bytes that nothing should write to
    scale_buf = torch.full((M * n_scale + 64, ), SENTINEL, dtype=torch.uint8, device="cuda")
    scale = scale_buf[:M * n_scale].view(M, n_scale)
    config = PrecisionConfig(out_dtype=torch.float8_e4m3fn, c_mx_scale=scale, c_microblock_size=32)
    with opt_flags.scoped_opt_flags_constraints({"is_persistent": False}):
        y = matmul(a, b, None, precision_config=config, epilogue=quantize, fused_activation=swiglu)
    got = upcast_from_mxfp(y, scale, torch.bfloat16, axis=-1).float()
    acc = a.float() @ b.float()
    g, lin = acc[:, ::2].clamp(max=LIMIT), acc[:, 1::2].clamp(-LIMIT, LIMIT)
    want = g * torch.sigmoid(ALPHA * g) * (lin + 1)
    wrong = (got - want).abs() > 0.15 * want.abs() + 0.1  # fp8 e4m3 rounding stays below 15%
    past_end = int((scale_buf[M * n_scale:] != SENTINEL).sum())
    print(f"N={N} (yN={y_n}, {n_scale} scale blocks per row): {int(wrong.sum())}/{wrong.numel()} output elements wrong, "
          f"{past_end} bytes written past the end of the scale ten

items.title: [interpreter] Debug mode is never actually set, so `tl.device_assert` and integer overflow checks silently do not fire as on the GPU
items.author: Hughshine
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug


With `TRITON_INTERPRET=1`, turning on debug mode (`TRITON_DEBUG=1`, `@triton.jit(debug=True)` or `debug=True` at launch) has no effect: the interpreter's options keep `debug=False`. So everything that only runs in debug mode, such as `tl.device_assert`, the integer overflow checks and `tl.expect_zero`, silently does nothing, while the same kernel on the GPU with `TRITON_DEBUG=1` asserts.

```python
import os
import sys

os.environ.update(TRITON_INTERPRET="1", TRITON_DEBUG="1")  # read when triton is imported

import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def assert_kernel(x_ptr):
    x = tl.load(x_ptr + tl.arange(0, 4))
    tl.device_assert(x >= 0, "negative element")


@triton.jit
def overflow_kernel(x_ptr, y_ptr):
    offs = tl.arange(0, 4)
    tl.store(y_ptr + offs, tl.load(x_ptr + offs) + 1)


fired = 0
for name, run in [
    ("device_assert", lambda: assert_kernel[(1, )](torch.tensor([1.0, -1.0, 1.0, 1.0]))),
    ("int32 overflow check", lambda: overflow_kernel[(1, )](torch.full((4, ), 2**31 - 1, dtype=torch.int32),
                                                             torch.empty(4, dtype=torch.int32))),
]:
    try:
        run()
        print(f"{name}: did not fire")
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"{name}: {type(e).__name__}: {e}")
        fired += 1
sys.exit(0 if fired == 2 else 1)
```

Observed on main @23d6832c42 (exit code 1):
```
device_assert: did not fire
int32 overflow check: did not fire
```
Expected, as on the GPU (both kernels with `TRITON_INTERPRET=0` and `TRITON_DEBUG=1` print ``Assertion `negative element` failed`` and ``Assertion `int32 overflow detected for operation add` failed``), and as the interpreter prints once its debug flag is set by hand (`interpreter_builder.options = dataclasses.replace(interpreter_builder.options, debug=True)`):
```
device_assert: InterpreterError: AssertionError('negative element')
int32 overflow check: InterpreterError: AssertionError('int32 overflow detected for operation add')
```

**Root cause.** These checks are emitted only when `builder.options.debug` is set ([semantic.py#L1940](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/23d6832c426e79a9b269d6252b11f17041bd35b5/python/triton/language/semantic.py#L1940)). The interpreter's builder is created once with `InterpreterOptions()` ([interpreter.py#L408](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/23d6832c426e79a9b269d6252b11f17041bd35b5/python/triton/runtime/interpreter.py#L408)), whose `debug` is `False`, and `InterpretedFunction.run` ([interpreter.py#L1668-L1672](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/23d6832c426e79a9b269d6252b11f17041bd35b5/python/triton/runtime/interpreter.py#L1668-L1672)) never sets it, unlike `JITFunction.run` ([jit.py#L737](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/23d6832c426e79a9b269d6252b11f17041bd35b5/python/triton/runtime/jit.py#L737)). Since #4589 (v3.2.0), which moved the debug check into `device_assert`; in v3.1.0 the interpreter asserted.

**Possible fix.** Resolve the flag in `InterpretedFunction.run` as `JITFunction.run` does (`InterpreterOptions` is frozen, so replace and restore it):
```diff
--- a/python/triton/runtime/interpreter.py
+++ b/python/triton/runtime/interpreter.py
@@ -1671,2 +1671,8 @@ class InterpretedFunction(KernelInterface[T]):
         fn = self.rewrite()
-        return GridExecutor(fn, self.arg_names, grid, self.pre_run_hooks)(*args, **kwargs)
+        options = interpreter_builder.options
+        debug = kwargs.get("debug", self.kwargs.get("debug")) or triton.knobs.runtime.debug
+        interpreter_builder.options = dataclasses.replace(options, debug=debug)
+        try:
+            return GridExecutor(fn, self.arg_names, grid, self.pre_run_hooks)(*args, **kwargs)
+        finally:
+            interpreter_builder.options = options
```
Tested on main @6fe3348e6 with `test_debug.py` run under the interpreter (all pass with the change). With it, interpreter tests run with `TRITON_DEBUG=1` that deliberately overflow integers (for example some `test_bin_op` cases) now report the overflow, as they already do on the GPU in debug mode.


### Environment details

Triton: main @23d6832c42 (also 3.2.0 to 3.8.0)
GPU: NVIDIA L40S (the interpreter runs on the CPU; the GPU only for the comparison)

items.title: `@triton.jit` helper names leave out pointer constness and namedtuple field names, so calls that differ only there share one function
items.author: Hughshine
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug


A `@triton.jit` helper called from a kernel is compiled once per argument types, under a name built from the types' `mangle()`, and a second call whose types give the same name reuses the first call's function. Two parts of the argument types are not in that name, so calls that differ only there wrongly share one function:

- **pointer constness** (`pointer_type.mangle`): a helper called with a `tl.const` pointer and with a plain pointer of the same element type fails to compile on main (`'tt.call' op operand type mismatch`), since #11294 gave const pointers their own IR type;
- **namedtuple field names** (`tuple_type.mangle`): a helper called with namedtuples of two classes whose fields have the same types in the same order uses the first class's field names for both, so `t.a` reads the wrong field, silently (3.4.0, 3.8.0 and main).

```python
import sys
from collections import namedtuple

import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def read(ptr):
    return tl.load(ptr)


@triton.jit
def const_kernel(x_ptr: tl.const, y_ptr):
    tl.store(y_ptr, read(x_ptr) + read(y_ptr))  # one const pointer, one plain pointer


AB = namedtuple("AB", ["a", "b"])
BA = namedtuple("BA", ["b", "a"])  # the same field names in the other order


@triton.jit
def diff(t):
    return tl.load(t.a) - tl.load(t.b)


@triton.jit
def tuple_kernel(p, q, out):
    tl.store(out + 0, diff(p))
    tl.store(out + 1, diff(q))


bad = False
y = torch.ones(1, device="cuda")
try:
    const_kernel[(1, )](torch.ones(1, device="cuda"), y)
    print("const and plain pointer:", y.item(), "(expected 2.0)")
except Exception as e:
    print("const and plain pointer: fails to compile:", type(e).__name__, str(e).strip().splitlines()[-1])
    bad = True

one, ten = torch.tensor([1.0], device="cuda"), torch.tensor([10.0], device="cuda")
out = torch.zeros(2, device="cuda")
tuple_kernel[(1, )](AB(a=one, b=ten), BA(b=ten, a=one), out)  # t.a - t.b is 1 - 10 for both
print("two namedtuple classes:", out.tolist(), "(expected [-9.0, -9.0])")
bad |= out.tolist() != [-9.0, -9.0]
sys.exit(1 if bad else 0)
```

Observed on main @23d6832c42 (exit code 1; the compile error also prints the MLIR module to stdout and this to stderr: `error: 'tt.call' op operand type mismatch: expected operand type '!tt.ptr<f32, "constant">', but provided '!tt.ptr<f32>' for operand number 0`):
```
const and plain pointer: fails to compile: RuntimeError error encountered during parsing
two namedtuple classes: [-9.0, 9.0] (expected [-9.0, -9.0])
```
3.8.0 gives `2.0` for the first part (const pointers had the plain pointer's IR type before #11294) and the same wrong `[-9.0, 9.0]` for the second; 3.4.0 gives the same as 3.8.0.

**Root cause.** `mangle_fn` builds the name from the arguments' `mangle()` ([code_generator.py#L32-L41](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/23d6832c426e79a9b269d6252b11f17041bd35b5/python/triton/compiler/code_generator.py#L32-L41)) and `call_JitFunction` reuses a function whose name already exists ([#L1452-L1454](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/23d6832c426e79a9b269d6252b11f17041bd35b5/python/triton/compiler/code_generator.py#L1452-L1454)). `pointer_type.mangle` returns only the element type ([core.py#L728-L729](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/23d6832c426e79a9b269d6252b11f17041bd35b5/python/triton/language/core.py#L728-L729)) and `tuple_type.mangle` only the element types ([#L822](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/23d6832c426e79a9b269d6252b11f17041bd35b5/python/triton/language/core.py#L822)), although both types compare these parts in `__eq__` and the helper's code depends on them.

**Possible fix.** Put the missing parts into the names (`K` as #1340 did `u` for unsigned integers):
```diff
--- a/python/triton/language/core.py
+++ b/python/triton/language/core.py
@@ -726,7 +726,8 @@
         return self
 
     def mangle(self) -> str:
-        return f"P{self.element_ty.mangle()}"
+        const = "K" if self.const else ""
+        return f"P{const}{self.element_ty.mangle()}"
 
 
 class block_type(dtype):
@@ -819,7 +820,8 @@
         return tuple(values, self), cursor
 
     def mangle(self):
-        return 'T' + '_'.join(ty.mangle() for ty in self.types) + 'T'
+        names = self.fields if self.fields is not None else [""] * len(self.types)
+        return 'T' + '_'.join(f"{n}_{ty.mangle()}" if n else ty.mangle() for n, ty in zip(names, self.types)) + 'T'
 
 
 class slice_type(dtype):
```
Tested on main @23d6832c42 by applying both methods at run time: the script prints `2.0` and `[-9.0, -9.0]` and exits 0, and `test_tuple.py` with `test_frontend.py` passes as before (969 passed). The pointer part alone was tested as a source patch on main @6fe3348e6 (`python/test/unit/language` unchanged apart from one new passing test). I did not add the pointer's address space, which `__eq__` also compares; I could not make a pointer with another address space reach a helper call. #12349 is another case of two different helpers sharing one name, from the function's name rather than its argument types.


### Environment details

Triton: main @23d6832c42 (both parts); 3.4.0 and 3.8.0 (namedtuple part only)
GPU: NVIDIA L40S (sm_89); the failing step is in the Python frontend

Happy to turn it into a PR with regression tests for both repros (const + plain pointer to the same helper, and two namedtuple classes with matching field types), crediting you, unless you'd rather send it yourself. I'll test it on an RTX A6000 (sm_86).

items.title: [Bug]: Kimi K3 / MLA unit tests on SM107: two KDA files skip SM107, a cute_dsl_mla routing case contradicts the perf table, and an indexed-pool decode test compares two code paths bit-exactly
items.author: lucifer1004
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

- TensorRT-LLM main @ e88d19ca3b, PyTorch backend
- GPU with compute capability 10.7 (SM107). Item 2 is a host-side routing test (it monkeypatches the SM version) and fails independently of the GPU.

### Who can help?

Related: #19960 (adds the `test_cute_dsl_mla` case below and extends Kimi K3 to SM107), #18599 (the `(96, 1)` entry in the FP8 perf table), #18938 (the KDA decode kernel and dispatch).

### Reproduction

Three test-only problems seen when running the Kimi K3 / MLA unit tests on SM107. They are grouped here to keep the noise down. None of them is a product bug as far as I can tell. Each item lists the fix I verified.

**1. Two KDA test files skip everything on SM107**

`tests/unittest/_torch/modules/kimi_kda/test_kda_cache_soundness.py:57` and `test_kda_prefill_state_parity.py:40` gate on

```python
torch.cuda.get_device_capability(0) in {(10, 0), (10, 3)}
```

with reason "Kimi K3 is supported only on Blackwell (SM100/SM103)". The runtime predicate `is_kda_optimized_supported()` (`_torch/modules/kimi_kda/_kda_kernels.py:66`) accepts `(100, 103, 107)`, and the neighbouring files (`test_kda_decode_op.py`, `test_kda_prefill_op.py`) already gate on it. So on SM107 these two files report 6 and 15 skips and cover nothing.

Fix: gate on `is_kda_optimized_supported()` like the other files. With `(10, 7)` added, `test_kda_cache_soundness.py` gives 5 passed and 1 skipped on SM107; the remaining skip is its own runtime condition, "could not obtain a recycled cu_seqlens tensor ID". `test_kda_prefill_state_parity.py` gives 15 passed.

Related stale comment: the `_has_supported_gpu()` comments in `test_kda_decode_op.py:33` and `test_kda_prefill_op.py:38` still say the predicate "accepts SM100/SM103 only; SM107 takes the FLA fallback".

**2. `test_cute_dsl_mla.py::test_mla_generation_routes_wide_head_fp8_verify_away_from_trtllm_gen[103-96-1-True-False-cute_dsl_mla]` fails independently of the GPU**

```
pytest tests/unittest/_torch/attention/test_cute_dsl_mla.py -k routes_wide_head
E       AssertionError: assert 'trtllm_gen' == 'cute_dsl_mla'
```

The case `(103, 96, 1, True, False, "cute_dsl_mla")` ("Single-token H=96 is unchanged (measured perf-table entry)") goes through the FP8 perf gate. `_PERF_MIN_BATCH_FP8[(96, 1)] = 8` (`attention/backends/fmha/cute_dsl_mla.py:419`), but `_select_mla_generation_fmha` always builds a decode batch of `batch_size = 4` (`test_cute_dsl_mla.py:148`). So the gate rejects CuTe DSL MLA and the selection falls through to the TRTLLM-Gen stub. The code behaves as the table says; the expectation is wrong for batch 4.

Fix: either expect `"trtllm_gen"` for that case (verified: the parametrization then gives 10/10 passed), or add a `batch_size` parameter to the helper and assert `"cute_dsl_mla"` at batch 8, which would test the table entry the comment refers to.

**3. `test_kda_decode_op.py::test_optimized_decode_updates_indexed_recurrent_state_pool_in_place` (all 3 ids) fails on SM107**

```
torch.testing.assert_close(indexed_output, local_output, rtol=0, atol=0)
E       Mismatched elements: 2154 / 21504 (10.0%)
E       Greatest absolute difference: 0.00048828125
```

The test compares two different code paths bit-exactly:

- The "local" reference calls `_run_production_decode(...)` without `ssm_state_indices`. `KimiKDALinearAttention.forward_decode` then routes to `forward_decode_fallback` (`ssm_state_indices is None`), which runs separate q/k/v/g projections.
- The indexed call passes `ssm_state_indices` and takes the optimized path with the fused `qkvg` projection.

On SM107 the two GEMM shapes round differently, by one bf16 ulp on 10% of the elements. That difference then also shows up in the fp32 recurrent state. Each path is deterministic: two local runs are bit-identical. Running the same core output through `_project_output` twice is bit-identical too.

Fix: compute the local reference on the same path with dense indices, so that the test checks only the pool addressing:

```python
dense_indices = torch.arange(batch_size, dtype=torch.int32, device="cuda")
local_output, local_cache = _run_production_decode(
    optimized,
    hidden_states,
    copy.deepcopy(initial_cache),
    slot_indices=dense_indices.long(),
    ssm_state_indices=dense_indices,
)
```

With this, the indexed output and the indexed recurrent state are bit-identical to the reference for `many-dense-pool`, `many-strided-pool` and `compact-dense-pool`. The test then gives 3 passed on SM107. I have not checked whether the two paths happen to agree bit-exactly on SM100/SM103.

### Expected behavior

These tests run and pass on SM107 (items 1 and 3), and item 2 passes on any GPU.

### Actual behavior

On SM107, item 1 skips everything and item 3 fails as shown above. Item 2 fails independently of the GPU.

### Additional notes

All three fixes are test-only. I can put them in one PR.

items.title: [Bug]: DeepSeek-V4.1 vision tower fails on SM107: cuDNN SDPA "No valid execution plans built" during KV-cache profiling
items.author: lucifer1004
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

- GPU: Vera Rubin, compute capability 10.7
- TensorRT-LLM main (`tensorrt_llm/_torch/models/deepseek_v41_vision.py` unchanged up to 0372799d15), PyTorch backend
- torch 2.14.0+cu132 with its bundled cuDNN 9.24.0, NVRTC 13.4.92
- Model: `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash` (`DeepseekV41ForConditionalGeneration`, vision encoder enabled), TP4/EP4

### Who can help?

_No response_

### Information

- [ ] The official example scripts
- [x] My own modified scripts

### Reproduction

`trtllm-serve` on the model above, with the multimodal encoder enabled, dies on every rank while estimating KV-cache capacity, in the dummy image encode:

```
_util.py configure_kv_cache_capacity -> _encode_dummy_inputs
modeling_deepseekv41_multimodal.py encode_multimodal_inputs
deepseek_v41_vision.py -> F.scaled_dot_product_attention
RuntimeError: cuDNN Frontend error: [cudnn_frontend] Error: No valid execution plans built.
```

Standalone (1 GPU, compute capability 10.7, torch 2.14 + cuDNN 9.24), the same shape the vision attention uses for the 8192-patch profiling dummy:

```python
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F
x = torch.randn(8192, 3 * 1024, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
q, k, v = (t.reshape(8192, 16, 64).transpose(0, 1).unsqueeze(0) for t in x.chunk(3, -1))
F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v)  # RuntimeError: ... No valid execution plans built.
```

### Expected behavior

The server starts and image requests are served, as on SM100/SM103.

### actual behavior

Startup fails as above. Only `disable_mm_encoder: true` gets the server up (text only).

### additional notes

Root cause:
- PyTorch 2.14 (CUDA >= 13 builds) prefers the cuDNN SDPA backend on every SM 10.x device, including 10.7, and does not fall back to another backend when cuDNN plan building fails.
- cuDNN 9.24 offers only runtime-compiled engines (eng8/eng10) for SM 10.7 SDPA forward, and all of them fail NVRTC compilation (`CUDNN_STATUS_INTERNAL_ERROR_COMPILATION_FAILED`). This holds for every shape that dispatches to cuDNN (head_dim 32/64/128, BF16/FP16, contiguous or strided), with NVRTC 13.2 or 13.4. cuDNN 9.25.1.1, 9.26.1.1 and 9.27.0.42 provide an engine (eng18) that builds on SM 10.7.
- A try/except fallback in the model is not safe: after a failed build PyTorch caches a null graph for that shape and the next call on the same shape segfaults. Reported upstream as pytorch/pytorch#201420.
- The vision tower's unit tests are CPU-only, and the V4.1 GPU tests (added with #19727) are text-only and do not run on SM 10.7, so CI does not cover this path.

Vision tower forward on one Vera Rubin GPU (full 32-layer tower + aligner, real weights, BF16; 1022x1022 image = 5329 patches / 8192-patch profiling dummy):

| SDPA backend | 5329 patches | 8192 patches |
|---|---|---|
| cuDNN 9.24 (as shipped) | fails | fails |
| FLASH | 30.8 ms | 53.0 ms |
| EFFICIENT | 44.6 ms | 86.3 ms |
| MATH | 260 ms | 567 ms |
| cuDNN 9.27 | 22.8 ms | 35.5 ms |

Against an FP32 reference (the checkpoint's `inference/vision.py`), every BF16 backend has a relative L2 error of 3.5–3.8% at the aligner output (MATH in BF16: 3.7%), so the choice of backend is within BF16 noise.

Proposed fix: on SM 10.7 with cuDNN < 9.25, exclude only the cuDNN backend around the vision SDPA call; leave every other configuration unchanged, since cuDNN is the fastest backend where it works. PR to follow.

items.title: [Performance]: DSpark: DSparkSpecMetadata.prepare() synchronizes the CUDA stream every iteration, defeating the overlap scheduler
items.author: lucifer1004
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

- 4 GPUs, TP4 / EP4 decode server, PyTorch backend
- DeepSeek-V4-family target with the embedded DSpark drafter (`DSv4DSparkWorker`), draft length 5
- `disable_overlap_scheduler: false`, CUDA graphs on (`cuda_graph_config` batch sizes 1–16)
- TensorRT-LLM main: the code below is identical on current main. The measurements were taken on an earlier commit with the same `prepare()`.

### Who can help?

@NVIDIA/trt-llm-torch-spec-decoding

### Information

- [ ] The official example scripts
- [x] My own modified scripts

### Reproduction

Serve a DSpark model with the overlap scheduler and CUDA graphs on. Run single-request decode and profile one rank with Nsight Systems. Then look at the CUDA API calls inside the `_prepare_inputs` NVTX range of a decode iteration.

The cause is in `DSparkSpecMetadata.prepare()` (`tensorrt_llm/_torch/speculative/dspark.py`). On every iteration it resets the scratch row of the rolling-window state by assigning Python scalars to elements of CUDA tensors:

```python
worker._ctx_len[scratch] = 0
worker._valid_len[scratch] = 0
worker._position_initialized[scratch] = False
```

In PyTorch, `cuda_tensor[i] = <python scalar>` wraps the scalar in a CPU tensor and copies it with `copy_()`. That is a pageable host-to-device copy, followed by `cudaStreamSynchronize` on the current stream. `torch.cuda.set_sync_debug_mode("error")` turns each of these assignments into `RuntimeError: called a synchronizing CUDA operation`.

The same pattern is used in three more places, each costing one more stall per request arrival or completion:
- slot release in `prepare()`, when a request has left the batch;
- `_assign_slot()`, on both the reset path and the new-slot path;
- `_seed_context_windows()`: `_position_initialized[slot] = True`.

`_advance_generation_state()` already resets the same scratch row with `.zero_()`, which does not synchronize.

### Expected behavior

`prepare()` runs on the host while the previous iteration's CUDA graph is still executing under the overlap scheduler, so it should not block the host. Writing the constants with `.zero_()` / `.fill_()` enqueues the same writes on the same stream, in the same order relative to the running graph and the next one, without a host sync.

### Actual behavior

Nsight Systems, rank 0, batch 1, inside `_prepare_inputs` of each decode iteration, in code order:

| API | Bytes | Memory | Followed by |
|---|---|---|---|
| `cudaMemcpyAsync` H2D | 4 | pinned | – (`batch_indices`) |
| `cudaMemcpyAsync` H2D | 8 | **pageable** | `cudaStreamSynchronize` **~6.8 ms** (`_ctx_len[scratch] = 0`) |
| `cudaMemcpyAsync` H2D | 8 | pageable | `cudaStreamSynchronize` ~12 us (`_valid_len[scratch] = 0`) |
| `cudaMemcpyAsync` H2D | 1 | pageable | `cudaStreamSynchronize` ~14 us (`_position_initialized[scratch] = False`) |
| `cudaMemcpyAsync` H2D | 8 | pinned | – (`mapping` -> `_batch_to_slot`) |

- **Where the first sync ends:** about 5 us after the last GPU operation on that stream finishes. That operation is the post-graph sampling work, which runs right after the previous iteration's graph.
- **What follows the sync:** the host still spends about 2.2 ms before the next graph reaches the GPU. This covers the rest of `_prepare_inputs`, the eager kernels of the next step and the ~0.37 ms `cudaGraphLaunch` call itself.
- **GPU idle:** about 2.2 ms per iteration, against about 8.8 ms of graph execution.
- **Sync count:** these three are the only `cudaStreamSynchronize` calls in a decode iteration (3.0 per step on average).

So this one implicit sync turns the overlap scheduler back into a serial loop. DSpark does enable the overlap scheduler (`support_overlap_scheduler()` returns True).

### Additional notes

I have a fix that replaces these assignments with in-place `.zero_()` / `.fill_(True)` and adds a sync-debug-mode unit test. I will open a PR that links here.

items.title: [BUG] CuTe DSL >= 4.6: FlashAttention-4 SM100 backward with block-sparse masks spills registers, up to 1.8x slower than 4.5.3 (same kernel source)
items.author: janhuenermann
items.body_excerpt:
### Which component has the problem?

CuTe DSL

### Bug Report

**Describe the bug**

With the same kernel source, CuTe DSL 4.6.0.dev0 and later generate PTX for the FlashAttention-4 SM100 backward kernel (`flash_attn.cute.flash_bwd_sm100.FlashAttentionBackwardSm100`) that spills registers. The spills appear when the kernel is specialized for block-sparse attention with a `mask_mod`. That is the path `torch.nn.attention.flex_attention(..., kernel_options={"BACKEND": "FLASH"})` takes. With CuTe DSL 4.5.3, the same source compiles to PTX with no spills, or almost none. The kernel is at the 128-register cap (512 threads per CTA), so the extra pressure becomes local-memory traffic. On B200 the backward kernel is 22% slower with a sliding-window mask and 82% slower with a document mask. The dense, causal, GQA and native `window_size` specializations of the same kernel are not affected.

This looks like the backward counterpart of #3701 (forward kernel, 4.7/4.8 vs 4.5.1), and it narrows down where the regression landed. 4.5.3 is fine. 4.6.0.dev0 already regresses, and it is the first release whose PTX header says `Based on NVVM 23.0.0` (4.5.3: `NVVM 20.0.0`).

**Backward kernel GPU time**, ms (B200, bf16, head dim 128, 16 heads; median of 50; main backward kernel only, from the torch profiler; a repeat run agrees within 1% for the block-sparse rows and within 5% for the others)

| attention | 4.5.3 | 4.6.0.dev0 | 4.8.0 ¹ |
|---|---|---|---|
| full, batch 2 × 8192 | 2.039 | 2.010 (−1%) | 2.084 |
| causal, 2 × 8192 | 1.121 | 1.140 (+2%) | 1.177 |
| GQA causal (32 q / 4 kv heads), 2 × 8192 | 2.287 | 2.266 (−1%) | 2.366 |
| native sliding window 1024 (`window_size`), 2 × 16384 | 0.714 | 0.713 (0%) | 0.756 |
| **block-sparse `mask_mod`: sliding window 1024**, 2 × 16384 | 0.858 | **1.045 (+22%)** | **1.027 (+20%)** |
| **block-sparse `mask_mod`: document mask** (causal within random-length documents), 1 × 32768 | 1.279 | **2.329 (+82%)** | **2.209 (+73%)** |

The 4.5.3 and 4.6.0.dev0 columns run the same FA4 source (b20, see "Same source" below).
¹ The 4.8.0 column runs FA4 4.0.0b32, the latest release at the time of testing (b33 has a byte-identical backward kernel). FA4 changed between b20 and b32, so this column shows that the regression persists; it is not a clean A/B.

**The same PTX files assembled by one ptxas** (CUDA 13.0, V13.0.88, `ptxas -arch=sm_100a -O3 -v`)

| backward specialization | PTX from | spill stores / loads | SASS instr. | IMAD | STL / LDL |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| causal | 4.5.3 (CUDA 12.9 / NVVM 20.0.0) | 0 / 0 B | 3496 | 242 | 0 / 0 |
| causal | 4.6.0.dev0 (CUDA 13.3 / NVVM 23.0.0) | 0 / 0 B | 3360 | 216 | 0 / 0 |
| sliding window `mask_mod` | 4.5.3 | 0 / 0 B | 3800 | 294 | 0 / 0 |
| sliding window `mask_mod` | 4.6.0.dev0 | 124 / 228 B | 4528 | 703 | 31 / 57 |
| sliding window `mask_mod` | 4.8.0 (CUDA 13.4 / NVVM 23.0.0) ¹ | 260 / 264 B | 4192 | 318 | 65 / 55 |
| document `mask_mod` | 4.5.3 | 28 / 16 B | 4512 | 653 | 7 / 4 |
| document `mask_mod` | 4.6.0.dev0 | 204 / 204 B | 5952 | 1049 | 51 / 42 |
| document `mask_mod` | 4.8.0 ¹ | 184 / 184 B | 5456 | 968 | 46 / 37 |

All of these are at 128 registers (`.reqntid 512`), with warp-specialized budgets (`setmaxnreg.inc` 136/152, `setmaxnreg.dec` 88/24). The PTX files have no `.local` declarations, so ptxas introduces the spills from register pressure in the NVVM 23 PTX. The SASS that 4.8.0 ships through its own ptxas has 50 STL / 42 LDL for the document mask and 35 / 26 for the sliding window (causal: 2 / 2).

**Likely pressure region.** `CUTE_DSL_COMPILER_OPT="remarks{ptx}" CUTE_DSL_LINEINFO=1` on 4.8.0 marks `flash_attn/cute/block_sparse_utils.py:1564` in `get_block_sparse_iteration_info_bwd`. That line loads the block-sparse count and index tensors: `curr_q_cnt = q_cnt[batch_idx, head_idx, n_block]` and `q_idx[batch_idx, head_idx, n_block, None]`. #3701 found the same kind of small metadata-tensor load for the forward kernel (`cu_seqlens` in the varlen scheduler). Here the IMAD count rises together with the spills (document mask: 653 → 1049). We suspect the address arithmetic of these indexed loads, but have not verified it.

**Steps/Code to reproduce bug**

The attached `nvvm23-sm100-bwd-repro.zip` has the scripts, the nine PTX files and our raw results. Its README has more detail.

*1. No GPU needed.* Assemble the attached PTX pair:

```
ptxas -arch=sm_100a -O3 -v ptx/bwd.document_mask.fa4-b20.cutlass-dsl-4.5.3.nvvm20.ptx -o /dev/null
    16 bytes stack frame, 28 bytes spill stores, 16 bytes spill loads
ptxas -arch=sm_100a -O3 -v ptx/bwd.document_mask.fa4-b20.cutlass-dsl-4.6.0.dev0.nvvm23.ptx -o /dev/null
    152 bytes stack frame, 204 bytes spill stores, 204 bytes spill loads
```

*2. On a B200: time the backward* with the script below (FA4 through `flex_attention`, about 50 lines), once per environment:

```
python3.12 -m venv nvvm20 && . nvvm20/bin/activate
pip install torch==2.14.0 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu130
pip install torch==2.14.0 numpy flash-attn-4==4.0.0b19 nvidia-cutlass-dsl==4.5.3 quack-kernels==0.5.0 apache-tvm-ffi==0.1.11
python minimal_repro.py

python3.12 -m venv nvvm23 && . nvvm23/bin/activate
pip install torch==2.14.0 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu130
pip install torch==2.14.0 numpy flash-attn-4==4.0.0b20 nvidia-cutlass-dsl==4.6.0.dev0 quack-kernels==0.5.3 apache-tvm-ffi==0.1.12
python minimal_repro.py
```

Hi @janhuenermann , I'd like to investigate this issue and work on a fix, including reproducing the register-spill regression and adding a regression test if appropriate.

Would it be possible to assign this issue to me? Please let me know if someone is already working on it or if there's any preferred direction for the investigation.

comments.author: brandon-yujie-sun
comments.body: @dongxiao92

comments.author: dongxiao92
comments.body: Hey @janhuenermann , I did some investigation and could reproduce your issues. Basically it's a specific pattern in PTX triggering pathological transformation in ptxas. We have started to work with compiler team to see how to fix it. Meawhile, there're a few options for you to WAR it: - option1: using O2 in cute.compile for impacted kernels. This is the most straightword path in my understanding. - option2: removing the cutlass prefix in kernel name through `FlashAttentionBackwardSm100.kernel.set_name_prefix("", remove_cutlass_symbol=True`. But this API is only available from 4.6.2 so an update will be necessary. - option3: patching the FA4 code. I list the perf results with different WARs below. Could you help to comment which one may be helping your case before we have a clean fix in future release?

comments.author: janhuenermann
comments.body: Thanks @dongxiao92! For now, we'll be staying on 4.5.3 and use the default settings. I'm aware of using `O2` as a fix. However we'd like to avoid running into unintended side-effects and slow-downs.

items.title: [cake deslop] balanced_gqa_decode (2): retire the experimental package (~10.7K lines) superseded by backend="cake" balanced decode
items.author: yyihuang
items.body_excerpt:
**Background.** #5474 (2026-09-22) and #5490 (2026-09-23) added `flashinfer/experimental/balanced_gqa_decode` for #4832. It provides on-device load-balanced BF16 paged GQA decode, with packed-row MTP for q_len 3..8, through the top-level experimental API `flashinfer.prepare_balanced_batch_decode_with_kv_cache` (sm_100a/sm_103a, JIT only, no AOT entry). The package has 13 files and 9,428 lines: 3 kernels (row 2,373, mtp32 2,379, mtp64 2,390), 3 bindings (313/320/320), 2 shared headers (297), 4 Python files (923) and a 113-line README. Outside the package are the 84-line wrapper `flashinfer/decode.py:290-373`, the export `flashinfer/__init__.py:86-88`, a 634-line test, a 563-line test-only host mirror of the device planner (`tests/test_helpers/cake_balanced_gqa_plan.py`) and `benchmarks/bench_cake_balanced_gqa_decode.py` (558 lines). The first round, #5806, was closed by #5954 (merged 2026-10-05, +685/−11,987). That PR removed the per-arch trees (17 → 13 files), added the 3-record `PROGRAMS` registry and the shared headers, and regenerated the kernels with ABI-neutral codegen changes on the same #5490 compute body. It deferred the interleaved KV view and folding the packed row count into one template; both are still open. No PR has touched the package since #5954, so nothing was re-added. Meanwhile, #5750 (2026-09-30) shipped the production generation of the same family in `csrc/cake_fmha`, and #5855, #5933 and #5913 kept changing it. #5750 also rewrote this unit's benchmark (+402/−77) to time the production kernels. Counts are from main @ 3184bbea6e.

**Findings**
- **Superseded by production.** `trtllm_batch_decode_with_kv_cache(backend="cake")` accepts the same contract (`flashinfer/cake_fmha.py:1091-1122`): contiguous query, head_dim 128, page 16, HND, 8 q-heads per KV head, no sinks/window/LSE, scalar scales, batch ≤ 1024. It routes these calls to `decode_balanced_bf16` / `_mtp_n32` / `_mtp_n64` (`cake_fmha.py:131-135`). The production kernels (`csrc/cake_fmha/cuda/decode_balanced_bf16{,_mtp_n32,_mtp_n64}/default.cu`, 2,724/3,505/3,505 lines) are newer:
  - normalised similarity to the experimental kernels is 0.852 (row) and 0.340 (MTP);

items.title: [PrimTS decode] [Perf] Multi-token GQA decode (q_len > 1) runs 1 token per CTA when page size != 32
items.author: xuanzic
items.body_excerpt:
### Before submitting

- [x] I have searched existing issues and did not find a solution or an existing report.

### Environment

```text
- GPU: B200 (SM100) / B300 (SM103)
- FlashInfer ToT; nvidia-cutlass-dsl 4.8.0
- torch: 2.13.0+cu130
```

### Bug description

## Summary

Performance issue, not a correctness bug.

For fixed multi-token decode (spec-decode / MTP verify, `q_len > 1`), PrimTS only runs the q_len-aware grouped-Q selector (`_apply_auto_grouped_q_mma_config`) when `num_tokens_per_page == 32`. With any other page size, the config falls back to `_swaps_tile_fields_for_heads`. That function sizes `tile_size_q` from the GQA ratio alone (`h_r = num_qo_heads / num_kv_heads`) and ignores `q_len`. So for `h_r` 5..16 it gives **1 token per CTA**: a `q_len = 4` step launches 4 Q CTAs per (request, KV head), and each of them runs the full KV mainloop.

Page size 64 is common in serving (e.g. vLLM), so this path is what serving hits for GQA models with MTP / EAGLE.

**Code** (`flashinfer/attention/prims_ts/kernels/fmha_decode/fmha_decode_config.py`, line numbers at `main`):

- **The gate:** [L4376](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/main/flashinfer/attention/prims_ts/kernels/fmha_decode/fmha_decode_config.py#L4376) in `_apply_auto_grouped_q_mma_config` (L4347).

  ```python
      or cfg.num_tokens_per_page != 32      # any other page size -> return None
  ```

- **The fallback:** [L3660](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/main/flashinfer/attention/prims_ts/kernels/fmha_decode/fmha_decode_config.py#L3660), `_swaps_tile_fields_for_heads`.

  ```python
  h_r = num_heads_q // num_heads_kv
  if groups_tokens_heads_q:
      tile_size_q = next((tile_q for tile_q in (8, 16, 32) if h_r <= tile_q), 0)
  ```

## Expected behavior

For `q_len > 1`, tile and launch selection should account for `h_r * q_len` regardless of page size. Either the grouped-Q selector runs for page sizes other than 32, or the fallback picks the tile from `h_r * q_len`.


### Minimal reproduction

```python
## Minimal reproduction

- It times `prims_ts.BatchDecodePagedTSWrapper` (the backend `flashinfer_benchmark.py` uses for `--backends prims-ts`) on random HND paged K/V with a causal mask and fixed `q_len`.
- It compares page size 32 vs 64 at `q_len` 1 and 4, and prints the resolved launch config. 

**Evidence that the gate is the cause:** at `q_len = 1`, page 32 and page 64 resolve to the same config and the same time. At `q_len = 4`, page 32 groups 2–4 tokens per CTA, while page 64 falls back to 1 token per CTA and runs slower.

**Example** (Llama-3.3-70B TP8 shape, BF16; change `page_size` between 32 and 64 and `q_len` between 1 and 4):


import math, torch
from flashinfer.attention import prims_ts
from flashinfer.testing.utils import bench_gpu_time

hq, hkv, d = 8, 1, 128                    # Llama-3.3-70B at TP8 (h_r = 8)
batch, kv_len, q_len, page_size = 32, 32768, 4, 64
dt, dev = torch.bfloat16, torch.device("cuda")

ppr = math.ceil(kv_len / page_size)
kv = (0.5 * torch.randn(batch * ppr, 2, hkv, page_size, d, device=dev)).to(dt)  # HND paged K/V
block_tables = torch.randperm(batch * ppr, device=dev, dtype=torch.int32).view(batch, ppr)
q = torch.randn(batch, q_len, hq, d, device=dev).to(dt)
out = torch.empty_like(q)

w = prims_ts.BatchDecodePagedTSWrapper("HND")
w.plan(dev, batch, hq, hkv, d, page_size, kv_len, max_seq_len_q=q_len,
       q_data_type=dt, kv_data_type=dt, o_data_type=dt,
       mask_type="causal", seq_lens=[kv_len] * batch)
cfg = w._plan_state.config               # private: resolved launch config
print(cfg.tile_size_q, cfg.q_tokens_per_cta)  # page 32: 32, 4   page 64: 8, 1

run = lambda: w.run(q, kv, None, block_tables, bmm1_scale=d ** -0.5, out=out, validate=False)
times = bench_gpu_time(run, dry_run_iters=10, repeat_iters=50, use_cuda_graph=True)
print(f"{sorted(times)[len(times) // 2] * 1e3:.1f} us")
```

**Problem shapes:**

items.title: In a loop, `acc -= tl.sum(x, 1)` silently adds the sum instead of subtracting it
items.author: Hughshine
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

**TL;DR.** In a loop that reduces a loaded tile along its last axis and accumulates the result, `acc -= tl.sum(x, 1)` silently returns the sum with the wrong sign, `acc += tl.max(x, 1)` returns `-inf`, and `acc = acc * 0.5 + tl.sum(x, 1)` fails to compile. Root cause: `TritonGPUOptimizeThreadLocality` moves the cross-thread part of the reduction after the loop, and accumulates the per-thread partial sums with the loop's update op (`-`) instead of the reduction's own op (`+`); likewise `+` instead of `max` for `acc += tl.max(x, 1)`. Possible fix: rewrite only when the update is the reduction's own op applied to `acc`, as #11370 did before it was reverted.

Reproducer (a 32x512 fp32 matrix of ones reduced per row in four blocks of 128 columns; the loop subtracts the four block sums, so every row has to end at -512):

```python
import sys

import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def kernel(x_ptr, out_ptr, K, BK: tl.constexpr):
    rm = tl.arange(0, 32)
    acc = tl.zeros([32], dtype=tl.float32)
    for k0 in range(0, K, BK):
        x = tl.load(x_ptr + rm[:, None] * K + (k0 + tl.arange(0, BK))[None, :])
        acc -= tl.sum(x, axis=1)
    tl.store(out_ptr + rm, acc)


x = torch.ones(32, 512, device="cuda")
out = torch.empty(32, device="cuda")
kernel[(1, )](x, out, 512, BK=128)
print(out[:3].tolist(), "(expected -512.0 in every row)")
sys.exit(1 if (out != -512.0).any() else 0)
```

Observed on main @6fe3348e6 (NVIDIA L40S, exit code 1); the 3.8.0 wheel and an H100 print the same:
```
[512.0, 512.0, 512.0] (expected -512.0 in every row)
```
Expected `-512.0` in every row. Each row ends at +512: the loop added the four sums instead of subtracting them. With the change below the script prints `[-512.0, -512.0, -512.0]` (exit code 0, on the L40S and on an H100).

<details>
<summary>The same with the control, `acc += tl.max(x, 1)`, `acc = acc * 0.5 + tl.sum(x, 1)` and a torch reference</summary>

Reproducer (a 32x512 fp32 matrix reduced per row in four blocks of 128 columns; the first update is the control, it is the combiner of `tl.sum`):

```python
import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def kernel(x_ptr, out_ptr, K, BM: tl.constexpr, BK: tl.constexpr, UPDATE: tl.constexpr):
    rm = tl.arange(0, BM)
    acc = tl.zeros([BM], dtype=tl.float32)
    for k0 in range(0, K, BK):
        x = tl.load(x_ptr + rm[:, None] * K + (k0 + tl.arange(0, BK))[None, :])
        if UPDATE == "acc += tl.sum(x, 1)":  # control
            acc += tl.sum(x, axis=1)
        elif UPDATE == "acc -= tl.sum(x, 1)":
            acc -= tl.sum(x, axis=1)
        elif UPDATE == "acc += tl.max(x, 1)":
            acc += tl.max(x, axis=1)
        else:
            acc = acc * 0.5 + tl.sum(x, axis=1)
    tl.store(out_ptr + rm, acc)


def reference(x, BK, update):  # the loop evaluated in order
    acc = torch.zeros(x.shape[0], device=x.device)
    for b in x.split(BK, dim=1):
        if update == "acc += tl.sum(x, 1)":
            acc = acc + b.sum(1)
        elif update == "acc -= tl.sum(x, 1)":
            acc = acc - b.sum(1)
        elif update == "acc += tl.max(x, 1)":
            acc = acc + b.amax(1)
        else:
            acc = acc * 0.5 + b.sum(1)
    return acc


BM, BK, K = 32, 128, 512
torch.manual_seed(0)
x = torch.randint(-3, 4, (BM, K), device="cuda").float()  # small integers: every result is exact in fp32
for update in ["acc += tl.sum(x, 1)", "acc -= tl.sum(x, 1)", "acc += tl.max(x, 1)", "acc = acc * 0.5 + tl.sum(x, 1)"]:
    want = reference(x, BK, update)
    out = torch.zeros(BM, device="cuda")
    try:
        kernel[(1, )](x, out, K, BM=BM, BK=BK, UPDATE=update, num_warps=4)
        got, ok = out[:3].tolist(), "OK" if torch.equal(out, want) else "WRONG"
    except Exception as e:
        got, ok = f"{type(e).__name__}: {str(e).strip().splitlines()[-1]}", "COMPILE ERROR"
    print(f"{update:32s} got {got}  expected {want[:3].tolist()}  {ok}")
```
On main @6fe3348e6 (NVIDIA L40S); 3.8.0 and an H100 print the same:
```
acc += tl.sum(x, 1)              got [3.0, -10.0, -9.0]  expected [3.0, -10.0, -9.0]  OK
acc -= tl.sum(x, 1)              got [3.0, -10.0, -9.0]  expected [-3.0, 10.0, 9.0]  WRONG
acc += tl.max(x, 1)              got [-inf, -inf, -inf]  expected [12.0, 12.0, 12.0]  WRONG
acc = acc * 0.5 + tl.sum(x, 1)   got RuntimeError: PassManager::run failed  expected [-0.375, -26.5, -6.625]  COMPILE ERROR
```
Before the `RuntimeError` the compiler prints this assertion and the MLIR reproducer:
```
OptimizeThreadLocality.cpp:338: virtual void mlir::triton::gpu::{anonymous}::TritonGPUOptimizeThreadLocalityPass::runOnOperation(): Assertion `isa<BlockArgument>(accumOperand)' failed.
```
</details>

**When it triggers.** Measured on main (L40S); each item changes one thing relative to the reproducer:
- The 48 combinations of the update `acc + r`, `r + acc`, `acc - r`, `r - acc`, `acc * r`, `tl.maximum(acc, r)`, `tl.minimum(acc, r)` or `acc * 0.5 + r`, with `r` = `tl.sum`, `tl.max` or `tl.min` of `(x, 1)` and `acc` starting at 0 or 2: 9 right (the 8 whose update is the combiner of `r` applied to `acc`, plus `acc * tl.sum(x, 1)` from 0, which stays 0), 33 wrong, and the 6 `acc * 0.5 + r` fail to compile. The outputs are identical on 2.2.0, 2.3.1, 3.0.0, 3.1.0, 3.2.0, 3.3.1, 3.4.0, 3.5.0, 3.6.0, 3.7.1 and 3.8.0, except that 2.2.0 to 3.2.0 abort the process for the 6 instead of raising.
- Also wrong: `a, b = b * 2, a + tl.sum(x, 1)` (the update reads another loop-carried value), and `m = tl.maximum(m, tl.max(x, 1), propagate_nan=tl.PropagateNan.ALL)` when all elements of one thread in a block are NaN (3 instead of 100; right when no thread has only NaN in a block, for example on data without NaN).
- Right, because the pass leaves them alone: `acc += tl.sum(x * x, 1)` and `acc += tl.sum(x, 1) * 0.5` (the reduction must take the `tl.load` result itself and feed the update directly), `acc` loaded from memory instead of `tl.zeros`/`tl.f

items.title: [Performance]: CuTe DSL MLA decode split-KV cap of 32 leaves the GPU idle at long context and small batch
items.author: lucifer1004
items.body_excerpt:
### Proposal to improve performance

The CuTe DSL MLA decode (`trtllm::cute_dsl_mla_decode_*_blackwell`, `attention/backends/fmha/cute_dsl_mla.py`) caps split-KV at 32: `CuteDSLNVMlaDecodeBlackwellRunner._MAX_SPLIT_KV = 32` for the tactic grid and `_SPLIT_PLAN_MAX_SPLIT = 32` for the per-request plan. For long-context decode with few requests and few heads per rank (for example Kimi K3 at TP8, 12 heads per rank, 1M-token context, batch 1), 32 splits of 2-CTA clusters fill only a fraction of one wave, so most SMs idle. On Rubin single GPU (200-SM engineering sample), FP8 KV, q = 8, batch 1 at 1M tokens, raising the cap from 32 to 128 makes the decode op 1.17x faster with a uniform split and 1.51x faster with the per-request plan.

Two related points:

1. The cap cannot simply be raised for everyone: with a larger grid, uniform batches of 4+ requests get many empty split slots on the BF16 kernel (BF16, B8 at 16K: +124% with a uniform split, +46% with the plan, on the same GPU), so it should be a deployment knob, default 32.
2. The per-request plan is computed against the global cap, while the kernel clamps each request's split count to the step's tactic grid (`split_kv` of the default tactic for the batch bucket, often 8 or 16). When the grid is smaller than the plan, the plan's wave-quantized makespan is computed for split counts that never run. Capping the plan at the step's grid makes the planner choose among the plans that can actually run.

Proposal: `TLLM_CUTE_DSL_MLA_MAX_SPLIT_KV` (read at import, default 32, clamped to the variable split-KV reducer's 256) sets both caps; the uniform-split reducer takes the generic capacity when the cap is above 32; and the plan is capped at the step's tactic grid. With the default, the only change is item 2. PR to follow (draft, stacked on the #20538 PR, whose vectorized plan kernel keeps planning cheap at large caps).

items.title: [Perf] DeepSeek-V4 MoE gate (trtllm::gate_forward) takes 5-7.5 µs per layer at decode: one warp per token
items.author: lucifer1004
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

- GPU: Vera Rubin, compute capability 10.7, single node, TP4/EP4
- TensorRT-LLM main, PyTorch backend, CUDA graphs
- Model: `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash` (384 routed experts, top-6, sqrt-softplus scoring with bias; hash-routed layers), batch 1 decode

### Who can help?

@NVIDIA/trt-llm-torch-models-devs

### Information

- [ ] The official example scripts
- [x] My own modified scripts

### Reproduction

Profile a single-request decode with nsys (`--cuda-graph-trace=node`) and look at `gate_forward_kernel` (`kernels/moe/routing/customMoeRoutingKernels.cu`), launched from `DeepSeekV4MoeRoutingMethod._apply_native` via `torch.ops.trtllm.gate_forward`.

### Expected behavior

Scoring and top-6 selection over 384 fp32 logits for one token should take a couple of µs.

### Actual behavior

In the served model the kernel takes 7.5 µs per MoE layer (40 layers, about 0.3 ms per decode step). The kernel runs one warp per token: each lane handles 12 experts, then a warp-level reduceTopK picks 6 experts; with one token there is one warp on the whole GPU, and the kernel does not use PDL.

Single-GPU timing on Vera Rubin (CUDA graph replay, µs per call), against a Triton kernel with one 4-warp program per token and 6 argmax rounds (same fast-math scoring as the CUDA kernel):

| | `gate_forward` | Triton |
|---|---|---|
| 384 experts, top-k, M = 1 / 6 / 32 | 5.2 / 5.1 / 5.3 | 2.4 / 2.6 / 2.6 |
| 384 experts, hash, M = 1 / 6 / 32 | 3.8 / 4.0 / 4.2 | 1.4 / 1.6 / 1.6 |
| 256 experts, top-k, M = 1 / 6 / 32 | 3.5 / 3.5 / 3.8 | 2.3 / 2.7 / 2.7 |

The selected experts are identical (including order) in 36 cases (384/256 experts x top-k/hash x with/without the image mask x M = 1/4/6/8/32/256); weights differ by at most 1.8e-7 (summation order).

End-to-end (TP4/EP4, same server configuration, only the gate changed): decode step period 5.97 ms -> 5.83 ms (-0.14 ms); GSM8K (100 questions) 99 -> 97, passkey 8K/32K/128K 5/5 in both.

### Additional notes

The open #20192 adds a 128-expert / top-3 specialization to the same kernel; it does not change the one-warp-per-token structure.

Spreading one token over more threads (or several warps cooperating on the top-k) in the CUDA kernel would likely give the same gain without a Triton dependency in `routing.py`. We have the Triton version working and are happy to send either as a PR, whichever maintainers prefer.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and checked the documentation and examples for answers to frequently asked questions.

items.title: VisitorRowReduction::Callbacks::reduction is declared to return ElementCompute but has no return statement
items.author: VaggelisGian
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

`VisitorRowReduction::Callbacks::reduction` in `include/cutlass/epilogue/threadblock/fusion/visitor_store.hpp` (lines 551-560) is declared to return `ElementCompute` but contains no `return` statement; control flows off the end of a non-void function, which is undefined behavior. Compilers flag it (`-Wreturn-type` / nvcc equivalent).

The result is currently benign because the only call site (line 508) discards the return value. The function also duplicates the existing shared helper `fragment_reduce` (line 214) that the Col and Scalar reduction visitors already use at lines 330 and 748.

### Suggested fix

Either change the signature to `void`, or delete the private duplicate and call `fragment_reduce<RegReduceFn, RoundStyle>(reduce_buffer, result)` like the sibling visitors.

items.title: maximum_active_blocks wrappers pass int into CudaHostAdapter* and no longer compile
items.author: VaggelisGian
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

Since 3.4, `GemmUniversalBase::maximum_active_blocks` takes a `CudaHostAdapter*`:

```cpp
// include/cutlass/gemm/device/gemm_universal_base.h:350
static int maximum_active_blocks(CudaHostAdapter *cuda_adapter = nullptr)
```

but the 2.x-style device wrappers still declare the pre-3.4 signature `(int smem_capacity = -1)` and forward the int into that pointer parameter, which does not convert:

```cpp
static int maximum_active_blocks(int smem_capacity = -1) {
  return UnderlyingOperator::maximum_active_blocks(smem_capacity);   // int -> CudaHostAdapter*: error
}
```

Calling any of these wrappers fails to compile:

```
error: argument of type "int" is incompatible with parameter of type "cutlass::CudaHostAdapter *"
```

Affected call sites (all forwarding `smem_capacity`):

- `gemm/device/gemm_universal.h:393-394`
- `gemm/device/gemm_universal_adapter.h:738-739` (2.x alias path)
- `gemm/device/rank_k.h:462`
- `gemm/device/rank_2k.h:499`
- `gemm/device/symm.h:554`
- `gemm/device/gemm_universal_with_broadcast.h:337`
- `gemm/device/gemm_universal_streamk_with_broadcast.h:337`
- `gemm/device/gemm_universal_with_absmax.h:355`
- `gemm/device/gemm_with_k_reduction.h:366`
- `gemm/device/gemm_layernorm_mainloop_fusion.h:336-337`

The 3.x adapter (`gemm_universal_adapter.h:270`) already updated its own declaration correctly (`maximum_active_blocks(int /* smem_capacity */ = -1)` ignoring the value), so only these forwarders were missed. Nothing in-tree calls them anymore (the profiler moved to the new API), which is why CI does not see it.

Reproduction: compile a TU that calls e.g.

```cpp
#include "cutlass/gemm/device/gemm.h"
using Gemm = cutlass::gemm::device::Gemm<float, cutlass::layout::ColumnMajor,
                                         float, cutlass::layout::ColumnMajor,
                                         float, cutlass::layout::RowMajor>;
int n = Gemm::maximum_active_blocks();
```

with nvcc or g++ against the current headers; it errors at the forwarded argument.

### Suggested fix

Drop the unused parameter in the ten wrappers to match the base signature (`maximum_active_blocks()` with no arguments), mirroring what `gemm_universal_adapter.h:270` already does.

items.title: [BUG] Constexpr missing in dynamic control-flow regions
items.author: nodeeeeee
items.body_excerpt:
### Which component has the problem?

CuTe DSL

### Bug Report

## Motivation

I encountered this while implementing FlashAttention. The implementation naturally groups the load and MMA paths into JIT methods on a compile-time configuration object, and selects between them using the runtime warp index. A reduced version looks like this:

```python
class FlashAttention:
    @cute.jit
    def load(self, tensor, pipeline):
        ...

    @cute.jit
    def mma(self, tensor, pipeline):
        ...


@cute.jit
def fa4_device_body(
    fa: cutlass.Constexpr[FlashAttention],
    tensor: cute.Tensor,
    storage,
):
    warp_idx = cute.arch.make_warp_uniform(cute.arch.warp_idx())

    pipeline = make_pipeline(
        storage=storage,
        num_stages=fa.num_stages,
    )

    if warp_idx < 4:
        cute.arch.setmaxregister_decrease(fa.num_producer_regs)
        fa.load(tensor, pipeline)
    else:
        cute.arch.setmaxregister_increase(fa.num_mma_regs)
        fa.mma(tensor, pipeline)
```

Here, `self` in `FlashAttention.load()` and `FlashAttention.mma()` is a compile-time method receiver. The `fa` parameter in `fa4_device_body()` refers to the same kind of compile-time object, made explicit by its `Constexpr` annotation.

Writing the device body as an actual instance method makes this code compile, but only because the compiler has a special case that excludes a receiver whose name is literally `self`. Passing the same object as a named `Constexpr[FlashAttention]` parameter should have equivalent staging semantics, but currently does not.

## Problem

CuTe DSL treats `Constexpr[T]` parameters as compile-time Python meta values. They do not have an MLIR representation and must not become arguments or results of runtime control-flow regions.

However, when a method is called through a `Constexpr` receiver inside a dynamic `if`, the receiver is incorrectly captured as a region argument:

```python
class Receiver:
    @cute.jit
    def store(self, output):
        ...


@cute.kernel
def kernel(receiver: cutlass.Constexpr[Receiver], output: cute.Tensor):
    tidx, _, _ = cute.arch.thread_idx()

    if tidx == Int32(0):
        receiver.store(output)
```

The region analyzer currently treats the base object of every method call as a mutable runtime value, except when its name is literally `self`.

Consequently, `receiver` is added to the values carried through the dynamic `if`. Lowering then attempts to flatten the plain Python `Receiver` instance into MLIR values and fails with:

```text
error[TYPE_DYNAMIC_EXPR_UNSUPPORTED]:
A value carried through this `if` is a plain Python value (Meta value)
(a `Receiver`) that cannot be turned into a Runtime value (Staged value)
```

This means `self.method()` works because of the existing `self` special case, while an explicitly annotated `receiver: Constexpr[Receiver]` does not, despite having the same staging semantics.

## Root cause

`Constexpr` is a property of the original function parameter binding. The AST preprocessor removes parameter annotations while transforming the function, so the later control-flow region analysis no longer knows which names refer to `Constexpr` parameters.

`RegionAnalyzer.visit_Call()` therefore sees only a method call on a Python object and adds its receiver to `invoked_args`.
