items.title: [Feature][CAKE] mHC: slows when other streams hold SMs; fixed eps / iterations; host cost
items.author: abcdabcd987
items.body_excerpt:
**Package:** `cake_mhc_train_backend` (#6897).
**Related:** #6486. The tensors kept outside `save_for_backward` are filed separately.
**Commit:** [617845d1](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/commit/617845d1a3aeadf2b95fb0e5d6a12383b192a963), GB200, PyTorch 2.14.

Thanks for #6897. At GLM-5.3-Flash shapes (four streams, hidden 4096, T 14928-16263 per rank) it is 2.9x faster per connection than our kernels (forward + replay + backward), with a 47% lower step peak and FP32 parameter gradients 13-16x closer to FP64. We are switching that model to it.

## 1. Persistent grids slow down when other streams hold SMs

The forward and backward grids are sized for all 152 SMs. Communication kernels hold some SMs during training. We measured with a spin kernel kept resident on a side stream (one GPU):

| Kernel on the side stream | `forward_prepare` | `backward_finish` | our connection backward |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| none | 0.219 ms | 0.447 ms | 2.018 ms |
| 16 CTAs × 640 threads | 0.245 ms | 0.802 ms (+80%) | 2.076 ms (+3%) |
| 152 CTAs × 128 threads (one per SM) | 3.598 ms | 3.826 ms | 5.399 ms |

With one CTA resident on every SM, both kernels wait for the side kernel to exit, as the cooperative RMSNorm and conv1d backwards do (filed separately).

**What we need:** kernels that keep their speed while communication kernels hold some SMs.

## 2. Fixed configuration

The kernels are built for:
- `rms_eps` 1e-5, `hc_eps` 1e-6 and 20 Sinkhorn iterations;
- hidden 4096;
- contiguous BF16 streams.

There is no head (stream-mean) kernel.

**What we need:** eps and iteration counts set at run time, if that is cheap, and other hidden sizes.

## 3. Host overhead

`forward_prepare` takes about 0.44 ms of CPU against 0.22 ms of GPU. At small T (4096) a checkpointed step becomes host-bound: 2.75 ms of CPU per step.

**What we need:** less host time per call.

items.title: [Tracking] GLM-5.3-Flash performance optimization on Hopper (SM90)

items.title: [BUG] CuTe DSL: export_to_c fails for a --gpu-arch other than the current GPU's
items.author: hwanseoc
items.body_excerpt:
### Which component has the problem?

CuTe DSL

### Bug Report

**Describe the bug**

`export_to_c` fails on the plain C path (no `--enable-tvm-ffi`) when the function was compiled for a different arch than the current GPU. For example, `--gpu-arch sm_90a` on a B200:

```text
JIT session error: Symbols not found: [ _cuKernelGetAttribute, _cudaDeviceGetAttribute, _cudaFuncSetAttribute, _cudaGetDevice, _cudaKernelSetAttributeForDevice, _cudaLaunchKernelEx, _cudaLibraryGetKernel, _cudaLibraryLoadData ]
error: Error dumping object file: Failed to dump object file with PIC relocation
```

The same export works for the native arch, and it also works if I load the runtime libraries `RTLD_GLOBAL` first. My guess is that no execution engine gets built for an arch the GPU can't run, so `libcute_dsl_runtime.so` never gets loaded before the object dump.

**Steps/Code to reproduce bug**

```python
import ctypes, sys, tempfile

import cuda.bindings.driver as cuda
import cutlass
import cutlass.cute as cute
from cutlass.cute.runtime import make_fake_stream


@cute.kernel
def noop_kernel(x: cutlass.Int32):
    pass


@cute.jit
def noop(x: cutlass.Int32, stream: cuda.CUstream):
    noop_kernel(x).launch(grid=(1, 1, 1), block=(32, 1, 1), stream=stream)


if "--preload" in sys.argv:
    for lib in cute.runtime.find_runtime_libraries(enable_tvm_ffi=False):
        ctypes.CDLL(lib, mode=ctypes.RTLD_GLOBAL)
fn = cute.compile(noop, cutlass.Int32(0), make_fake_stream(), options="--gpu-arch sm_90a")
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
    fn.export_to_c(tmp, "noop", function_prefix="noop")
print(f"cutlass-dsl {cutlass.__version__}: exported", flush=True)
```

```console
$ python repro.py
JIT session error: Symbols not found: [ _cuKernelGetAttribute, ... ]
$ python repro.py --preload
cutlass-dsl 4.8.0: exported
```

**Expected behavior**

`export_to_c` works for any `--gpu-arch` the compiler accepts, with no manual preloading.

**Environment details (please complete the following information):**
 - Environment location: Bare-metal
 - nvidia-cutlass-dsl 4.8.0 and 4.7.0 (cu13), cuda-python 13.4.1
 - B200, driver 580.159.03, Ubuntu 22.04, Python 3.12

**Additional context**

#2859 had the same error on the TVM-FFI path and was fixed in 4.3.3; the TVM-FFI path does export cross-arch now. The plain C path still fails. Workaround: preload `cute.runtime.find_runtime_libraries()` with `RTLD_GLOBAL`.

items.title: [BUG] SM90 TMA GEMM mainloops rely on elect_one_sync() electing lane 0 (TMA issuer vs. PipelineTmaAsync is_leader)
items.author: builtin-pb
items.body_excerpt:
### Which component has the problem?

CUTLASS C++

### Bug Report

**Describe the bug**

**Summary.** Most SM90 TMA GEMM mainloop collectives work only if `elect.sync` elects lane 0, because two threads are chosen by different rules: the TMA issuer is the elected lane, while the producer's arrival comes from warp-group thread 0. PTX does not say which lane `elect.sync` elects, and if another lane were elected the kernel would hang. We suggest deriving the leader from the election in the mainloop warp, as in-tree code already does elsewhere.

Paths and lines are at main `0b55a2f`.

#### Evidence

**TMA issuer.** These collectives call `producer_acquire` and issue the TMA copies only inside `if (lane_predicate)`, where `lane_predicate = cute::elect_one_sync()`, that is, `elect.sync` with a full mask:

| Collective (`include/cutlass/gemm/collective/`) | elect / `producer_acquire` lines |
|---|---|
| `sm90_mma_tma_gmma_ss_warpspecialized.hpp` | 320 / 374 |
| `sm90_mma_tma_gmma_ss_warpspecialized_fp8.hpp` | 318 / 372 |
| `sm90_mma_tma_gmma_rs_warpspecialized.hpp` | 401 / 457 |
| `sm90_sparse_mma_tma_gmma_ss_warpspecialized.hpp` | 415 / 458 |
| `sm90_sparse_mma_tma_gmma_ss_warpspecialized_fp8.hpp` | 426 / 469 |
| `sm90_mma_array_tma_gmma_ss_warpspecialized.hpp` | 370 / 425 |
| `sm90_mma_array_tma_gmma_ss_warpspecialized_fp8.hpp` | 368 / 422 |
| `sm90_mma_array_tma_gmma_ss_warpspecialized_fp8_blockwise_scaling.hpp` | 463 / 543 |

The non-warp-specialized `sm90_mma_tma_gmma_ss.hpp` (lines 365 and 504) and the SM90 implicit-GEMM conv collective (`conv/collective/sm90_implicit_gemm_gmma_ss_warpspecialized.hpp:558–559, 612`) have the same pattern.

**Producer arrival.** `PipelineTmaAsync::producer_acquire` performs `arrive_and_expect_tx` only when `params_.is_leader` is set (`include/cutlass/pipeline/sm90_pipeline.hpp:533–535`, and 555–557 in the token overload). This arrival is the stage's only producer arrival. The kernels set `is_leader = warp_group_thread_idx == 0`:
- `sm90_gemm_tma_warpspecialized.hpp:324`;
- `sm90_gemm_tma_warpspecialized_cooperative.hpp:471`;
- `sm90_gemm_tma_warpspecialized_pingpong.hpp:463`;
- the array cooperative and pingpong kernels, lines 522 and 531;
- `sm90_mma_tma_gmma_ss.hpp:334`.

The mainloop warp is warp 0 of the producer warp group, so warp-group thread 0 is its lane 0.

#### Cause

PTX ISA 9.4 (§9.7.15.15, `elect.sync`) promises only that the election is deterministic, with the same leader for the same `membermask` every time. It does not say which lane. If another lane were elected:
- that lane would call `producer_acquire` without being the leader, so nothing arrives on the full barrier;
- lane 0 would not enter the `if` at all;
- the TMA's complete-tx would only drive the transaction count negative.

The phase would never complete. Consumers would block in `consumer_wait`, then the producer in `producer_acquire` once every stage is used.

#### Suggested fix

Precedents for deriving the leader from the election:
- on the same `PipelineTmaAsync`, `examples/88_hopper_fmha/kernel/fmha_kernel_tma_warpspecialized.hpp:205, 210` and `sm120_gemm_tma_warpspecialized_cooperative_asymmetric_dma.hpp:443, 448`;
- in the SM100 kernels, e.g. `sm100_gemm_tma_warpspecialized.hpp:465`.

For the SM90 kernels, that would be:

```cpp
mainloop_pipeline_params.is_leader =
    warp_group_role == WarpGroupRole::Producer &&
    producer_warp_role == ProducerWarpRole::Mainloop && lane_predicate;
```

Restrict it to the mainloop warp. The `MainloopAux` warp in the blockwise kernels also has the Producer role and calls `producer_acquire` from all lanes. Giving it a leader would add a second `arrive_and_expect_tx` per stage.

This works because the kernel's `elect_one_sync()` and the collective's later one use the same full mask, and PTX guarantees the same leader for the same mask. Two more changes go with it:
- `sm90_mma_tma_gmma_ss.hpp` would need `lane_predicate` computed before `is_leader` is set;
- the debug-build `brkpt` checks in `producer_acquire` (`sm90_pipeline.hpp:542–544` and 564–566), which fire when the leader is not lane 0, would need to go. They already assume lane 0 for the FMHA and SM120 kernels above.

The alternative is to gate the TMA issue in each affected collective on lane 0 instead of `elect_one_sync()`.

#### Scope

- Unaffected: some collectives call `producer_acquire` from all 32 lanes and issue TMA only from the elected lane, so lane 0 always arrives:
  - the mixed-input collectives (`sm90_mma_tma_gmma_rs_warpspecialized_mixed_input.hpp:684/694`, and the array variant at 774/784);
  - the non-array FP8 blockwise collective (577/587–588).

  The epilogue's TMA loads are also unaffected, because one elected lane both posts the expect-tx and issues the copy.
- Current hardware: the kernels run today, so current hardware evidently elects lane 0 here. The code also states that intent:
  - `sm90_mma_tma_gmma_ss.hpp:356` says "Set predicate for the lowest lane_id in the warp";
  - `sm90_pipeline.hpp:286` says "We have exactly one thread elected in the Producer as the 'leader'";
  - CuTe's fallback without `elect.sync` returns `(threadIdx.x % 32) == 0` (`include/cute/arch/cluster_sm90.hpp:197`).

#### Why there is no PR

The fix can go in the kernels (`is_leader` from the election) or in each affected collective (TMA issue gated on lane 0), so we'd rather follow your preference than guess. Tell us which and we'll write the PR.

**Steps/Code to reproduce bug**

Found by reading the source against the PTX ISA. There is no runtime reproduction.

**Expected behavior**

The lane that issues the TMA loads is the lane that arrives with the expected bytes.

**Environment details**

Source analysis; no runtime environment involved. Hopper (sm_90a).

items.title: [DOC] Dynamic-layout guide example uses incompatible singleton strides
items.author: 0z5a
items.body_excerpt:
## Report incorrect documentation

**Location:** [Framework integration guide, dynamic-layout code example](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/91843b71d90737e0a9b86f7d9df213cff5a3526f/media/docs/pythonDSL/guides/framework_integration.rst), at the v4.8.1 source revision.

**Problem and reproduction:** The example assumes that singleton dimensions of `b` have stride 1, but the shown PyTorch construction retains stride 4:

```python
import torch
from cutlass.cute.runtime import from_dlpack

b = torch.empty(32, 1, 1, 1, 4).permute(3, 4, 1, 0, 2)
print(b.stride())  # (4, 1, 4, 4, 4)
from_dlpack(b).mark_layout_dynamic(leading_dim=0)
# Expected strides[leading_dim] == 1, but got 4
```

The same mismatch affects the later `leading_dim=2` example. The `t1` and `t2` examples also print `t2` and `t3`, respectively, before those variables have been defined.

**Verification:** Ran the six positive examples t0–t5 in a GH200 environment with the main editable core and torch 2.11.0, and an H100 environment with CuTe DSL 4.8.1 and torch 2.13.0. The original and a print-only repair fail at the stride check. Using explicit singleton strides and correcting the print variables makes all six layouts match the documented output in both environments. This checks tensor-layout metadata, not GPU kernel performance; deliberate-error snippets elsewhere in the guide are outside this report.

**Suggested fix:** Construct `b` with `torch.empty_strided((1, 4, 1, 32, 1), (1, 1, 1, 4, 1))`, and print the variables just defined.

items.title: [Store] Does Mooncake store plan to support awareness of layers, chunk ordering, and TP?
items.author: Hadigan
items.body_excerpt:
It looks like the current Mooncake store does not have awareness of layer granularity, chunk order (earlier vs. later chunks), or TP ranks. This can cause problems during cache eviction:

1. The store might evict KVs for only some layers, forcing prefill to recompute all layer KVs for those tokens.
2. The store might evict the KVs corresponding to the earliest chunk(s) of a token sequence, forcing prefill to recompute KVs for all chunks/tokens.
3. The store might evict KVs produced by some TP ranks, forcing all TP ranks to recompute KVs.

I think the Mooncake store should be aware of layers, chunk ordering, and TP. On eviction, it should evict a token’s KV caches for all layers and for all TP ranks together (i.e., keep KV state complete per token). 
From the chunk-order perspective, eviction policies should prefer removing KVs for later chunks first rather than evicting early-chunk KVs that make prefill expensive.

items.title: [Core/Auth] Distribute the auth token to ray up and autoscaler nodes via file_mounts
items.author: MortalHappiness
items.body_excerpt:
`ray up` clusters need the token on the head and every worker, without putting it on a command line. Passing it as an env var in the start commands puts it in `ps` on both ends of the SSH command and twice in the `ray up` console log.

Change:

- In `_set_up_config_for_head_node` (`autoscaler/_private/commands.py`), before the file mounts are rewritten, add a file mount for `~/.ray/auth_token` unless `RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled` is set locally or the YAML already mounts that path. The source follows token precedence: `RAY_AUTH_TOKEN` written to a 0600 temp file, else `RAY_AUTH_TOKEN_PATH`, else `~/.ray/auth_token` (created with `generate_and_save_token` if missing). The autoscaler reuses `file_mounts` for workers.
- `ray up` creates a missing token through the C++ token loader function that #67049 adds, so it follows the same rules, and never overwrites a token file that holds a token.
- Opting out: the user sets `RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled` on the nodes in the cluster YAML. `ray up` never copies the local auth mode to the nodes.
- Existing `ray up` clusters update their worker nodes once after upgrading: the new file mount changes the autoscaler's runtime hash, so each worker reruns its setup commands and restarts Ray. Instances aren't relaunched; in Docker mode the container restarts to pick up the new mount. Call this out in the PR so it reaches the release notes.
- Also cover `--no-monitor-on-head`, which skips `_set_up_config_for_head_node`.
- The fake multi-node docker provider skips worker `file_mounts` (`disable_node_updaters`), and the head's `ray start` runs at container start, before `ray up` syncs files. So add the token file to the shared `node_spec["volumes"]` in `fake_multi_node/node_provider.py`, mounted read-only at `/home/ray/.ray/auth_token`. The fake command runner must then skip `ray up`'s `~/.ray/auth_token` upload, because `docker cp` can't overwrite a read-only single-file mount.
- Test: a fake-provider cluster with `RAY_AUTH_MODE=token` scales up a worker that joins. It runs in the "core: HA integration tests" CI job (tag `ha_integration`).

Checked: `rsync -avz` keeps mode 0600. In Docker mode, file mounts are rsynced to the host and bind-mounted into the container at the expanded `~/.ray/auth_token`; this comes from reading `command_runner.py` and hasn't been run on a real cluster.

items.title: [Data] Converting multi-chunk variable-shaped tensor columns to pandas skips the dense fast path
items.author: rayo5o
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

#66122 made `TensorDtype.__from_arrow__` return one dense view when a variable-shaped tensor column has uniformly shaped rows. That only happens for a single chunk ([pandas.py#L436-L452](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/f4f37d399886529c69c201cca9a714ace9c7c06e/python/ray/data/_internal/tensor_extensions/pandas.py#L436-L452)). With two or more chunks, each chunk still goes through `to_numpy()`, which returns one ndarray per row, and the rows are then stacked one by one. The PR left this out of scope ([description](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/66122), [review](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/66122#pullrequestreview-5242470499)).

`iter_batches` runs into this whenever a batch spans two blocks. `Batcher` joins blocks with the same schema through `pa.concat_tables`, so the column reaches `__from_arrow__` with one chunk per block.

Proposed change: in the multi-chunk branch, convert each chunk with `tensor_array_to_numpy()`. If every chunk comes back dense with the same row shape, join them with one `np.concatenate`. Otherwise keep the current path, which also covers the dense-plus-ragged case that #66122 mentions. Chunks sit in different buffers, so this still copies once and is not zero-copy like the single-chunk case. It replaces the per-row stacking with one contiguous copy.

Measured with `iter_batches(batch_size=..., batch_format="pandas")` over a materialized dataset whose blocks hold uniformly shaped `ArrowVariableShapedTensorArray` rows. In "aligned", each block is one batch, so every batch column has 1 chunk. In "crossing", each block is half a batch, so every batch column has 2 chunks. "crossing + prototype" applies the change above inside the benchmark process only. Median of 5 runs, each in a fresh process.

| rows | batch size | layout | total | inside `__from_arrow__` |
|---|---:|---|---:|---:|
| 65,536 × (128,) float32 | 1024 | aligned | 144 ms | 9.6 ms |
| | | crossing | 346 ms | 156 ms |
| | | crossing + prototype | 209 ms | 27 ms |
| 2,048 × (224, 224, 3) uint8 | 64 | aligned | 120 ms | 8.0 ms |
| | | crossing | 172 ms | 82 ms |
| | | crossing + prototype | 160 ms | 62 ms |

Most of the gain is with small rows, where per-row work dominates: the conversion goes from 156 ms to 27 ms and the whole loop from 346 ms to 209 ms. With image-sized rows both paths are mostly the copy itself, so the change helps less (82 ms to 62 ms). Output was checked to be the same in all three layouts.

I couldn't find an open issue or PR for this. #67236 also edits `__from_arrow__`, but only adds null-row checks around this branch.

I'll open a PR for this. cc @marwan116 @rayhhome since it follows up on #66122.

<details>
<summary>Benchmark script</summary>

Run each layout in a fresh process, e.g. `python bench.py --layout crossing --prototype --shape 224x224x3 --dtype uint8 --batch-size 64 --rows 2048`.

```python
"""iter_batches(batch_format="pandas") on a uniformly shaped variable-shaped
tensor column, with batches that come from one block vs. span two blocks.

One run per process. Prints one JSON line.

  python multichunk_iter_batches_bench.py --layout aligned|crossing \
      [--prototype] [--shape 128] [--dtype float32] [--batch-size 1024] [--rows 65536]

aligned:   rows_per_block == batch_size, so every batch column has 1 chunk.
crossing:  rows_per_block == batch_size // 2, so every batch column has 2 chunks.
--prototype replaces the multi-chunk branch of TensorDtype.__from_arrow__ inside
this process only (per-chunk tensor_array_to_numpy + one np.concatenate), to
estimate what a fix would buy. Ray source is not modified.
"""

import argparse
import json
import time

import numpy as np
import pyarrow as pa

import ray
from ray.data._internal.tensor_extensions import pandas as tpd
from ray.data._internal.tensor_extensions.arrow import (
    ArrowVariableShapedTensorArray,
    tensor_array_to_numpy,
)

p = argparse.ArgumentParser()
p.add_argument("--layout", choices=["aligned", "crossing"], required=True)
p.add_argument("--prototype", action="store_true")
p.add_argument("--shape", default="128")
p.add_argument("--dtype", default="float32")
p.add_argument("--batch-size", type=int, default=1024)
p.add_argument("--rows", type=int, default=65536)
args = p.parse_args()

shape = tuple(int(s) for s in args.shape.split("x"))
rows_per_block = args.batch_size if args.layout == "aligned" else args.batch_size // 2
num_blocks = args.rows // rows_per_block

# Instrument __from_arrow__: chunk counts and time spent inside it.
stats = {"calls": 0, "chunks": {}, "seconds": 0.0}
orig_from_arrow = tpd.TensorDtype.__from_arrow__


def prototype_from_arrow(self, array):
    if isinstance(array, pa.ChunkedArray) and array.num_chunks > 1:
        parts = [tensor_array_to_numpy(c) for c in array.iterchunks()]
        if all(p.dtype != object for p in parts) and len(
            {p.shape[1:] for p in parts}
        ) == 1:
            return tpd.TensorArray(np.concatenate(parts))
    return orig_from_arrow(self, array)


inner = prototype_from_arrow if args.prototype else orig_from_arrow


def timed_from_arrow(self, array):
    n = array.num_chunks if isinstance(array, pa.ChunkedArray) else 1
    stats["chunks"][n] = stats["chunks"].get(n, 0) + 1
    stats["calls"] += 1
    s = time.perf_counter()
    out = inner(self, array)
    stats["seconds"] += time.perf_counter() - s
    return out


tpd.TensorDtype.__from_arrow__ = timed_from_arrow

ray.init(num_cpus=4, include_dashboard=False, log_to_driver=False)

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
tables = []
for b in range(num_blocks):
    rows = [
        rng.random(shape).astype(args.dtype) if args.dtype.startswith("float")
        else rng.integers(0, 255, shape).astype(args.dtype)
        for _ in range(rows_per_block)
    ]
    tables.append(pa.table({"x": ArrowVariableShapedTensorArray.from_numpy(rows)}))
ds = ray.data.from_arrow(tables).materialize()
assert ds.num_blocks() == num_blocks

checksum = 0.0
s = time.perf_counter()

items.title: [Inductor] flex_attention fails with NameError: FloatTrueDiv when the default scale is symbolic
items.author: Jeremalloch
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

`flex_attention` with `scale=None` computes the default scale as
`1 / sqrt(query.size(-1))`. Under `torch.compile(dynamic=True)`, the head
dim can be a `SymInt`, so the default scale becomes a sympy expression.
The Inductor flex lowering puts that expression into the generated Triton
template source as the `SM_SCALE` constexpr. The generated module then
fails to load with `NameError: name 'FloatTrueDiv' is not defined`.

An explicit Python float `scale` avoids the error.

## Reproducer

```python
import torch
from torch.nn.attention.flex_attention import flex_attention


def attention(x, head_dim):
    # head_dim is an int argument, so dynamic=True traces it as a SymInt.
    q = x.view(1, x.shape[1], -1, head_dim).transpose(1, 2)
    # The default scale is 1 / sqrt(q.size(-1)), a symbolic float here.
    return flex_attention(q, q, q)


compiled = torch.compile(attention, fullgraph=True, dynamic=True)
for tokens in (128, 256):
    x = torch.randn(1, tokens, 1024, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
    compiled(x, 64)
```

## Observed behavior

The first call fails during Inductor lowering:

```
torch._inductor.exc.InductorError: LoweringException: NameError: name 'FloatTrueDiv' is not defined
  target: flex_attention
  ...
  args[5]: FloatTrueDiv(1.0, OpaqueUnaryFn_sqrt(ToFloat((s53//((s53//s28))))))
```

The generated template's `inductor_meta` contains
`'SM_SCALE': FloatTrueDiv(1.0, OpaqueUnaryFn_sqrt(ToFloat((s53//((s53//s28))))))`,
while `'QK_HEAD_DIM': 64` is concrete. The error comes from
`PyCodeCache.load` when it executes the generated module. The forward
lowering fails, so the backward is not reached.

## Expected behavior

The compiled function runs and matches eager. Inductor already specializes
the head dim (`QK_HEAD_DIM: 64`), so it can also emit a concrete
`SM_SCALE`, or pass a symbolic scale as a kernel argument.

## Versions

H100 80GB, CUDA 13.0 wheels, Python 3.12.3.

| torch | triton | Result |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `2.15.0.dev20261005+cu130` (git `7bf52b3a`) | `3.9.0+gitaad2a60d` | Fails |
| `2.16.0.dev20261021+cu130` (git `ea870f7f`) | `3.9.0+gitfc8d31a5` | Fails |

With `flex_attention(q, q, q, scale=0.125)`, the same reproducer compiles
and runs forward and backward on both versions.

## Probable cause

`torch/_inductor/kernel/flex/flex_attention.py` calls
`kernel_options.setdefault("SM_SCALE", scale)` in the forward and backward
lowerings. When `scale` is a sympy expression, the template writes its
`repr` into the generated source. The sympy function names
(`FloatTrueDiv`, `OpaqueUnaryFn_sqrt`, `ToFloat`) are not defined in that
module. A fix could evaluate the scale from the specialized head dim, or
pass a symbolic scale as a runtime kernel argument.

## Context

We first hit this in TorchTitan, which then compiled each Qwen3.5
vision-encoder block with `torch.compile(fullgraph=True)`. Packed images
give a different token count on every step. TorchTitan has since removed
per-block compilation (pytorch/torchtitan#4895), and its own recipes no
longer reach this path. The reproducer above shows that the Inductor bug
remains on the latest nightly.

items.title: Support Context Cache for Improved Conversation Efficiency
items.author: Jeffwan
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 Feature Description and Motivation

In many large language model (LLM) scenarios, especially multi-turn conversations or sessions where the user interacts repeatedly with the same context (e.g. chatbots, agents, assistant-like use cases), it’s critical to efficiently re-use past prompt / history information without repeatedly sending the entire conversation back to the model.


Several popular APIs already support explicit context caching or context handles:

- [Anthropic Claude’s prompt caching](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/prompt-caching) uses cache identifiers to rehydrate previous contexts.
- [Google Gemini context caching](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/caching?lang=python) provides context_cache_id to continue conversations.
- [Moonshot Kimi context caching](https://platform.moonshot.cn/docs/guide/use-context-caching-feature-of-kimi-api) allows explicit reuse of context handles.
- [Volcengine](https://www.volcengine.com/docs/82379/1396491) also offers conversation_id for session reuse.



We’d like to introduce an optional context caching interface in AIBrix, so that:

- Clients can pass in a conversation/session ID or similar handle when making requests.
- AIBrix can reuse already-processed KV cache / embedding context for that session, reducing repeated computation.
- Expose:
  - A way to create a new context handle (first request)
  - A way to continue using an existing handle (subsequent requests)
  - A way to explicitly clear / expire handles (or auto-timeout)

This would likely require:

- Storing partial KV cache (or references) indexed by conversation/session IDs.
- Coordinating with AIBrix’ current GPU memory management and eviction mechanisms.
- Ensuring multi-tenant isolation and clean up on failures.

### Use Case




-  New API fields (e.g. context_id, clear_context).
- Internal engine / scheduler support to associate context ID with existing KV cache.
- Metrics to track cache hit/miss rate, and memory usage of stored contexts.

### Proposed Solution

items.title: [experimental] SM120 DSA indexer: `backend="sm120"` of `dsa_indexer_topk` (tracking issue)
items.author: lucifer1004
items.body_excerpt:
**Owner:** @lucifer1004

**Use case:** the DeepSeek Sparse Attention lightning indexer on SM12x for serving DeepSeek-V3.2, DeepSeek-V4 / V4.1 and GLM-5.x. Today vLLM and SGLang run it on SM120 as two steps:
1. DeepGEMM's MQA logits, written out as a `[rows, context]` fp32 matrix;
2. a separate top-k: vLLM's, SGLang's, or GVR.

This backend computes the same scores, bit-identical to DeepGEMM's `fp8_mqa_logits`, `fp8_fp4_mqa_logits` and `fp8_fp4_paged_mqa_logits`, and selects the exact top-k for both forms:
- **ragged (prefill):** no score matrix is materialized;
- **paged (decode):** a logits scan followed by one selection launch, with speculative verify up to `next_n` 16.

It supports FP8 and MXFP4, 32 or 64 heads, and `top_k <= 4096`. Every launch is fixed by the shapes, so a call is CUDA-graph capturable. Ties at the k-th score always go to the larger key id, so the selection is deterministic.

**Relation to existing work:**
- `cake_dsa_indexer` is the BF16 training form on SM100 / SM103 / SM107. This adds `backend="sm120"` to the same public `dsa_indexer_topk`.
- `cake_deepgemm`'s SM120 paged MQA logits cover the logits only.
- #3965 (LiteTopK) is a fused prefill indexer for SM100.
- The b12x DSA indexer in `experimental/b12x` also targets SM12x. This backend differs in three ways:
  - its scores are DeepGEMM's bit for bit;
  - its selection is exact and deterministic (compare #6735);
  - it was faster than b12x in every cell where b12x ran in our comparison.

**Performance:** measured on an RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (188 SMs) with CUPTI and a flushed L2, against the fastest of these for each cell: DeepGEMM logits plus vLLM, SGLang, FlashInfer or GVR top-k, and b12x.

| Form | Cells | Geomean speedup | Slowest cell |
|---|---|---|---|
| Prefill, indices only | 152 | 1.11x | 0.992x |
| Decode | 126 | 1.05x | 0.977x (H32 top-k 512, B32, `next_n` 2, 64K) |

Also checked:
- **RTX PRO 5500** configuration (170 SMs, 112 MB L2): the tests pass and spot checks show the same picture.
- **GB10 / SM121** (DGX Spark, 48 SMs, 24 MB L2): the tests pass, and most cells are at parity or faster (up to 1.4x). Two known gaps there:
  - MXFP4 H32 prefill on rows of 32K-40K keys is up to 0.68x. Its resident route assumes a large L2.
  - Decode with `next_n` 6 is 0.967x.

**Reason for the experimental path:**
- It is a new backend with its own kernels and JIT module.
- It is not yet wired into vLLM or SGLang.
- Its routing thresholds (resident classes, when logits are kept in L2) are tuned on 188-SM, 128 MB-L2 parts and need tuning by L2 size for smaller ones such as GB10.

**Graduation plan:** graduate within four weeks of the PR merging, once:
1. the backend is wired into vLLM's or SGLang's DSA indexer path and validated end to end (accuracy and serving benchmarks);
2. the routing adapts to L2 size and SM count, closing the GB10 gaps above;
3. the experimental CI lane runs `tests/experimental/test_sm120_dsa_indexer.py` on SM120.

Implementation PR to follow.

Hi TensorRT-LLM team,
Deploying a large MoE model (Kimi-K2.7-Code-NVFP4, 384 experts) on 8x RTX PRO 6000 (SM120) via the pytorch backend, trtllm-serve, version 1.3.0rc20. Two related findings we wanted to raise:

1. MoeConfig.backend's pydantic Literal doesn't include MEGAMOE_CUTEDSL/MEGAMOE_DEEPGEMM, even though create_moe.py's dispatch logic already handles both as real branches. Setting moe_config.backend: MEGAMOE_CUTEDSL in extra_llm_api_options.yaml fails pydantic validation before create_moe.py is ever reached, even though the underlying backend selection logic supports it. This looks like the config schema hasn't caught up to the dispatch logic yet.
2. More fundamentally: none of the EP-capable MoE backends currently work on SM120 in this build.
 - MEGAMOE_CUTEDSL / MEGAMOE_DEEPGEMM: both explicitly require SM100/SM103 ("MegaMoECuteDsl requires SM100 family (SM100 or SM103); got SM120"), and fall back to CutlassFusedMoE.
 - WIDEEP: not SM-gated, but its GEMM compute still routes through the same CUTLASS kernel that produces silently incorrect output on SM120 in our testing, and additionally hit a binding mismatch in this build (run_moe() is missing value for argument '_37') before we could evaluate EP itself.
 - CUTEDSL (b12x): the only backend we've confirmed produces correct output on SM120, but has no EP support at the flashinfer level (num_local_experts != num_experts raises NotImplementedError in b12x_fused_moe).

Net result: there is currently no correct + EP-capable MoE path for SM120 in this stack, which limits per-GPU memory headroom for large-expert-count models on this hardware class.
Questions:

1. Is SM120 support planned for any of the MegaMoE/WideEP paths, or is SM100/SM103-first prioritization intentional for the near term?
2. Should we file the MoeConfig.backend schema gap as a separate, smaller issue, since that looks like a straightforward fix independent of the larger EP question?
3. Is there a recommended path for SM120 users running large MoE models today, or is CUTEDSL/no-EP the expected configuration for this hardware class in the current release?

Happy to share full repro steps/configs if helpful. Thanks for your work on this — appreciate the pointers.

shortlist.title: [Feature Request][MP] Concurrent multi-turn benchmark for memory-budget-aware KV offload and retrieval
shortlist.author: shivankur-code
shortlist.body_excerpt:
**Label**
new feature; multiprocess mode / benchmarking, if applicable.

**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

I'd like to help evaluate memory-budget-aware KV offloading and retrieval for concurrent, multi-turn conversations. Before changing any policy, I'd like to agree on a small workload and the specific limitation it should test.

The concrete starting point is MP prefetch admission: the current controller limits in-flight requests by count, while their L1 footprints can differ a lot. Eight short-prefix loads and eight long-prefix loads are very different memory and transfer workloads. The existing [controller design](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/dev/docs/design/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/overall.md#max-in-flight-limiting) already calls out memory-based admission as a possible improvement.

I found #4529, which addresses this directly with byte-aware admission and aging, so I'm not proposing another implementation of that queue. What I'd like to check is how the existing approach behaves when conversations grow over successive turns, compete with one another, and overlap stores with retrievals under a fixed budget. I haven't run this experiment yet, and I'm not reporting a reproduced serving failure or claiming this coverage is absent everywhere.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

Start with a focused benchmark/test extension using the existing engine-bench infrastructure from #5489, rather than a new scheduler. Initial scope would be one serving engine (vLLM), MP mode, one GPU and DRAM L1 plus local filesystem L2. No P2P or distributed placement changes.

The workload would:

- Interleave short and long conversations. Each conversation keeps its exact previous token prefix and appends subsequent turns, including generated output. Turns within one conversation remain ordered; different conversations run concurrently, with configurable think time.
- Use a deterministic seed and a working set large enough to produce actual tier pressure. Verify useful prefix hits and actual L2 reads, rather than assuming a large prompt exercises off-GPU retrieval.
- Sweep concurrency and context lengths at fixed GPU and host-cache budgets. Include an ample-capacity control and separate cold-start from warmed measurements.
- Compare no external offload, eager offload, and existing eviction-aware lazy offload. Evaluate #4529 separately on a pinned compatible revision, with its author's agreement. Deadline/fallback interactions from #5255 would be a follow-up, not a requirement to merge all pending work together.

The first deliverable would be a reproducible workload, a documented run matrix, and a report showing:

- p50/p95/p99 time to first token, inter-token latency, and requests meeting agreed latency targets;
- per-conversation queueing time and whether long conversations repeatedly lose admission;
- useful hit tokens, actual transfer bytes, allocation failures/fallbacks, and evictions;
- separate GPU KV-pool usage, GPU temporary/pinned-for-transfer usage, and host L1 allocated/staging bytes, identifying any unavailable measurements rather than estimating them as results.

If this exposes a reproducible problem that existing work doesn't cover, I'd bring back a narrowly scoped fix with regression tests. Fewer transferred bytes alone would not count as success if response latency or useful reuse gets worse. Any cancellation/timeout tests must keep buffers charged and protected until transfer completion or confirmed abort; returning a fallback result doesn't make outstanding I/O safe to forget.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

- Just lower the current in-flight request count or increase L1 capacity. Both are useful controls, but neither tells us how mixed-size conversations behave at equal resource budgets.
- Contribute tests directly to #4529 instead of adding a benchmark workload. I'm happy to do this if that is the more useful boundary.
- Build a new global scheduler or cost model. I'd rather avoid that before there is evidence of a gap in the existing policies.
- Compress L2 storage. That's a separate experiment: smaller serialized objects don't automatically reduce the engine's GPU-resident KV pool, since data may be reconstructed on load. Copying KV off GPU also isn't proof that its GPU blocks have been reclaimed.

**Additional context**

Related work I want to coordinate with:

- #4847: merged eviction-aware lazy offload.
- #4529: byte-aware MP prefetch admission, including small-load ordering and aging.
- #5255: optional prefetch deadline and recompute fallback.
- #5837 / #5838: L1 allocated-byte eviction accounting.
- #5489: merged tier-pressure benchmark.
- #5780, particularly #5782 / #5783: cost-aware admission and serving qualification. This request should complement those experiments, not duplicate them.
- #4557: earlier shared-L2 QoS proposal, including in-flight byte limits; closed, but relevant prior discussion.

Would this mixed-size, growing-prefix workload be useful as a separate benchmark contribution, or should it live under one of the existing threads? In particular, I'd appreciate guidance from the prefetch/benchmark maintainers and the authors of #4529 and #5780 on the scope before starting implementation. The first step is agreeing on that boundary, not changing defaults or claiming a new policy.

shortlist.title: [good-first-issue] tests: make flaky vllm_bench throughput comparisons reproducible
shortlist.author: maobaolong
shortlist.body_excerpt:
Parent tracker: #5313 · Onboarding: #3372

## Confirmed flaky behavior

`k3-multiprocess-test / vllm / vllm_bench / zmq` changes its throughput verdict without a source update:

| Build #5340, September 29, 2026 (UTC) | Result |
| --- | --- |
| [Original job](https://buildkite.com/lmcache/k3-multiprocess-test/builds/5340#01a0eab1-a517-4a38-8163-b0ec7cfaff63) | LMCache throughput **7.34% slower** than baseline; fails the 5% limit |
| [Retry](https://buildkite.com/lmcache/k3-multiprocess-test/builds/5340#01a0eaba-4671-4f79-a910-4a02cfa0cadf) | LMCache throughput **0.62% faster** than baseline; passes |

Both are `dev` builds of **`9e8226dd49728769843bf6f586b00b33ab616125`**, with no PR-base merge, vLLM **`0.30.1rc1.dev244+g0da126676`**, and torch **`2.13.0+cu130`**. Both baseline and LMCache completed all 50 requests with 500400 input tokens. This is an intermittent benchmark verdict, not an installation failure.

The inputs are not reproducible across those attempts: the original uses seed `1790644335`, the retry `1790645482`. Each attempt uses the same seed for its own baseline/LMCache pair, but the default `RANDOM_SEED` comes from `date +%s`. The seed change is a confirmed confounder; it is **not proven to be the sole cause** of the throughput fluctuation.

## Bounded good-first task

Make this benchmark's inputs reproducible across retries, and make the comparison auditable. This is the first test-harness improvement for the confirmed flake, not a production performance optimization.

1. Replace the clock-derived default seed with a documented stable default; continue honoring an explicit `RANDOM_SEED` override.
2. Save a small comparison manifest next to `baseline.json` and `lmcache.json`: effective seed, model, request count and lengths, actual checkout SHA, installed vLLM/torch versions, and the two throughput values/verdict. Keep any new diagnostics local to this workload.
3. Preserve separate attempt results when used in CI. Follow the existing result-directory/cleanup conventions, and ensure the manifest is accessible in the job log or a public Buildkite artifact rather than merely naming a container-local file.
4. Add focused CPU-only regression coverage using stub benchmark commands: default seed is repeatable, both sides receive it, an override is honored, and success/failure summaries retain the actual numbers.

Keep the 5% throughput limit, request/token checks, and cache-retrieval validation. Do not add blanket retries, remove assertions, or present a fixed seed as proof of a resolved performance issue. #5227 already added retry mitigation; this task addresses reproducibility within the workload.

Starting points, checked at `42be9c7439a1eb0b17bf6b7565a894a9743fd052`:

- [Workload seed and result comparison](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/42be9c7439a1eb0b17bf6b7565a894a9743fd052/.buildkite/k3_tests/multiprocess/scripts/workloads/vllm/vllm-bench.sh).
- [Result cleanup/copying](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/42be9c7439a1eb0b17bf6b7565a894a9743fd052/.buildkite/k3_tests/multiprocess/scripts/cleanup.sh).
- [Buildkite step and existing retry policy](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/42be9c7439a1eb0b17bf6b7565a894a9743fd052/.buildkite/k3_tests/multiprocess/pipeline.yml).

## Acceptance

- [ ] Default inputs are identical across attempts; explicit overrides still work.
- [ ] A reviewer can recover both results, the effective inputs, versions, and verdict from public job output/artifacts.
- [ ] Stubbed CPU coverage exercises default/override and passing/failing results.
- [ ] GPU validation reports first-attempt results with a fixed seed; remaining fluctuation is reported as unresolved rather than hidden.
- [ ] Existing behavioral assertions and thresholds remain effective.

## Reproduce the CI workload

The evidence below comes from CI; this issue does not claim a local GPU reproduction. Use a dedicated Linux x86_64 GPU test host with Docker and NVIDIA Container Toolkit, two available CUDA GPUs capable of running separate `Qwen/Qwen3-14B` servers, sufficient host RAM for the default 80 GiB LMCache buffer (plus the mock L2 storage for the L2 case), and disk/network access for the image, wheels, and model. CI uses CUDA 13.0, Python 3.12, and a 1 GiB `/dev/shm`. A maintainer can run the GPU validation for a contributor who only has a CPU machine.

These commands build the public CI image recipe, explicitly start Bash, and pin the historical LMCache and vLLM revisions. They are a reproduction recipe, not a fully locked copy of every historical dependency or GPU scheduling condition. Run from a fresh directory; make the actual PR against current `dev`.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache.git
cd LMCache
git checkout 9e8226dd49728769843bf6f586b00b33ab616125
docker build -t lmcache-flake-ci \
  -f .buildkite/k3_harness/ci-base.Dockerfile .
docker run --rm --gpus '"device=0,1"' --shm-size=1g \
  --entrypoint bash \
  -v "$PWD:/workspace/LMCache" -w /workspace/LMCache \
  -e MAX_JOBS=1 \
  -e INFERENCE_ENGINE=vllm \
  -e LMCACHE_REQUEST_TRANSPORT=zmq \
  -e LMCACHE_PR_BASE_MERGE=never \
  -e PINNED_VLLM_VERSION=0.30.1rc1.dev244+g0da126676 \
  -e PINNED_VLLM_ARCHIVE_INDEX_URL=https://wheels.vllm.ai/0da126676e38f5dc1b02b2c4f48dc85f90f5a79f/cu130 \
  lmcache-flake-ci -c '
    set -e
    source /opt/venv/bin/activate
    command -v git uv python3 nvcc gcc g++
    nvidia-smi
    git config --global --add safe.directory /workspace/LMCache
    .buildkite/k3_tests/multiprocess/run.sh vllm_bench
  '
```

Use the linked failed and passed jobs as the initial reproduction pair. For subsequent GPU runs, record the actual checkout SHA, installed package versions, GPU model, input settings, and first-attempt result. A green retry alone does not show that the underlying fluctuation was fixed.

## Claim and contribution rules

This is primarily for a new contributor. Claim **one active sub-issue at a time** by commenting `/claim` here; check existing comments and ass

shortlist.title: [RFC / Feature] SPICY-KV: 28.6x–50x Pre-RoPE Algebraic Multigrid KV Compression for RadixAttention & Long-CoT (91.7%–100% RULER Recall & 100% Shared-Prefix Multi-Query Reuse)
shortlist.author: Yuge-Y
shortlist.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [ ] If this is not a feature request but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [ ] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Motivation

### Motivation: Compressing `RadixAttention` Shared Prefixes & Long-CoT (`<think>`) Traces by 28.6x–50x

Hi `SGLang` team! We evaluated our newly released Pre-RoPE Algebraic Multigrid KV compression framework (**SPICY-KV**: *SPectral Invariant Coarse-graining with dYadic KV renormalization*) across both the **NVIDIA `RULER` benchmark suite** (`28.6x` / `3.5%` KV and `50.0x` / `2.0%` KV on `DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B` & `1.5B`) and **4-Turn Shared-Prefix Multi-Query Reuse** (compressing a shared prefix once and answering 4 distinct sequential user queries without re-prefilling, directly mirroring `SGLang`'s **`RadixAttention`** tree nodes).

We wanted to share why existing eviction (`SnapKV`, `PyramidKV`, `H2O`, `StreamingLLM`) and post-RoPE token-merging (`KVMerger`, `CaM`) baselines break down on `RadixAttention` shared prefixes and extreme compression ratios, and discuss a 4-byte per-node kernel calibration hook for `FlashInfer` / `Triton` paged attention:

1. **Why Observation-Window Eviction (`SnapKV`, `H2O`) Fails on Shared `RadixAttention` Prefixes:** Eviction methods score prefix tokens using only the trailing observation window of the *first* prompt. When subsequent turns query different branches or facts in the cached prefix, evicted tokens are permanently gone (`62.5%` multi-query recall for `SnapKV`, `25.0%` for `PyramidKV`, `0.0%` for `H2O`).
2. **Why Post-RoPE Token Merging (`KVMerger`, `CaM`) Hits `0.0%` on `RULER`:** Linearly merging post-RoPE keys across positions $t_1 \neq t_2$ causes destructive trigonometric phase cancellation. `SPICY-KV` inverts RoPE ($R_{\Theta, t_i}^{-1}$, or taps pre-RoPE / MLA latent vectors $c_t^{KV}$) and applies **two-level moderated-step mean centering ($B_{\text{step}}=128$)** to strip `k_proj.bias` sink cones and cumulative causal drift.
3. **Hybrid Algebraic Multigrid ($C/F$) Splitting + 2nd-Order Subgrid Variance Closure:** Retains $C$-point landmarks (including cross-block bridge hubs and causally dilated bound-value spans) at exact $1\times$ resolution ($m_c=1, \sigma_c^2=0$) with exact positions $t_c$, coalesces $F$-point background bulk in unrotated space, and closes the **Softmax Jensen Inequality Gap** ($\mathbb{E}[e^{q^\top k}] > e^{q^\top \mathbb{E}[k]}$) by tracking intra-cluster subgrid key variance $\sigma_m^2$ via the Law of Total Variance:
   $$s_m = \frac{q_T^\top R_{\Theta, \bar{t}_m} \tilde{k}_m}{\sqrt{d_k}} + \log(m_m) + \frac{\lVert q_T \rVert_2^2 \sigma_m^2}{2 d_k}$$

---

### Headline Results: NVIDIA `RULER` (`7B` & `1.5B`) & 4-Turn Shared-Prefix Reuse

| Method | `1.5B` `RULER` @ **28.6×** (`3.5%` KV) | `1.5B` `RULER` @ **50.0×** (`2.0%` KV) | `7B` `RULER` @ **28.6×** (`3.5%` KV) | `7B` `RULER` @ **50.0×** (`2.0%` KV) | **4-Turn Shared-Prefix Reuse** |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| `FullKV` (100% Oracle) | `100.0%` (`0.0000` KL) | `100.0%` (`0.0000` KL) | `91.7%` (`0.0000` KL) | `91.7%` (`0.0000` KL) | `100.0%` (`16/16`) |
| **🌶️ `SPICY-KV (Regime 2)`** | **`100.0%` (`0.0077` KL)** | **`87.5%` (`0.2647` KL)** | **`83.3%` (`0.0374` KL)** | **`58.3%` (`0.2835` KL)** | **`100.0%` (`16/16`)** |
| **🌶️ `SPICY-KV (Regime 1)`** | **`100.0%` (`0.0120` KL)** | **`83.3%` (`0.2019` KL)** | **`91.7%` (`0.0360` KL)** | **`66.7%` (`0.1845` KL)** | **`100.0%` (`16/16`)** |
| `SnapKV` | `41.7%` (`0.4241` KL) | `12.5%` (`0.8089` KL) | `33.3%` (`0.4452` KL) | `16.7%` (`0.9163` KL) | `62.5%` (`10/16`) |

### Proposed `SGLang` Integration Discussion
We'd love architectural feedback from the `SGLang` maintainers on:
1. **4-Byte Per-Slot Calibration Metadata in `Triton` / `FlashInfer` Paged Kernels:** Passing two FP16 scalars per cached node—log-mass $\log(m_m)$ and subgrid key variance $\sigma_m^2$ (4 bytes/node total, `< 0.4%` memory overhead)—into the online softmax loop (`score += log_m[j] + 0.5 * q_norm_sq * sigma_sq[j] / d_k`).
2. **`RadixAttention` Prefix Node Coarsening:** Compressing cold/shared `RadixCache` prefix blocks by $20\times\text{–}28.6\times$ via `SPICY-KV` single-pass hybrid $C/F$ restriction so `RadixCache` can hold $20\times+$ more concurrent prefix trees in GPU HBM without query-specific eviction blindness.

shortlist.title: [Bug] Decode Throughput Inconsistency Between bench_serving and Engine Logs
shortlist.author: leepoly
shortlist.body_excerpt: ### Checklist - [x] 1. I have searched related issues but cannot get the expected help. - [x] 2. The bug has not been fixed in the latest version. - [x] 3. Please note that if the bug-related issue you submitted lacks corresponding environment info and a minimal reproducible demo, it will be challenging for us to reproduce and resolve the issue, reducing the likelihood of receiving feedback. - [x] 4. If the issue you raised is not a bug but a question, please raise a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions/new/choose Otherwise, it will be closed. - [x] 5. Please use English, otherwise it will be closed. ### Describe the bug Hi, I encountered an inconsistency in decode throughput reporting. When benchmarking with the bench_serving script, the reported TPOT is **much lower** than the decode throughput logged by the engine. This gap is significant for **small models or high concurrency settings**. ### Reproduction #### start the server ``` python -m sglang.launch_server \ --model-path Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B \ --trust-remote-code \ --tp 1 \ --load-format dummy \ --port 30000 --host 127.0.0.1 ``` #### benchmark (seqlens 2048 concurrency 16) ``` python3 -m sglang.bench_serving \ --backend sglang \ --dataset-name random \ --random-range-ratio 1.0 \ --random-input-len 2048 \ --random-output-len 256 \ --num-prompts 16 \ --max-concurrency 16 \ --host 127.0.0.1 \ --port 30000 ``` Observed Results: - The bench_serving script reports a median TPOT of 4.45 ms, equating to a token throughput of 224 $\times$ 16 = 3584 tokens/second. - However, the engine logs show a decode throughput of 7026 tokens/second. The gap between these metrics is significant and raises concerns about potential discrepancies in throughput measurement. Please let me know if you need additional details or logs to assist in troubleshooting. ### Environment Python: 3.10.0 (default, Mar 3 2022, 09:58:08) [GCC 7.5.0] CUDA available: True NVIDIA H800 GPU CUDA_HOME: /usr/local/cuda NVCC: Cuda compilation tools, release 12.6, V12.6.85 CUDA Driver Version: 535.129.03 PyTorch: 2.5.1+cu124 sglang: 0.4.1.post5 flashinfer: 0.1.6+cu124torch2.4 triton: 3.1.0 transformers: 4.48.0 torchao: 0.7.0 numpy: 1.26.4

comments.author: YEXINGZHE54
comments.body: I think it's just a difference between  long-time metric and short-time peak metric. From the perspective of bench_serving, estimating token throughput using TPOT (Time Per Output Token) provides a comprehensive evaluation over the entire testing period. On the other hand, the throughput printed in the engine log refers to the number of tokens generated within a single logging interval (which can be understood as the time for 40 consecutive decodes) divided by the time taken. Clearly, the data in the engine log is influenced by various factors, including: the potential interleaving of the prefill phase between decodes, which extends the total time; additionally, the amount of remaining memory also affects the number of tokens output per decode. Of course, the core issue here is that the engine log records short-term peak throughput, and similar results might be obtained if using the P25 (25th percentile) of TPOT for estimation.

comments.author: Tshiyao
comments.body:
I think I've found the cause. In multiple tests, when the backend is specified as "sglang," the `flush_cache` function is called to clear the cache.

 If `flush_cache` is executed successfully, there will be an inconsistency in the Decode Throughput between `bench_serving` and `engine logs`, specifically, `bench_serving` will be lower than `engine logs`. 

If `flush_cache` fails, the difference in Throughput between the two is within an acceptable range.

I speculate that the time loss caused by the successful execution of `flush_cache` might be the reason. The Decode Throughput in `engine logs` is not affected by this, but `bench_serving` is. I'm still not sure how to fix it. Does anyone have any suggestions?

When the backend is specified as "sglang," the following code is called to flush the cache，code in [here](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/9cf407729441a18561ee5a8b2c1e3e535ba817f9/python/sglang/bench_serving.py#L961):
```python
# Flush cache
if "sglang" in backend:
    requests.post(base_url + "/flush_cache")
```

The specific implementation of `flush_cache` can be found [here](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/9cf407729441a18561ee5a8b2c1e3e535ba817f9/python/sglang/srt/managers/scheduler.py#L1677):
```python
def flush_cache(self):
    """Flush the memory pool and cache."""
    if len(self.waiting_queue) == 0 and (
        self.running_batch is None or len(self.running_batch.reqs) == 0
    ):
        self.tree_cache.reset()
        self.tree_cache_metrics = {"total": 0, "hit": 0}
        if self.grammar_backend:
            self.grammar_backend.reset()
        self.req_to_token_pool.clear()
        self.token_to_kv_pool.clear()

        if not self.spec_algorithm.is_none():
            self.draft_worker.model_runner.req_to_token_pool.clear()
            self.draft_worker.model_runner.token_to_kv_pool.clear()

        self.num_generated_tokens = 0
        self.forward_ct_decode = 0
        self.spec_num_total_accepted_tokens = 0
        self.spec_num_total_forward_ct = 0
        torch.cuda.empty_cache()
        logger.info("Cache flushed successfully!")
        if_success = True
    else:
        logging.warning(
            f"Cache not flushed because there are pending requests. "
            f"#queue-req: {len(self.waiting_queue)}, "
            f"#running-req: {0 if self.running_batch is None else len(self.running_batch.reqs)}"
        )
        if_success = False
    return if_success
```

comments.author: ptimizeroracle
comments.body:
I went through both sides of this with the current code (main @ 99b9109). Happy to turn any of it into a fix if wanted, but evidence first.

**The two numbers are different estimators, not two measurements of the same thing:**

| | bench_serving | engine log |
|---|---|---|
| definition | TPOT-derived, per request: `(latency − ttft)` over `output_len − 1`, averaged across the whole run, client-side | `num_generated_tokens / gap_latency` where `gap_latency` is the time since the previous log line (`scheduler_components/metrics_reporter.py:799,894`) |
| window | entire run: queueing, any cold start, `[DONE]` tail included | one reporting interval, near-instantaneous |

So bench < engine is expected whenever the run has any ramp-up: the engine line reads close to a short-window peak, the bench number is a whole-run average.

Three smaller things verified along the way (all `python/sglang/benchmark/serving.py` unless noted):

1. TPOT arithmetic is the standard upstream vLLM formula (`(latency − ttft)/(output_len − 1)`, `:1136`): sound.
2. `itl` is recorded per stream **event**, not per token (`:334-337`, `:466+`). Events carrying several tokens (stream-interval batching, speculative decoding) contribute one itl sample, so `len(itl) < output_len − 1` and ITL percentiles conflate event latency with token latency. A retokenized correction already exists, but only for the `sglang-oai` backends (`:1131-1135`, `:1145-1155`); the completions/chat paths don't get it. I wrote CPU unit tests pinning this behavior (sum(itl) + [DONE]-tail == latency − ttft exactly; mean(ITL) > TPOT for the same request from denominators alone). Happy to PR them.
3. `should_flush_cache` is `("sglang" in backend AND SGLANG_IS_IN_CI) or --flush-cache` (`:1467-1471`), not default-on, so the cold-start mechanism discussed earlier in this thread needs CI or the explicit flag to apply to a default run.

If it's useful, the options I see: (a) a note in the bench output clarifying the window difference vs engine logs, (b) an engine-side long-window average for apples-to-apples runs, (c) extending the retokenized ITL path to the other backends. Which, if any, would you want?

shortlist.title: Restart-proof KV cache for llama-server: 40K-token TTFT 155s to 6s after reboot
shortlist.author: qqkzlm
shortlist.body_excerpt:
Every restart wipes your prefill. Server crash, box reboot, model reload — a 40K-token agentic prompt pays the full ~155s prefill again before the first token.

I patched llama-server to persist KV-cache prefix checkpoints to disk and auto-restore the longest matching prefix on boot. Same prompt after a restart: **first token in ~6s instead of ~155s** (2.1s disk read once + decode). No client changes, no re-architecture — the server just remembers.

Measured on GTX 1080 8GB, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, `-c 92160`:

- Cold: 151s prefill → first token at ~155s
- Warm (post-restart): 2.1s disk read (first request only) → first token at ~6s
- Checkpoints keyed by model + ctx + KV quant (wrong config = ignored, never corrupted); disk-budget eviction included

Single-commit patch (86KB): https://github.com/qqkzlm/llama-cpp-prompt-disk-cache — `git am` onto the PrismML `prism` branch, four flags (`--slot-save-path`, `--checkpoint-min-step`, `--ctx-checkpoints`, `--prompt-cache-disk-budget`).

One MoE lesson from the same box: keep experts on GPU, let KV follow the layers — pushing 20 MoE layers to CPU collapsed prefill 265→30 tok/s, which no cache can fix.

Happy to upstream behind a flag if maintainers are interested.

comments.author: qqkzlm
comments.body:
Update to the README since this went up — three things worth calling out for anyone trying it:

**1. Prebuilt CUDA binaries exist for both platforms.** The `v0.2.3` release ships `llama-server-win-cuda-v0.2.3.zip` and `llama-server-linux-cuda-v0.2.3.tar.gz`. The Linux package is built for `sm_61`/Pascal, so it also runs on GTX 10-series. No build needed:

```bash
./llama-server -m model.gguf -c 32768 --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 \
  --slot-save-path /var/tmp/kvstore/model \
  --prompt-cache-disk-budget 20 --checkpoint-min-step 2048 --ctx-checkpoints 64
```

**2. Only one flag is actually required.** `--slot-save-path` is the only one you must pass — `--prompt-cache-disk-budget` and `--prompt-cache-disk-path` are silently ignored without it, and entries land in `<slot-save-path>/pdcache`. `--prompt-cache-disk` is **enabled by default**, so passing it is optional; use `--no-prompt-cache-disk` to turn the cache off.

**3. Cache hits require a byte-identical prompt prefix.** Only the common prefix from token 0 onward is reused. If you prepend a timestamp or a random ID, everything after it misses and the cache is effectively unused. Put stable content first (system prompt, tool definitions, long docs) and per-turn content last — opencode / Claude Code already do this, so it works out of the box.

The README now has a "when does the cache hit / when does it miss" section covering this, a flag-duty table, and a Chinese-first three-step guide (the repo README is now Chinese-primary). A Windows `start-llama-server.bat` is included in the zip if you want a prompt-driven launcher instead of a command line.

Still happy to upstream this behind a flag if maintainers are interested — the whole feature is one commit touching `tools/server/server-prompt-disk.cpp` (~900 lines) plus slot/task integration.

Part of #3372. This is a community tracker for small, independently claimable improvements to flaky tests.

## The problem

Recent PR CI contains assertions that race background work and an intermittent hang that can occupy a runner for almost six hours. These failures consume contributor time and make unrelated PRs harder to validate.

The initial triage reviewed GitHub Actions `Test` runs from September 13-23, 2026 and recent `k3-unit-tests` failures. These are selected examples, not a complete inventory or a measured repository-wide flake rate. The test code was checked against `dev` at [21571dae80c6](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/commit/21571dae80c64ab4d141be571744494995270160).

The initial tasks cover:

- **Health-monitor exit:** a fixed 200 ms sleep precedes a thread-exit assertion; two PRs have same-checkout failed/passed attempts.
- **Health-monitor fallback/recovery:** a fixed 200 ms sleep precedes a state assertion; failure logs show fallback completing after the assertion.
- **RESP wait diagnostics:** a same-checkout rerun passes after an almost-six-hour hang near the RESP test boundary. The exact blocked operation remains unproven; this task adds bounded waits and diagnostics, not a speculative production fix.

## Initial tasks

- [x] #5314: Synchronize health-monitor exception-driven exit
- [ ] #5315: Synchronize health-monitor fallback/recovery phases
- [ ] #5316: Bound RESP waits and add stalled-operation diagnostics

## September 22–29 follow-up tasks

The follow-up scan covered **September 22, 2026 04:31 UTC through September 29, 2026 04:31 UTC**. It inspected 1,338 GitHub Actions run records across `Test`, `CPU Device Tests`, and `Operator: CI`, and 2,106 Buildkite build records across the active LMCache pipelines, then examined relevant failed jobs and retry logs. These inventory counts are not a repository-wide flake rate or a claim that every failed log was exhaustively analyzed.

Each new task below includes a failed/passed pair within the **same `dev` Buildkite build**, with the same LMCache checkout and vLLM/torch versions. PR-head-only matches with an unverified base merge, dependency/version changes between attempts, and one-off failures were not used as confirmation.

- [ ] #5403: Preserve separate baseline/LMCache raw timings for `long_doc_qa`. Build #5294 changes from 50.3% TTFT improvement (fail) to 70.4% (pass); #5291 provides a second pair.
- [ ] #5404: Retain L2 data-flow diagnostics after `long_doc_qa_l2` performance failures. Build #5287 changes from 1.49x TTFT speedup (fail) to 1.54x (pass).

These are independently claimable **reproducibility and diagnostics improvements for confirmed intermittent test verdicts**. They deliberately keep the existing performance/data-flow assertions. Contributors can develop the scoped regression coverage with CPU-only command stubs. Existing health-monitor/RESP tasks and ongoing MQ, distributed-storage, and observability work were checked to avoid duplicate newcomer assignments. Intermittent model-output mismatches were not turned into generic timing-hardening tasks or described as harmless flakes.

shortlist.title: [Bug]:  Gemma 4 fails to initialize with per-token-head KV cache quantization
shortlist.author: lisp19
shortlist.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment
The output of python collect_env.py ```text Use the builtin dockerfile to build & manually merge PR https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/39018 for turing devices base compatibility Main commit hash:726efe177bf22874743d11dfdfef9247dbfb5ff0 ```
### 🐛 Describe the bug Gemma 4 fails to initialize in vLLM V1 when `--kv_cache_dtype int8_per_token_head` is enabled. The same issue also affects `fp8_per_token_head`. The failure is caused by Gemma 4's hybrid attention layout using two different KV head dimensions: - sliding/local layers use `head_dim = 256` - global/full-attention layers use `head_dim = 512` With per-token-head KV quantization, each KV head also stores scale metadata per token. That extra scale payload breaks the exact 2:1 page-size ratio between the 512-dim and 256-dim layers, so V1 KV page-size unification fails during initialization. Minimal reproduction: ```bash vllm serve \ --kv_cache_dtype int8_per_token_head ``` Observed result: ```text (Worker_TP1 pid=248) ERROR 04-19 14:16:08 [multiproc_executor.py:971] File "/usr/local/lib/python3.12/dist-packages/vllm/v1/core/kv_cache_utils.py", line 942, in unify_kv_cache_spec_page_size (Worker_TP1 pid=248) ERROR 04-19 14:16:08 [multiproc_executor.py:971] raise NotImplementedError( (Worker_TP1 pid=248) ERROR 04-19 14:16:08 [multiproc_executor.py:971] NotImplementedError: The page size of the layer is not divisible by the maximum page size. Cannot unify by adjusting block_size. ``` Why this happens: - local layer page-size factor: `(256 * 1 byte * 2) + 8 = 520` - global layer page-size factor: `(512 * 1 byte * 2) + 8 = 1032` `1032` is not divisible by `520`, so the current page-size unification logic cannot reconcile the two layer types by changing `block_size` alone. Relevant code paths: - `vllm/model_executor/models/gemma4.py` - `vllm/model_executor/layers/attention/attention.py` - `vllm/v1/core/kv_cache_utils.py` - `vllm/v1/kv_cache_interface.py` - `vllm/v1/worker/gpu/attn_utils.py` - `vllm/v1/worker/gpu_model_runner.py` ## Environment | Item | Value | |---|---| | **Commit** | [`726efe177bf22874743d11dfdfef9247dbfb5ff0`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/commit/726efe177bf22874743d11dfdfef9247dbfb5ff0) | | **GPU** | 2× NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2080 Ti (22 GB, CC 7.5, Turing) | | **CUDA Driver** | 580.126.18, CUDA 13.0 | | **Python** | 3.12 (Docker) | | **Model** | Gemma4-31B AWQ 4-bit (`google/gemma-4-31b-it`), also reproduced with `cyankiwi/gemma-4-31B-it-AWQ-4bit` | I'm still new to this project, so if this report doesn't match the community's preferred format or I've misunderstood something basic, corrections are very welcome. Potential direction for a fix: I want to post a temporary workaround PR later for reference later, which as I tested, can solve this problem. But it certainly needs more review and discussion. ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

shortlist.title: [Bug]: Persistent KV offload cache is not namespaced by model revision
shortlist.author: mindungil
shortlist.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment
The relevant output of python vllm/collect_env.py ```text ============================== System Info ============================== OS : Ubuntu 24.04.3 LTS (x86_64) GCC version : (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0 CMake version : version 3.28.3 Libc version : glibc-2.39 ============================== PyTorch Info ============================== PyTorch version : 2.11.0+cu130 CUDA used to build PyTorch : 13.0 ============================== Python Environment ============================== Python version : 3.12.3 Python platform : Linux-6.8.0-136-generic-x86_64-with-glibc2.39 ============================== CUDA / GPU Info ============================== Is CUDA available : True GPU models and configuration : GPU 0: NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPU 1: NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPU 2: NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPU 3: NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition Nvidia driver version : 580.126.09 cuDNN version : 9.18.1 ============================== Versions of relevant libraries ============================== flashinfer-python==0.6.14 numpy==2.3.5 nvidia-cuda-runtime==13.0.96 nvidia-cudnn-cu13==9.19.0.56 nvidia-nccl-cu13==2.28.9 torch==2.11.0 transformers==5.13.1 triton==3.6.0 ============================== vLLM Info ============================== vLLM Version : 0.23.1rc1.dev1312+g97a668152 git sha : 97a668152 ```
This issue concerns deterministic cache-path construction and is independent of the GPU architecture. ### 🐛 Describe the bug Persistent native KV offloading tiers derive their cache namespace from `FileMapper.fields`. The fingerprint includes the model name, KV dtype, cache geometry, and parallelism, but not the model revision. Two deployments using the same model repository name and persistent offload root, but different model revisions, therefore produce the same `FileMapper.base_path`. Block keys are derived from token content rather than model weights, so the newer deployment can report a filesystem or object-tier hit and load KV produced by the older weights. This can silently change model output after a model update. The problem is specific to persistent secondary tiers and survives engine restarts. #### Minimal reproduction On current `main` (`97a668152`): ```python from vllm.v1.kv_offload.file_mapper import FileMapper common = dict( root_dir="/tmp/cache", model_name="org/model", tokens_per_hash=16, blocks_per_file=1, tp_size=1, pp_size=1, pcp_size=1, dcp_size=1, rank=0, dtype="float16", ) # There is currently no model-revision input to distinguish these deployments. revision_a = FileMapper(**common) revision_b = FileMapper(**common) assert revision_a.base_path == revision_b.base_path ``` The revision cannot currently be represented by `OffloadingModelConfig` or passed through `FileMapper.from_offloading_spec`. vLLM already has an immutable resolved commit for Hugging Face models, even when the user does not explicitly pass `--revision`. For the locally cached `facebook/opt-125m` used to verify this: ```text ModelConfig.revision = None ModelConfig.hf_config._commit_hash = "27dcfa74d334bc871f3234de431e71c6eeba5dd6" ``` #### Observed behavior Persistent cache paths are identical for different revisions of the same model repository when the remaining cache configuration is unchanged. Existing KV files can consequently be treated as valid after deploying different weights. #### Expected behavior Different resolved model revisions should use different persistent cache namespaces. Deployments using the same resolved revision should continue to share a namespace. A possible fix is to: 1. add the resolved model revision to the normalized offloading model config; 2. prefer the Hugging Face config's resolved commit hash and fall back to the requested revision; and 3. include the revision in the `FileMapper` fingerprint when available. For local models without revision information, omitting the field can preserve the existing cache path. #### Affected components - `vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/offloading/config.py` - `vllm/v1/kv_offload/config.py` - `vllm/v1/kv_offload/file_mapper.py` - filesystem and object secondary tiers that use `FileMapper` #### Duplicate check I searched open and closed issues and pull requests for combinations of `FileMapper`, model revision, fingerprint, stale KV, filesystem tier, and offloading. I did not find an existing report or change covering model-revision namespacing. I have a focused fix and regression tests ready and plan to submit a PR. ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

shortlist.title: [RFC]: Add GDS offload for mooncake-store based on existing TENT gds transport
shortlist.author: tong1heng
shortlist.body_excerpt:
### Changes proposed

## Summary

Add opt-in GDS SSD offloading to mooncake store by reusing the existing TENT GDS transport.

The implementation adds:

1. A client-local, fixed-size GDS backing file exposed as a TENT `file://` segment and managed by an aligned extent allocator.
2. A first-class `ReplicaType::GDS` with storage identity, generation, offset, value size, and allocation size in store metadata and wire serialization.
3. Required dual-write behavior for enabled `BatchPut`: memory/NoF writes and GDS writes are submitted in parallel and waited on before finalization.
4. A GDS-only creation fallback when memory replica allocation fails because of capacity or tenant quota.
5. Memory-first `BatchGet` selection, followed by a local matching GDS replica, while retaining existing NoF, local-disk, and disk fallbacks.
6. TENT/Transfer Engine capability checks and GDS buffer-registration tracking needed for sub-slice cuFile requests.

The feature is enabled through environment variables and requires no changes to upstream vLLM, so existing deployments remain unchanged when it is disabled.

## Motivation

Mooncake store currently supports POSIX and `io_uring` file offloading. Its existing data path is as follows:

1. **Write path:** when memory usage in a global segment (CPU memory) reaches the configured eviction watermark, mooncake master selects objects for offloading and places them in the background offload queue. The client then reads the objects from the global segment and writes them to the configured file backend through POSIX or `io_uring`. After the file write completes, the master records the file-backed replica and may release the corresponding memory replica.
2. **Read path:** the client first queries the master for the object's replica metadata and prefers an available memory replica. If the object is no longer present in memory, the client loads it from the file backend through POSIX or `io_uring` and returns the data to the caller.

This data path becomes a bottleneck when host memory is constrained. GPU-to-CPU and CPU-to-SSD bandwidths are not matched: GPU data must first be copied into CPU memory and then written to SSD. **When GPU production outpaces this two-step pipeline, CPU memory and CPU-side file I/O cannot drain the global segment fast enough. Some KV cache is consequently discarded before it can be completely offloaded, preventing more valid KV cache from being offloaded to the SSD even when sufficient SSD capacity remains.**

GPUDirect Storage (GDS) addresses this mismatch by supporting GPU-to-SSD DMA, so the data can bypass the CPU staging path. The GDS transport has already been integrated into TENT, **but the data path between TENT and mooncake store has not yet been connected.** An earlier draft PR (#2731) attempted to add GDS offload at the mooncake store layer by introducing a separate GDS context. This approach would duplicate cuFile resource management and make mooncake store responsible for transport-specific details that already belong to TENT.

Therefore, the central design goal of this change is to preserve the existing separation of mooncake store and TENT while connecting the two components: TENT owns all GDS cuFile operations, transport selection, and buffer registration, while mooncake store owns only object and replica metadata, allocation/lifecycle decisions, and transfer-request submission. Mooncake store should reuse the existing Transfer Engine and TENT GDS transport instead of introducing another GDS/cuFile implementation. This keeps the GDS data path composable with store's replica semantics and avoids a second, divergent GDS context in mooncake store.

## Non-goals

- Replacing the existing `enable_ssd_offload`/`LOCAL_DISK` POSIX or `io_uring` path.
- Providing remote reads from another client's local GDS file. A remote GDS descriptor falls back to the existing memory, NoF, local-disk, or disk paths.
- Recovering a client's GDS index after restart or promising crash/durability semantics for the local file.

## Architecture

```text
RealClient (env opt-in)
  +-- client
      +-- GdsStorageManager
      |    +-- aligned extent allocator
      |    +-- file:// backing segment handle
      |    `-- storage_id + generation + read leases
      +-- TransferSubmitter::submitFile
      |    `-- TransferEngine / TENT GDS / cuFile
      `-- MasterClient RPCs
           `-- MasterService: GDS storage identities and replicas

BatchPut:
  reserve local extent
    +-- BatchPutStart -> MEMORY/NoF PROCESSING replicas
    +-- BatchAddGdsReplicaStart -> GDS PROCESSING replica
    `-- submit both write paths -> wait -> commit + BatchPutEnd

BatchGet:
  local MEMORY -> any MEMORY -> matching local GDS -> NoF/disk fallbacks
```

### Local GDS storage

`GdsStorageManager` creates/truncates and preallocates the configured backing file, opens it once through `openSegment("file://...")`, and allocates raw value extents aligned to 4 KiB. Reservations are move-only and automatically aborted unless committed or explicitly preserved after an uncertain RPC. A reference-counted read lease keeps an extent alive until all GDS read futures finish.

Each client registers a `storage_id` and `storage_generation` with the master. The generation changes when the file is recreated, preventing an old metadata descriptor from addressing the same offset in a new file.

### Store metadata and RPCs

`ReplicaType::GDS` is an independent replica type rather than an alias for `LOCAL_DISK`:

```text
GdsDescriptor {
  owner_client_id
  storage_id
  storage_generation
  value_offset
  value_size
  allocated_size
}
```

The master exposes storage registration/unregistration, `BatchAddGdsReplicaStart`, and `BatchCreateGdsOnlyObjects`. GDS replicas use the existing `PROCESSING` -> `COMPLETE` lifecycle, participate in `BatchPutEnd` / `BatchPutRevoke`, and are removed during stale-client cleanup. MessagePack serialization uses a stable explicit replica type value and validates the six-field G
